docs.title: Nereus
docs.text:
A composable API platform: reefs add the APIs, Nereids look after them, installed at runtime. An Internal Developer Platform is one profile of it.

Install the CLI

  • Start

    From nothing to a reef and its Nereid, in six short steps.

  • Concepts

    Reef, Nereid and Mandate: the model in a few pages.

  • Guides

    One goal per page: install, operate, grant access, use a reef.

  • Reference

    Every command, every reef, every word.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Every technique, method, practice, quote, book, author, film, paper and reference that the project and its predecessors mention, harvested on 2026-10-27 to show how much context surrounds a project, and to credit it (Credit what we use, #332). The owner (Silvio) suggested most of them; the evidence below credits each one only where a file says who brought it, so many stay unknown.

docs.title: How this list was made
docs.text:
Six read-only agents harvested one source each and a script merged their rows by name; three more agents checked the books, papers, quotes, myths and the most repeated items on the web. The sources:

  • nereus: Nereus repository.
  • wasp-idp-docs: wasp-idp (docs/).
  • wasp-idp-rest: wasp-idp (code, commits, issues).
  • platform-api: platform-api (the former name of Nereus).
  • early-platform-api: early-platform-api (a private earlier copy).
  • drive: raw sessions on Drive (#pontos/raw).

The columns:

  • Author / origin and Year: as the source states them; when the web check found different values, the Verified column says so.
  • Brought by: who put it into the conversation, from the evidence (a session file that marks who said what, a "Credit" section, an issue label). unknown means the only evidence is a commit by Silvio co-authored by Claude, which does not say who proposed the idea.
  • Verified: yes with the page opened; known, page not opened when the checker recognised a classic but did not open the page; differs when the page gives another author or year; checked in the session when the raw session says it was checked then; linked in the source, not opened; project practice for the project's own rules, which have nothing outside to check; not confirmed on the web when the check could not open or find the text (often a quote inside a book or a report); not checked.
  • Where: the first places it appears, <source>:<path>:<line>; (+N) counts the other places.

docs.title: Conflicting attributions
docs.text:
Places where two sources, or a source and the web, disagree about who wrote it, when, or who brought it.

Reference Conflict A mostly complete chart of Neural Networks (Neural Network Zoo) CONFLICT (dates): Claude says first published 2016 by van Veen and the 2019 version adds Leijnen (from memory), while the chart itself shows 2019; occurrences: 3 Building Evolutionary Architectures years differ: 2017, 2017; 2nd ed. 2022 Caranguejos com Cérebro (Manguebeat manifesto) the web gives Fred 04 (Fred Zero Quatro) and DJ Renato L. 1991: Wikipedia dates the manifesto 1991 (source says 1992) and credits DJ Renato L. as co-author Extreme Programming Explained brought_by differs between sources: Claude (Anthropic), Silvio Forer effect (Barnum effect) CONFLICT: Silvio thought humility relates to the Forer effect; Claude corrected that Forer is about accepting vague generic descriptions as personal (horoscopes), and the closer one is Dunning-Kruger; occurrences: 2 Kubernetes static pods and mirror pods (analogy for core) CONFLICT: S25/117:5 says Silvio recalled static pods, but the register at S25/117:19 says the analogy was brought by Claude; occurrences: 3 Lean Inception (book and method) the web gives Paulo Caroli 2017: Fowler site page is dated 22 Feb 2022 (revision history from 2017); book Lean Inception on Leanpub dates from 2017, not 2018 PACT: action-state communication for multi-agent systems the web gives Chen Huang, Yuhao Wu, Wenxuan Zhang 2026: arXiv title is What Should Agents Say? docs.title: Thinking in platforms
docs.text:
What Nereus takes from Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante's book: a platform is the operating model of knowledge work, not a tool for developers only. Nereus already holds that thesis, an Internal Developer Platform being one profile of it (Vision); the book gives it words, a history and a model. The owner read it and chose these lessons (2026-11-13).

  • Source: Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante, Thinking in Platforms: Platform engineering as the operating model for work in the AI era (Weave Intelligence, 2026), Kindle edition. The quotes come from the owner's reading highlights; the pages are the Kindle edition's. The same authors wrote the State of AI in Platform Engineering report, summarised in its reference page.

docs.title: The lessons
docs.text:
• The production system is itself a product. "A production system is the overall way an organization turns effort into results" (p. 17). Ford went from letting it "happen" to treating it as a product "worked on, improved, tested, and refined continuously" (p. 15). Platform engineering is "the discipline of deliberately designing, building, and improving platforms for knowledge work, and treating those platforms as products" (p. 23). Here: the project's own way of working (the pillars, the hooks, the skills, the board) is designed and improved like the platform it builds (Continuous learning and improvement).
  • A platform is not only for developers. The book's examples go beyond software: an "internal marketing platform", a "patient tracking platform" (p. 20). Here: an IDP is one profile of Nereus; a reef can serve any recurring knowledge work.
  • Replace negotiation with paths. Without a platform, "work crosses the boundary through ad hoc negotiation rather than through a well-designed interface" (p. 60): urgent requests, "who owns this?", the wrong person. "Designed interfaces make boundaries reliably accessible" (p. 62), and "good paths don't eliminate communication altogether, they remove the need for constant clarifying, coordinating, and renegotiating around recurring work" (p. 62). Here: the Nereus API is that interface (The Nereus API is the one door); a deployment that needed a specialist becomes "a self-service path any developer could trigger" (p. 9).
  • Autonomy grows, it does not shrink. Platforms, "when designed well, increase autonomy rather than reducing it" (p. 22), and the book lists "creativity requires unlimited freedom" among the misconceptions (p. 54). Here: a team still chooses its tools, as a Nereid behind a reef's contract, and switches them without changing a command (ADR 0011, reefs, Nereids and Mandates).
  • Standardization is a floor. "Standardization is a compounding floor, not a ceiling on what is possible" (p. 59). Against "our situation is too complex to standardize" (p. 62): once primitives "are stable, reusable, and connected through clear rules, variation no longer has to be rebuilt from scratch each time" (p. 63). Here: reefs are the primitives and composition is the rule (Simple on the surface, consistent underneath, Progressively extensible).
  • A platform evolves or it is a process. "A platform that doesn't evolve is not a platform, it's an imposed process" (p. 59); a better approach that emerges is absorbed and raises the floor for everyone. A platform is "operated and observed, then refined based on user feedback" (p. 26), with "close interaction with users to set abstractions correctly" (p. 57). Here: Metrics and real users decide, and an experience that works becomes a possible feature.
  • Exceptions harden. Without that care, "workarounds multiply, exceptions harden, and over time the platform turns back into the accidental system it replaced" (p. 28). Here: every fix gets an issue, and a stand-in names the feature that ends it (Rules).
  • Start thin. "Most platform efforts fail not by starting too small, but by starting too broad" (p. 30); the book names the Thinnest Viable Platform (p. 29). Here: good enough first, the walking skeleton (How we work).
  • Learn, then adjust. "The objective isn't to perfect the plan, but to tighten the learning loop" (p. 31). "Plans still exist, but as dynamic hypotheses", and "learning without adjustment is pointless" (p. 31). Here: what an attempt teaches is kept, and it changes how the work happens.
  • AI amplifies what is there. "If the way an organization produces products is unstructured or suboptimal now, it'll only get worse with AI" (p. 10). Here: agents run on top of clear interfaces, documented workflows and deterministic checks (AI and teams, Deterministic first).

docs.title: Where this project stands
docs.text:
The book places production systems on two axes: whether the design is explicit or implicit, and whether ownership is concentrated or fragmented (p. 36-37). Implicit design with fragmented ownership is the artisanal system: informal coordination, negotiation, high variance. Implicit design with concentrated ownership is the hero-based one: expertise in few heads, high ownership, fragile scale.

Explicit design with fragmented ownership is the bureaucratic one: prescribed process, weak accountability, "compliance becomes the safest strategy because accountability for outcomes is diffuse" (p. 49). Explicit design with concentrated end-to-end ownership is the platform.

Nereus starts close to hero-based: one owner holds most of the context, and every agent works through the owner.

Each written rule, hook, skill and issue an agent can carry out alone moves the design from implicit to explicit, toward the platform quadrant; the risk to watch on that path is the bureaucratic one, rules kept because they exist and not because they still serve, so each rule names its reason and is reviewed when it stops paying (#871, the review of the pillars).

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text: • Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante, Thinking in Platforms (2026): why platforms, the model to reason about them, and how to start, harden and scale a platform initiative.

docs.title: Where it is heading
docs.text:
The Nereus API is the one door for every client: the CLI, a portal, an IDE reading an app.yaml, an agent asked to "create a Postgres for greeting-api". None needs a kubeconfig, and all speak of reefs, not of the tools behind them (ADR 0002).

An Internal Developer Platform is one profile of it: a platform serves any recurring knowledge work, as the "internal marketing platform" and the "patient tracking platform" of Thinking in Platforms do (Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante, p. 20; Thinking in platforms).

Each box in a plane is a candidate reef: Delivery is release (ADR 0010), Identity is authentication (ADR 0006), Data would be database. A reef arrives at runtime with its contract, and the Nereids added to it fill the box (ADR 0003, ADR 0010).

What the API adds over the Kubernetes API each reef already extends:

  • Composition. An app declaration or a golden path becomes several Instances at once: a release, a database, an identity.
  • What crosses the planes. Authentication, authorization by team, policy, cost and several clusters belong to the platform, not to one reef or cluster.
  • Moving parts from day one. Platform teams pick tools from the CNCF Landscape and soon have code depending on each choice. Here a team tries a tool as a Nereid and, if it does not fit, adds another to the same reef and switches its default Mandate, with no command, client or app declaration to change (ADR 0002, ADR 0011).

What runs today: What is built; what comes next and the ideas being refined: Roadmap. The vision, goals and sequence of the MVP: Inception.

docs.title: What guides the work
docs.text:
"Nothing new under the sun, except the AI agents" (the owner, 2026-11-03): the practices here are old ones (Agile, XP, flow, WIP limits), and what is new is who carries them out.

The project calls these pillars so that it orients itself by them, and so that its agents understand what the project's people value (the owner, for now) and come to value it too. That lets an agent collaborate better and register ideas during its own work. Their number is not a problem: the agents help remember them (the owner, 2026-11-03).

This page holds the one full list; other pages point to it or highlight part of it.

Twenty-four pillars, in the owner's words:

  • the Agile Manifesto
  • Extreme Programming, adjusted to AI agents
  • short cycles and frequent deliveries
  • continuous learning and improvement
  • costs as a lever
  • open source first
  • deterministic first, AI only where it is good
  • transparency
  • metrics and real users decide
  • every interaction tells the story
  • a platform progressively extensible in its capabilities
  • every fix gets an issue
  • eat your own dog food
  • issues an agent can carry out alone
  • every commit follows Conventional Commits
  • courtesy and respect with everyone
  • security from the first slice
  • no personal data in a command or a log (a direction until there is an audit trail)
  • credit what we use
  • the Nereus API is the one door, and it cannot lie
  • the same quality for fewer tokens
  • simple on the surface, consistent underneath
  • no single control point
  • an experience that works becomes an exploration of a possible feature

Where a pillar is a known technique, it names its source and links it.

docs.title: The Agile Manifesto
docs.text:
Follow the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, above all working software over comprehensive documentation and working software is the primary measure of progress. So every slice ends with a scene a person runs from the CLI, the walkthrough shows the output commands really print, and progress is measured by what runs (#57), not by what was written. Documentation follows the software.

Learn more: the Manifesto (2001) and its twelve principles, where "working software is the primary measure of progress" is the seventh.

docs.title: Extreme Programming, adjusted to AI agents
docs.text:
Extreme Programming, adjusted to work with AI agents: Kent Beck's Extreme Programming (XP), from Extreme Programming Explained (1999), in small steps that each end in working software. With an agent on one side of the pair:

  • Small releases and continuous integration: one issue per deliverable, one pull request each, checked with the scene on k3d before it merges.
  • Test-first and the scene: each slice starts from the scene a person will run; tests and checks run on every change, for people and agents alike. With an agent, test-first is kept at the level of behaviour: the contract (the scene, the CLI examples, a test of the behaviour) comes first and is seen failing; the red-green-refactor micro-cycle on every small step is optional (the rule, #1153).
  • Pair programming: agents implement in parallel, a coordinating agent reviews and merges, and the owner decides what the issue does not hold, one question at a time.
  • The planning game: the board's order is the plan; the owner reprioritizes it, and forecasts come from what was delivered (#95), not from estimates.
  • Collective ownership and simple design: every rule lives in the repository (CLAUDE.md, ADRs, specs, skills); anything learnt goes back there, in the same session.

Agent contribution and the XP practices that fit this era: #40; recording and telling the experience: #113.

Learn more: Martin Fowler's summary of Extreme Programming; Don Wells's extremeprogramming.org, with its rules on small releases, pair programming and the planning game; Martin Fowler's Continuous Integration. How well the practices work with an agent as one side of the pair is the project's own observation, measured in #113.

docs.title: Short cycles, frequent deliveries
docs.text:
Each cycle ends in something delivered: an issue small enough to close in hours, a pull request merged once the checks and the review pass, main always working.

The checks run locally for now: GitHub Actions is off to save its cost, and CI will run inside the platform itself, on BuildKit (#848, the build reef). A long branch, a big pull request or an issue In Progress for days means cut again. Flow metrics (#95) show whether the cycles stay short. Good enough now, improve later: ship the thinnest slice that works end to end, then widen it.

Learn more: each slice starts as a walking skeleton (Alistair Cockburn): "a tiny implementation of the system that performs a small end-to-end function", widened afterwards. The flow metrics (cycle time, work item age, throughput) are those of The Kanban Guide.

docs.title: Continuous learning and improvement
docs.text:
Every attempt, even a dropped idea, leaves what it taught: an issue (improvement, feature, bug), a rule or decision in the repository (CLAUDE.md, an ADR, a spec, a skill, the glossary), or a measurement: agent runs (#113), forecasts against delivery (#95), software quality (#102). A discarded idea closes with its lesson on its issue. What is learnt then changes how the work happens: the way of working is itself reviewed and reorganized, as this list of pillars was (#871).

Learn more: "A platform that doesn't evolve is not a platform, it's an imposed process", and "the objective isn't to perfect the plan, but to tighten the learning loop" (Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante, Thinking in Platforms, p. 59 and p. 31; Thinking in platforms).

docs.title: Open source first
docs.text: Before building, look for an open source tool or a native resource that already does it, and integrate it with the model of reefs and Nereids. Build only when none fits, and the issue says which ones were evaluated and why each falls short. Time, tokens and money are not spent rebuilding what a tool already does.

docs.title: Deterministic first, AI only where it is good
docs.text:
Plain code, rules and checks where they do the job; Artificial Intelligence (AI) only where it does better, such as a summary, a classification or an extraction. A first version may be an agent following a rule; it then evolves into a script, a hook, a test or a check that does the same every time.

When a rule depends on an agent remembering it, propose what enforces it: scripts/board/queue claim refuses an item someone else holds, and claude-guard-main-clone refuses a change in a main clone.

A check that starts with exceptions keeps them in a ratchet (the owner, 2026-11-16): an allowlist of what exists today, which only shrinks, so a fix lowers it in the same change and nothing new joins it; make kubeconfig-ban (#1529) is the first, the personal-data check (#1680) the next, which warns and never blocks until Nereus has an audit trail. Learn more: Ratchets in software development (qntm, 2021).

docs.title: Transparency
docs.text: Decisions, designs and the way the work happens are written in the repository: the ADRs (Architecture Decision Records), the specs, the agent guides and the issues.

docs.title: Metrics and real users decide
docs.text:
A feature lives or dies by what it measures and by its users, not by opinion.

Learn more: a platform is "operated and observed, then refined based on user feedback", with "close interaction with users to set abstractions correctly" (Thinking in Platforms, p. 26 and p. 57; Thinking in platforms).

docs.title: Costs as a lever
docs.text: Every cost is measured (#56, #57, #113), but not everything must be solved at no cost. When a measured bottleneck costs more in time or quality than the money that removes it (a higher AI plan when usage limits stall the work, a paid service when a free one blocks a decision), the spend is made and recorded with what triggered it. The figures live in the private repository (#31); this one keeps only the method.

docs.title: Every interaction tells the story
docs.text:
Every exchange, person and agent, agent and agent, is a chance to tell how the project evolves: the question that changed a design, the failure CI caught, the limit that stopped an agent. The story is kept as it happens: decisions on their issues, moments and figures in the log of #113 (figures in the private repository), the panel's rounds, the board's metrics.

It feeds the talks, the deck and the courses (#33), and the platform's Inception (#24): the platform will record and tell its own construction.

docs.title: Progressively extensible
docs.text:
The platform grows its capabilities step by step. nereus init only prepares a cluster; every capability is a reef added at runtime and looked after by a Nereid (ADR 0002, ADR 0011), each adding its own commands to the CLI. A new capability (secrets, authentication, cost, a portal) is one more reef, not a new release of the core. The skills, metrics and rules of the project grow the same way.

Learn more: Kubernetes grows the same way, its API extended by custom resources and the operator pattern; the split of a contract from what fulfils it follows Gateway API's GatewayClass and Crossplane's composite resource definitions (ADR 0010, reefs are objects added at runtime). Once primitives "are stable, reusable, and connected through clear rules, variation no longer has to be rebuilt from scratch each time" (Thinking in Platforms, p. 63; Thinking in platforms).

docs.title: Every fix gets an issue
docs.text: Every fix, even a small one, gets its own issue, and the pull request that makes it closes it. A fix found mid-task opens its bug issue first, so the metrics count every fix: the queue's flow (#95), software quality (#102), the agents' work (#113): how often things break, how fast they are fixed, what kept breaking.

docs.title: Eat your own dog food
docs.text:
The platform is used to build itself. Each capability the project needs (an always-on environment deployed continuously, #159; its metrics, #113; its board, #137) becomes a capability of the platform as soon as it can, and the project is its first user. Until the platform does it, plain files and scripts do, and are replaced. Until a running Nereus receives them, every session records its metrics in the private repository (#31). This is the Inception of #24 made a habit.

Learn more: eating your own dog food.

docs.title: Issues an agent can carry out alone
docs.text:
Every issue lets an agent take it from the board and deliver it without more confirmation. It holds:

  • its context
  • the decisions taken (who, when)
  • the dependencies and what they deliver
  • the facts checked in the code
  • the names a person will see or type
  • a "Done when" the agent can check itself

An open question that changes what a person sees is answered before the issue is ready, or the issue says which recommendation to follow. Questions to the owner are for what the issue cannot hold. This is the Definition of Ready that autonomous agents (#25) will need.

docs.title: Every commit follows Conventional Commits
docs.text:
Every commit follows Conventional Commits, no exception: <type>(<scope>)!: <description>, the type one of feat, fix, docs, chore, refactor, test, ci, build, perf, style, revert, bump.

The history is data: Commitizen (cz.yaml) derives the versions from it, starting at 0.1.0 (#55), and the metrics read it: fixes against features (#102), what each agent run delivered (#113), whether every fix had its issue.

.githooks/commit-msg refuses a message outside the format (make hooks), and CI checks every commit of a pull request with scripts/check-commit-message, both through cz check.

docs.title: Courtesy and respect with everyone
docs.text: Every exchange is courteous and respectful, between people, agents, and both, in issues, comments, reviews, pull requests, commit messages, the panel's rounds and reports. Disagreement goes to the idea, never to the person; a review names what to change and why; a question is answered, or said plainly that it cannot be yet. Agents follow it as people do. A code of conduct for contributors comes with going public (#9).

docs.title: Security from the first slice
docs.text:
Security is designed in from a feature's first slice. Auditing, authorisation and secrets handling are provided for in the architecture: every action in a cloud says which identity, which Nereid and on whose request it ran (spec 0005).

The baseline is OWASP's (#237): every spec's security section names the categories its slice touches and what covers each, and what is designed or built is reviewed against them (#235), so a gap is an issue, not a rewrite. The project prepares for the regulations its users answer to, SOX, the GDPR and the LGPD, with DevSecOps in its own delivery (#238).

docs.title: No personal data in a command or a log
docs.text:
A command should not take personal data, and a log should not record it (the owner, 2026-11-16). A person is named by a Nereus object, a User or a team, by its name or id, never by an e-mail, a phone number or a document: what a person types lands in the shell's history, the API's access log, the audit trail and the object itself, and none of them can be cleaned later.

It is a direction, not yet a hard rule: Nereus has no audit trail yet, so the check that follows it (#1680) keeps its ratchet but only warns, never blocks a change (the owner, 2026-11-16); it blocks once the audit trail exists. The design to follow meanwhile: a person named by a User or a team, an invite that carries the e-mail in the request body (#1679), a list read from a file or a Secret (#1686).

The staff of a talk is a team of Users named once, not a list of e-mails on the command line (#218).

The personal data a feature needs (an e-mail to deliver a prize, a sign-up) is entered on a form that sends it in the request body, kept in one place the person can delete, and referred to everywhere else by an opaque id; what stays after a deletion is anonymized. Learn more: OWASP lists personal data among the data to exclude from logs (Logging Cheat Sheet); the LGPD and the GDPR ask for data minimisation.

docs.title: The Nereus API is the one door, and it cannot lie
docs.text:
The Nereus API is the single point of communication between the platform and the outside world: the CLI, the portal, an IDE and the agents talk to it, and what is behind it stays behind it (ADR 0018). A new command reaches the cluster through it, never through a kube context; the commands not yet moved keep the kubeconfig, a stand-in ADR 0018 names and ends one command group at a time.

The name says why: Nereus knows everything and cannot lie, in the owner's words, and Hesiod's Theogony (233 ff.) calls him "truthful Nereus who tells no lies". So the API answers what it read, and what it did not read it says it did not: nereus doctor (#799) shows a check that did not run as skipped, never pass, and a person with no login gets a shorter answer, never a different one.

Learn more: without a platform, "work crosses the boundary through ad hoc negotiation rather than through a well-designed interface"; the answer is to "replace negotiation with paths" (Thinking in Platforms, p. 60 and p. 62; Thinking in platforms).

docs.title: The same quality for fewer tokens
docs.text: Before an activity, an agent weighs whether the way it plans to do it could reach the same quality for less: a smaller answer, fewer subagents or a narrower brief, a lighter model for mechanical work, a script instead of an agent. It does the cheaper way, or suggests it when the choice is the owner's. Quality comes first: a saving that brings rework is no saving. scripts/metrics/order (#803) measures it per order and agent.

docs.title: Simple on the surface, consistent underneath
docs.text:
What a person types first is the familiar, welcoming form; what it reaches underneath behaves like everything else in the platform. The root form nereus invitation create is the familiar one, and underneath the invitation is a kind of the authentication reef, with the same verbs, output and errors as every other noun (spec 0007, ADR 0013).

Learn more: "Standardization is a compounding floor, not a ceiling on what is possible" (Thinking in Platforms, p. 59; Thinking in platforms).

docs.title: An experience that works becomes an exploration of a possible feature
docs.text: When something done by hand works, the project asks whether it could be a Nereus feature, and records the exploration as an issue, with what happened and what it taught. It is an exploration, not a commitment: the owner's triage decides whether it goes on. Coordinating six sessions by hand to bring their work to main became #956 (an agents' merge queue in Triton).

docs.title: No single control point
docs.text:
Control (identity, authorization, quota, policy) is enforced in layers: the cloud, Kubernetes, the Environment and the Nereus API. One layer failing or misconfigured must not collapse the platform, and no one layer is the only place a rule lives.

What holds today: the Nereus API checks every request against the person's roles and bindings, and fails closed when its authorization store is down; the nereus-admins group is the emergency exit, which does not depend on that store, and nereus doctor warns when it was used (spec 0011, #1644). What does not yet: Kubernetes RBAC derived from the bindings, and cloud policy, so today the Nereus API is still the one layer that enforces them.

Learn more: a platform should not make one component the single place where control is held (Thinking in Platforms, Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante, 2026; Thinking in platforms).

docs.title: Credit what we use
docs.text:
Every technique, practice or pattern the docs use is named, credited and linked, with what the project takes from it, in the style of evidence-based medicine (the owner, #332):

  • an ADR has a ## Prior art section before its Consequences (ADR 0012, every error message says what happened and how to fix it, is the first)
  • a spec or a page has a "Learn more" line
  • this page names the source of each pillar that is a known technique

A claim of effect cites its evidence (a study, a book, a measurement) or says it is the project's own observation. Every link is opened before it is cited, and no author or year is guessed. The deck does the same (docs/presentations/references/, #202).

An agent that notices a technique, practice or study that could improve the product, code or process opens a Proposal issue with proposed-by-agent: the technique named and credited, links, evidence, where it applies here and a recommendation. It never adopts it on its own: the owner decides whether, when and how.

docs.title: How every feature is born
docs.text:
A principle being refined (#28) for every feature:

  • Security and the quality attributes from the start. Every idea is discussed under security, the other "-ilities" and their fitness functions before it is built.
  • Alpha, beta, stable. Alpha is a proof of concept that never reaches production; beta works and has the minimum to be presented; stable comes after it ran, was tested and collected metrics, preferably from real users.
  • Early adopters. A feature can go to a chosen group of users first.
  • Edge and stable channels. Everything merged to main is deployed to an edge environment where every test runs (smoke, performance, penetration); only graduated features are promoted to stable.

The helm Nereid (#8) is the first to go through it, as alpha.

docs.title: 0001. Record architecture decisions
docs.text:
In short

Every architecture decision is recorded in docs/adr/, one file per decision in Nygard's format. A number is valid only once its ADR is merged into main. Status: Accepted (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25).

Status: Accepted (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The project starts from ideas worked out in conversation: a model of layers, how Controllers are installed and how they extend the CLI. Without a record, each decision gets argued again, and someone reading the code later cannot tell a rule from an accident.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Record every architecture decision in docs/adr/, in the format of Michael Nygard: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences. One file per decision, named NNNN-short-title.md.

  • Status is Proposed, Accepted, Superseded by NNNN or Rejected.
  • A number is valid only once its ADR is merged into main. A draft in a branch, a pull request or a work order carries no number: it is named by its title, and takes the next free number when it is merged. Two drafts never claim the same number, and a dropped draft leaves no hole.
  • Until the first release (v1.0.0), an ADR may be rewritten in place when its decision changes: the number stays, the file may be renamed to the new words, and a line at the end says *Rewritten <date> ...*. The history keeps the old text.
  • From v1.0.0 on, an accepted ADR is not edited, except to change its status. A changed decision is a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
  • An ADR states what was decided and why. Open questions are listed as such, never presented as decided.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
Editorial addition (#332): credits only; the Context, Decision and Consequences are unchanged.

  • Michael Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions" (2011) (Cognitect blog): the format this ADR adopts (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences), one short file per decision, numbered and kept with the code, and a superseded decision kept rather than erased.
  • Architecture decision records, the community's hub (adr.github.io): templates, tools and the other formats that grew from Nygard's.
  • Thoughtworks Technology Radar, "Lightweight Architecture Decision Records" (thoughtworks.com): ADRs kept in the repository next to the code, rather than in a wiki.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The ADRs are the place to learn the rules. CLAUDE.md summarises them and points here.
  • A pull request that adds an ADR checks the next free number against main right before it is merged, and renames the file and its links when another ADR took that number first.
  • Before v1.0.0 an ADR always says what is decided now, at the cost of reading git log to learn what it said before.

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session (order 20261025-1724): ADRs may be rewritten in place until v1.0.0; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

Rewritten 2026-10-26 from order 20261026-0508 (divergence 2 of the idea timeline of 2026-10-25): a number is valid only once the ADR is merged; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

docs.title: 0002. Conceptual model: reef, Instance, Mandate, Nereid, Tool
docs.text:
In short

The platform is five layers plus Vendor: reef, Instance, Mandate, Nereid and Tool. A reef is a capability, an API group, and may exist with no Nereid. Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
An Internal Developer Platform offers capabilities (a database, an environment, a login, a place for secrets) that are delivered differently in each place: a Postgres in the cluster or a managed one, Keycloak or Auth0, Azure Key Vault or OpenBao. Without a shared vocabulary, the API ends up knowing each implementation by name, and swapping one means changing the API.

Kubernetes already solved this for storage and traffic: a PersistentVolumeClaim names a StorageClass, the StorageClass names a provisioner, and the provisioner is the only part that knows the storage backend and holds its credentials. Gateway API does the same with Gateway, GatewayClass and controllerName.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The platform is described in five layers, plus Vendor as an attribute:

Layer Answers Kubernetes Platform reef what exists? traffic entry secrets, authentication, release Instance which occurrence, whose? Gateway shop-edge secret/google-sso, a database for an app Mandate which Nereid handles this reef here, with which parameters? GatewayClass aws-alb, StorageClass vault (secrets by azure-key-vault), corporate (authentication by keycloak) Nereid who fulfils the contract? the provisioner, gateway.k8s.aws/alb azure-key-vault, keycloak, sao Tool what does it work with? the ELB API Azure Key Vault, the Auth0 Management API Vendor (attribute) whose thing is it? AWS Microsoft, Auth0, local
  • A reef is a capability, an API group <reef>.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009). A reef can exist with no Nereid; it then waits. The core reef is built in.
  • A Nereid is a controller installed in the platform, top-level, with a name global to the platform. One Nereid may look after many reefs, as one controller manager looks after many kinds; one reef may have many Nereids. Its name is free: the Tool's name (keycloak) or a name from the myth (sao, nereus nereid suggest).
  • A Nereid owns its authentication and its default target parameters (for example authentication=workload-identity and a default vaultUrl), as the provisioner holds the credentials and the StorageClass only selects. They are set once, when the Nereid is added.
  • A Mandate binds one reef to one Nereid. It may override the Nereid's target parameters with --param (a Nereid may serve several vaults); one Mandate per reef is the default. A Mandate's match may also route requests (ADR 0017).
  • The platform's own kinds are Reef, Nereid and Mandate, in the API group core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, owned by the core reef (ADR 0009). Today's code names them Interface, Implementation and a per-reef class such as CloudClass, in platform.wasp.silvios.me (current code, to be renamed).
  • The API knows reefs and Instances, never a Nereid by name. It reads what the Nereid publishes in status and acts on that.
  • The person asking names the reef, never the Tool. The Mandate, when not given, is the reef's default, and it is recorded in the Instance's status.
  • The word is Nereid; Controller, as in Kubernetes, is the mechanism that runs it (ADR 0011). "Driver", "plugin" and "provider" are not used for either.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text: • Kubernetes storage classes and Gateway API (StorageClass; GatewayClass): a claim names a class, the class names who fulfils it, and only that part knows the backend; the model takes that split for every capability, with the Mandate in the role of the class.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Swapping a Nereid (Keycloak for Auth0) changes no API code: only which Mandate is the default and what the Nereid publishes.
  • Each reef needs a written contract: the fields a Nereid must publish for the API and the CLI to work, and the capabilities it must offer (for secrets, client-side encryption, ADR 0011).
  • Credentials of a Tool are never repeated per Mandate: they live with the Nereid.

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1724): "Mandate" is the working term and "Instance" keeps its name. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1805): the kinds are Reef, Nereid and Mandate in core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1.

docs.title: 0003. nereus init prepares the platform; reefs and Nereids are added at runtime
docs.text:
In short

nereus init prepares a cluster with the built-in core reef, the tenancy reef and a profile's reefs; every other capability arrives later as a reef, with Nereids added at runtime. Status: Accepted (2026-11-24, by the owner; proposed 2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25). What init installs is revised by ADR 0014.

Status: Accepted (2026-11-24, by the owner; proposed 2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
In the project this one grew from, platform init installs the whole platform: identity, API, every controller, ingress, observability. Adding or swapping a capability means changing init, and there is no way to run the platform with less, or with something else.

There is one exception to "less": secrets. Every other reef needs a place for credentials, and the first Nereid that keeps secrets needs something to exist outside the cluster before any Nereid runs (in Azure: a Key Vault, a Managed Identity federated with the cluster's issuer). That chicken-and-egg can only be solved by the person's own login, once.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
nereus init prepares a cluster with the built-in core reef, then installs the reefs of a profile (ADR 0014, profiles: core is only the engine, and a profile lists what to install). The secrets reef is not fixed at init: it comes when the profile, or a Nereid it installs, requires it. Every other capability arrives later as a reef, added by name, and Nereids that look after it:

# Core only, the default profile core: to build piece by piece
nereus init

# A local platform on k3d: core, then the profile internal-developer-platform: authentication with
# keycloak, after what keycloak requires, the secrets reef kept by OpenBao
nereus init --profile internal-developer-platform

# A platform whose first secrets Nereid is Azure Key Vault
nereus init --target azure

# Every other reef and its Nereids, added at runtime
nereus reef list
nereus reef apply authentication --from-file ./reefs/authentication/
nereus nereid apply keycloak --reef authentication
  • The profile decides whether the secrets reef comes with init (#420). core, the default, installs nothing beyond core (#424). internal-developer-platform installs authentication with the keycloak Nereid, which requires the secrets reef: so the secrets reef, its first Nereid, the reef's default Mandate vault, and the Mandate's RSA key come first, with its public key published in the Mandate's status for the CLI (ADR 0011). With no target that Nereid is openbao, with OpenBao in dev mode in its Pod (in memory: a restart makes a new key, which init and the Mandate's status say). A Nereid that needs secrets declares that it requires the reef; nothing installs secrets because it is secrets.
  • With --target azure, init still installs the secrets reef with Azure Key Vault, since the cloud bootstrap needs it; how a profile follows the target is left to its own issue (ADR 0014).
  • Adding the secrets reef again is not part of the person's flow once a profile installed it. nereus reef create secrets fails as any create of a thing that exists (ADR 0013), and the message points to nereus reef list; nereus reef apply secrets reports reef/secrets unchanged, or configured when it changed something.
  • --target <provider> decides the first secrets Nereid and provisions what it needs to be reachable. For azure: Key Vault, Storage, DNS zone and a Managed Identity, with the RSA key of the secrets reef (ADR 0011). Init uses the person's own az login, since no Nereid exists yet; from then on, the Nereid uses workload identity, with no stored secret.
  • The cluster's issuer is made public: the OIDC discovery document and the JWKS of the cluster are published to the Storage account, and the Managed Identity is federated with that URL, so Azure accepts tokens signed by the local cluster.
  • Undercloud and overcloud. A local k3d cluster (the undercloud) bootstraps and provisions the overcloud (for example AKS); then the platform pivots to the overcloud, the federated credential moves to the overcloud's issuer as an explicit step, and the undercloud is deleted.
  • nereid apply records the Nereid (name, image, reefs, parameters) and runs its image as a Deployment. The Nereid reports Ready in its status when it is up.
  • Until the Platform API exists, the CLI does this with the kubeconfig, as helm does. The API itself becomes one more Nereid added this way; after it, everything goes through the API.
  • init installs the chart nereus with Helm (amended 2026-11-05, #1044): the kinds, the namespace and the Nereus API come from cli/src/nereus/charts/nereus, the API through helm upgrade --install nereus in nereus-system, so the cluster holds a release a HelmRelease can take over later (#1045). Helm runs with the same kube context and kubeconfig as the Kubernetes client, and no other credential; it is the one tool besides the client, checked at init's prerequisites step (4.0 or newer, for --take-ownership and --force-conflicts, which takes a kind or an object changed in the cluster back to the chart's). The kinds come before it from their own chart, cli/src/nereus/charts/nereus-reefs, as templates with helm.sh/resource-policy: keep (amended 2026-11-05, #1050): helm upgrade --install nereus-reefs updates them on every run, and helm uninstall never deletes one. The chart holds the Installation too (#1051), named by installation.name, its id kept by lookup of the stored one; init still creates it with the client before Helm, until #1055. The profile's reefs stay with the client.
  • Removing a Nereid removes its Deployment and the commands it added to the CLI (ADR 0004).

docs.title: The Vault kind
docs.text:
The secrets Nereid is installed once; each vault it keeps is a Vault, a kind of the secrets reef (secrets.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1), one object per vault inside that Nereid. A person names the vault a secret goes to with --vault, and leaves it out to use the default vault (order 20261026-0640):

# The default vault, when --vault is left out
nereus secrets apply google-sso --from-file google-sso.json

# Another vault the same Nereid keeps
nereus secrets apply google-sso --from-file google-sso.json --vault team-a

kubectl get vaults.secrets.getnereus.dev
#   NAME     NEREID   DEFAULT   FINGERPRINT
#   default  openbao  true      SHA256:aA57xN3...
#   team-a   openbao            SHA256:Qm9vY2...

apiVersion: secrets.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Vault
metadata:
  name: team-a
spec:
  nereid: openbao
  default: false
  params: {}          # where the Nereid keeps it: a path, a Key Vault URL
status:
  publicKey: {}       # what the Mandate's status.publicKey holds today (ADR 0011)
  • One Nereid, many vaults: the Nereid is not installed again for a second vault; a new Vault object is enough, and the Nereid makes it ready.
  • One default: at most one Vault has spec.default: true, and a secret with no --vault goes to it. A command that would make a second default fails and names the current one.
  • The profile that installs the secrets reef (ADR 0014) creates its default vault, as it creates the default Mandate vault today.
  • No --vault exists yet: on 2026-10-26 the CLI has no secrets command at all (nereus secrets apply is designed in ADR 0011, not built), so the flag is born with the command.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Kubernetes default StorageClass (kubernetes.io, "Storage Classes"): a claim that names no storageClassName gets the class annotated storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true". A secret with no --vault takes the default Vault the same way; Nereus allows one default, where Kubernetes takes the most recent of several.
  • cert-manager Issuers (cert-manager.io, "Issuer"): one installed cert-manager serves many Issuer and ClusterIssuer objects, each a certificate authority it signs with. A Vault is the same shape: one secrets Nereid, many vaults as objects.
  • Cluster API, bootstrap and pivot (clusterctl move): a temporary bootstrap cluster creates the management cluster, and clusterctl move transfers the resources to it; the undercloud and overcloud take the same shape and the word "pivot".

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A platform is the set of reefs and Nereids in it. Two installations can differ in what they offer.
  • Adding a Nereid is running code with permissions in the cluster. Once the API exists, nereid apply is for platform admins only, and images are pinned by digest. Before that, whoever holds the kubeconfig already has that power.
  • The order matters (the secrets reef and its Nereid come first, a Nereid that installs others before them); init takes the first part on itself, and the rest has to be visible to the person running it: each output ends with Next steps: (ADR 0013).
  • With --target, the platform starts with a cloud dependency; with no target, the secrets Nereid runs in the cluster (OpenBao), when the profile requires it.
  • After a plain nereus init (the profile core), nereus nereid apply keycloak is refused until a Nereid looks after the secrets reef, as any Nereid whose required reef has none.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How a Vault relates to the Mandate: ADR 0011 says the key belongs to the Mandate, which picks the target vault through its params. Recommendation: the key and the target move to the Vault, and the Mandate only binds the reef to its Nereid.

  • The default vault's name: default, or vault as the default Mandate is named today.

  • Whether init prints what the person's login granted, so it can be removed afterwards (least privilege).

  • How OpenBao, the secrets Nereid of nereus init with no target, is unsealed after a restart. Demos may run it in dev mode or with auto-unseal; the production answer is open.

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1724): init installs the secrets reef, its first Nereid, the default vault Mandate and the reef's RSA key. Rewritten 2026-10-26 (order 20261026-0508, divergence 4): the secrets reef is not fixed at init; the profile decides, and keycloak requires it (#420). Revised 2026-10-26 (order 20261026-0640): the default profile is core (#424); the Vault kind, one object per vault inside the secrets Nereid; the ADR stays Proposed.

docs.title: 0004. Reefs and their Nereids extend the CLI with their own commands
docs.text:
In short

Each reef describes its commands as data published in status, and the CLI builds them at runtime, grouped by reef, never by Nereid or Tool. Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: If reefs and Nereids are added at runtime (ADR 0003), the CLI cannot know their commands in advance. Shipping a new CLI release for each would undo the point. The Azure CLI solves a similar problem with extensions, but an extension is code installed on the client.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Each reef describes the commands it serves, and the CLI builds them at runtime:

  • The commands are grouped by reef, never by Nereid or Tool: adding the secrets reef adds nereus secrets apply, whichever Nereid keeps the secrets.
  • The description of the commands (names, arguments, flags, help text, examples) is data, not code, published in status.
  • The CLI caches these descriptions when it lists reefs or logs in, as kubectl caches API discovery.
  • Running a command reaches the reef's resources or the Nereid that handles it under the reef's Mandate. In the first test, the CLI reaches the Nereid through the Kubernetes API's Service proxy, with no Platform API and no login. Later the Platform API sits in between and decides who may run what.
nereus reef apply secrets --from-file ./reefs/secrets/
nereus secrets --help
nereus secrets apply google-sso --from-file google-sso.json

docs.title: Amendment: named options and the answer's steps (2026-11-09)
docs.text:
Decided by the owner on 2026-11-09 for #1290 (a command a Nereid publishes appears under its reef, takes named options, and can open the browser and write the Mandate's params), the generic mechanism the github Nereid's app-register uses first:

  • Every Nereid of a reef publishes into the reef's group. The same path published by two Nereids is one command, routed by --mandate: the Nereid of that Mandate, else the reef's default Mandate's; a path one Nereid publishes goes to it. --mandate is the option the CLI adds to every published command of a reef with several Nereids, unless the command declares it; a Mandate whose Nereid does not publish the command is refused, naming it. The CLI's own commands of a reef still win.
  • Named options: a command declares options (name, help, required, pattern) beside its positional arguments; the CLI checks each value against its pattern before sending it, and sends the options by name.
  • The answer's steps: POST /run answers JSON with output, error and exitCode, and may ask two steps the CLI carries out as the person's client, in this order:
  • browser (url, callback, timeoutSeconds, optional form): the CLI listens on 127.0.0.1 only, generates a state and checks it on the callback, opens the URL (or, with a form, a local page that POSTs it, for GitHub's manifest flow, served once at an unguessable path), keeps only the listed callback parameters, and refuses every request after the first valid callback. {{callback}} and {{state}} in the URL and the form become the listener's callback URL and that state.
  • mandateParams (mandate, params): the CLI merges the params into the spec of that Mandate, which must be one the answering Nereid serves on this reef (ADR 0005: the person, through the CLI, writes spec), and prints core/mandates/<name> configured (...).
  • The Nereid stays stateless: after a browser step, the CLI posts the command again with the original options plus everything the steps collected (collected), until an answer asks no browser step, at most five rounds. A failed answer (exitCode other than 0) runs no step.
  • nextSteps (a list of lines, #1291): the CLI closes the run with them in its own Next steps: block (ADR 0013), after the other steps, so a line like the App's install URL comes after the Mandate is written.
  • No step carries a secret: a Nereid answers with secret names, never their values.
  • A Mandate made with no params names, in the Next steps of mandate create, every command its Nereid publishes with a required --mandate option, the Mandate filled in and the other required options as placeholders (#1291: nereus authentication app-register --mandate github --org <org>).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A reef extends the MCP door the same way: its Nereid's contract lists its tools, and the Nereus API serves them at /mcp (ADR 0029).
  • No client-side code is downloaded: a Nereid cannot run anything on the user's machine.
  • Swapping a Nereid changes no command a person types.
  • What a Nereid publishes is untrusted input: validated before the CLI renders or routes it.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How a reef's contract becomes commands: built from the schema of its resources, published by its Nereids for actions that are not resources, or both (ADR 0010).

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

Amended 2026-11-09 from the owner's decisions on #1290; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-09.

docs.title: 0005. One writer per field: spec by the API, status by the Nereid
docs.text:
In short

The API writes spec; each Nereid writes only its own part of status. A field that needs two writers is split. Status: Proposed (2026-10-17).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-17)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: With Nereids swapped and added at runtime, several processes touch the same objects. When two of them write the same field, the last write wins and the bug shows up far from its cause.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The API (or the CLI, before the API exists) writes spec: what was asked.
  • Each Nereid (its controller) writes only its own part of status: what it did and what it publishes. When several Nereids look after the same reef side by side, each writes under its own key, status.nereids.<name>.
  • Choosing which Nereid handles a request is a Mandate's spec (ADR 0002), written through the API.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Kubernetes API conventions, "Spec and Status" (kubernetes/community; Kubernetes objects): spec is the desired state, written by its user, and status the observed state, written by the system; this ADR takes the split as is and adds one key per Nereid under status.
  • The controller pattern (Kubernetes, "Controllers"): a control loop that reads the desired state, works towards it and reports what it observes.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every new field is designed with its writer. A field that needs two writers is split.
  • Reading status is how the API and the CLI learn what a Nereid offers: endpoints, commands (ADR 0004), readiness.
  • One handover, for held objects (ADR 0031): while an object carries the hold of a soft gate, the authorization reef's gate Nereid is the one writer of its status; the kind's own Nereid writes it from the moment the API lifts the hold.

Aligned in wording 2026-10-25 from voice session (reef, Nereid, Mandate, nereus); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

docs.title: 0006. Authentication is a reef: the person signs in through OIDC, the platform proves itself through a Mandate, and the User belongs to core
docs.text:
In short

authentication is a reef: logins are always OIDC, the platform proves itself outwards through a Mandate per identity, and the User belongs to core. Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25, 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-12, amended 2026-11-15).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25, 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-12, amended 2026-11-15)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The first swap to prove is authentication: the same login and the same API working with Keycloak or with Auth0, side by side or one after the other, without losing anything (ownership, credentials, teams, authorship). Two things get in the way when a platform relies on one identity provider: the person is identified by the provider's sub, which changes with the provider, and teams are groups inside the provider.

The platform needs an identity too, towards the systems it acts on: a GitHub App to read a private repository (#927, the catalog Nereid's SourceUnreachable of #904), to clone one for a build (#1070) or to publish a package (#1250). #234 (the platform's own identity towards external systems) asked where it sits in the model. The first version of ADR 0024 (the scm reef) put the App in the scm reef; the owner moved it here on 2026-11-09, since a token for ghcr.io is not a source host's concern.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
authentication is a reef, API group authentication.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009). It answers two questions: who the person is (inwards, OIDC), and who the platform is towards an external system (outwards, a Mandate per identity).

The contract of a login is always OIDC. The API and the CLI only speak OIDC: a bearer token the API validates against a JWKS, plus authorization code with PKCE, device code and refresh for the CLI. Each authentication Nereid that serves login publishes in status: issuer, jwksUrl, audience, cliClientId, authorizeParams and emailClaim. The contract binds only those Nereids (owner, 2026-11-10): one that publishes no status.oidc, as github, serves Token only and never takes part in a login.

The first one, the local keycloak Nereid (#407), writes them in its Mandate's status.oidc: issuer, jwksUrl, audience (nereus-mcp), clientId (claude, the claude.ai connector's public client, with PKCE S256), cliClientId (nereus-cli, the public client of nereus login, #605: PKCE S256 on a loopback callback, or the device flow), authorizeParams, emailClaim, and storage: memory while Keycloak runs in dev mode.

Two optional fields name the client a coding agent logs in to /mcp with (#1880): mcpClientId (claude-code, PKCE S256, aud: nereus-mcp) and mcpCallbackPort (33418), the one loopback port its redirect http://localhost:<port>/callback allows. The Nereus API publishes them at /.well-known/nereus-configuration beside cliClientId, and nereus mcp client add claude-code passes them to claude mcp add; a Nereid that leaves them out serves no coding agent.

The protocol with the person's origin belongs to the Nereid. Google, a corporate SAML IdP or GitHub are sources the Nereid brokers: a SAML IdP is an identity provider in a Keycloak realm or an enterprise connection in Auth0. There is no "SAML Nereid"; a lighter broker (Dex) would be another Nereid that still issues OIDC.

Several Nereids at once, one default (owner, 2026-11-10, #1311). The reef takes keycloak, auth0, an Entra ID one and github side by side. Each Mandate binds the reef to one Nereid with its parameters, and a request picks its Mandate by ADR 0017's selection rule (the Nereids that serve the request, then match on the nearest owner, then the default, then the only one). The credentials a Nereid needs are secrets, named in a parameter (credentials=secret:google-sso):

# The default Mandate: the platform's login
nereus nereid apply keycloak --reef authentication
nereus mandate create corporate \
  --reef authentication \
  --nereid keycloak \
  --param identityProvider=google \
  --param credentials=secret:google-sso \
  --default

# An Organization overrides it with another Nereid, for itself and its Projects
nereus nereid apply auth0 --reef authentication
nereus mandate create acme-auth0 \
  --reef authentication \
  --nereid auth0 \
  --match owner=organization/acme
  • The default Mandate is the platform's login.
  • An Organization overrides it with a Mandate whose match names it; the Mandate covers its Projects.
  • A Project, or several, may pick another Mandate to compare two Nereids side by side (the comparator, #1316). The tenancy has no Team kind: "a team" is a match on its Projects (ADR 0015).
  • The e-mail domain is not a Mandate parameter: the matchEmailDomain of the first versions is gone, and a domain belongs to an Organization (below).

Identifier-first login, by e-mail domain only (owner, 2026-11-10). The domain of the address points to the Organization that verified it (its domains, ADR 0015), and the Organization to its Mandate by match; a domain no Organization verified gets the default. Never per person: telling, before any password, whether an address exists or where it sits is user enumeration (OWASP A07). The address goes to the Nereid's issuer as OIDC's login_hint.

nereus login asks nothing (owner, 2026-11-10):

# The default Mandate, or the one used last
nereus login

# The Mandate of the address's domain; the address goes on as login_hint
nereus login --email maria@example.com

# One Mandate, by name
nereus login --mandate acme-auth0

The API accepts the token of any Ready login Mandate, told apart by iss (owner, 2026-11-10). The API reads the token's iss, finds the Mandate whose status.oidc.issuer equals it, and validates the token against that Mandate's jwksUrl and audience; any other issuer is refused.

  • An Organization may require its own Mandate (requireMandate: true, ADR 0015): an e-mail of its verified domains then enters only with a token of the Mandate that matches the Organization ("enforce SSO").
  • Never per resource owner: a person who works in two Projects with two Nereids keeps working with one token.

A machine is the one exception to OIDC (owner, 2026-11-14): a Machine of core signs in with a key pair it made itself, and the Nereus API checks its assertion against the public key, with no login Nereid involved, so it holds the same on every installation. The metrics intake ADR holds the details.

The person is a User of core, not a sub, and no authentication Nereid owns it. User is a kind of core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009), like Reef, Nereid and Mandate: the person exists in the platform before, and independently of, any authentication Nereid. The platform generates the User's id. An authentication Nereid only links an external identity (its issuer and the token's sub) to a User; it never creates, keys or deletes the User, and the User is not keyed by a Nereid's name (the API never names a Nereid):

apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: User
metadata:
  name: u-7f3k2p
spec:
  name: maria
  email: maria@example.com
  identities:
    - {issuer: "http://localhost:8180/realms/nereus", sub: 3f2a9c1e-...}
    - {issuer: "https://example.us.auth0.com/", sub: "google-oauth2|1088..."}

The reason: a company changes its authentication tool far more often than its e-mail domain. Moving from Keycloak to Auth0, or to any other tool, must keep every User, and with it what each person owns. Owners, authorship and team members store the User's id, never a sub. Teams belong to the platform, not to the identity provider.

The tests sign in with a real Google account through single sign-on (SSO), brokered by the keycloak Nereid and then by an Auth0 one: the same User must come out of both.

A new sub is linked only after an e-mail code. The first login of any sub sends a single-use code to the token's verified e-mail, through a notification reef whose Nereid can be a real mail server or a local one that writes the message where only an admin can read it. The code never appears in the API response or on the screen of the person logging in. A sub is never linked to an existing User because the e-mail matches: whoever controls an IdP that issues that e-mail would take the account.

Two stand-ins in the first slice of teams and authorization (owner, 2026-11-15, ADR 0027, spec 0011), until the notification reef exists:

  • The first identity is linked by the token's verified e-mail. An administrator creates the User with its e-mail (nereus user create maria --email maria@example.com); the first sign-in of a token with email_verified: true and that e-mail links its {issuer, sub} to the User. It trusts the email_verified claim of the instance's own issuer, also when that issuer brokered another identity provider. A token whose e-mail is not verified links nothing, and a second identity on the same User is not linked at all. The e-mail code above replaces it.
  • The User's id is the object's name (core/users/maria), not an id the platform generates; spec.email is required and unique, spec.displayName optional, and the identities are written only by the Nereus API. A generated id, with the name kept as a field, replaces it.

The platform's identity towards an external system is a Mandate (owner, 2026-11-09, #234). A GitHub App is a Mandate of the github Nereid: its id and its private key are Mandate parameters, the key a plain secret of the secrets reef, read by the Nereid through a SecretBinding (ADR 0023's pattern). There is no --vendor and no Application kind: the model of ADR 0011 holds, and the CLI never names an implementation (cli/tests/test_boundaries.py::test_the_cli_never_names_an_implementation); github appears only in nereid apply and mandate create:

nereus secrets create github-app-key --from-env GITHUB_APP_KEY
nereus nereid apply github --reef authentication --reef scm
nereus mandate create github \
  --reef authentication \
  --nereid github \
  --param appId=123456 \
  --param privateKey=github-app-key

The github Mandate sits next to the login ones and is never the default (owner, 2026-11-10): a Token picks it as the only Nereid that mints tokens.

  • The App's status is the Mandate's status: Ready, NotInstalled, InvalidCredentials, NotRegistered (neither appId nor privateKey: no App yet, run app-register, #1291) or MissingParam (only one of the two), with the App's installations and the permissions granted (nereus mandate get github). There is no verify command.
  • A second App is a second Mandate, chosen with --mandate wherever a command needs the platform's identity, or by its match; with none, ADR 0017's selection rule among the Mandates that mint tokens.
  • The App has one webhook: its secret is a Mandate parameter (webhookSecret), and its URL points at the scm reef's receiver, which checks the signature (ADR 0024).
  • Creating the App from a manifest, in the browser, is an action of the github Nereid (ADR 0010, Nereid actions; ADR 0004, the commands a Nereid publishes), not a flag of mandate create; the key goes from GitHub to the Nereid, never through the person's machine. The Nereid answers with the App's id and the key's secret name, and the CLI, as the person's client, writes them to the Mandate's spec (owner, 2026-11-09): one shape of Mandate for a new App and an existing one, and ADR 0005 holds (#1275).
  • The App stands for this installation of Nereus towards GitHub, not for an org (owner, 2026-11-10): app-register names it nereus-<installation>, after the one Installation of the nereus namespace, without repeating the prefix and within GitHub's 34 characters; --name names it when that name is taken, since a name is unique across GitHub (#1291).
  • One github Nereid serves the authentication and the scm reefs, opt-in: the internal-developer-platform profile does not install it, since it needs an App the person owns.
  • The same App can broker a person's GitHub login through the keycloak Nereid (#1282); the person stays a User of core.

A consumer gets a short-lived credential as a Token, the reef's first kind (owner, 2026-11-09). A person or a Nereid asks it; the Nereid of the Mandate mints an installation token narrowed to one repository and to permissions no wider than the App's, writes it to a Secret in the requester's namespace, and refreshes it before its hour ends while the Token exists. A consumer never holds the App's key. The catalog Nereid is the first consumer (#1274); the build (#1070) and the publish copy (#1250) follow.

Kind spec (the person, or a Nereid as a client) status (the Nereid only) Token repository, permissions, mandate (empty: ADR 0017's selection rule) observedGeneration, conditions, mandate, secretRef (namespace and name), expiresAt 
nereus authentication token create catalog \
  --repository example/app \
  --permission contents=read
# ✓ authentication/tokens/catalog created (expires in 1h, mandate github)

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• OpenID Connect Core 1.0, Authentication Request and ID Token Validation: login_hint is a "hint to the Authorization Server about the login identifier the End-User might use to log in", and the issuer "MUST exactly match the value of the iss (issuer) Claim"; the address of --email and the way the API tells one Mandate's token from another's.
  • OWASP, Authentication Cheat Sheet, "Authentication and Error Messages": "an application should respond (both HTTP and HTML) in a generic manner", whether or not the account exists; the reason the discovery looks at the domain, never at the person.
  • Slack, Set up SAML single sign-on for Slack: "choose whether SSO is required for all members, required for all members excluding guests, or optional"; the shape of an Organization's requireMandate.
  • GitHub, Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App: a token that expires after an hour, narrowed to repositories and permissions, the shape of Token.
  • GitHub, Registering a GitHub App from a manifest: the browser flow and the one-time code exchanged for the App's key.
  • Flux, GitRepository, and Argo CD, Private repositories: both reach GitHub with a GitHub App's credential held by the controller, never by the person.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Swapping Keycloak for Auth0 costs each person one login and one code; nothing they own changes hands, since the User stays in core and only gets one more identity.
  • The User kind joins core next to the kinds of ADR 0014 (profiles: core is only the engine); the issue that builds it decides its exact fields.
  • Each authentication Nereid must deliver a verified e-mail in the access token, under the claim it publishes in emailClaim (Auth0 needs a post-login Action for this).
  • Authorization (who is admin, which teams) is the platform's job, outside the identity provider.
  • The github Nereid sits next to keycloak, which unblocks #1282 (keycloak brokers a GitHub login through the App) and #91 (the auth0 Nereid). The order of that work: #1313 (several Nereids per reef and the selection rule), #1314 (the API accepts several issuers, and requireMandate), #1315 (identifier-first login by e-mail domain).
  • A login by e-mail tells which Nereid an Organization's domain uses, and nothing about a person: the answer is the same for every address of a domain (OWASP A07, user enumeration).
  • The authentication reef gains its first kind, Token: it leaves contracts.REEFS_WITHOUT_KINDS (#794) when #1274 builds it.
  • The order of the work: #1273 (the github Nereid's Mandate proves a GitHub App installed), #1274 (the Token), #1275 (the App from a manifest); ADR 0024's Connection follows (#1281).
  • OWASP A01 (broken access control: one repository per token, a Secret only in the requester's namespace), A02 (cryptographic failures: the App's key sealed on the client, never outside openbao in clear) and A07 (identification and authentication failures: an hour-long token instead of a personal one) are the categories the platform's identity touches.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The workload identity of each Nereid towards a cloud (federation, no stored secret) stays with spec 0005 for the cloud reef; a system that accepts no federation, as a GitHub App, gets a Mandate of this reef. Whether an Entra ID app registration or a Slack app also becomes a Mandate here waits for its first use.
  • How the Nereid writes a Token's Secret in the requester's namespace. Recommendation for #1274: a Role on Secrets granted per namespace that asks a Token, never a ClusterRole, held by an admission policy to the Secrets the Nereid owns.
  • How a login learns the Project, when a Project has its own Mandate (the comparator, #1316). A login has no owner, and the address's domain leads only to the Organization. Until #1316 decides, --mandate is the way.

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

Rewritten 2026-10-26 from order 20261026-0508 (divergence 3 of the idea timeline of 2026-10-25): the User belongs to core, independent of the authentication Nereid; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25 (voice files 27, 28, 32 and 90).

Rewritten 2026-11-09 from the owner's decisions on #927 and #234 (the platform's identity towards an external system is a Mandate of this reef, the Token is its kind; #1280); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-09/.

Rewritten 2026-11-12 from the owner's decisions of 2026-11-10 (#1311: several Nereids at once, login by e-mail domain, the tokens the API accepts); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-10/ and #pontos/raw/2026-10-24/0000-voice-07-platform-landscape-api-groups-controllers.md.

Amended 2026-11-15 from the owner's decisions refining #897 into spec 0011 (decision 4: the first identity linked by verified e-mail, the User's name as its id, both stand-ins; ADR 0027); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-15/.

docs.title: 0007. Public by design: Apache-2.0, no identifying data in the history
docs.text:
In short

The project is Apache-2.0 and public by design: no identifying data in any commit, and public names chosen as if already public. Status: Accepted (2026-10-17).

Status: Accepted (2026-10-17)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The repository starts private and is meant to be opened, so other projects can build their platform with it. When a repository goes public, its whole history goes with it, and the names it chose (API group, image names, commands) become a contract with whoever uses it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• License: Apache-2.0, the license of Kubernetes, Helm, Argo and Crossplane: companies can adopt it without legal review, and it carries a patent grant.
  • No identifying data in any commit: no e-mails, personal or company names, internal domains, tenant or account ids, tokens. Examples use example.com, maria@example.com, 123456789012. Personal notes live in CLAUDE.local.md, which is gitignored.
  • Public names are chosen as if already public: the Kubernetes API group, image names and CLI commands.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: • A leaked value is fixed by rewriting history before the repository is opened, which gets harder with every clone. Review diffs for identifying data before each push.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The API group of the CRDs: answered by ADR 0009, <reef>.getnereus.dev, a domain the project controls.
  • Contributions: whether to require DCO sign-off (Signed-off-by) from the first external contribution.

Aligned in wording 2026-10-25 from voice session (reef, Nereid, Mandate, nereus); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

docs.title: 0008. The CLI is written in Python, with uv and typer
docs.text:
In short

The CLI is written in Python, managed with uv, with typer for commands and the official kubernetes client. Status: Accepted (2026-10-17).

Status: Accepted (2026-10-17)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The first slice (spec 0001) needs a CLI that talks to a cluster and builds command groups at runtime from what reefs and Nereids publish (ADR 0004). Go gives one static binary and the kubectl/helm/k3d toolchain (client-go, cobra); Python gives a faster start and simpler dynamic command building.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The CLI is written in Python, managed with uv, with typer for commands and the official kubernetes client for the cluster. The binary name is set in one place: the [project.scripts] entry of pyproject.toml (platform in today's code, nereus in the new design).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The proof of concept moves faster: commands built from data are plain Python objects, with no code generation.
  • Users need a Python runtime; uv tool install covers it. Distribution as a single binary is harder and is revisited before the project is opened.
  • The fake Controller (spec 0001) can share the language, but it does not have to: it only speaks HTTP and writes status.

Aligned in wording 2026-10-25 from voice session (reef, Nereid, Mandate, nereus); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

docs.title: 0009. Each reef is an API group <reef>.getnereus.dev, starting at v1alpha1
docs.text:
In short

Each reef is its own API group <reef>.getnereus.dev, starting at v1alpha1; the platform's own kinds live in core.getnereus.dev. Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25; the first version was Accepted).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25; the 2026-10-17 version was Accepted)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR 0007 asks for an API group on a domain the project controls, not a personal one. The proof of concept used platform.wasp.silvios.me, a personal domain, for every CRD. The project now has the domain getnereus.dev, and each capability is a reef (ADR 0002), so the group can say which reef a resource belongs to.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Each reef is its own API group: <reef>.getnereus.dev, starting at version v1alpha1 (secrets.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, authentication.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1).
  • The platform's own kinds (Reef, Nereid, Mandate) live in the core reef's group, core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1.
  • The domain is kept in one constant in the CLI and in the generated manifests, so changing it is a one-line change plus a regeneration.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The CRDs of today's code still use platform.wasp.silvios.me; renaming them is a change of its own, and clusters created before it are recreated, with no migration.
  • The old group stays in the history. Before opening the repository, either rewrite the history or accept that it stays visible.
  • A reef's version moves on its own (v1alpha1, v1beta1, v1), independent of the others.

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1805): the platform's own kinds live in core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1.

docs.title: 0010. Reefs are added at runtime; commands are grouped by reef
docs.text:
In short

A reef is added at runtime from its contract, and a Nereid is added on its own and looks after one or more reefs. The release reef has four kinds. Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
