ADR 0002 says the person asking names the reef, never the Tool. Naming a command group after whoever fulfils it (platform helm repo add) would expose the Tool and would not survive a swap: Flux has no helm repo, and its sources may be Git repositories.

Helm, Flux and Argo CD all take something from a source and keep a version of it running in a cluster. Kubernetes keeps the same split for traffic: a GatewayClass exists in the cluster and names a controllerName; the person writing a Gateway never names the load balancer. Crossplane does it for infrastructure: a CompositeResourceDefinition is the contract, and Compositions fulfil it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A reef is added at runtime, from its contract, and listed with the others:

nereus reef apply release --from-file ./reefs/release/
nereus reef list

A Nereid is added on its own, top-level, and looks after one or more reefs; a reef with no Nereid waits:

nereus nereid apply helm \
  --reef release \
  --image ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/release-helm-controller:0.1.0
  • Its commands are served under the reef's group: nereus release ... (ADR 0004).
  • Several Nereids may look after one reef. Which one handles a request is chosen by a Mandate (ADR 0002), the reef's default one when the request names none: nereus mandate create ... --default.

The release reef, release.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, has four kinds (#445), each named for one question, in the namespace Nereus runs in:

Kind Answers Fields (spec) Status (written by a Nereid) Repository where it comes from type (http, oci, git), url, optional secretRef (a secret of the secrets reef) ready, nereid, conditions Source what repositoryRef, chart (name, version); later kustomize or manifests instead of chart, in the same kind ready, resolvedVersion, nereid, conditions Target where to optional environmentRef (an environment of the environment reef, which knows the cluster and its credentials), namespace ready, nereid, conditions Release a Source running in a Target optional mandate (the reef's default when absent), sourceRef, targetRef, values phase (Pending, Progressing, Ready, Failed), version, nereid, mandate, and a Ready condition in the reef's reasons
  • A Target with no environment is the cluster Nereus runs in, until the environment reef exists.
  • Who writes which status (ADR 0005): a Release's, the Nereid of its Mandate; a Repository's, a Source's and a Target's, the Nereid of the reef's default Mandate.
  • A Nereid keeps its Tool's objects next to the reef's, on purpose: the flux Nereid writes a Flux HelmRepository for each Repository and a Flux HelmRelease for each Release (its chart template from the Source), each owned by the Nereus object it comes from, and translates their Ready condition into the reasons the reef declares (Released or Indexed, Progressing, ReleaseFailed or IndexFailed), keeping its status and message (#528); Flux's other conditions stay on Flux's objects. Swapping Flux for Argo CD or plain Helm changes the second object, never the first.

A reef has two levels of commands:

  • Configuring the reef, done by a platform admin: where things come from (repository), what (source) and where they go (target).
  • Using the reef, done by a developer: its Instances (release), which name a source and a target that already exist.

The commands are nereus <reef> <kind> <verb> <name>, with long options and kubectl's verbs (ADR 0013). A kind named after its reef takes the reef's own verbs: nereus release create is nereus release release create, as nereus environment create will be nereus environment environment create.

# The admin, once: the Nereid and the reef's default Mandate
nereus nereid apply flux \
  --reef release

nereus mandate create flux \
  --reef release \
  --nereid flux \
  --default

# configure
nereus release repository create codecentric \
  --url https://codecentric.github.io/helm-charts \
  --type http

nereus release source create keycloak \
  --repository codecentric \
  --chart keycloakx \
  --version 7.0.1

nereus release target create dev-identity \
  --environment dev \
  --namespace identity

# use
nereus release create keycloak \
  --source keycloak \
  --target dev-identity \
  --values-file keycloak-values.yaml \
  --mandate flux

nereus release list

Repositories are typed (http, oci, git). A Nereid says in a Repository's status when it does not take its type: the flux Nereid takes http and oci, not git yet.

GitOps is a way of making releases, a Mandate of the release reef in ADR 0002's terms, not a reef of its own: a gitops reef would leave plain Helm out.

The contract of a reef is a Kubernetes API, the API group <reef>.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009). Adding a reef applies the CRDs of its contract (for release: its repositories, sources, targets and releases), so the platform's API is extended through Kubernetes itself: validation by OpenAPI schema, discovery, RBAC per resource, kubectl and watches come with it. Nereids reconcile those resources and write their status.

Inspired by Crossplane, not built on it. The model borrows the shape of a CompositeResourceDefinition, but the platform does not depend on Crossplane. Crossplane stays free to be what ADR 0002 makes of any other project: a Tool, used by a Nereid.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Gateway API's GatewayClass (gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io): the class names a controllerName, and the person writing a Gateway never names the load balancer.
  • Crossplane's composite resource definitions (docs.crossplane.io): a definition is the contract, and Compositions fulfil it; the contract of a reef takes the shape, not the dependency.
  • Flux's source and helm controllers (fluxcd.io, HelmRepository; HelmRelease): where a chart comes from apart from what is released and where; the release reef's Repository, Source and Release take the same split, and the flux Nereid writes those objects.
  • Custom resources and the operator pattern (Kubernetes, "Operator pattern"): the API is extended at runtime with CRDs, and a controller reconciles them.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Swapping Helm for Flux changes no command a person types: only which Nereid the Mandate names.
  • Configuration and use are separate resources, so permissions split along the two levels without extra design (admins write repositories, sources and targets, developers write releases).
  • Repositories, sources, targets and releases are Instances in the cluster instead of state in a Nereid's volume: a new Nereid inherits them.
  • reef, nereid and mandate share one shape: the noun, the verb and the name as an argument, top-level (nereus nereid apply helm, nereus reef apply release).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How a contract is written and turned into commands. To decide: how a reef is packaged (--from-file today; an image or an OCI package next), how the CLI builds commands from its schema, and how a contract is versioned. Today the CLI builds the release reef's commands from the contract it pins (#445), a stand-in for commands built from any reef's schema.
  • How the Platform API sits in front of the reefs. kubectl reaches the CRDs of one cluster; the Platform API is the one door for every client (the CLI, a portal, an IDE, an agent), none of which should need a kubeconfig. It composes reefs and owns what crosses them: authentication (ADR 0006), authorization by team, policy, cost, several clusters.
  • Actions that are not resources. source apply and release create map to resources; release rollback, sync or logs are actions. Likely both mechanisms stay: commands built from the contract's schema for resources, and commands a Nereid publishes for actions (ADR 0004).
  • What a target is beyond the cluster Nereus runs in: an environment of the environment reef names the cluster and its credentials; whether a Target may also name a cluster directly is open.
  • Where the reef's objects live: today the namespace Nereus runs in; a namespace per organization and project comes with them.
  • Who upgrades the Tool (#449): nereus nereid apply flux installs Flux before the Nereid, as the openbao Nereid runs OpenBao (owner, 2026-10-26): the source and helm controllers, from Flux's install.yaml pinned by version and digest. Who upgrades it, what the CLI does to a Flux it finds, and whether deleting the Nereid uninstalls it are open.

The first Release the platform makes itself (order 20261026-0840, step 2; #597): Keycloak. The keycloak Nereid writes it itself, by server-side apply through the reef's default Mandate: a Repository codecentric, a Source keycloak (keycloakx 7.0.1), a Target keycloak (the namespace Nereus runs in) and a Release keycloak with the chart's values. While the release reef has no default Mandate it writes nothing and reports Ready=False (NoReleaseNereid, naming nereus nereid apply flux --reef release); it reports WaitingForRelease until the Nereid of that Mandate reports the Release Ready, ReleaseFailed with the Release's own message when it fails, and only then applies its realm and publishes status.oidc, reaching Keycloak through the chart's Service. So the keycloak Nereid requires the release reef, besides secrets. The Source, the Target and the Release are owned by the core/nereids/keycloak object, so deleting the Nereid lets Kubernetes' garbage collector delete them, and Flux uninstalls Keycloak; the shared Repository has no owner, and nereus nereid delete keycloak deletes it once no Source names it (owner, 2026-10-26).

A Nereid that needs a Helm chart writes its own Release (owner, 2026-10-30, #597), with the customisations it needs, through the chart's native options where possible (its values, extraInitContainers, extraVolumes); the CLI only installs the Nereid and never customises a chart. What a Nereid adds to its chart runs from its own image when it needs one (NEREID_IMAGE, pinned by digest), as the login theme of #598 will.

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25. Rewritten again 2026-10-26 (order 20261026-1748, #445): the release reef's four kinds (Repository, Source, Target, Release) and their fields, from the owner's walkthrough deck of 2026-10-26; source became repository and the chart moved from the release to the source; the syntax sugar of a kind named after its reef. Amended 2026-10-26 (order 20261026-1843): the flux Nereid installs Flux itself. Amended again (order 20261026-0840, step 2): Keycloak is a Release of this reef. Amended 2026-10-30 (#597): the keycloak Nereid writes that Release itself, and every Nereid that needs a chart writes its own.

docs.title: 0011. Reefs, Nereids and Mandates, managed with top-level commands
docs.text:
In short

Reefs, Nereids and Mandates are managed with top-level commands, with --reef and --nereid as the flags everywhere; a Mandate binds one reef to one Nereid. Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-17, rewritten 2026-10-25)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The model's words changed twice. The first ADRs said Concept and Controller; the Lean Inception of #79 changed them to Interface and Implementation, managed under a platform system group, with an Implementation installed into an Interface and one active Instance per Interface. The owner's voice sessions of 2026-10-25 reviewed the CLI command by command on the MVP's journey (secrets first, then authentication with two identity brokers side by side) and found:

  • A capability and whoever fulfils it are different things: a reef can exist with no Nereid, and one controller can look after several reefs, as in Kubernetes. Nesting the Nereid under the reef is wrong.
  • A Tool's credentials repeated in every Class or Instance are wrong: they belong to the controller's installation, as a StorageClass's provisioner holds them.
  • A secret travelling in plain text inside the platform can be captured in logs, even over HTTPS.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Words. A reef is the contract of a capability, an API group (ADR 0009); a Nereid fulfils one or more reefs; a Mandate binds one reef to one Nereid (ADR 0002). Controller stays the mechanism, in ADRs and code: each Nereid runs as a Kubernetes controller that reconciles and writes status (ADR 0005). Instance, Tool and Vendor keep their meaning from ADR 0002.

Commands that change the platform are top-level nouns, with --reef and --nereid as the flags everywhere:

nereus reef list
nereus reef apply authentication --from-file ./reefs/authentication/

nereus nereid suggest --reef authentication
nereus nereid apply keycloak \
  --reef authentication
nereus nereid apply sao \
  --reef authentication \
  --image ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/authentication-auth0-controller:0.1.0

nereus mandate create corporate \
  --reef authentication \
  --nereid keycloak \
  --default

nereus status
  • Nereid names are global to the platform and free: the Tool's name or a name from the myth, suggested by nereus nereid suggest. --reef repeats when one Nereid looks after several reefs.
  • --image names an image other than the one the CLI pins for that name.
  • nereus status shows the mechanism: one row per reef and Nereid pair, columns REEF, NEREID, VERSION, STATUS, AGE.
  • nereus nereid list shows the Nereids: one row per Nereid, columns NEREID, REEFS, IMAGE, STATUS, AGE; nereus nereid get <nereid> adds the image's title, description and digest. --param is the only flag for parameters (no --set), and --reef the only flag naming a reef (no --implements).
$ nereus status
REEF            NEREID           VERSION  STATUS  AGE
authentication  keycloak         0.1.0    Ready   3m
                sao              0.1.0    Ready   3m
core            built-in         0.1.0    Ready   38m
secrets         azure-key-vault  0.1.0    Ready   8m

$ nereus nereid list
NEREID           REEFS           IMAGE                                                               STATUS  AGE
azure-key-vault  secrets         ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/secrets-azure-key-vault-controller:0.1.0   Ready   8m
keycloak         authentication  ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/authentication-keycloak-controller:0.1.0   Ready   3m
sao              authentication  ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/authentication-auth0-controller:0.1.0      Ready   3m

The kinds and their fields, in core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009): Reef.spec holds the contract (API group, version, commands); Nereid.spec.reefs (a list), Nereid.spec.image and Nereid.spec.params (authentication and default target parameters); Mandate.spec.reef, Mandate.spec.nereid, Mandate.spec.params (overrides) and Mandate.spec.default. A reef's own objects key their entries by reef (reef: in a Cloud access entry). Today's names (spec.interface, interface:) are current code, to be renamed.

Where parameters live.

  • The Nereid owns its authentication and its default target parameters, set once at nereid apply (authentication=workload-identity, a default vaultUrl). A Nereid may serve several targets (several vaults). The first secrets Nereid, its default Mandate vault and the Mandate's RSA key are made by nereus init (ADR 0003), never by the person.
  • The Mandate may override the target parameters with --param and adds the parameters of its own choice (identityProvider, credentials=secret:<name>); the common case needs only --reef and --nereid.
  • An Instance's fields are generic: fields the reef defines, common to its Nereids. A Nereid ignores what it does not use and says so in status. What one Nereid needs and the others lack becomes a new common field of the reef, never a Nereid-specific kind.

A reef's contract may require capabilities of every Nereid. The secrets reef requires client-side encryption: every secrets Nereid publishes a public key for each Mandate naming it and decrypts inside its own boundary, and the CLI encrypts each secret before sending it, with envelope encryption (an AES-256-GCM data key encrypts the value; the Mandate's RSA-OAEP-256 public key wraps the data key). The key belongs to the Mandate, not to the reef or the Nereid: a Mandate picks the target vault, and a Nereid may serve several vaults through its params. nereus secrets apply encrypts with the key of the Mandate it targets, the reef's default one unless a Mandate is named. The CLI stays provider-agnostic; only the Nereid differs:

Nereid The private key Azure Key Vault (--target azure) a non-exportable RSA key in Key Vault; the Nereid calls Key Vault to decrypt OpenBao, local k3d with no target a non-exportable RSA key of the Transit engine (rsa-4096, exportable and allow_plaintext_backup false; reading the key returns its public key); the Nereid calls Transit to decrypt, which uses OAEP with SHA-256 for the hash and MGF1 (RSA-OAEP-256), checked against OpenBao 2.7.1 fallback, a Nereid with no vault Sealed Secrets style: the private key in a cluster Secret 
$ nereus secrets apply google-sso --from-file google-sso.json
encrypted locally with the public key of mandate vault (envelope: AES-256-GCM + RSA-OAEP-256)
secret/google-sso stored by nereid azure-key-vault (2 keys, values hidden)

Log redaction stays, whatever the encryption.

Repositories and images: one per Nereid's Tool, named <reef>-<tool>-controller (secrets-azure-key-vault-controller, authentication-keycloak-controller); the image is ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/<reef>-<tool>-controller while the monorepo holds them.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• The Lean Inception (Paulo Caroli) (martinfowler.com): the workshop of #79 that first exercised the model on the MVP's journey.
  • Kubernetes storage classes (StorageClass): the provisioner holds the credentials and the class selects the target with parameters; the Nereid and the Mandate split them the same way.
  • Sealed Secrets (Bitnami) (github.com/bitnami-labs/sealed-secrets): the controller holds the private key, and kubeseal encrypts on the client with its public certificate; the secrets reef's contract takes the same shape, and the fallback Nereid the same storage of the key.
  • OpenBao's Transit secrets engine (openbao.org, API): encryption as a service, with RSA keys (rsa-2048, rsa-3072, rsa-4096), keys not exportable by default and a decrypt endpoint; the local secrets Nereid decrypts through it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• ADR 0002's words changed for people: reef, Nereid, Mandate. The legacy platform system interface ..., platform system install ... and platform system interface use ... map to nereus reef ..., nereus nereid apply ... and nereus mandate create ... --default (docs/agent/cli.md).
  • No secret value crosses the platform in plain text: the API, the logs and the cluster see only the envelope, until the Nereid writes it to its vault.
  • The reef's schema must be designed for every Nereid it expects, at the risk of a lowest common denominator; new common fields are the way out.
  • The code still names Interface and Implementation; renaming it is a change of its own.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Published (#404): the Nereid writes the key in its Mandate's status.publicKey (pem, algorithm, fingerprint, version, and where the vault keeps it, storage); version grows by one each time the key changes, and storage: memory says the vault keeps nothing across a restart (OpenBao in dev mode). Until the API exists, the CLI reads it through the kubeconfig, so the trust is the cluster's TLS and RBAC, and nereus init prints the fingerprint.
  • How the key is rotated, and how the CLI pins it (trust on first use, with nereus secrets apply) (open).

Rewritten 2026-10-25 from voice session; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1724): init makes the first secrets Nereid and its Mandate; OpenBao Transit keys are non-exportable; "Mandate" is the working term. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1805): nereid list and status columns, --param and --reef as the only flags. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1812): the fields of the kinds, and nereid get. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-2158): the public key is the Mandate's, published in its status, and its OAEP hash.

docs.title: 0012. Every error message says what happened and how to fix it
docs.text:
In short

Every error message, from the CLI or a Nereid, follows eight rules: what happened, the cause, how to check, how to fix, what changed, no traceback, and a fitness function. Status: Proposed (2026-10-19).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-19)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Reviewing #321 (install stops at once when the Controller refuses the cloud Instance) and #327 (the issuer refusal names the undercloud and Kubernetes' default issuer, not k3s), the owner decided on 2026-10-19: "error messages must always be meaningful and, whenever possible, suggest what must be done to fix them".

The rule exists only in pieces today. platform init names the setting to fix and says Nothing was changed.; spec 0005 asks the plans of a cloud Implementation to be written "in plain words". Nothing asks it of every message, and the cases that triggered the decision show the gap:

  • The refusal of the cloud Instance reads "the cluster presents k3s's default issuer ...": it is generic (which cluster?), it names the Kubernetes distribution instead of the object the person knows, and it gives no cause and no way out.
  • make docs dies with a 40-line traceback when its port is taken (#330): an expected error, shown as if it were a bug.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Every error message, from the CLI or from a Nereid, follows eight rules:

  1. What happened, in the person's words, naming the object: the undercloud of installation tailwind, never the cluster, never the Kubernetes distribution (such as k3s).
  2. The probable cause, when it is known.
  3. How to check: a command the person runs, when there is one.
  4. How to fix: a command ready to copy, or who has to act (an admin of the subscription runs ...).
  5. What changed: the message says whether anything changed (Nothing was changed.).
  6. Never a traceback for an expected error. Tracebacks are for bugs, and show with --debug.
  7. Nereids too. A refusal in status carries the fields message, cause, check and fix. The CLI only shows them, cleaned, since what a Nereid publishes is untrusted input, and never names the Nereid (ADR 0002). One line per field, each with its own length limit.
  8. A fitness function guards it. The CLI's error type requires fix=, and each error path has a test that checks its fix line.

The format, on the refusal of #327:

✗ plan     the Controller refused the Instance: IssuerNotPublic
  what     the undercloud of installation tailwind presents Kubernetes' default issuer,
           https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local, which Azure cannot reach
  cause    probably created by nereus init without --target azure (k3d is the default)
  check    kubectl get --raw /.well-known/openid-configuration
  fix      nereus init --target azure --installation-name tailwind
  Nothing was changed.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
These rules are not new; they gather what these communities already teach:

  • Jakob Nielsen's usability heuristic #9, "Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors" (1994) (Nielsen Norman Group): an error in plain language that says what went wrong, why, and suggests the fix (rules 1 to 4).
  • Command Line Interface Guidelines, "Errors" (clig.dev): catch expected errors and rewrite them for humans, keep tracebacks out of them, and suggest the next command (rules 4 and 6).
  • Elm, "Compiler Errors for Humans" (Evan Czaplicki, 2015) (elm-lang.org): errors that teach and point to the fix, shown in the person's terms rather than the tool's (rules 1 and 4).
  • Kubernetes API conventions on conditions, and kstatus's Stalled (API conventions, "Typical status properties"; kstatus): a condition carries a machine-readable reason and a human message, and Stalled says a Controller cannot progress without help; the Controller side of rule 7 builds on both.

Learn more: the four links above, in that order, go from the principle to the CLI and then to the Controller.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A person reading an error knows what failed, why, how to confirm it and what to run next, without reading the code or asking.
  • Existing messages are brought in line as they are touched, not in one sweep.
  • Every new error path costs a fix line and its test; an error with no known fix says who has to act instead.
  • A Controller's refusal becomes structured data in status, with limits the CLI enforces.
  • Follow-ups: #327 applies these rules to the issuer refusal and adds the refusal fields to spec 0005's Stalled condition; #330 makes make docs say its port is taken, and how to pick another, without a traceback.

Aligned in wording 2026-10-25 from voice session (reef, Nereid, Mandate, nereus); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25.

docs.title: 0013. Command conventions: one shape, kubectl's verbs (create, apply, delete), dry runs, examples, and refusals that list what to run
docs.text:
In short

Commands share one shape, nereus <noun> <verb> <name>, with kubectl's verbs, dry runs, examples, and refusals that list the commands to run. Status: Proposed (2026-10-18, rewritten 2026-10-25, amended 2026-10-29, 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-15).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-18, rewritten 2026-10-25, amended 2026-10-29, 2026-11-03 and 2026-11-15)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR 0010 gave the commands that extend the platform one shape: a noun, a verb, and the name as an argument (nereus reef apply release). Reviewing the commands of spec 0005 (PR #151), the owner asked for more than the shape: how a command behaves when what it creates already exists, how a person changes it, how they check a change before making it, and how a person or an agent learns to use a command. Every command added later, by the CLI or by a Nereid, should answer these the same way, so a person who learned one command knows them all.

The first version of this ADR, decided in an earlier review, used add (fails when the thing exists) and remove. On 2026-10-25 the owner replaced them with kubectl's own verbs: a person who knows kubectl should not learn a second vocabulary for the same three acts.

On 2026-10-29, designing the secrets reef's commands (#529) and porting the Keycloak login (#89), the owner sharpened four points: what create and apply each take, what a reef's commands mean without a kind, how an output line names an object that lives inside another, and which commands take --dry-run.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The shape stays ADR 0010's: nereus <noun> <verb> <name>, with the platform's nouns top-level (reef, nereid, mandate) and a reef's nouns under its group (nereus release source apply). Options are long-form (--reef, --nereid), one per line in examples.

The verbs:

Verb Does When it exists create creates, from the flags given and the defaults this CLI pins fails, and the error lists the commands to run instead apply creates or updates, declaratively, from files only: --from-file <path> (a .yaml file or a whole folder of them) or --path <path> (one local file or folder, given once) updates it, or reports it unchanged list shows every one, as a table get shows one delete deletes refused while something depends on it, naming the command that frees it

The verbs are kubectl's: create, apply and delete mean what kubectl create, kubectl apply and kubectl delete mean. add and remove are not verbs. nereus reef delete authentication deletes.

create builds an object from flags; apply takes only files or whole folders of .yaml (owner, 2026-10-29), as kubectl does. create fails when the object exists, and leaves it unchanged: nereus mandate create corporate --reef authentication --nereid keycloak --default. To change an object built from flags, write it as a file and apply the file, as kubectl create --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - does:

# Build a secret from two environment variables
$ nereus secrets create google-oauth --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET
secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth created (key SHA256:Xy3…)

# Write it as a file instead of creating it
$ nereus secrets create google-oauth --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET --dry-run --output yaml > secrets/google-oauth.yaml

# Apply a whole folder of them
$ nereus secrets apply --from-file secrets/
secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth configured
secrets/vaults/default/secrets/github-app unchanged

nereus reef apply secrets --from-file ./reefs/secrets/ applies a reef from its folder. Installing a reef or a Nereid by its name (nereus nereid apply keycloak --reef authentication, nereus reef apply cloud, --image <reference>) is not decided here: #487 (the verb that installs a reef or a Nereid by name, with apply kept for files) holds it, and until it closes those commands keep today's form.

Each reef declares a default kind (owner, 2026-10-29): nereus <reef> <verb> is nereus <reef> <default kind> <verb>, so nereus secrets create is nereus secrets secret create, as nereus release create is already nereus release release create. The reef's contract declares it with the annotation core.getnereus.dev/default-kind: "true" on that kind's CRD, on one kind at most. A shortcut at the top of the CLI is the same idea one level up (the first: nereus login for nereus authentication login, #89): allowed, with no limit per reef, each decided by the owner. nereus workload and nereus template are both shortcuts into catalog (ADR 0016).

Every noun takes the five verbs, as kubectl's resources do: create, apply, delete, get and list, for the platform's nouns and a reef's alike. Both create and apply are valid for every noun: create from flags, apply from files.

A noun Nereus ships and nobody writes takes only get and list (owner, 2026-11-17, #1700): the presentations reef's schema, the deck outline's JSON Schema of each outlineVersion, shipped with the CLI and the API; nothing creates, applies or deletes it.

Four more verbs, for what the five do not say (owner, 2026-11-02, ADR 0020):

Verb What it does Example deploy creates or updates a Delivery, across reefs nereus workload deploy hello@dev --image <reference> render writes a template's files, with Copier nereus template render python-service --path ./hello logs reads what a thing prints nereus workload logs hello-dev --follow publish publishes an artifact with the platform's credential nereus release source publish nereus

can-i asks before acting (owner, 2026-11-15, ADR 0027): nereus authorization can-i <verb> <reef>/<kinds> [--owner <kind>/<name>] [--user <name>] asks the question the Nereus API asks before it acts and changes nothing, so it takes no --dry-run. The answer names the binding that grants it, and the exit code is 0 for yes and 1 for no, for scripts. With no --user it answers for the caller; asking about another User is itself a permission. The shortcut nereus can-i is the same command. A rule of a role names it as any other verb (authorization:can-i:get).

# May bruno create Environments in the Project payments?
$ nereus authorization can-i create environment/environments --owner project/payments --user bruno
no: no binding gives bruno create on environment/environments at project/payments

request is a right, approve and reject are commands (owner, 2026-11-24, ADR 0031): request is the right to ask for a verb a soft gate holds, never a command; a person who may request but not create runs the ordinary create and gets an object held Pending, and can-i answers no, but may ask, naming the gate. nereus authorization approval approve <name> --reason <text> and reject record one decision each on an Approval.

@ names a pair: hello@dev is sugar for hello --environment dev. The argument rule, and why deploy refuses a bare name, are in ADR 0020.

Output lines end in kubectl's words: created, configured (updated), unchanged, deleted, plus rendered at <path> for render, which changes no object. They name the object by its full path (owner, 2026-10-29), as Azure's resource ids do: the reef, then each kind in the plural followed by its name, parents before children, never shortened, even when a word repeats. The platform's own kinds (Reef, Nereid, Mandate) are under core:

secrets/vaults/default created
secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth created (key SHA256:Xy3…)
secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth/secretbindings/keycloak created
release/repositories/codecentric created
release/releases/keycloak created
core/reefs/secrets created
core/nereids/openbao configured
core/mandates/default unchanged (reef: secrets, nereid: openbao, default)

A path is read without knowing the reef: release/releases/keycloak keeps release twice, so nobody learns an exception. A Mandate's line adds, in a parenthesis, the reef and the Nereid it binds and whether it is the reef's default: core/mandates/flux created (reef: release, nereid: flux, default), core/mandates/reference configured (reef: release, nereid: fake, no longer the default) (owner, 2026-10-26, order 20261026-1843): a Mandate is a binding, and the line says what it binds.

A refusal lists what to run. Every error follows ADR 0012 (every error message says what happened and how to fix it); for a command that refuses, its fix gives the command or commands that would do what the person meant, each with what it does:

$ nereus secrets create google-oauth --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET
✗ secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth already exists. To change it, run:
  # write it as a file, then apply the file
  nereus secrets create google-oauth --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID --from-env GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET --dry-run --output yaml > google-oauth.yaml
  nereus secrets apply --from-file google-oauth.yaml

Every output ends with Next steps:: a blank line before and after the label, then the command to run next, indented two spaces.

core/reefs/secrets created (secrets.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1)

Next steps:

  nereus nereid apply --help

--dry-run on every command that changes something, no exception (#242, owner, 2026-10-29): create, apply and delete of every noun, and every other imperative command. It shows exactly what would change, the objects and, for a cloud, the requests of a plan, and changes nothing; with --output yaml it prints the objects, ready for apply --from-file. #242 (every command that changes something has --dry-run) tracks the commands that miss it.

Lists come in alphabetical order, and --sort-by changes it (owner, 2026-11-02, #808): status and every list by name; --sort-by takes kubectl's path into each object (--sort-by .metadata.creationTimestamp), in every form of --output, and refuses a field no row has. A table whose order means something keeps it: the steps of a plan, the checks of doctor, what a profile installs.

--examples on every command and group (#243), next to --help: each example is a line saying what it does, then the command; -o json prints them for agents. In every code block of the docs and the deck, a comment line comes before each command and a blank line between commands.

Commands a reef or a Nereid adds follow the same conventions, and the CLI checks them as untrusted input before rendering them (spec 0003).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• kubectl get --sort-by (Kubernetes, "Command line tool (kubectl)"): a path into each object, the form --sort-by takes as it is.
  • kubectl create, kubectl apply and kubectl delete (Kubernetes, "Managing Kubernetes objects"): imperative creation that fails when the object exists, next to a declarative create-or-update, and the verb that deletes; the three are taken as they are. The output lines (created, configured, unchanged, deleted) are what kubectl prints per object, and kubectl create --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f - is the way from flags to a file, in the project's own observation.
  • Azure resource ids (Azure REST API, "Resources - Get By Id"): /subscriptions/{guid}/resourceGroups/{resource-group-name}/{resource-provider-namespace}/{resource-type}/{resource-name}, as in /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/rg-demo/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/kv-demo/secrets/google-oauth: the provider first (here, the reef), then type and name in pairs, types in the plural, a child after its parent, and a repeated word kept (Microsoft.Batch/batchAccounts). The output lines' full path follows it.
  • Command Line Interface Guidelines (clig.dev): examples first in the help, --dry-run for commands that change something, and errors that suggest the next command.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• nereus reef create fails when the reef exists, naming apply; nereus reef apply on a reef that exists reports unchanged or configured (in today's code, platform system interface add behaves as create, #18).
  • Today's code and the docs written before 2026-10-25 say add and remove; they map to apply (or create) and delete (The CLI design).
  • The code and the decks' recorded outputs adopt the 2026-10-29 amendment in #523 (the CLI's commands adopt the amended conventions): the full-path output lines, apply from files only, create from flags, --dry-run everywhere. Each reef's own commands follow it from their first slice (the secrets reef, #530).
  • Each reef's contract names its default kind with the annotation; a reef without one has no nereus <reef> <verb> shortcut.
  • cli/tests/test_help.py grows to check these conventions on every command: --dry-run where a command changes something, a description for each example.
  • A new command is reviewed against this list before it merges; a command that needs another verb or behaviour gets an ADR that extends this one.

Aligned in wording 2026-10-25 from voice session (reef, Nereid, Mandate, nereus). Rewritten 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1741): the verbs are kubectl's, create, apply and delete, replacing add and remove. Rewritten again 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-1805): every noun takes create, apply, delete, get and list; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25. Amended 2026-10-26 (order 20261026-1843): a Mandate's output line names its reef, its Nereid and whether it is the default. Amended 2026-10-29 (owner, while designing the secrets reef, #529, and porting the Keycloak login, #89; #522): create builds from flags and apply takes only files or folders, each reef declares a default kind, output lines name the object by its full path as Azure's resource ids do, and every imperative command has --dry-run; installing a reef or a Nereid by name stays open in #487. Amended 2026-11-03 (the owner's decisions of 2026-11-02 in #835, the delivery model of the internal-developer-platform profile; #843, the delivery reef's ADR): no limit of shortcuts per reef, the verbs deploy, render, logs and publish, and the @ sugar. Amended 2026-11-15 (the owner's decisions refining #897 into spec 0011, decision 19; ADR 0027): the verb can-i; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-15/. Amended 2026-11-17 (the owner's go on #1700, the deck outline's JSON Schema): a read-only noun takes only get and list. Extended 2026-11-24 with the right request and the commands approve and reject (ADR 0031, #2118); raw data in #pontos/raw/2026-11-24/.

docs.title: 0014. Profiles: core is only the engine, and a profile lists the reefs, Nereids and Mandates to install
docs.text:
In short

Core is only the engine; a profile lists the reefs, Nereids and Mandates to install, run as the commands a person would type. It revises what nereus init installs (ADR 0003). Status: Proposed (2026-10-26).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-26)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Today nereus init installs the core kinds and, with them, the secrets reef, the openbao Nereid, the default vault Mandate and the Mandate's key (ADR 0003 (init prepares core and secrets; reefs and Nereids come at runtime), #404, #406). Every other reef comes later, one command at a time: nereus reef apply, nereus nereid apply, nereus mandate create (ADR 0011, #409). A person who wants a working platform has to know which reefs, Nereids and Mandates to apply, and in which order.

Two things are mixed in init today. One is the engine: the kinds that let reefs, Nereids and Mandates exist at all. The other is a choice of capabilities, the secrets reef, made for the platform Nereus is built for first. Nereus is meant as a generic engine, and the Internal Developer Platform is one use of it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Core is only the engine. The core reef is the Reef, Nereid, Mandate and Profile kinds of core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, plus the User of ADR 0006 (the person belongs to core, not to an authentication Nereid), and nothing else. Core installs no other reef: the secrets reef, the openbao Nereid and the vault Mandate move into a profile. This revises what nereus init does since #406 (ADR 0003); the change is planned here and made in its own issue.

A profile is a list of what to install: reefs, Nereids and Mandates. It runs as the commands a person would type, nereus reef apply, nereus nereid apply and nereus mandate create (ADR 0013), so a profile adds nothing the commands cannot do. The install order is not written in the profile: it comes from each Nereid's requirements (spec.requires, from the image's label core.getnereus.dev/requires). For example, keycloak requires the vault, so the vault comes first.

# Core only, the default: to build piece by piece
nereus init

# The Internal Developer Platform: secrets, authentication, authorization, policy and environments
nereus init --profile internal-developer-platform

# A sketch of the profile; its exact fields belong to the issue that builds it.
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Profile
metadata:
  name: internal-developer-platform
spec:
  reefs: [secrets, release, authentication, authorization, policy, environment]
  nereids:
    - {name: openbao, reefs: [secrets]}
    - {name: flux, reefs: [release]}
    - {name: keycloak, reefs: [authentication]}
    - {name: openfga, reefs: [authorization]}
    - {name: kyverno, reefs: [policy]}
    - {name: vcluster, reefs: [environment]}
  mandates:
    - {name: vault, reef: secrets, nereid: openbao, default: true}
    - {name: flux, reef: release, nereid: flux, default: true}

Profiles are named by purpose, never by size. There are two:

Profile What it installs core core only, nothing else, the default: for building piece by piece internal-developer-platform the first full profile: Nereus as an Internal Developer Platform with interchangeable pieces. The secrets reef with openbao and the vault Mandate, release with flux and the flux Mandate, authentication with keycloak (Keycloak itself a Release of release), authorization with openfga, policy with kyverno, and environment with vcluster (open source, a virtual cluster on the local k3d)
  • The name internal-developer-platform is written in full on purpose: "IDP" is often read as Internal Developer Portal. The docs use no short name and no alias.
  • There is no minimal, default, empty or full: the profile of core alone is named after what it installs, core (it was empty until order 20261026-0640).

Nereus is a generic engine, and the Internal Developer Platform is its first distribution: a profile. Other domains may come as other profiles on the same engine.

A profile never carries a secret. Credentials reach a Nereid through the secrets reef after the profile is installed (nereus secrets apply, encrypted on the client, ADR 0011), never through the profile.

nereus init with no --profile installs core, core alone (#424). The full platform comes only when asked for, with --profile internal-developer-platform. A plain init stays fast and installs nothing a person did not ask for; the trade-off is one more flag to see something working. This reverses the first decision (order 20261026-0006), which made internal-developer-platform the default.

The name is "Profile", with no word from the sea: it says what it is to a person who meets it for the first time.

docs.title: Origin
docs.text:
All decided by the owner: on 2026-10-25 (order 20261025-2359, which supersedes order 20261025-2352) and on 2026-10-26 (orders 20261026-0003, 20261026-0006, 20261026-0035 for the environment reef, and 20261026-0640 for the default core and the decisions below).

Decided on 2026-10-26 (order 20261026-0640), on the open points of order 20261026-0508:

  • The stand-in stays: keycloak's requirements on the secrets and release reefs are written in the CLI's table of the local Nereids until each local Nereid has its own image label.
  • A cloud target refuses --profile and installs Azure Key Vault as its secrets Nereid; accepted until the issue that joins profiles and targets.
  • #414 (the secrets Reef missing after nereus init in one CI run) stays open until its cause is found, with no rush.
  • Core holds the User kind (ADR 0006): confirmed.
  • Every ADR stays Proposed until the profile internal-developer-platform runs complete, with its five reefs. The orders are in Drive #pontos/beach/.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Istio installation profiles (istio.io, "Installation Configuration Profiles"): istioctl install --set profile=<name> picks a set of components. default, demo, minimal, remote, empty, preview and ambient are mostly named by size or stage. Nereus takes the empty base and the idea of one command that installs a known set, and names its profiles by purpose instead.
  • Debian tasksel (wiki.debian.org/tasksel): during installation, a person picks a task ("web server", a desktop), and tasksel installs the packages for it. A Nereus profile is the same shape: a task named by purpose, made of pieces that also install one by one.
  • Helm umbrella charts (helm.sh, "Complex Charts with Many Dependencies"): one chart that lists its subcharts as dependencies. A profile differs in two ways: it lists pieces that each keep their own commands, and it leaves the order to the Nereids' requirements.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• nereus init installs core, then the profile through the same code paths as nereus reef apply, nereus nereid apply and nereus mandate create. Built in #420: --profile empty (now core, the default since #424) and --profile internal-developer-platform, whose keycloak Nereid requires the secrets reef, so the secrets reef comes as that requirement (order 20261026-0508); ADR 0003 is rewritten with it. The profiles are a table in the CLI (cli/src/nereus/profiles.py) until the Profile kind exists.
  • --target azure (ADR 0003) still decides the first secrets Nereid (Azure Key Vault). The issue that builds --profile settles how the profile's secrets entry follows the target.
  • The policy reef and the kyverno Nereid do not exist yet. The profile installs the other reefs of its list: authorization with openfga and its default Mandate openfga (#1655, spec 0011), which turns the check on in the Nereus API, and environment with vcluster. The teams reef, which no Nereid serves, is applied by a lane of its own before openfga, which reads its Teams and Members. The environment reef is the first PoC's environment API group (an environment was a virtual cluster); an azure-aks Nereid may come later as its interchangeable alternative, decided when the first real environments are provisioned.
  • The order comes from the Nereids. A Nereid's image declares what it requires (core.getnereus.dev/requires): keycloak's must name the secrets reef for the vault to come first. Every local Nereid's Dockerfile declares it since #1368, which retired the requires column of the CLI's table that stood in for it.
  • The default init stays fast, since it installs core alone; the time SLO of init (spec 0004) is checked in CI on that path, and the profile's own time shows in nereus profile apply.
  • nereus profile apply <name> layers a profile on core (#425), idempotent as kubectl apply: the demo is nereus init, then nereus profile apply internal-developer-platform, and nereus init --profile <name> is the shortcut for both. nereus profile list and nereus profile describe <name> show the built-in profiles; nereus profile create (custom profiles) is parked.
  • The profile is a setting of init (#426): spec.profile in init.yaml, besides --profile; the flag wins over the file.
  • The Profile kind joins core (ADR 0009). First the CLI ships the profiles and runs them. Later the applied Profile becomes an object in the cluster.
  • Later, better than good enough:
  • The Profile is applied as a resource in the cluster, and nereus status shows the drift between what the profile asks for and what runs. The PoC's hand-written "Divergences" list becomes a CI check.
  • An engine-boundary test proves that a reef outside the platform domain can be added without touching core.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-10-30): the tenancy reef counts as part of core
docs.text:
Every nereus init applies the tenancy reef, the default core profile included, and a cloud target too (#646, #651). This does not change the decision above: core is still only the engine, and a profile still lists the reefs, Nereids and Mandates a person chooses. The tenancy reef counts as part of core, not as a choice of a profile, for three reasons:

  • The API keeps the tree, as it keeps the core kinds (ADR 0015, tenancy: a tenancy reef whose kinds come from each instance, with one fixed shape): the reef has no Nereid, no Mandate and no secret, so applying it installs no capability a person did not ask for.
  • Whatever says whose a thing is points to it: the catalog, an Environment, a resource Instance and a Mandate's match name an owner in the tenancy group, so every installation needs the tree before its first reef with an owner.
  • It is still a reef, not more kinds in core.getnereus.dev: each instance applies its own kinds from its reefs/tenancy/, and a tenancy Nereid may come later to sync the tree with another system; ADR 0015 says why tenancy is not in core.

So "core installs no other reef" reads: no other reef that a Nereid looks after. nereus status shows the tenancy reef Ready with no Nereid (#651), and nereus profile describe names it under every profile.

Origin: the open points of #646 (the tenancy reef's CRDs and admission), recorded in #651 by an agent on 2026-10-30; pending the owner's review, as the whole ADR.

Proposed 2026-10-26 from orders 20261025-2359, 20261026-0003 and 20261026-0006; the environment reef added from order 20261026-0035; the default core from order 20261026-0640; keycloak requires the release reef, which releases Keycloak, from order 20261026-0840 (step 2). Raw data in Drive #pontos/beach/. Amended 2026-10-30 from #651: the tenancy reef counts as part of core.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11-05): the order lives in thetis, the installer Nereid
docs.text:
A profile installed from the chart nereus runs in the cluster, in thetis' reconcile (#1053, parent #1049). The chart's value profile writes the Profile named nereus (spec.profile), and thetis, a Nereid that comes up with core, runs the profile's steps: the same profiles.steps that nereus init --profile runs, from the CLI's own package in its image. The order still comes from each Nereid's requirements, never from the profile. It now lives in that reconcile, not in init and not in Helm hooks.

  • Why a Nereid: each Nereid's step resolves its image by digest for the nodes' platform, reads the image's labels, creates its Secrets, and waits for it to report Ready. Helm cannot do that at run time, and its hooks order only the creation of objects and stay out of the release.
  • The status shows each step (Done, Waiting with why, Pending) and a Ready condition; a Nereid whose required reef has no Ready Nereid waits and names it.
  • thetis' rights are wide: it writes CRDs, admission policies, Deployments, Secrets and each Nereid's RBAC, so its ClusterRole holds bind and escalate.
  • The Profile is the embryo of the Operator of #77 (the Platform resource): one description of the platform, kept reconciled after the install.
  • The first profile thetis installs is secrets, the secrets reef with openbao alone; #1054 brings internal-developer-platform.
  • nereus init --profile runs no step of the profile (#1055): it passes the profile to the chart nereus as a value, then waits for the profile's Nereids and the Profile to be Ready, printing each Nereid's time. nereus profile apply still runs the same steps from a laptop.

Origin: decided by the owner on 2026-11-05, in #1049 and #1053.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11-08): the Profile wins
docs.text:
thetis keeps a Profile's Nereids installed, so a Nereid leaves the platform through the Profile, never by a delete by hand (#1231, from #1056). thetis runs the Profile's steps every 30 s and puts back a Nereid of the profile deleted by hand; that stays, as with Flux.

  • spec.exclude lists the Nereids of the profile a person left out: thetis does not install them and deletes them, the last installed first, as nereus nereid delete does. Leaving out a Nereid that a kept one requires is refused, naming it.
  • nereus profile apply <profile> --without <nereid> writes that list, repeated for each Nereid; the list given replaces the one the Profile holds, as apply does. It waits until thetis reconciled it. The profile itself stays the chart's value.
  • nereus nereid delete refuses a Nereid the Profile holds, --force or not, naming the Profile and the profile apply line that leaves it out.

Origin: decided by the owner on 2026-11-08, in #1231.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11-11): a profile is one YAML file the chart renders into the Profile's spec
docs.text:
Status of this amendment: Proposed.

A profile is one YAML file, keyed by reef, that the chart nereus ships and renders into the spec of the single Profile named nereus; thetis installs what that spec describes (#1363). It replaces the sketch of the Decision above, which named openfga and kyverno, which no profile installs:

profile: secrets
reefs:
  - name: secrets
    nereids:
      - name: openbao
        # Optional: with none, <registry>/<nereid>-controller:<chart version>, the convention (#1364).
        image: {repository: ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/openbao-controller, tag: 0.1.0, digest: "sha256:..."}
    mandates:
      - {name: default, nereid: openbao, default: true}
  • The files live at cli/src/nereus/charts/nereus/profiles/<name>.yaml, outside templates/. The chart renders the one its value profile names under spec: with .Files.Get, and fails on a name with no file. There is still one Profile, named nereus, and spec.profile stays the name; spec.exclude is unchanged.
  • A Nereid serving a second reef is repeated there by name, without its image. A Mandate's params are never secret, as the Decision says of a profile.
  • thetis reconciles the object's spec, what this installation asked for; the CLI (profile apply, describe, list, init) reads the files. One parser, profiles.py: load(name) reads a file, from_spec(spec) reads an object, both into one dataclass that steps() takes.
  • spec.reefs is required (#1370): thetis, nereus status and nereus nereid delete read the spec alone, never the file of its name; a spec with no reefs is refused (the CRD, and thetis in the Profile's status).
  • One profile per installation: profiles are alternatives, not layers; composing them waits for a marketplace.
  • The order is never in the file: it comes from what each Nereid requires, its image's label core.getnereus.dev/requires, read from the registry; the label wins (#1368). With no registry answering (nereus profile describe or --dry-run with the network off), the offline list cli/src/nereus/requires.yaml stands in: make chart writes it from the labels of controllers/*/Dockerfile, and a test fails when a Dockerfile that names a Nereid lacks the label or when the list differs from the labels.
  • An image the profile pins runs as pinned; the local registry (NEREUS_NEREIDS_REGISTRY, NEREUS_NEREIDS_TAG) rewrites its repository prefix and its tag, and drops its digest only when it names another registry or another tag than the pinned ones (#1403). A release pins tag and digest (#1369). Replaced on 2026-11-12, below: nothing rewrites an image.
  • Reef contract versions stay in contracts.pinned; the ClusterRole stays generated by make chart.

The steps: the profile secrets first, as a walking skeleton, with spec.reefs optional and the other profiles falling back to their list in the CLI (#1365); internal-developer-platform and core as files, the entrance becoming ingress with its versions in the profile (#1366); Mandates from the file (#1367); the order from the image label (#1368); tag and digest pinned by a release (#1369); spec.reefs required (#1370).

Prior art: Istio's manifests/profiles/*.yaml (one file per profile, rendered by the installer), Flux's OCIRepository.ref (a tag for people, a digest for the machine), Crossplane's Configuration lock.

Origin: decided by the owner on 2026-11-11, in #1363.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11-12): the Profile names every image, and thetis installs it as written
docs.text:
The list of images is a parameter of what thetis is asked to install: the Profile (#1425). The chart writes every Nereid's image into the Profile's spec, and thetis installs each one as written: no convention and no registry override inside thetis.

  • The convention moves to the chart (#1364): for a Nereid the profile file leaves without image:, the template writes the one the profile pins for it in another reef, else <nereids.registry>/<nereid>-controller:<nereids.tag>; nereids.tag defaults to the chart's version. profiles.filled is the same rule in Python, and a test holds both equal.
  • Where the images come from is the installer's choice, the chart's values nereids.registry (default ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus) and nereids.tag. The CLI's init passes the local registry, or the one NEREUS_NEREIDS_REGISTRY names, for a cluster that cannot reach the local one, such as Nereus inside an Environment.
  • thetis refuses a spec with a Nereid and no image in the Profile's status: that spec was not rendered by this chart. NEREUS_NEREIDS_REGISTRY and NEREUS_NEREIDS_TAG leave thetis' Deployment; LOCAL_REGISTRY stays, the local registry's address from a Pod, so thetis reads an image's labels there.
  • This replaces the rewrite of #1363 and #1403: a pinned digest is never dropped, and a local build is named by the values the chart is given, not by thetis' environment.

Origin: decided by the owner on 2026-11-12, in #1425, after #1406's recorded run found that thetis inside an Environment cannot reach the local registry.

docs.title: 0015. Tenancy: a tenancy reef whose kinds come from each instance, with one fixed shape
docs.text:
In short

Tenancy is a reef whose kinds come from each instance, with one fixed shape: every kind is a tree node with an optional parent, and one kind is the boundary. Status: Proposed (2026-10-30, rewritten 2026-11-12, amended 2026-11-15).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-30, rewritten 2026-11-12, amended 2026-11-15)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Nereus is born multi-tenant (#21, Organization and nested Projects): the tenancy model is part of the product, not something added later. On 2026-10-29 the owner settled its levels: an Organization is the top level of separation, the boundary of people, permissions and isolation; a Project always sits under an Organization, and a Project may sit under another Project. Nested Projects take the place of Backstage's Domain and subdomain, and a leaf Project plays the part of Backstage's System, so there is no System kind.

The catalog reef (#559, the catalog reef: Workload, Package and their types) and the resource reefs (#560, the resource reefs and how a Mandate picks their Nereid) both need to say whose a thing is, and that question could not be answered until two others were: whether a Project is a Kubernetes namespace, and where the tenancy kinds live.

A namespace does not fit. A namespace exists once per cluster and does not nest. A Project nests (nereus holds triton), and the same Project runs in several environments: the Triton of nereus (the kept k3d cluster) and the Triton of a pr-<n> vcluster are one Project in two namespaces, on two clusters. Hierarchical namespaces would give the nesting but not the second cluster, and the project that provided them is archived.

The kinds differ from one instance to another. This instance of Nereus is organised as Organizations and Projects. A company with its own structure (departments and squads, say) may run its own instance of Nereus with its own tenancy kinds; what the platform must not do is force one vocabulary on every company, nor let the catalog break when the vocabulary changes. A reef is a contract, an API group with its kinds (ADR 0002, ADR 0010), and ADR 0011 says an Instance's fields are common to every Nereid of the reef. If the kinds were free, the catalog would have to reference any kind ({apiVersion, kind, name}), and catalog check would no longer know what a parent or a boundary is: the fixed thing has to be the shape of a kind, not its name.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Tenancy is a reef, tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, and its kinds come from each instance. The group is fixed; its CRDs are applied from the instance's reefs/tenancy/ as any reef is (ADR 0010). This instance applies Organization and Project; another instance may apply its own kinds, and its catalog still works, because the contract is the shape of every kind of the group, not the kind names:

  • Every kind of the group is a node with an optional spec.parent: {kind, name}; a node with no parent is a root. The kind of a parent is one of the group's own kinds.
  • One CRD of the group carries the annotation tenancy.getnereus.dev/boundary: "true": the kind that isolates (people, billing, isolation), as core.getnereus.dev/default-kind marks a reef's default kind (ADR 0013, command conventions). Here it is Organization.
  • Whatever points to the tree names owner: {kind, name} inside the group, never an apiVersion: the catalog's Workloads and Packages, an Environment of the environment reef, a Mandate's match. The field replaces the spec.project of the first proposal.
  • catalog check climbs spec.parent to the root without knowing the kinds: it resolves every owner, refuses a cycle or a parent that does not exist, and finds the boundary by the annotation.

On this instance:

# reefs/tenancy/: the kinds of this instance, applied with nereus reef apply
# tenancy/organizations/getnereus.yaml: the boundary
apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Organization
metadata:
  name: getnereus

# tenancy/projects/nereus.yaml: the monorepo, under the Organization
apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Project
metadata:
  name: nereus
spec:
  parent: {kind: Organization, name: getnereus}
  repository: https://github.com/getnereus/nereus

# tenancy/projects/triton.yaml: a Project under another Project
apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Project
metadata:
  name: triton
spec:
  parent: {kind: Project, name: nereus}

# catalog/workloads/triton.yaml: the catalog points to the tree by kind and name
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Workload
metadata:
  name: triton
spec:
  owner: {kind: Project, name: triton}

Another instance, with its own kinds (a placeholder company, acme.example.com), keeps the same shape and the same catalog field:

# that instance's reefs/tenancy/ applies Department (boundary) and Squad
apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Squad
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  parent: {kind: Department, name: platform-engineering}

# its catalog, the same field
spec:
  owner: {kind: Squad, name: payments}

The commands follow ADR 0013: nereus tenancy <kind> <verb> <name>, built from the reef's schema, as the release reef's are; the output names the object by its full path, parents before children; nereus reef apply lists the kinds the reef created (owner, 2026-10-30).

# Apply the tenancy reef of this instance
$ nereus reef apply tenancy --from-file reefs/tenancy/
core/reefs/tenancy created (tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1: organizations, projects)

# The boundary
$ nereus tenancy organization create getnereus
tenancy/organizations/getnereus created

# A Project under the Organization
$ nereus tenancy project create nereus \
    --parent organization/getnereus \
    --repository https://github.com/getnereus/nereus
tenancy/organizations/getnereus/projects/nereus created

# A Project under another Project
$ nereus tenancy project create triton \
    --parent project/nereus
tenancy/organizations/getnereus/projects/nereus/projects/triton created

Next steps:

  nereus catalog apply --from-file catalog/

A Project is not a namespace. A Project is an object of the platform, cluster-scoped, with its parent in spec; the namespace is only where a Project runs, one per environment (triton on nereus, the kept k3d cluster, triton again on the pr-<n> vcluster). The API projects who may act on a Project into the namespaces where it runs; it has to stand in front of the reefs in any case (ADR 0010, open question on the Platform API).

The permissions are relations, in the authorization reef. The tenancy reef holds the tree; who may do what on it is the authorization reef's job, with its openfga Nereid (ADR 0027), permission flowing down the tree and never up. One OpenFGA type, node, serves every tenancy kind (owner, 2026-11-15, spec 0011, decision 11): the kinds come from each instance, and the model is fixed, versioned with the Nereid, so it cannot name them. A node's id is its kind in lowercase, a slash and its name (node:project/triton), and its parent is another node or, for a root, the one instance. A new tenancy kind on another instance changes no model, only tuples.

type node
  relations
    define parent: [instance, node]
    define granted: [grant#subject with rule_matches]
    define can: granted or can from parent

The first sketch of this ADR had one OpenFGA type per tenancy kind, with an instance writing its own model over its own kinds; it was dropped because a model fixed with the Nereid could not follow each instance's kinds.

The boundary kind carries domains and requireMandate (owner, 2026-11-10, #1311). Both are optional fields of the kind annotated boundary, whatever its name; here, Organization. The authentication reef reads them (ADR 0006): a login by e-mail finds the Organization by the address's domain, and the Organization's Mandate by match (ADR 0017).

apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Organization
metadata:
  name: acme
spec:
  domains: [example.com]
  requireMandate: true
  • domains: the e-mail domains of the Organization. A domain counts only once verified: the Organization's admin publishes a DNS TXT record the API gives, and the API checks it. Until then the domain is Unverified in status and takes no part in the login's discovery or in requireMandate.
  • requireMandate: true: an e-mail of the verified domains enters only with a token of the Mandate that matches the Organization. The API refuses the field while no authentication Mandate matches the Organization, so nobody is locked out.
  • A team is a match on Projects. The tenancy has Organization and Project, no Team kind: a Mandate for "one or more teams" matches their Projects, until the tenancy gets teams.

The first version has no tenancy Nereid: the API keeps the tree, as it keeps the core kinds. A Nereid comes when the tree is synced from or to another system (Keycloak groups, a human-resources system); OpenFGA's tuples are written from the tree by the authorization reef's openfga Nereid (ADR 0027). That work is what makes tenancy a reef rather than two more kinds in core: core is the mechanism (Reef, Nereid, Mandate) and never has a Nereid.

Sharing across Projects or Organizations goes by publishing or by access, never by a permission climbing the tree. A Project runs its own copy from a published Package (a chart in an OCI registry, installed through the release reef, as Keycloak is today), or talks to the running thing through its audience (Triton, for agents and people of any Project); the registry decides who pulls.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• GitLab groups and subgroups (docs.gitlab.com): one kind of node nests "up to 20 levels" (five or fewer recommended), and a member's permissions are "inherited from the group into all subgroups"; the Project that nests and the permission flowing down take that shape.
  • Google Cloud's resource hierarchy (docs.cloud.google.com): an organization at the root, folders that "can contain projects and other folders", and "IAM roles granted on a folder resource are inherited by all project and folder resources in that folder"; the Organization as boundary and the nested node come from here too.
  • Gateway API's ParentReference (shared_types.go): "identifies an API object (usually a Gateway) that can be considered a parent of this resource (usually a route)", with group, kind and name, used by every route kind; owner: {kind, name} is that reference with the group fixed.
  • Kubernetes namespaces (kubernetes.io): "Namespaces cannot be nested inside one another and each Kubernetes resource can only be in one namespace"; the reason a Project is not a namespace.
  • Hierarchical Namespace Controller (github.com/kubernetes-sigs/hierarchical-namespaces): "hierarchical policies and delegated creation to Kubernetes namespaces"; the alternative weighed and dropped, nesting inside one cluster only, with the repository archived in April 2025.
  • OpenFGA and Google's Zanzibar (openfga.dev): an authorization model "combines one or more type definitions", each listing its relations, and a relationship tuple is "a user, relation, and object"; its model syntax "closely follows the original syntax in the" Zanzibar paper. The relations over the tree are written in that model.
  • GitHub's verified domains (Verifying or approving a domain for your organization): the owner of an organization proves a domain by following "the instructions under 'Add a DNS TXT record' to create a DNS TXT record with your domain hosting service"; the way an Organization's domains are verified.
  • Backstage's Domain, System and Component are the model the owner reacted to (#21): nested Projects replace Domain and subdomain, and a leaf Project plays System's part; the project's own observation.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• spec.project becomes owner: {kind, name} in everything that points to the tree: the catalog's Workloads and Packages (#559), an Environment, a resource Instance and a Mandate's match (#560). The CLI gets a current owner in its config so --owner is optional when several things are created for the same Project (owner's ask, #559).
  • A new reef that needs to say whose a thing is reuses the field and the climb to the root; none of them learns a kind name.
  • Each instance owns its reefs/tenancy/; the kinds of this instance (Organization, Project) are the reference ones, shipped with nereus init, and the first entries are Nereus itself: Organization getnereus, Project nereus, and core, nereids, triton and docs under it.
  • Permissions are not free from Kubernetes RBAC: the API projects them into the namespaces where a Project runs, and the authorization reef holds the relations.
  • The output of nereus reef apply grows a list of the kinds it created, for every reef.
  • The boundary kind's shape grows two optional fields, domains and requireMandate; #1314 (the API accepts several issuers) builds requireMandate, and #1315 (identifier-first login) builds domains and their verification, deciding the TXT record's name and the status fields.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• A depth limit: a limit (four levels, for example) until a case asks for more, as #21 (Organization and nested Projects) suggested; not decided.
  • How permissions are projected from a Project into the namespaces where it runs, per environment, and what the API does when a Project runs on a cluster it does not own.
  • The tenancy Nereid: when the tree is synced with Keycloak groups or a human-resources system, which side is the source, and what status it writes on each node. OpenFGA's tuples are settled (ADR 0027): the tree is the source, and the authorization reef's openfga Nereid reads it, so tenancy still needs no Nereid of its own for them.
  • The Organization of nereus init: where the first Organization and Project come from on a fresh cluster (#21's "what the first slice becomes").
  • Two Organizations that claim one domain. Recommendation for #1315: the first to verify it holds it, and the second is refused.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-10-29 (the levels, #21) and 2026-10-30 (a Project is not a namespace; a tenancy reef with kinds per instance and one fixed shape), in a design session with a second opinion and research by subagents; raw data in Drive #pontos/beach/opinions/2026-10-30/ (the session brief, the proposal as YAML, the opinions and research) and #pontos/raw/2026-10-30/.

Rewritten 2026-11-12 from the owner's decisions of 2026-11-10 (#1311: an Organization's domains and requireMandate, teams as a match on Projects) and of 2026-11-12 (a domain is verified by a DNS TXT record); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-10/ and #pontos/raw/2026-11-12/.

Amended 2026-11-15 from the owner's decisions refining #897 into spec 0011 (decision 11: one OpenFGA type, node, for every tenancy kind; ADR 0027); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-15/.

docs.title: 0016. The catalog reef: Workload and Package, three characteristics, configurable types
docs.text:
In short

A catalog reef holds two kinds split by lifecycle, Workload for what runs and Package for what is published, with three characteristics and configurable types. Status: Proposed (2026-10-30, rewritten 2026-11-03).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-30, rewritten 2026-11-03)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
While the wasp-idp deck's "Developer Control Plane" part was ported as a Nereus deck (#541, the Developer Control Plane deck, PR #557), its golden-path slide showed nereus catalog create hello-api --system greeter --template python-service, a command with no counterpart in the CLI design (docs/agent/cli.md). The owner reacted to the model behind it, Backstage's: a Component (which the owner never knew the meaning of), under a System, under a Domain, with its type as a free string. The design session of 2026-10-29 and 2026-10-30 turned that reaction into three refinements: the catalog's kinds (#559, the catalog reef: Workload, Package and their types), the tenancy model (#21, Organization and nested Projects, ADR 0015) and the resource reefs (#560, the resource reefs and how a Mandate picks their Nereid, ADR 0017).

The diagnosis that held through the session: Backstage classifies software for a portal, to look at; Nereus classifies it for a control plane, to act on. A type says what shape a thing has; a platform needs to know what it must do for the thing, and only that can be checked by a script. The owner's provocation, that classifying software by Backstage's words may be looking at the problem from an older time, was tested against the ways software is delivered in 2026 (micro-frontends, a BFF, edge sites, serverless functions, agents, MCP servers, inference endpoints, workers of a workflow engine, operators): every one of them is something that runs, something that is published, or both from one repository, and a type alone fits few of them without a qualifier.

The owner asked for the model to be proved on Nereus itself, dogfooding and inception, never on a generic example: the Nereids openbao, keycloak and flux, Triton, the CLI, the images, the docs site, the kept k3d cluster. The brief, the opinions and the research behind this ADR are private raw data on the owner's Drive.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A catalog reef, catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, with two kinds split by lifecycle: Workload for what runs and Package for what is published. There is no Component, no System (a leaf Project of the tenancy tree plays that part, ADR 0015) and no API or Resource kind: an API is a Workload with an audience, and a resource is an Instance of its own reef (ADR 0017), which the catalog reads and never writes. A thing that runs and is published, such as the CLI's repository that is also a Package, is two entries.

A Workload has three characteristics, each the answer to one question, as plain fields of spec:

Field The question Values runs does it stay up, or run until it completes? always, once trigger what makes it work? a list of event (something changed: the cluster, a queue, a file), request (someone asks), schedule audience who talks to it? a list of programs, people, agents; [] means nobody

The platform reads only these three. They are what the reefs and catalog check act on, and they stay fixed: adding one is a change to this ADR. In OIDC an aud claim names who a token is for, another meaning of the word; the catalog's audience says who talks to a Workload.

Types are configurable objects; the characteristics are not. A WorkloadType is a name plus the answers it fills in for runs and trigger, as a StorageClass is a name plus the parameters its provisioner takes: the list of types changes with a file, never with an ADR, and the platform never reads a type's name. A Workload names its type and may override runs or trigger when the type does not fit. audience is required on every Workload and never comes from a type: both service Workloads of Nereus (Triton, for agents and people; the Keycloak server, for people, programs and agents) would override any default, so a default would be wrong more often than right, and "who is this for?" is the one question no type can answer.

The initial WorkloadTypes, in catalog/workload-types/:

Type What it is runs trigger controller watches the API and acts when something changes (every Nereid) always event service stays up and answers requests (an HTTP or gRPC API, a BFF) always request web-app an application that builds the page on each request, used by people always request static-site files, served as they are always request worker stays up consuming a queue or a topic, no port always event job runs to completion on a schedule once schedule function runs to completion on each call and scales to zero, as Knative Serving does once request, event

static-site and web-app share the same answers: the name is for people and for search (nereus catalog list --type static-site), the characteristics are for the platform; site and web were dropped as names that do not explain themselves. A "files only" characteristic comes when the edge reef (#470, publishing a reef's endpoint at a hostname) needs it. function stays in the set with no function in Nereus yet: it costs one file. The docs site is a static-site; the portal, later, a web-app.

A Nereid and the tool it runs are two entries. The keycloak Nereid is a controller with audience: []: nobody talks to it; the CLI writes an object to the API and the Nereid acts. The Keycloak server is the tool the Nereid runs: people log in on it, the CLI exchanges tokens with it, the claude.ai connector authorizes agents through it. The server reaches the catalog as an Instance of the authentication reef, which the catalog only reads; nobody writes a catalog file for it.
