A Package has a type, a registry and an audience. type comes from configurable PackageTypes (cli, library, image, chart, reef, module); the packaging format follows from the registry and is not a field. registry says where it is published, with the same values as ADR 0010's Repository types where they overlap (git, oci, http) plus pypi, npm and maven. A PackageType holds only spec.registries, the registries it allows, the minimum catalog check needs to refuse a registry the type does not take; more fields come when a real Package asks for them. A reef that is only YAML files today is a Package with type: reef and registry: git: the same files are on GitHub for anyone, and when the reef ships as an OCI package only registry and the name change. The owner's cut of what is published by consumer (Package for programs, App for people) fails on Nereus's first published thing, the CLI, which is both; App waits.

source has repository, ref and path. ref is structured as Flux's GitRepository.spec.ref (the owner's choice over one string): branch, tag, semver, name (a full Git reference, such as refs/pull/420/head) or commit, with Flux's precedence, commit over name over semver over tag over branch, and commit with branch meaning the commit must be on that branch. Workloads use ref: {branch: main}; a published Package names its tag or a semver range. The catalog Nereid writes the resolved commit in status.source.commit.

Every entry names its owner in the tenancy tree (ADR 0015) as owner: {kind, name}, never a namespace and never an apiVersion.

A Workload says nothing about where it is delivered. One Workload runs in several Environments, so a delivery's namespace and running image live in the Delivery's status (ADR 0020, the delivery reef). runtime is for what runs outside a Delivery, and runtime.namespace is allowed only with runtime.kind: Deployment, which cannot be found without it, as Triton today.

A Workload may name its chart: spec.chart: {package: <name>} references a Package of type: chart, with no new kind. With no spec.chart, the delivery reef uses the curated chart app-template.

The first entries are Nereus itself, one file each in a catalog/ folder at the repository's root:

# catalog/workloads/triton.yaml: the room and the MCP door in one Pod, one entry until
# #508 (the bridge that splits Triton's room from the door)
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Workload
metadata:
  name: triton
spec:
  owner: {kind: Project, name: triton}
  type: service                 # runs: always, trigger: [request]
  audience: [agents, people]    # always written here, never from the type
  source:
    repository: https://github.com/getnereus/nereus
    ref: {branch: main}
    path: controllers/triton/
  runtime:
    kind: Deployment
    namespace: triton
    name: triton

# catalog/workloads/openbao.yaml: the controller of the secrets reef; nobody talks to it
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Workload
metadata:
  name: openbao
spec:
  owner: {kind: Project, name: nereids}
  type: controller              # runs: always, trigger: [event]
  audience: []
  source:
    repository: https://github.com/getnereus/nereus
    ref: {branch: main}
    path: controllers/openbao/
  runtime:
    kind: Nereid
    name: openbao

# catalog/packages/nereus.yaml: the CLI, installed by people and pulled by CI
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Package
metadata:
  name: nereus
spec:
  owner: {kind: Project, name: core}
  type: cli
  registry: pypi
  name: nereus
  audience: [people, programs]
  source:
    repository: https://github.com/getnereus/nereus
    ref: {branch: main}         # no tag yet; a published version names its tag
    path: cli/

# catalog/packages/openbao-image.yaml: the image of the openbao Nereid, one image per Nereid (#611)
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Package
metadata:
  name: openbao-image
spec:
  owner: {kind: Project, name: nereids}
  type: image
  registry: oci
  name: localhost:5111/openbao-controller
  audience: [programs]
  source:
    repository: https://github.com/getnereus/nereus
    ref: {branch: main}
    path: controllers/openbao/

# catalog/workload-types/service.yaml
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: WorkloadType
metadata:
  name: service
spec:
  runs: always
  trigger: [request]

# catalog/package-types/cli.yaml
apiVersion: catalog.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: PackageType
metadata:
  name: cli
spec:
  registries: [pypi, npm, oci]

The commands follow ADR 0013 (command conventions): nereus catalog <kind> <verb> <name>, kinds singular, workload the reef's default kind; apply from files, create from flags, list --type, get, delete, and check. Output lines name the object by its full path with the owner and the type in a parenthesis:

# Register what the repository says it has
$ nereus catalog apply --from-file catalog/
catalog/workloads/triton created (owner: Project/triton, type: service)
catalog/workloads/openbao created (owner: Project/nereids, type: controller)
catalog/packages/nereus created (owner: Project/core, type: cli, registry: pypi)
catalog/packages/openbao-image created (owner: Project/nereids, type: image, registry: oci)

Next steps:

  nereus catalog check

# Search by type
$ nereus catalog list --type static-site
WORKLOAD  OWNER         TYPE         AUDIENCE  DELIVERIES  STATUS
docs      Project/docs  static-site  people    0           Ready

The catalog lists what it has, one row per Workload, and DELIVERIES counts the Workload's Deliveries, read from the delivery reef and never written. What was deployed, one row per Workload and Environment pair, is nereus delivery list (ADR 0020).

nereus catalog check is deterministic: it joins each entry to the tenancy tree, the types, the registries, and the reefs and Mandates that fulfil it. It fails on a contradiction, when the file says something impossible (a registry the type does not allow, an owner that does not exist), and only points at a gap, when the catalog tells the truth and the platform cannot fulfil it yet, each gap with its issue, ! instead of ✗. On Nereus today it finds three gaps and no contradiction, and a PR passes with gaps:

$ make catalog-check
✓ tenancy: 1 organization, 5 projects, every owner resolves
✓ types: every workload type and package type resolves, every registry allowed
! catalog/workloads/triton: audience people, agents, no edge reef (#470)
! catalog/workloads/triton: uses nats, no messaging reef (#576)
! catalog/packages/nereus: not found on pypi
0 contradictions, 3 gaps

make catalog-check joins the local checks before a PR that touches the catalog or the tenancy (docs/agent/rules.md), since CI is off.

Registering an existing thing is apply; a template comes before the catalog. The catalog entry is a file in the repository and the file is the truth, so Triton, which already exists, is imported with nereus catalog apply --from-file catalog/. A template writes files into a folder, new or existing, including the new catalog/workloads/<name>.yaml, and the same apply registers the new entry and leaves Triton unchanged. Creating the repository is #279 (the repository reef). --template leaves the catalog's create. The golden-path slide of #541 (the Developer Control Plane deck) shows that order, the template first (the next Nereid of the backlog, edge-cloudflare of #470, in place of hello-api) and catalog apply second. create with flags stays for writing the file (--dry-run --output yaml).

Template is a kind of the catalog, and nereus template is a shortcut of nereus catalog template (ADR 0013); this replaces the owner's decision of 2026-10-30 that templates are a reef of their own. The verb is render, with Copier: create makes the Template object and apply takes only files. There is no type field in the first slice, since Copier treats every template the same.

# Write a template's files, then register what they say
$ nereus template render python-service \
    --path ./hello \
    --param name=hello
✓ catalog/templates/python-service rendered at ./hello

Next steps:

  nereus catalog apply --from-file ./hello/catalog/

A current owner in the CLI's config (a proposal, owner's ask): a command sets the current Project, and other repeated references, so --owner becomes optional when several resources are created for the same service or Project, as kubectl config set-context --current --namespace and gcloud config set project do; the flag wins over the config, and the output line names the owner used. The shape, nereus config set owner project/triton, goes into docs/agent/cli.md with the catalog's commands.

The first slice, three pull requests (owner, 2026-11-03, #574): the kinds, the commands and six entries, Workloads triton, openbao, keycloak and flux, Packages nereus and openbao-image (#902); catalog check and make catalog-check (#903); one catalog Nereid, in an image of its own as every Nereid since #611, writing status: a Workload's readiness, a Package's presence in its registry, the resolved commit of a source (#904).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Open Application Model, workload types (oam-dev/spec, 4.workload_types.md): a workload type carries characteristics as labels, replicable, daemonized ("if the workload exits, this is considered a fault, and the system must fix it"), exposed ("have a service endpoint with a stable name for network traffic") and podspecable; the catalog's runs and audience are those two characteristics with the owner's words, and trigger is the project's own addition. In OAM a "trait" is an operational add-on, which is why the catalog says characteristics, as plain fields.
  • Backstage's system model (backstage.io, System model): "A component is a piece of software, for example a mobile feature, web site, backend service or data pipeline", with API, Resource, System and Domain around it; the catalog takes the idea of a repository-owned entity and replaces Component with the lifecycle split and the characteristics, System and Domain with the tenancy tree (ADR 0015), and Resource with the resource reefs' own Instances (ADR 0017).
  • Copier (copier.readthedocs.io): "A library and CLI app for rendering project templates", whose goals include bringing existing projects up to date as a template changes; the engine behind nereus template render.
  • Kubernetes storage classes (StorageClass): "a way for administrators to describe the classes of storage they offer", a name plus a provisioner and parameters, created by administrators; a WorkloadType and a PackageType are configurable the same way, a name plus the answers it fills in, with the platform reading only the answers.
  • Knative Serving (knative.dev, Serving): revisions "automatically scaled up and down according to incoming traffic", down to zero; the function type takes that shape, runs: once on each request or event.
  • Flux's GitRepository (fluxcd.io, GitRepository): spec.ref with branch, tag, semver, name and commit, "with latter listed fields taking precedence over earlier ones"; source.ref takes the same fields and precedence.
  • kubectl's verbs and kubectl config set-context (Kubernetes, Managing Kubernetes objects): apply from files as the way to register what a repository declares (ADR 0013), and a current context that spares a repeated flag, the model of the current owner in the CLI's config.

The claim that types alone strain on Nereus's own entries (a Nereid is a worker only by elimination, the docs site needs "files only" on day one, Triton is both a service and the room's operator) is the project's own observation, from modelling the catalog on the repository and the live cluster.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The platform acts on three answers it can check, never on a type's name: a new kind of software is a new WorkloadType file, not a change to the reef, and catalog check stays deterministic.
  • Every Workload says who talks to it; catalog check can join audience to the edge and authentication reefs and say what is exposed with nothing publishing it, which is Triton today (#470).
  • The catalog never writes a Nereid's tool: the Keycloak server, a database or a topic reach it as Instances of their reefs; one writer per field holds (ADR 0005), the repository's file writes spec, the catalog Nereid writes status.
  • The golden path is two commands of one reef, a template that writes files and catalog apply that registers; the deck of #541 (the Developer Control Plane deck) and docs/agent/cli.md adopt the catalog's commands, kinds singular, --owner and the structured ref.
  • catalog check becomes a local check before a PR, and its three gaps of today are the next work: #470 (publishing a reef's endpoint at a hostname), #576 (the messaging reef), publishing the CLI on PyPI.
  • The proposal on the Drive used spec.project, site, web and a one-string ref; this ADR replaces them with owner, static-site, web-app and the structured ref.

docs.title: What the catalog Nereid writes
docs.text:
Decided by the owner on 2026-11-03 (#904, the catalog Nereid writes status); controllers/catalog/README.md has every reason.

  • A Workload's readiness: runtime.kind: Nereid reads the Ready condition of the core Nereid object it names; runtime.kind: Deployment reads the Deployment's availability.
  • A Package's presence: pypi and oci are looked up, any other registry is Unknown (RegistryNotChecked); a lookup with no answer never reads as found or as absent.
  • The resolved commit: status.source.commit, with its own condition SourceResolved, apart from Ready, from branch, tag, name or commit; semver stays Unknown until its issue. No credential reaches the Nereid until the scm reef (#927, the GitHub App connection), so a private repository answers SourceUnreachable.
  • nereus catalog check reads a Package's presence from status when the Nereid has answered that very spec, and looks up PyPI itself otherwise, so make catalog-check needs no Nereid.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How a Workload lists the resources it needs (a database, a topic, a cache): the owner's idea of a chart carrying the Kubernetes objects plus a Score application spec makes Score a candidate format for that list, to weigh when the first resource reef is built (ADR 0017).
  • App (what people install: mobile, desktop, a browser extension) waits until Nereus has one to prove it on; the CLI stays a Package for people and programs.
  • The current owner in the CLI's config: its command's shape and where the value lives (the CLI's own config, never the person's kubeconfig).

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-10-30 in a design session on the catalog (#559, the catalog reef: Workload, Package and their types), tenancy (#21, Organization and nested Projects) and the resource reefs (#560, the resource reefs and how a Mandate picks their Nereid); raw data in Drive #pontos/beach/opinions/2026-10-29/, #pontos/beach/opinions/2026-10-30/ (the brief, the opinions, the research and the YAML proposal) and #pontos/raw/2026-10-29/.

Rewritten 2026-11-03 from the owner's decisions of 2026-11-02 and 2026-11-03 (#835, the delivery model of the internal-developer-platform profile; #843, the delivery reef's ADR): runtime.namespace and the running image, spec.chart, the Template kind and the DELIVERIES column; raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-02/ and #pontos/raw/2026-11-03/. Amended the same day (owner, #574): one image per Nereid, so openbao-image replaces the local-nereids image, which #611 had already retired.

docs.title: 0017. Resource reefs: a small contract kind per family, the provider in the Mandate, and a Mandate's match
docs.text:
In short

Five resource reefs, each a small contract kind per family, with the provider chosen in the Mandate and a Mandate selected by its match. Status: Accepted (2026-11-14, by the owner; proposed 2026-10-30, rewritten 2026-11-12).

Status: Accepted (2026-11-14, by the owner; proposed 2026-10-30, rewritten 2026-11-12)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A platform provisions resources for the things that run on it: a database, a queue or a topic, a cache, a bucket, a hostname. The clouds offer each of them in their own way (a Postgres on RDS has multiAz, a topic on NATS has JetStream), and the owner, in the design session of #560 (the resource reefs and how a Mandate picks their Nereid), leaned towards one kind per engine or per provider offering, so that nothing of a provider is lost.

ADR 0011 (reefs, Nereids and Mandates) says the opposite: an Instance's fields are generic, common to every Nereid of the reef, and what one Nereid needs and the others lack becomes a common field of the reef, never a Nereid-specific kind. A kind per engine would amend it, and would change the command a person types on every swap of provider, against ADR 0002 (the person asking names the reef, never the Tool).

The research asked for by the owner (on the owner's Drive, private) shows what teams do with Crossplane, the project closest to this problem: a generic kind bound to provider classes was tried and dropped in 2020 as the lowest common denominator, and teams now build two layers, a small contract kind on top (an engine, a size) and typed, provider-specific objects one layer down, picked by a selector or a class. It also shows how the platforms pick an implementation (Humanitec by the most specific criteria, StorageClass and IngressClass by a default, Score by the first match), and that a cache's contract is small and distinct from a database's.

The order comes from the dogfooding: Nereus itself runs Triton on NATS with no reef (#483, Triton as the messaging reef) and publishes Triton through a tunnel made by hand (#470, publishing a reef's endpoint at a hostname: an edge reef with a cloudflare Nereid). No Workload of the catalog (#559, the catalog reef) asks for a database yet.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Five resource reefs, in the order the dogfooding asks. Each is a reef in ADR 0002's sense: an API group <reef>.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, fulfilled by Nereids, bound by Mandates.

Order Reef Kinds Why now 1 messaging Queue, Topic Triton uses NATS with no reef (#483) 2 edge hostname, certificate, DNS Triton behind a tunnel made by hand (#470) 3 database Database when a Workload of the catalog asks 4 cache Cache when a Workload of the catalog asks 5 storage Bucket when a Workload of the catalog asks

DNS lives in edge. The other families of the research (data lake, streams, AI services, about 35 in all) enter one by one when catalog check (#559) points at the gap, each as its own reef or kind, never decided in advance.

A small contract kind per family, with engine. The kind carries owner: {kind, name} (the node of the tenancy tree it belongs to, #21, Organization and nested Projects), engine and the fields every engine understands. What only one provider has goes in the Mandate's params, written once by the admin; what a person chooses per request and every engine understands becomes a common field of the kind, as ADR 0011 asks. ADR 0011 stays as it is: the person writes the contract, the Mandate holds the provider.

# The person asks (Instance): the small contract
apiVersion: messaging.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Topic
metadata:
  name: triton-orders
spec:
  owner: {kind: Project, name: triton}
  engine: nats

# The admin decides once (Mandate): the provider's part
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Mandate
metadata:
  name: messaging-nats
spec:
  reef: messaging
  nereid: nats
  match: {engine: nats}
  params: {jetstream: "true", replicas: "3"}

spec.match on the Mandate picks the Nereid; the most specific wins. The rule:

  • A match holds when every key it names equals the request. A key the match does not name is not looked at.
  • owner holds down the tree (owner, 2026-11-10, #1311): a match on a node of the tenancy tree (ADR 0015) holds for that node and for every node under it, so a Mandate matching an Organization covers its Projects.
  • Among the Mandates whose match holds, the one whose match contains every other matching one wins (the most specific, by containment). On owner, the nearest node wins: a Project's own Mandate before its Organization's.
  • The empty match is the reef's default (spec.default: true and no match mean the same).
  • --mandate on the request forces one Mandate, as today.
  • The keys are engine, environment and owner; kind only in a reef with several resource kinds (messaging, with Queue and Topic).
  • nereus mandate create refuses a match identical to an existing one, and a partial overlap (two matches that can both hold on one request and neither contains the other), with an error that follows ADR 0012 (error messages) and gives the fix to copy. A tie is refused when the Mandate is made, never when a resource is asked. Two matches that differ only in owner, one node above the other in the tree, are not an overlap: the nearest wins.
  • The output line of a request names the Mandate resolved and its Nereid.

The selection rule is the same for every reef (owner, 2026-11-10, #1311). A reef may have several Nereids at once, and a request picks its Mandate in this order:

  1. Only the Nereids that serve the request take part. A Nereid serves a request when it publishes what the request needs: the kind, for a request of a kind; status.oidc, for a login (ADR 0006).
  2. The Mandate whose match holds, the most specific one, by the rule above.
  3. Else the reef's default.
  4. Else the only one, when a single Mandate is left.

--mandate skips the order. A request that reaches the end with no Mandate, or with several, fails with the Mandates that exist and the --match that would catch it (ADR 0012).

# The authentication reef with three Mandates:
#   corporate   keycloak  the default
#   acme-auth0  auth0     match: owner=organization/acme
#   github      github    no match, not the default; mints tokens only

# A login of a Project under acme:  acme-auth0 (step 2, the Organization's match covers its Projects)
# A login of anyone else:           corporate  (step 3; github publishes no status.oidc and is out at step 1)
# A Token:                          github     (step 4; the only Nereid that mints tokens, without being the default)

# The reef's default: what nereus init makes on k3d
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Mandate
metadata:
  name: cloudnative-pg
spec:
  reef: database
  nereid: cloudnative-pg
  default: true

# Postgres on nereus, the kept cluster, goes to RDS: the most specific match wins
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Mandate
metadata:
  name: database-postgres-nereus
spec:
  reef: database
  nereid: aws-rds
  match:
    engine: postgres
    environment: nereus
  params:
    accountId: "123456789012"
    region: us-east-1
    multiAz: "true"

# Triton's topic, through the messaging reef's Mandate for NATS
$ nereus messaging topic create triton-orders \
    --owner project/triton \
    --engine nats
messaging/topics/triton-orders created (mandate: messaging-nats, nereid: nats)

# The same request in two environments: nereus resolves the specific Mandate, pr-123 the default
$ nereus database create orders \
    --owner project/triton \
    --engine postgres \
    --environment nereus
database/databases/orders created (mandate: database-postgres-nereus, nereid: aws-rds)

$ nereus database create orders \
    --owner project/triton \
    --engine postgres \
    --environment pr-123
database/databases/orders created (mandate: cloudnative-pg, nereid: cloudnative-pg)

# A partial overlap is refused when the Mandate is made
$ nereus mandate create database-postgres-eu \
    --reef database \
    --nereid aws-rds \
    --match engine=postgres \
    --match region=eu
✗ core/mandates/database-postgres-eu overlaps database-postgres-nereus (engine=postgres) and neither contains the other. To fix it, run:
  # name the environment too, so one match contains the other
  nereus mandate create database-postgres-eu --reef database --nereid aws-rds --match engine=postgres --match environment=nereus --match region=eu
  Nothing was changed.

The same match picks who delivers into an environment. An Environment (the environment reef) is only the request, with no technology in its spec, and its name is a disposable label (nereus for the kept k3d cluster today, the name of the k3d cluster itself; never prod, owner 2026-10-30 and 2026-11-23), so that migrating data, restoring a backup or swapping the cluster under a Workload changes the environment, not the Workload; the Nereid of its Mandate materializes it (a kept cluster, a vcluster, a managed container service) and writes what it made in status. A Mandate of the release reef with a match on the environment picks the Nereid that knows how to deliver there, so nereus release create is the same command whatever the environment is made of.

A cache reef of its own, Valkey by default. The in-memory contract is small (get and set with a time to live; the data may be lost) and differs from a database's, so a cache is not a Database with another engine. Valkey, Redis and Memcached are engines and params of the Cache kind; the reef's default Nereid runs Valkey. A durable, no-eviction Redis is a key-value database (database, engine: redis); CDN and HTTP caches belong to the edge reef.

apiVersion: cache.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Cache
metadata:
  name: sessions
spec:
  owner: {kind: Project, name: triton}
  engine: valkey

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Kubernetes StorageClass (Storage Classes): "When a PVC does not specify a storageClassName, the default StorageClass is used", and its parameters are provider-specific, read by the provisioner alone; the Mandate's empty match as the default and its params as the provider's part take the same split. Kubernetes keeps the newest of several defaults "to allow for seamless migration"; this ADR refuses the second one instead.
  • Kubernetes IngressClass (Ingress, "Default IngressClass"): "If you have more than one IngressClass marked as the default for your cluster, the admission controller prevents creating new Ingress objects that don't have an ingressClassName specified"; the refusal of an identical or overlapping match at mandate create moves that refusal to the moment the class is made.
  • Humanitec resource definitions (Resource Definitions): matching criteria on environment type, application, environment, resource id and class, each with a weight, and "when selecting with Matching Criteria, the most specific one is selected"; the most-specific rule is taken, by containment instead of weights, so that a tie cannot happen.
  • Crossplane composite resources (Composite Resources; Compositions): a composite resource names its Composition with compositionRef or selects one by labels with compositionSelector, and a Composition is "a template for creating multiple Kubernetes resources as a single composite resource"; the two layers (a contract kind over provider-specific objects) are the shape this ADR takes, with the Mandate in the place of the Composition. That Crossplane dropped its generic kinds in 2020 and that teams build two layers is the project's own reading of the research on the Drive.
  • Score resources (Score specification reference): a workload declares a resource by type, an optional class and params, and "it is up to the Score implementation to resolve the resource by name, type, or any other meta information available"; the contract kind with engine plays the part of type and class, and the Mandate the part of the implementation's resolution.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A person asks for a Topic, a Database or a Cache by its engine and never names a Tool or a provider; swapping NATS for Kafka, or CloudNativePG for RDS, changes a Mandate, not a command or a file of the person.
  • Every provider-only setting is written once, in a Mandate's params, by the admin; a setting a person needs per request becomes a common field of the kind, which is the way out of the lowest common denominator ADR 0011 already names.
  • The choice of Nereid is deterministic and refused early: with the overlap rule enforced at mandate create, every request resolves to one Mandate or to none, and a request with no Mandate fails with the Mandates that exist and the --match that would catch it (ADR 0012).
  • A reef takes several Nereids at once: the refusal "one Nereid per reef" of nereus nereid apply goes away (#1313), and the authentication reef is the first to use it (ADR 0006).
  • nereus mandate create grows --match <key>=<value> (repeatable) next to --param, and nereus mandate list shows the match of each Mandate; nereus status keeps one row per reef and Nereid pair (ADR 0011).
  • The messaging and edge reefs come first, so the two stand-ins of Nereus itself (NATS with no reef, the tunnel by hand) are retired by a feature of the platform, as #269 asks.
  • Each reef's commands follow ADR 0013 (command conventions): nereus <reef> <kind> <verb> <name>, kinds singular in commands, a default kind per reef (nereus database create is nereus database database create), full-path output lines, --dry-run everywhere.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How a Workload lists the resources it needs. The catalog's Workload (#559) has no list of resources yet; the owner's idea of a chart carrying the Kubernetes objects plus a Score application spec makes Score's resources a candidate format, to weigh when the first resource reef is built.
  • How a Workload gets the credentials of a resource. The first opinion proposed a binding through the secrets reef in the Service Binding layout (the Nereid writes the connection as a secret the Workload mounts); not decided.
  • The edge reef's kinds. #470 names the hostname and the cloudflare Nereid; whether a certificate and a DNS record are kinds of their own or fields of the hostname is decided there.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-10-30, in the design session on the catalog, tenancy and resource reefs (#21, #559, #560); the brief, the opinions and the three research files (research-crossplane.md, research-resource-families.md, research-mandate-matching.md) in Drive #pontos/beach/opinions/2026-10-29/ and 2026-10-30/ (private); the raw log under #pontos/raw/2026-10-29/.

Rewritten 2026-11-12 from the owner's decisions of 2026-11-10 (#1311: the selection rule for every reef, and a match on owner holding down the tree); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-10/.

docs.title: 0018. The Nereus API is the one door: clients talk to it, and the Kubernetes API stays behind it
docs.text:
In short

The Nereus API is the one door of the platform: clients talk to it with the person's token, and the Kubernetes API stays behind it. Status: Proposed (2026-10-30).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-30)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
docs/vision.md and the slide landscape of the deck (docs/presentations/nereus.yaml) draw the Platform API as "the one door for every client: the CLI, a portal, an IDE reading an app.yaml, an agent", where "none of them needs a kubeconfig". wasp-idp, where the idea comes from, built it: the platform CLI called its Platform API (GET /v1/me for platform whoami), and the API validated the person's token and acted on the cluster.

Nereus has no such API yet. Every reef is an API group served by the Kubernetes API (ADR 0002, ADR 0009), the CLI reaches it with the person's kubeconfig, and nereus-mcp runs on the person's machine and reads the cluster the same way, "until the Platform API exists". #54 (the first slice of the Platform API, after the CLI MVP) was closed as not planned on 2026-10-30.

The question came back with nereus whoami (#605): its first design sent the person's token to the Kubernetes apiserver (a SelfSubjectReview, the apiserver trusting the authentication reef's issuer through a structured AuthenticationConfiguration). The owner refused it the same day: "mandar para API do cluster, acho que está errado ... a CLI deveria se comunicar com a API do Platform API, que no caso aqui é o Nereus. E tudo o resto ficaria atrás dessa API."

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The Nereus API is the one door of the platform. The CLI, a portal, an IDE and the agents talk to it, with the person's token from the authentication reef (ADR 0006). Everything else sits behind it: the Kubernetes API with the reefs' kinds, the Nereids, the tools they drive. A client never needs a kubeconfig to use the platform.

  • It runs in the cluster: a Deployment and a Service nereus-api in nereus-system, installed by nereus init with the core reef (owner, 2026-10-30, over a process on the person's machine or a route inside nereus-mcp). Its public name is api.<domain>, api.getnereus.dev for Nereus itself (#577, the edge reef).
  • It validates the token, and only it: the issuer and the JWKS come from the default Mandate of the authentication reef (status.oidc), the audience is nereus-api. The Kubernetes apiserver is not taught to trust the issuer: a person's token never reaches it.
  • It acts on the cluster with its own identity (a ServiceAccount and its RBAC), and decides what the person may do (by group, later by team) before acting.
  • It speaks of reefs, never of tools (ADR 0002): its routes name reefs and their kinds, and it reads what the Nereids publish in status.
  • Its first slice is GET /healthz and GET /v1/me (#607), which nereus whoami calls. The rest of the CLI moves behind it one command group at a time; until a group moves, its commands keep using the kubeconfig, a stand-in this ADR names.
  • A check holds the door (#1529, owner 2026-11-14): scripts/checks/kubeconfig-ban, part of make checks, refuses any kubeconfig access in cli/src/nereus/ (a kube context, a client built from the kubeconfig, kubectl) outside the files scripts/checks/kubeconfig-allowlist names, each with a count that may only go down. Three exceptions are permanent: nereus init and what bootstraps an instance on a cluster (they need that cluster's credentials), the settings of the person's own machine, and cluster.py, which holds the doors themselves. Every other entry is a stand-in, removed by the issue that moves its commands behind the API.

docs.title: For a new feature
docs.text: Every new command, reef or screen reaches the platform through the Nereus API, from its first slice: a route in api/, called by the CLI or the portal with the person's token. It never adds a line to the allowlist; a feature that seems to need the kubeconfig is either part of nereus init and the bootstrap, or a sign that the API lacks a route, and gets that route instead.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• wasp-idp's Platform API (the project Nereus comes from, platform/api/src/platform_api/app.py and auth.py): one HTTP API for the CLI, the portal and the agents, a bearer token checked against the issuer's JWKS and the audience, GET /v1/me answering who the person is; the first slice and its token check are ported from it.
  • The API gateway pattern (microservices.io, Chris Richardson): "Implement an API gateway that is the single entry point for all clients."; the Nereus API is that single entry point, in front of the reefs instead of services.
  • The CNCF Platforms white paper (TAG App Delivery): a platform should "offer its capabilities through consistent interfaces and focus on the user experience"; one API for every client is how Nereus keeps its interfaces consistent.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• nereus whoami asks the Nereus API (#607); the AuthenticationConfiguration of the apiserver drafted for #605 is dropped.
  • Authentication, authorization by team, policy, cost and several clusters live in one place, the API, instead of in each client and in the apiserver's configuration.
  • The CLI keeps two ways to reach the platform for a while: the API for the groups already moved, the kubeconfig for the rest. Each move is its own issue; the stand-in ends when no command needs a kubeconfig. Moved: whoami, doctor, login (#1321); status, reef, nereid (#1322); registry but repository publish (#1324); mandate, secrets (#1323); release (#1514), its source publish too (#1518); build (#1515), build trigger (#1528) and build apply (#1594); delivery and workload deploy (#1516), workload logs (#1517); tenancy and config set owner (#1639); environment but environment kubeconfig (#1638).
  • nereus-mcp became a part of the API: ADR 0029 has it serve /mcp with the tools the reefs declare (#1806), and the nereus-mcp process, which read the cluster with the kubeconfig, is retired (#1810).
  • The API is one more workload to run, secure and publish: its image, its RBAC, its hostname (#577).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How the CLI finds the API's URL: published by the core reef or set with nereus config, decided in #607.
  • The framework of the API (Starlette or FastAPI with uvicorn, as nereus-mcp), decided in #607.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-10-30 in the session that built nereus login (#605): the correction of whoami and the choice of the API in the cluster; the raw log under #pontos/raw/2026-10-30/.

Rewritten 2026-11-14 from the owner's ban of the kubeconfig (#1529) and the request to make it the rule for every new feature; raw data in #pontos/raw/2026-11-14/.

docs.title: 0019. The messaging reef: threads, orders and claims as records, a bus behind a Nereid
docs.text:
In short

The conversation joins the messaging reef as records (Thread, Order, Claim, Message), with a bus behind a Nereid. Status: Proposed (2026-10-26).

Status: Proposed (2026-10-26)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Work orders reach the local agents through a stand-in: the voice session writes a Markdown file to a Google Drive folder (the beach, Beach), and scripts/beach/watch on each machine polls it and starts Claude Code on the orders assigned to its agent. A security review of the watcher found two gaps in its only gate, "the file's Drive owner is the trusted owner":

  1. Owner is not author. Drive keeps the owner when an editor changes a file, so anyone with edit access to the folder can rewrite an order that still passes the check.
  2. Checked is not what runs. The watcher checks the owner, then the run reads the order from Drive again; the text may have changed in between (a time-of-check to time-of-use gap).

The owner accepted that risk for now and made the replacement the priority: a messaging reef, where an order is a message of the platform rather than a file. The owner also asked for threads: with remote agents, every subject arrives in one conversation, and the person must work out which subject each message belongs to.

Two earlier ideas touch the same ground: a contract for Controllers to exchange events with the platform (#254), and a communication reef for queues and topics, RabbitMQ first (#257, #374, both closed since).

Since this was first written (2026-10-26):

  • Triton (controllers/triton) carries orders today: its door, an MCP server behind OAuth through the keycloak Nereid (#495), takes an order from the voice session and hands it to an agent's open Claude Code session over NATS; the orders and their status live on JetStream and survive a restart (#506); every agent joins NATS with its own login through NATS's auth callout (#497). The beach is its backup.
  • ADR 0017 (resource reefs) puts the machine side in this same reef: messaging holds Topic and Queue, fulfilled by a nats Nereid through the Mandate messaging-nats, and Triton becomes a Nereid of it (#576, #483).
  • ADR 0018 (the Nereus API is the one door) makes the Nereus API, not the Kubernetes API, what clients talk to.

Origin: the owner, in the voice session of 2026-10-26, through order 20261026-1236 (messaging reef design) and its addendum 01 (threads); raw data in Drive #pontos/beach/ and beach/replies/20261026-1236-messaging-reef-design/design.md, which holds the survey of buses in full.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The conversation joins the messaging reef, API group messaging.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009, ADR 0010), next to ADR 0017's Topic and Queue: its records are kinds of the same reef; a bus only carries notifications of those records, behind a Nereid (ADR 0002).

The records (kind names proposed, to decide with the owner):

Kind What it is Who creates it Thread one subject: a client-chosen id, a title, an optional issue; status sums it up (state, counts, last message) a person Order a work order to one agent, in one thread; immutable; an addendum is an Order with spec.amends a person with the publisher role Claim an agent takes an order; named after the order, so a second claim fails with AlreadyExists; records the digest it ran an agent's runner Message everything else in a thread: ack, question, answer, reply, done, failed, cancelled; inReplyTo names the record it answers a person or an agent

Separate kinds, rather than one message with a type field, because RBAC authorises by resource: only a publisher may create an Order, and an agent may create Claim and Message only.

A thread groups one or more orders. The common case is one order per thread, as an order and its replies folder are today; a follow-up order may join the same thread. Thread ids are chosen by the client, so a conversation can open several planned threads at once, and new ones on the way. Every record and every event carries its thread.

Deterministic first: routing (spec.to), the claim (create-if-absent), the digest and the end of a run are code; AI only runs the order's text.

Closing the two gaps:

  • An authenticated identity publishes. People publish through nereus or the Nereus API's /mcp with an OIDC token of the authentication reef (ADR 0006), through the Nereus API (ADR 0018), which acts as the person, so RBAC and the audit log see the person. A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy refuses a record whose spec.author is not the caller. Each agent has an identity of its own, as it has on NATS since #497.
  • The text checked is the text run. Order.spec is immutable (a CEL rule self == oldSelf); the Nereid writes status.digest; the runner reads the order once, checks the digest, records it in the Claim, and passes that text to the run on stdin.
  • Each run is isolated: a rootless container (podman first, a Kubernetes Job later) with the worktree only, no sudo, a one-hour GitHub App token scoped to the repository, egress limited to GitHub, the model's API and Nereus; pushing to main and merging are refused by a ruleset, not by the agent's restraint.

The bus is a Nereid, and not part of the first slice. A Kubernetes watch already delivers each change to a subscriber; the first Nereid only keeps the records and writes status. When #254's events or the number of subscribers need one, the bus is NATS with JetStream, the one Triton runs on and ADR 0017's nats Nereid serves (#576): it publishes one CloudEvent per record (type dev.getnereus.messaging.<kind>.created.v1, extension thread), with a reference to the record and never the order's body.

The terminal is the first client (ADR 0013 verbs), the voice session the second, through the /mcp tools of the Nereus API (ADR 0029) with the same nouns:

nereus thread create messaging-reef-design --title "Design the messaging reef"
nereus order create 20261026-1236-messaging-reef-design \
  --thread messaging-reef-design \
  --to ln28 \
  --from-file order.md
nereus thread list
nereus thread get messaging-reef-design
nereus message create \
  --thread messaging-reef-design \
  --in-reply-to messaging-reef-design-0004 \
  "fix first"
nereus order list --to ln28 --watch

$ nereus thread list
THREAD                  TITLE                       STATE      AGENT  LAST             AGE
messaging-reef-design   Design the messaging reef   working    ln28   claim, 13:09     34m
merge-readme-pr-437     Merge the README PR         needs-you  m15    question, 13:20  25m

Migration: Triton's door becomes a client of the Order kind: an order sent through it is a record, its JetStream status follows the Claim and the Messages; runs move into containers; then the Drive source is turned off and the beach retires.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• NATS and JetStream (docs.nats.io): subject-based routing with per-subject permissions, durable consumers, and a key-value create that fails when the key exists (key-value store); the recommended bus and the shape of the claim.
  • RabbitMQ (OAuth 2.0 backend, Kubernetes operators): the alternative, the working choice of communication until #257 closed.
  • Knative Eventing, Argo Events and Dapr pub/sub (triggers, EventBus, pub/sub): evaluated and not chosen as the reef's contract; Argo Events stays a candidate for "an order starts a Job".
  • CloudEvents (spec, extensions): the envelope of every event; the spec has no correlation attribute, so the thread travels as an extension.
  • Threads in chat systems: Matrix's m.thread relation and its root summary (spec), Zulip's topics (topics), Slack's thread_ts (messaging), and Google Chat's client-chosen thread_key (spaces.messages.create), the model for planned threads.
  • Kubernetes: immutability with CEL (blog), ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (docs) and user impersonation (docs).
  • Claude Code development containers (docs): unattended runs inside an isolated container with a firewall, and the warning that the container does not protect what it holds.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An order's author is a platform identity, audited by the API server, and the text a run receives is the text that was checked.
  • The voice session publishes with no secret of its own, but only while the instance behind /mcp is reachable: the reef depends on an always-on instance.
  • The beach watcher stand-in of docs/features.md gets its replacement; it retires when the Drive source is turned off.
  • The first slice needs no broker; the bus arrives with #254 and is swappable through a Mandate.
  • Agents need identities and RBAC roles of their own, and the repository needs a ruleset that makes merging without the owner impossible.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether Triton's door writes Order records itself, or the records replace the door's JetStream orders.
  • Whether the conversation kinds belong in messaging with ADR 0017's Topic and Queue, or in a reef of their own.
  • Where the always-on instance runs.
  • The kind names: Thread, Order, Claim, Message, or Conversation, WorkOrder, a core Lease.
  • Whether a thread closes only by a person's word, and whether a claim expires.
  • How an agent's NATS login (#497) maps to its identity on the Nereus API.
  • Whether an agent's question blocks its run or ends it.

Reviewed 2026-10-31 against Triton (#495, #497, #506), ADR 0017 and ADR 0018, at the owner's request, before its first merge; renumbered from the draft's 0015, taken by ADR 0015 (tenancy).

docs.title: 0020. The delivery reef: a Delivery takes a Workload to an Environment
docs.text:
In short

A delivery reef with one kind, Delivery, takes a Workload to an Environment; the Nereid, never the client, resolves an image tag to a digest. Status: Proposed (2026-11-03).

Status: Proposed (2026-11-03)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
make scene-golden-path (PR #836) took a developer's image to a namespace with today's commands and listed what hurts: nothing says what runs (gap 8), changing a tag takes three steps (gap 9), and a re-pushed tag is not pulled (gap 10). #835 (the delivery model of the internal-developer-platform profile) refined the path from that list, and the owner settled it on 2026-11-02.

The catalog (ADR 0016) says what exists, the release reef (ADR 0010) runs a chart in a Target, the environment reef says where. Nothing joins them: one Workload runs in several Environments, and a developer should not write a Repository, a Source, a Target and a Release to run an image.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A delivery reef, delivery.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, with one kind, Delivery, its default kind: one per Workload and Environment pair, cluster-scoped. The pair lives in spec. status says what runs.

apiVersion: delivery.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Delivery
metadata:
  name: hello-dev
spec:                                   # written by the client: the CLI, or the portal through the API
  workload: hello
  environment: dev
  image: registry.example.com/hello:a1b2c3d
  requestedAt: "2026-11-03T14:00:00Z"
status:                                 # written by the Nereid
  resolved:
    requestedAt: "2026-11-03T14:00:00Z"
    image: localhost:5111/hello:0.1.0   # what this resolution read: a new deploy of another image resolves again
    digest: sha256:9f2c1e
    port: 8080                          # read once with the digest, so a retry reads no registry
  digest: sha256:9f2c1e                 # what is running
  previousDigest: sha256:77ab40         # the only history for now
  namespace: hello-dev

The Nereid resolves a tag to a digest, never the client. The CLI is today's client, and a portal will call the same API, so the rule sits behind them and works the same for both (owner, 2026-11-03). The Nereid uses the platform's registry credential, so a person needs only their own login, as #835 decided for publishing.

  • Each deploy is a new request: the client writes spec.requestedAt, so a second deploy of the same tag changes spec, prints configured and reaches a re-pushed image.
  • One resolution per request: the Nereid resolves only when spec.requestedAt differs from status.resolved.requestedAt. A tag that moves with no new deploy never changes what runs in silence.
  • A digest stays as it is: an image given as hello@sha256:... is not resolved. The Release always carries the digest, so imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent is no longer a trap.
  • What this costs: --dry-run shows the tag, not the digest, and a tag that does not exist fails after deploy printed created or configured, with the reason in status. --wait brings that reason to the terminal.

The Nereid writes the release reef's objects. It writes a Release with the curated chart app-template, or the chart the Workload names in spec.chart (ADR 0016), and the Source and the Target that Release needs, so a developer configures nothing of the release reef. The namespace is the Delivery's name. The keycloak and vcluster Nereids already write their own Release. The flux Nereid still does the installing, with #828 (a Release reaches its Target's Environment) taking it into the Environment.

The port comes from the image's ExposedPorts, overridden in the Workload, with a clear error when both lack it. Secrets, databases and health checks go in the Workload; Score waits.

One Nereid per platform it delivers to, with no new noun. The kind Target and init --target already use the other word. The first Nereid is kubernetes: it delivers to a Kubernetes Environment through Release. A destination that is not Kubernetes is another Nereid, behind another Mandate, with the same nereus workload deploy and no Release.

A Delivery's name is generated once and never changes: <workload>-<environment>. When that name belongs to another pair (hello in dev-x and hello-dev in x), it takes a short suffix from the hash of the pair (hello-dev-x-3f9a); the same hash shortens a name that is too long. The limit is 53 characters, a Helm release's, since the Release takes the Delivery's name; the CRD checks it with CEL.

How the CLI reads the argument:

Typed Read as hello@dev the pair; @ is sugar for --environment hello --environment dev the pair hello-dev the Delivery's name hello a Workload with a single Environment, except in deploy

The Delivery's name is tried before the Workload. When both match different targets, or a Workload runs in several Environments, the error lists the candidates and picks none (ADR 0012).

deploy never guesses: it takes the unique name, hello@dev or hello --environment dev, and refuses a bare hello even with one Environment, so it cannot change target in silence when a second Environment appears.

The commands follow ADR 0013. nereus workload deploy creates or updates a Delivery, and nereus delivery has the five verbs. nereus workload list shows what the catalog has, and nereus delivery list shows what was deployed: the two are different questions (owner, 2026-11-03). The deck is docs/specs/cli/reefs/delivery.yaml.

# Take a Workload to an Environment
$ nereus workload deploy hello@dev \
    --image registry.example.com/hello:a1b2c3d
✓ delivery/deliveries/hello-dev created

Next steps:

  nereus delivery get hello-dev

# What the catalog has
$ nereus workload list
WORKLOAD  OWNER          TYPE     AUDIENCE  DELIVERIES  STATUS
billing   Project/shop   service  programs  0           Ready
hello     Project/hello  service  people    2           Ready

# What was deployed
$ nereus delivery list \
    --workload hello
NAME         WORKLOAD  ENVIRONMENT  DIGEST         READY
hello-dev    hello     dev          sha256:9f2c1e  True
hello-stage  hello     stage        sha256:77ab40  True

Stand-ins, for the issues that build them: workload deploy and nereus delivery (#845) and workload logs (#846) reached the cluster with the kubeconfig until their group moved behind the Nereus API (ADR 0018): the first two through it since #1516, workload logs and --follow since #1517, streamed by the API from inside the Environment. The kubeconfig stays only while the instance offers no sign-in. This ADR creates none itself.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Kubernetes, images (kubernetes.io, Images): "Tags can be moved to point to different images, but digests are fixed", and with IfNotPresent "the image is pulled only if it is not already present locally"; the reason the Release carries the digest.
  • Flux's HelmRelease, triggering a reconcile (fluxcd.io, HelmReleases): the annotation reconcile.fluxcd.io/requestedAt queues a reconcile when its value differs from .status.lastHandledReconcileAt; spec.requestedAt and status.resolved.requestedAt take that shape. The same page describes .spec.kubeConfig, which "can apply and manage resources on a remote cluster", the way a Release reaches an Environment.
  • bjw-s app-template (bjw-s-labs, App Template): "a companion Helm chart that works alongside the Common Library to deploy any application in Kubernetes"; the curated chart, used since PR #836, instead of a chart of our own.
  • Kargo (docs.kargo.io, Core concepts): a Stage is "a promotion target" and Freight "references specific revisions of artifacts"; the Delivery plays the Stage's part for one Workload and holds one digest, with no pipeline. Update channels, if they come, should read Kargo first.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One command takes an image to an Environment and one row says what runs: gaps 8, 9 and 10 of PR #836 close with #845.
  • The catalog stays a reader (ADR 0016): nereus workload list only counts Deliveries, and the running image lives in the Delivery's status.
  • A Delivery applied from a file with a tag resolves once, and applying the same file again prints unchanged. Moving to a re-pushed tag takes nereus workload deploy or a new spec.requestedAt.
  • Security (OWASP A10, server-side request forgery): the Nereid contacts a registry a person named, with the platform's credential; #845 validates the reference and sends that credential only to the registry it belongs to. Authorization is by owner for now, then the authorization reef.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Rollback: status.previousDigest is the only record; no command uses it yet.
  • History of a Delivery: whether more than one previous digest is kept, and where.
  • Update channels: an idea, not designed.
  • Which registries a Delivery may name: a list per Organization or Project is a candidate for when the authorization reef exists.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-11-02 in the review of #835 (the delivery model of the internal-developer-platform profile), and of 2026-11-03 in the design of #843 (this ADR): nereus delivery list apart from nereus workload list, the Nereid kubernetes and what it writes, and the Nereid resolving the digest. Raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-02/ and #pontos/raw/2026-11-03/.

docs.title: 0021. The registry reef: a Registry and its Repositories, read with a credential, published through the platform
docs.text:
In short

A registry reef with Registry and Repository kinds; images are read with one read-only credential per Registry, over TLS, and published through the platform. Status: Proposed (2026-11-05).

Status: Proposed (2026-11-05)

docs.title: 844 (prove the nodes pull from a zot inside the cluster) showed that a cluster's nodes can pull from a registry that runs in the cluster, with no cluster recreated. #847 asks for the reef that makes it a capability, and #848 (the build reef) needs somewhere to publish. ADR 0017 (resource reefs) does not list this reef, so it needs a decision of its own.
Decision
docs.text:
A registry reef, registry.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, with two cluster-scoped kinds. One writer per field (ADR 0005). The commands follow ADR 0013, and the deck is docs/specs/cli/reefs/registry.yaml.

Kind spec (the person) status (the Nereid only) Registry (default) owner, mandate observedGeneration, conditions, steps, nereid, pullAddress, internalAddress, namespace, readCredential Repository registry, owner the same base fields, image, identity, pushIdentity (#1010; credentialSecret before it)

No port in spec. Kubernetes allocates the NodePort, and the Nereid copies the result into status.pullAddress. A Pod cannot reach localhost:<port>, so builds and the delivery Nereid use status.internalAddress: a person names the pullAddress in nereus workload deploy, and the kubernetes Nereid finds the Registry that holds it (#1014). It calls the internal address only when it stays in the namespace registry-<name>, which an admission policy holds, and only while it looks up an image of that Registry, so an answer from another registry never sends it there.

A Registry answers only over TLS (#1064) (owner, 2026-11-06). The platform has one registry CA, made with a new k3d cluster: its name constraints, critical, permit only localhost and names under svc.cluster.local and exclude every IPv4 and IPv6 address (RFC 5280 checks each name type on its own, and containerd trusts the CA for every registry), so a node that trusts it trusts nothing else on the internet and no IP address. Only its certificate reaches the host, in the CLI's state folder (~/.local/state/nereus/clusters/<cluster>/registry/ca.crt), which every node mounts at /etc/nereus/registry; the key is made in memory and goes straight into the Secret registry-ca in nereus-system, of type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt and tls.key, the shape cert-manager's CA Issuer reads, so the certificate reef (#1101, certificates as a reef) can take it over. A cluster made before keeps what it has until scripts/cluster/registry-trust brings it there. containerd trusts the CA for every registry (registries.yaml, configs: {"*": {tls: {ca_file: /etc/nereus/registry/ca.crt}}}), added to the system's roots, so public images still come over their own https. The zot Nereid reads registry-ca by name only and issues each Registry a certificate for localhost and <service>.registry-<name>.svc.cluster.local, kept in the Secret zot-tls of registry-<name> and renewed 30 days before its 90 days end; zot reloads it with no restart. It publishes the CA's certificate, never its key, in the ConfigMap zot-ca of the same namespace. Every reader trusts only that CA, never the system's roots: the kubernetes Nereid calls https://<internalAddress> with the CA read from zot-ca (RBAC names that ConfigMap; it never reads zot-tls) and sends the read credential only there, the zot Nereid checks its users over https, and nereus registry repository publish reads the digest over https through its port-forward. Plain HTTP gets no answer as a registry on the pull address nor on the internal address (OWASP A02).

Reading images takes a credential: one read-only credential per Registry (#1015) (owner, 2026-11-05). zot answers no anonymous read or write. The Nereid gives each Registry a user pull, allowed read on every repository, and keeps its password in two places, both written by the Nereid itself at the same moment:

  • the Kubernetes Secret zot-pull in registry-<name> (the kubernetes Nereid read it for its lookups until #1187 gave each Registry a read identity, the ServiceAccount read of registry-<name>, whose ten-minute tokens zot lets read, so that Nereid holds no Secret);
  • the secrets reef's secret registries/<name>-pull, key auth, the base64 of pull:<password> and nothing else, sealed with the public key of the vault's Mandate, in the CLI's envelope (owner, 2026-11-05: deterministic, and a rotation needs no person).

A Registry is read only by its owner and what is under it (#1075) (owner, 2026-11-05). The kubernetes Nereid gives a Delivery the Registry's read credential only when the Registry's spec.owner is the Workload's owner or one of its parents in the tenancy tree, climbed through spec.parent of any kind of the group, and is the Environment's owner or one of its parents as well (#1082, owner, 2026-11-06), since the Release puts the credential in the Environment's namespace; an Environment with no spec.owner is refused (fail closed); otherwise the Delivery is Ready False, reason RegistryNotOwned, before any lookup, since a lookup already reads with that credential. A node missing on the way refuses too. The credential stays only while the owner check approves it (#1085, owner, 2026-11-06): a refused Delivery whose Release carries a Registry's credential that the same pass did not approve (refused this way, refused before the check, or now naming an image of no Registry or of another one) loses that Release. Flux uninstalls the chart, the pull Secret goes with it and the app stops, since it ran on a credential it may no longer read; the Target stays. A refusal after the check approved the same credential (an image not found, a registry that does not answer) keeps the last good Release, as does a Release that carries no credential. A Registry with no spec.owner stays readable by every Delivery. The gate lives in the Nereid, not in the vault: the vault registries stays one, revisited when #990 (who may deliver to which Environment) settles who writes a Delivery.

status.readCredential names both. The vault registries holds only pull credentials, so allowing an Environment's namespace on the host (env-<nereid>-<env>) by name opens nothing else (OWASP A01). nereus registry create makes the vault when it is missing. A Delivery of an image from a Registry asks for the key with secretValues (#877), at nereus.pullAuth: the Release's values hold the dockerconfigjson as a template, {"auths":{"<pullAddress>":{"auth":"{{ .Values.nereus.pullAuth }}"}}}, which app-template renders with tpl into its Secret inside the Environment, and defaultPodOptions.imagePullSecrets names it. Flux's targetPath reads a value with Helm's --set parser, so a JSON value breaks; app-template's tpl takes the JSON, and the vault keeps only the base64 value, which the parser reads as one string. A credential per Environment goes with #953 (a private image with the platform's registry credential).

Publishing goes through the platform, and a tag is never overwritten. Each Repository has its own push credential, allowed read and create only, so a person uses only their own login. nereus registry repository publish runs on the kubeconfig, which ADR 0018 (the Nereus API as the one door) allows until the group moves:

  1. Apply the Repository and wait for Ready.
  2. Ask a token of its push identity and open a port-forward.
  3. Push with crane, the token as a Bearer, from a temporary folder removed on exit.
  4. Read the digest back from the registry with the Registry's read credential.

The push credential expires (#1010, amends the above). A Repository's push identity is the ServiceAccount push-<name> in builds, and zot takes its Kubernetes tokens through http.auth.bearer.oidc, mapped to a user bound to the ServiceAccount's uid, with the same read and create only. A token is for one Registry's audience and lasts ten minutes, so no Secret holds a push credential. This is not the token service below: zot's access control decides, so a push still cannot overwrite a tag. Spec 0009 (build security) has the details.

The first Nereid is zot, through its chart, behind the Mandate zot. Harbor stays possible as another Nereid. A token service does not qualify: in zot v2.1.23 a bearer push grants create and update (pkg/api/bearer.go), which would allow overwriting a tag.

A delete is refused while Repositories exist. A Repository name is unique per cluster in this slice.

# Ask for a registry
$ nereus registry create main
registry/registries/main created (mandate: zot, nereid: zot)

Next steps:

  nereus registry get main

# Where to pull from
$ nereus registry get main
NAME  NEREID  PULL-ADDRESS     READY
main  zot     localhost:31874  True

localhost:31874 is a NodePort, for an image reference on this cluster's nodes. Anything that reaches a node's port reaches this registry, over TLS only, and reads nothing with no password.

Next steps:

  nereus registry repository publish hello --registry main --image hello:v1

Stand-ins: create, apply, list, get, delete, purge and repository list|get|delete go through the Nereus API (/v1/registry/..., for nereus-admins) once the instance offers sign-in, and through the kubeconfig before (#1324, the two doors of #1322); repository publish too since #1328, its image through the API's /v2 (the amendment below). The API names the person on what it creates (metadata.annotations[getnereus.dev/created-by]). Who may create or publish is not enforced: owner has nothing behind it until the authorization reef (#897). The push user lives until rotated, retired by #1010 (the registry reef's push credential expires). The zot Nereid issues the Registry's certificates from the platform's registry CA until the certificate reef (#1101, certificates as a reef) does.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Kubernetes, NodePort (Service, type NodePort): "the Kubernetes control plane allocates a port from a range", and "Your Service reports the allocated port in its .spec.ports[*].nodePort field"; the reason spec holds no port and the Nereid copies it.
  • zot, access control (Authentication and authorization): "With an anonymousPolicy, a repository can allow anonymous actions which do not require user authentication", and "you can choose to allow any combination of read, create, update, or delete actions on specific paths"; anonymous reading and the per-repository read and create come from these.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The nodes pull from a registry the platform runs, and #848 has a place to publish.
  • Reading needs the Registry's read credential (#1015), but one credential serves every Environment allowed in the vault registries, so any of them can read every image of the Registry; the kubernetes Nereid gives it only to a Delivery whose Workload's owner (#1075) and Environment's owner (#1082) may both read the Registry, but a namespace allowed in the vault could still name another Registry's secret in a Release written by hand. Security (OWASP A01, broken access control): a credential per Environment is #953. The password no longer crosses plain HTTP: a Registry answers only over TLS (#1064, OWASP A02).
  • A Registry needs the secrets reef: without the vault registries it is not Ready (NoVault).
  • nereus registry collides with no command; the Nereid registry (#22, #691) stays under nereus nereid.
  • A person changes a tag's content by publishing a new tag, never by overwriting one.

docs.title: Open questions answered
docs.text:
No cluster ran for this design; test/scene-registry-reef (#1012) answers the three questions it left open, all yes:

  • containerd pulls under mixed policies: a node pulled with no password while another user could write (#1012); since #1015 it pulls only with the read credential, and with none it is refused.
  • zot's watcher sees a ConfigMap update: a new user and policy took effect with no restart of the Pod.
  • The allocated port survives a Helm upgrade: the NodePort and status.pullAddress stayed the same.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-11-02 in #847 and of 2026-11-05 on its design (#1011 delivers this ADR). Raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-05/.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11-13): publish pushes through the Nereus API's /v2 (#1328)
docs.text:
nereus registry repository publish no longer needs a kubeconfig (ADR 0018, the Nereus API as the one door). The Repository goes through /v1/registry, as since #1324, and the image through the API's /v2, which proxies the OCI Distribution API to the Registry's zot. release source publish (#1229) pushes the same way, so it now needs nereus login too.

  • The person's token, the Repository's push identity behind it. crane sends the person's Nereus token (registrytoken in a temporary Docker configuration); the API checks it and mints, itself, a token of the ServiceAccount push-<repository> of builds, for the audience nereus-registry-<registry>, of at most 600 seconds, cached for half its life. zot still sees only the push identity, with read and create, so a tag is still never overwritten. The /v2/ ping answers 401 with a Bearer challenge, as crane expects; --insecure is used only for a loopback instance URL.
  • Every /v2 method needs nereus-admins, reads too: the API would read with the push identity. Pulls by people outside nereus-admins are out of scope; nodes and Deliveries keep the read credential and the read identity (#1015, #1187).
  • Only the Distribution grammar passes: a repository name, then blobs/<digest>, blobs/uploads/[<id>], manifests/<tag or digest> or tags/list; a dot or empty segment, or any % in the raw path, is 404 with no call upstream. The upstream URL is built from the checked parts, over TLS that trusts only the Registry's ConfigMap zot-ca.
  • The API's grants are Roles the zot Nereid writes, never a ClusterRole (owner, 2026-11-13). Per Registry, in registry-<registry>, nereus-api-zot-ca (get of zot-ca alone); per Repository, in builds, nereus-api-push-<repository> (get and token create of push-<repository> alone), made and removed with its ServiceAccount; each bound to nereus-system/nereus-api alone. The Nereid holds what they grant (RBAC's escalation rule), and its admission policy holds their exact shape. The policy nereus-api-push-tokens stays as a second lock: the API asks only tokens of push-* in builds, for a registry audience, of at most 600 seconds.
  • Open: the API still holds create and update of ValidatingAdmissionPolicies (#1322), so it could change nereus-api-push-tokens; a follow-up issue takes it.

test/scene-registry-reef publishes with KUBECONFIG=/nonexistent, against a stand-in realm, and the same tag again is refused.

docs.title: 0022. A reef adds a screen to the portal as a Web Component its Nereid serves, named in its contract
docs.text:
In short

A reef adds a screen to the portal as a Web Component its Nereid serves, named in its contract, loaded at runtime. Status: Accepted (2026-11-08).

Status: Accepted (2026-11-08)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The portal (spec 0008, #729) is a PWA with no build and no framework: static/index.html, app.js and app.css, served by the nereus-portal Nereid on port 8081. It forwards /v1/* to the Nereus API (ADR 0018, the one door) and sends a Content Security Policy of default-src 'self', connect-src 'self' <issuer origin> and frame-ancestors 'none'. Reefs and their Nereids extend the CLI with their own commands (ADR 0004), and reefs are installed at runtime (ADR 0010); the portal has no such extension point, and #46 asks that "a new Controller adds screens without a portal release".

The owner asked on 2026-11-06 "microfrontends? Module? How?" (#1102, Tide in the portal; this is its step 1, #1103). Tide, the idea timeline, is the first screen that belongs to a reef that is not the portal: the ideas reef. The tabs already planned as portal features (#740 status, #750 orders, #777 threads) show the platform's own state, not a reef's.

The Nereid's contract today is GET / on its controller port (8080, inside the cluster only), an object such as {"name": "nereus-portal", "commands": []}. Errors follow ADR 0012: what happened, the cause, how to check, how to fix, in one line per field.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A reef adds a screen to the portal as a Web Component its Nereid serves. The options weighed:

Option What it is Fits Against Module of the portal One more tab in controllers/nereus-portal/static/ The fastest first slice Every capability needs a portal release; the portal grows to know every reef, the opposite of ADR 0004, ADR 0010 and #46 Microfrontend at runtime, Web Components The reef's Nereid serves an ES module that defines a custom element; its contract names it; the portal loads it when the reef is installed Mirrors ADR 0004 for the portal; no build and no framework, like the portal; same origin, so the CSP stays 'self' A small contract to design and keep stable Module Federation Webpack or Rspack federated bundles Mature for big SPA teams Needs a build and a shared runtime; the portal has neither single-spa A root config that mounts apps Framework-agnostic A second router and lifecycle on top of a 200-line app iframe The Nereid serves a whole page, framed Strong isolation Breaks the PWA's theme, language and sign-in; frame-ancestors 'none' today Backstage plugin The wasp-idp path (#30) Ecosystem A Backstage instance the portal does not have

The contract gains a screens list, versioned by a contractVersion field (an integer, 1 with this ADR; a Nereid with no contractVersion serves no screen). Each entry has exactly these fields; an unknown field makes the entry ignored, never half-loaded:

{
  "name": "doris",
  "commands": [],
  "contractVersion": 1,
  "screens": [
    {"tab": "Tide", "element": "nereus-tide", "module": "tide.js", "icon": "waves"}
  ],
  "assets": ["tide.css"],
  "uiPort": 8082
}
  • tab: the label of the tab. element: the custom element's tag name, which must start with nereus- and contain a hyphen. module: a file name of the Nereid's ui/ folder, no slash and no dot segment, ending in .js. icon: the name of an icon the portal already has, else the reef's own icon (below), else a default.
  • The portal's Nereid reads the screens from each Nereid's status.screens (the SDK copies the contract's list there, so the cluster holds one list and the API reads what Nereids publish, ADR 0018), and the portal asks the API for them (GET /v1/screens, built in #1105). A tab shows only while its reef is installed.

The portal's Nereid forwards /reefs/<reef>/ui/<file>, not the API (the open point of #1103, decided as recommended). The forward serves static files only, from an allow-list built from the contracts: GET only, a file that some screens entry names (module) or that sits in the Nereid's ui/ folder and is listed by the same contract in assets (an optional list of file names, such as a stylesheet or an icon), no query, no dot segment, backslash or percent-encoded slash (the check /v1 already has). It forwards to the reef's Nereid on its controller port, GET /ui/<file>, which answers only files it listed in the contract; anything else is 404. A Nereid may serve ui/ on a port of its own instead, named by the contract's optional uiPort (an integer from 1024 to 65535, copied to its status like screens; #1108), so a NetworkPolicy opens that port to the portal's pods without opening the Nereid's data, since it holds a port, not a path; the forward then targets that port. Same origin, so the CSP stays 'self' and no header is relaxed. The API does not carry code: it carries data.

The element's interface. The portal creates the element with document.createElement(element) after import("/reefs/<reef>/ui/<module>") and sets, as properties and never as globals:

  • api: an object with get(path), post(path, body) and delete(path), each a fetch bound to /v1 with the person's token; the token itself is never given. A path outside /v1 is refused.
  • lang: pt-BR or en, set again when the person switches the language.
  • The theme as CSS custom properties the portal defines on :root (--nereus-bg, --nereus-fg, --nereus-muted, --nereus-accent, --nereus-border, --nereus-radius, --nereus-font), which cross the shadow boundary; the palette follows prefers-color-scheme as the portal's does.
  • The element owns its shadow DOM (mode open) and its styles; the portal's CSS does not reach it.
  • The element reads and writes data only through /v1 (ADR 0018), never from the screen to the Nereid directly: connect-src has no other origin, so the browser enforces it.
  • It dispatches nereus-error (a CustomEvent whose detail has the ADR 0012 fields message, cause, check and fix) when it cannot work, and the portal shows that line in the tab. It sets no title, route or history of its own.
  • It may dispatch nereus-focus (a CustomEvent whose detail.focused is true or false) when it shows one item and when it goes back to its list (#1761): while focused, the portal hides its mark, its language switch and its tab bar, and the screen takes the whole view, as a phone app hides its tabs inside a detail.
  • It may dispatch nereus-signin (a CustomEvent whose detail.resume is a small JSON value, at most 1 KB) when a call still answers 401 after the portal's renewal, the sign-in having ended (#1910): the portal signs in again by a full redirect and, back, opens that screen at once and sets its resume property to that value before api, so the screen reopens where it was.

Each reef has its own icon (#1773, amended 2026-11-24): its Nereid's image declares it in the label <API_GROUP>/icon, next to /reef, /requires and /nereid, as the name of an icon of the portal's set (Material Symbols, filled, an underscore written as a hyphen: inventory-2), checked as a screen's icon is. A label, not a field of the contract: every Nereid's image has labels, while only some publish a contract, and a reef with no screen (metrics, release) still needs an icon for its status rows. nereus nereid apply copies the label to the Nereid's spec.icon, leaving a bad name out; GET /v1/status gives each row its reef's icon (the first Nereid by name whose first reef it is, then one that serves it next to its own), and core and the reefs the API keeps (tenancy, teams) get theirs from the CLI, having no image; GET /v1/screens gives a screen with no icon of its own its reef's; nereus reef get prints it. The portal draws a row's icon, else its reef's screen's (an older API), else the default; a name it does not have draws the default too. A reef's own SVG, served by its Nereid, is a later decision (#2206).

When a module fails to load (a 404, a syntax error, a customElements.define that throws, the element never defined within 10 seconds, or a nereus-error), the tab shows the error line of ADR 0012, with the reef and the file named, and the rest of the portal keeps working. The portal never retries on its own; the person reloads the tab.

The portal's built-in tabs (#740, #750, #777) stay modules of the portal: they are the platform's own, not a reef's, and need no contract.

Tide is the first consumer: the ideas reef's Nereid doris serves tide.js, which defines <nereus-tide>, and reads its notes from GET /v1/ideas/notes (#1107). It proves the extension point against a real screen, not an abstract one.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Custom Elements and Shadow DOM (WHATWG HTML Standard, custom elements): the browser's own component model, with no library; the contract is one tag name and one module.
