  • Backstage's frontend plugins (backstage.io): the portal loads a plugin's UI at runtime; Nereus keeps the idea and drops the build and the framework.
  • Module Federation (module-federation.io) and single-spa (single-spa.js.org): the microfrontend patterns weighed above; the pattern is the same (an independent team ships a screen), the mechanism here is the platform's.
  • Micro Frontends (micro-frontends.org, Cam Jackson on martinfowler.com): the case for Web Components as the integration contract between a shell and its parts.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The same contract carries a reef's MCP tools (ADR 0029, a tools list read with contractVersion 2), served by the Nereus API at /mcp.
  • A reef adds a screen with no portal release: install the reef and its Nereid, and the tab appears.
  • The Nereid SDK and templates/nereid learn the screens, assets and contractVersion fields and serve ui/ (#1105 builds the portal's side and the SDK's).
  • The portal's Nereid gains a read of the Nereids' status and a forward to another Nereid's controller port; its admission policy and Role change in the same issue. A screens entry cannot make the portal fetch anything outside the allow-list.
  • A reef's screen runs code in the portal's origin, with the person's token reachable through api. Installing a reef is therefore trusting its code as the portal's own (OWASP A08); the allow-list and the 'self' CSP limit where it can reach, not what it does with the data it may read. A signed module is a later decision.
  • The contract is versioned: a change that breaks an element's interface raises contractVersion, and the portal loads only the versions it knows, with the ADR 0012 line for the others.
  • Until v1.0.0 this ADR is rewritten in place when the decision changes (ADR 0001).

docs.title: Origin
docs.text: Decided as a recommendation on 2026-11-06 and 2026-11-08 in #1102 and #1103, from the owner's question about microfrontends; raw data in #pontos/raw/2026-11-06/ (Drive) for the voice session of that day. The reef's own icon was approved by the owner on 2026-11-24 in #1773, after #1838 gave the portal its icon set.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Signing the modules a Nereid serves, so the portal loads only code a Mandate approved.
  • Whether a screen may offer a command to the CLI as well, as ADR 0004 does for commands.
  • Isolating a reef's screen from the portal's origin (a sandboxed iframe or an origin of its own, with a narrow API over postMessage), so its code cannot reach the person's token; until then the portal keeps the browser's own fetch before any reef module loads, and its forward follows no redirect and sets each file's type from its extension (#1105).

docs.title: 0023. An external registry's push credential is the Repository's secret, read by the Nereid, never on the person's machine
docs.text:
In short

An external registry's push credential is the Repository's secretRef, read by the Nereid through a SecretBinding, never on the person's machine. Status: Proposed.

Status: Proposed

docs.title: 1229 (publishing goes through the platform) asks for nereus release source publish: a chart goes to an external OCI registry, ghcr.io/getnereus first, with no token on the person's machine, and the Source shows its digest. Until now, #850 (promote the seed images and the chart to ghcr.io/getnereus) copies by digest with crane and the owner's own token, on the owner's machine.
docs.text: The pieces are there. The release reef's Repository already has a secretRef, a secret of the secrets reef. A SecretBinding turns a secret into a Kubernetes Secret in a namespace the vault allows. The registry reef (ADR 0021) already takes a person's upload with a ten-minute token of a push identity, through a port-forward, with crane in a container (#1010). Each Registry also has a read identity whose ten-minute tokens a Nereid may ask for (#1187).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
An external registry's push credential is the target Repository's secretRef, read by the Nereid through a SecretBinding, never on the person's machine.

  • The secret holds one key, config.json, a docker configuration for the registry's host. The Nereid never opens it, so it does not care whose token is inside: a person's token today, a GitHub App's later (#1250, GitHub App token from the scm connection).
  • The CLI packages the chart with helm package and builds its OCI artifact with Helm's media types. It uploads the artifact to a Registry of the cluster as nereus registry repository publish uploads an image, to the registry Repository chart-<chart>. Then it applies the Source with spec.publish.from, the upload by digest. The registry reef is required, and the command says so when it is missing.
  • The Nereid of the Source's Mandate (flux today) asks a SecretBinding of the secret in its own namespace, for the copy alone, and deletes it once the copy is done. Before asking it, the Nereid checks that spec.publish.from names a Registry's own internal address, so a token never goes to another host.
  • The copy is a Job of three crane containers, each with only its own credential: pull reads the upload with a ten-minute read token of the Registry, push writes it to the target at its version's tag, and digest reads the tag's digest back. The Nereid compares that digest with the uploaded one, as scripts/registry/promote does. On a match it writes status.digest and the Source is Ready (Published), otherwise PublishFailed with crane's last line.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Flux's HelmRepository.spec.secretRef and OCIRepository.spec.secretRef name a docker configuration Secret the controller reads, never the user.
  • crane copy (go-containerregistry) copies by digest, and Helm pushes charts as OCI artifacts with the media types used here (Helm 3.8+, helm push).
  • GitHub Actions' GITHUB_TOKEN and the GitHub App tokens of #1250: a short-lived token held by the platform, not a personal one.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No person ever holds the external registry's credential; whoever may write the secret in the vault decides who publishes. The credential sits in nereus-system only while a copy runs.
  • The chart is pushed by tag, so Helm finds it by version, and checked by digest. A version uploaded before with another digest is refused, both in the cluster's Registry and at a target that forbids overwrites.
  • The flux Nereid gains a Role on Jobs, their Secrets and their Pods' logs in nereus-system, plus a read token of a Registry's read ServiceAccount, held by an admission policy to registry-*, the Registry's own audience and ten minutes (the same policy the kubernetes Nereid has, #1187).
  • The scene stands in for ghcr.io with a second Registry of the cluster, whose push token is the secret's content.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-11-08 on #1229 (the CLI flow, the Source's fields, the credential, the copy Job and this ADR). Raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-08/.

docs.title: 1250 replaces the personal token with a GitHub App token minted from the scm connection, with no change here: the secret's content changes, not who reads it.
0024. The scm reef: a Connection names a source host's organisation, reached through the App its scm Mandate names
docs.text:
In short

An scm reef holds what a source host is to Nereus: a Connection names an organisation, reached through the App its scm Mandate names, and a Mirror copies a repository. Status: Proposed.

Status: Proposed

docs.title: 927 asks Nereus to reach a source host as an application, not as a person. The first need is the catalog Nereid (#904): getnereus/nereus is private, so its entries report SourceResolved False SourceUnreachable ("a private one needs a connection"). Three more wait on the same answer: #1070 (a Build clones a private repository with a token minted for that build alone), #1250 (publishing to ghcr.io with a short-lived App token instead of a personal one) and #1255 (the forgejo Nereid mirrors a GitHub repository into the cluster).
docs.text:
The first version of this ADR put everything in the scm reef: the GitHub App (its id and key, with a vendor flag), a command to verify it and the Token lent to a consumer. Two of those are not a source host's concern: the App is the platform's identity towards GitHub, which #234 (the platform's own identity towards external systems) asks to keep in one place, and the token serves #1250, which publishes a package and reads no source. ADR 0006 (the authentication reef) now holds both: the App is a Mandate of the github Nereid, and the Token is a kind of the authentication reef.

What exists: nereus secrets create seals a value on the client with the vault Mandate's public key, and a SecretBinding turns a secret into a Kubernetes Secret in a namespace the vault allows; ADR 0023 (an external registry's push credential) has a Nereid read its credential that way, never the person. A working version exists outside this repository (wasp-idp's scm connection, its ADR 0025), with the per-organisation statuses this ADR keeps.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
An scm reef, scm.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, holds what a source host is to Nereus: an organisation reached, a repository mirrored, a push received. Who the platform is towards the host belongs to the authentication reef (ADR 0006). One writer per field (ADR 0005); the commands follow ADR 0013 (command conventions), and the deck is docs/specs/cli/reefs/scm.yaml.

Kind spec (the person, or a Nereid as a client) status (the Nereid only) Mirror from (a public https://<host>/<owner>/<repository>), interval (10m by default), mandate observedGeneration, conditions, nereid, mandate, repository, url, branch, commit, lastSync Connection (default) org, mandate (an scm Mandate, ADR 0011; empty: the reef's default), default observedGeneration, conditions, nereid, mandate, installationId, repositorySelection, permissions 
nereus nereid apply github --reef authentication --reef scm
nereus mandate create github-scm --reef scm --nereid github --param identity=github --default
nereus scm connection create example --org example
# ✓ scm/connections/example created (mandate github-scm)
nereus mandate create github-scm-labs --reef scm --nereid github --param identity=other-app
nereus scm connection create labs --org example-labs --mandate github-scm-labs
  • A Connection is one organisation of one host, reached through the App its scm Mandate names (owner, 2026-11-09). It names no vendor, no App and no key. --mandate keeps ADR 0011's meaning, a Mandate of the object's own reef: an scm Mandate, with none the reef's default. That Mandate's param identity names the authentication Mandate whose App reaches the organisation (ADR 0006); a second App is a second scm Mandate, so no command gains a flag that points into another reef. The host is the Nereid's, never an attribute the API reads.
  • The statuses are per organisation and stay on the Connection, in this order: NotInstalled (the App is not installed on the organisation), NotAllRepositories (installed on a selection), MissingPermissions (less than asked), Ready. There is no verify command: nereus scm connection get and list show the status.
  • Permissions start at metadata and contents read (owner, 2026-11-09), the least #904 needs. A feature that needs more widens them in its own issue, and the Connection reports MissingPermissions until the App's owner accepts the new ones.
  • --default on a Connection, one in the reef. A second default is refused.
  • One github Nereid serves both reefs, opt-in (owner, 2026-11-09): nereus nereid apply github --reef authentication --reef scm. The internal-developer-platform profile does not install it, since it needs an App the person owns. The scm reef's own Mandate says which Nereid serves Connections and, through identity, which App they use; Mandate names are global, so it takes its own name by the convention <nereid>-<reef> (github-scm; owner, 2026-11-09), which a second host follows too (forgejo).
  • The App has one webhook, received by the scm reef (owner, 2026-11-09): the webhook's secret is a param of the authentication Mandate (the App's), and its URL points at the scm reef's receiver, which checks the signature before anything reads the event. The push webhook of #914 (a push starts a build) builds on it.
  • Mirror copies one public repository into the cluster, with no Connection (#1255, owner, 2026-11-10): a public source needs no App. It goes through an scm Mandate like a Connection, and the CLI refuses one whose Nereid does not list mirrors in its status.kinds. The forgejo Nereid serves it through its own Mandate forgejo; the internal-developer-platform profile installs it, with forgejo as the scm reef's default, since the profile runs on open source and the github Nereid is not in it; a github-scm Mandate takes the default only when asked (#1327, owner, 2026-11-11): Forgejo from its upstream Helm chart through the release reef, on SQLite, its admin sealed into the secrets reef, copying from github.com only unless the setting MIRROR_ALLOWED_DOMAINS adds a host. One Mirror per place (<owner>/<repository>, any case); the oldest keeps it, the other is Taken.
  • No Token here: a consumer that needs to read a repository asks the authentication reef's Token (ADR 0006, #1274).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• GitHub, Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App: the installation and its repository selection, which the Connection's status reports.
  • GitHub, Validating webhook deliveries: the HMAC signature the scm reef's receiver checks.
  • Flux, GitRepository, and Argo CD, Private repositories: both reach GitHub with a GitHub App's credential held by the controller, never by the person.
  • wasp-idp's scm connection and its ADR 0025 (SCM connections in the platform API): the per-organisation statuses, ported here with Nereus's verbs.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The catalog Nereid resolves a private repository's commit with an authentication Token (#1274), with no Connection needed; SourceUnreachable stays for a repository no App reaches.
  • Another host needs only another Nereid serving both reefs: the commands and kinds stay.
  • OWASP A01 (broken access control: a Connection exposes an organisation's status, never a credential) and A08 (software and data integrity failures: a webhook event is trusted only after its signature checks) are the categories this reef touches; the key and the token are ADR 0006's.

Origin: the owner's cut of #927 into #1272, #1273, #1274 and #1275, and the decisions above, on 2026-11-09. Raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-09/.

Rewritten 2026-11-09 from the owner's decisions on #927 (the App is a Mandate of the authentication reef, the Token is its kind, no --vendor, no verify; #1280); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-09/.

docs.title: 1281 builds the Connection and the receiver, after #1273 (the github Nereid's Mandate); #927 closes with it.
0025. The platform receives metrics from anywhere through the CLI and the Nereus API: declared sources, a spool, late-send alerts with a heartbeat, and machine identities
docs.text:
In short

Metrics enter only through the Nereus API, with the CLI as the official client: declared sources, a spool, late-send alerts with a heartbeat, and machine identities. Status: Accepted (2026-11-14, by the owner; proposed the same day).

Status: Accepted (2026-11-14, by the owner; proposed the same day)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The owner asked on 2026-11-14 for one official way for the platform to receive metrics from anywhere: external scripts, external pipelines, agents through MCP, a laptop or a server that only drops files in a folder. The first client is the decision metrics of the journeys work (how many decisions wait for the owner, how long each waits), which the owner wants sent through the CLI from day zero, so the channel exists before anything else depends on it. The owner's words: the sending "must be well designed from day zero".

What exists today:

  • The metrics reef only scrapes. Its victoriametrics Nereid runs a VMAgent and a VMSingle in nereus-system; nothing outside the cluster can write a sample. #783 closes the push endpoint VMAgent opens by default, since any pod could forge series the portal shows as a Nereid's signals (#744); #784 puts vmauth in front of VictoriaMetrics and keeps its import and delete unrouted.
  • The Nereus API is the one door (ADR 0018), and it has no metrics route.
  • Authentication knows people and the platform's own identity outwards (ADR 0006: OIDC logins for a User, Mandates for a GitHub App), but no machine that signs in to the platform on its own: a systemd unit on a laptop cannot run nereus login in a browser.
  • Nereus assumes no vendor: the store, the registry and the git host are configured, so nothing in this channel may depend on VictoriaMetrics, Keycloak or GitHub.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Metrics enter the platform only through the Nereus API, and the CLI is the official client. A script, a pipeline, a cron job and an agent all send through nereus metrics send, or call the same route the CLI calls; nothing writes to the store directly. The route belongs to the metrics reef's API group, metrics.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009); no separate intake reef.

docs.title: A source is declared before it sends
docs.text:
A MetricSource is the metrics reef's first kind. It names the metric names a source may write, who may send as it, and how late it may be:

nereus metrics source create journeys \
  --owner project/nereus \
  --prefix journeys_ \
  --late-after 2h \
  --quiet-after 1d \
  --max-age 7d \
  --machine owner-laptop
  • --prefix is the only namespace the source may write: journeys_decisions_open is accepted, nereid_requests_total is refused. The API refuses a prefix that overlaps another source's (journeys_ and journeys_x_). Reserved for the platform and the tools it runs: nereus_, kube_, container_, vm_, up and ALERTS.
  • --owner is an Organization or a Project (ADR 0015); only a person who may create resources in that owner may create the source.
  • --late-after, --quiet-after and --max-age drive the late-send alerts and the accepted delay (below).
  • --machine binds the machine identities that may send as this source; any person allowed in the owner may send too.
  • The standard verbs of ADR 0013 apply: create, apply, list, get, delete. Every source is declared; there is no source made on the fly.

docs.title: Sending
docs.text:
# One sample
nereus metrics send journeys \
  --name journeys_decisions_open \
  --value 3 \
  --label journey=continuous-deploy

# A batch, JSON Lines from a file or a pipe
some-script | nereus metrics send journeys --file -

# Nothing to send: only says the source is alive
nereus metrics send journeys --heartbeat
  • The wire format is versioned JSON Lines (application/vnd.nereus.metrics.v1+jsonl), one sample per line: name, value, kind (counter, cumulative; gauge; or histogram, with its buckets), labels and timestamp (RFC 3339, required). The kinds follow OpenTelemetry's metric data model, so an OTLP entry for pipelines is one more decoder behind the same route. Names and labels follow Prometheus' rules; NaN and infinities are refused.
  • The CLI stamps the timestamp when a sample is made, never when it is sent. That makes every send idempotent with no key to remember: a retry repeats the same series and timestamp, which the store keeps once, while the same value sent at 10:00 and at 11:00 stays two samples.
  • The API stamps the labels that say where a sample came from: source and the source's owner. A sample that carries either, any label under getnereus.dev/, or job, instance, namespace or nereid, is refused: an outside sample never passes for a Nereid's signal, the risk #783 closes for VMAgent. Who sent it (a person or a machine) is not a label, so rotating a machine's key or sending once as a person does not split a series; it goes to the audit log.
  • The audit log keeps one line per request: when, the principal, the source, the samples accepted and refused.
  • The accepted window: a timestamp no older than the source's --max-age (default 7 days, so a laptop off for a long weekend still drains its spool) and no later than 5 minutes ahead (a clock ahead is always an error).
  • Limits, checked before parsing: request body 1 MiB, after decompression too; line length; 1000 samples per request; 1000 series per source; 60 requests per minute per source. Each is a default the MetricSource may override. A refused sample is named in the answer with its reason; the rest of the batch is accepted.
  • The metrics Nereid writes, the API does not. The API validates and stamps, then hands the batch to the metrics reef's Nereid, over the cluster network and with a credential of its own (a NetworkPolicy alone is the weakness #784 corrects). Only the Nereid writes to its store; another store (Mimir, a cloud's managed Prometheus) is another Nereid of the same reef, with the route and the CLI unchanged.
  • MCP: the Nereus API's /mcp exposes metrics_send, a tool the reef declares (ADR 0029), which calls the same route as the person. The portal escapes every label value it shows.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry: OTLP on the same route
docs.text:
Pipelines and services that already speak OpenTelemetry send without the CLI, through an OpenTelemetry Collector or an SDK exporter (owner, 2026-11-14):

# An OpenTelemetry Collector exporting to Nereus
exporters:
  otlphttp/nereus:
    endpoint: https://api.example.com/v1/metrics/sources/ci-pipeline
    auth:
      authenticator: nereus_machine   # a Machine's token, never a stored API key
  • Same route, another decoder: OTLP/HTTP (application/x-protobuf and application/json) is told apart by its content type. The source comes from the route and the token, never from an attribute; every rule above (prefix, reserved labels, limits, the accepted window, the audit log, the two clocks) holds the same.
  • Resource and scope attributes become labels, under the same refusals; an attribute that maps to a reserved label is refused, not renamed.
  • Histograms are accepted, explicit-bucket and exponential, since latency comes as a histogram from every SDK. The JSON Lines format gains the same kind (histogram, with its buckets), so the CLI and OTLP stay equal.
  • Delta temporality is converted to cumulative by the API, per series, so the store keeps one temporality. A delta series whose start time goes backwards (a restart) starts a new cumulative series, as the OpenTelemetry Collector's delta-to-cumulative processor does.
  • Summaries are refused with a reason: their quantiles cannot be aggregated, and OpenTelemetry keeps them only for compatibility.

docs.title: The spool: a folder of ready files
docs.text:
A machine that only produces files sends them by pointing the CLI at a folder:

nereus metrics spool /var/spool/nereus-metrics --source journeys
  • The folder is 0700, and a file is ready when it is in ready/. A producer writes tmp/<name>.jsonl and renames it into ready/ once complete, as Maildir does. The CLI reads only regular files up to a size limit and refuses symlinks.
  • ready/ is the truth: whatever is in it is still to send. Files go in name order, one request each. The watermark (state/watermark, written atomically) records only the last file sent and when; a file found in ready/ whose name sorts before it is still sent, and the CLI reports it.
  • What each answer does to a file:
Answer The file 2xx, all accepted moves to sent/ (kept --keep 7d, then deleted) 2xx, part refused moves to sent/; the refused lines go to rejected/<name>.jsonl with their reasons 400, 422 moves to rejected/ with <name>.reason 401, 403 stays in ready/; the run stops and says why 408, 429, 5xx, network stays in ready/, retried with backoff
  • One stuck file never blocks the queue: after a number of failed tries the CLI goes on with the next and reports the stuck one in its lag.
  • One run at a time: the CLI holds a lock on state/lock.
  • Every run is a heartbeat: a run with nothing in ready/ still makes contact. A one-shot run in a systemd timer is the lightest setup; --watch keeps the process up. Both are the same code.
  • Every run reports its own lag: the age of the oldest file in ready/ and the count of files in rejected/ travel with each request, and the API keeps them in the source's status.

docs.title: Late-send alerts and the heartbeat
docs.text:
A source has two clocks, both in its status, written by the API:

Clock Moves on Past its limit lastSeenTime every contact: samples or a heartbeat --late-after: condition Receiving=False, reason Late (the source is silent) lastReceivedTime accepted samples only --quiet-after, optional: reason Quiet (alive, but no data)
  • A spool that does not drain is reason Backlog: the source makes contact, but its reported lag grows.
  • A source that never sent counts from its creation, so a timer that never ran is caught.
  • The API compares, not the store: the logic lives with the MetricSource, so it holds with any store.
  • When the API itself was down, every source's clock restarts when it comes back, and one alert says the API was down, instead of one per source.
  • Quiet is only for a source that declares data must flow; a source that sends only when something happens leaves --quiet-after out.
  • Where an alert is delivered (the portal, a push to the phone, a spoken summary) is the notifications question of #278, outside this ADR.

docs.title: The source's health, kept as metrics by the platform
docs.text:
A heartbeat writes no sample of the source's, but the contact is not lost: the API records every request as the platform's own series, in the reserved nereus_ namespace, so a source's health has a history like any other signal.

Series What it says nereus_intake_requests_total{source, kind} contacts, kind = samples or heartbeat nereus_intake_samples_total{source, result} samples accepted or refused, with reason on refused nereus_intake_last_seen_timestamp{source} the last contact nereus_intake_last_received_timestamp{source} the last accepted sample nereus_intake_spool_lag_seconds{source} the oldest file still in ready/, as the spool reported it nereus_intake_spool_rejected{source} files in rejected/

A source is healthy when its condition Receiving is True: seen within --late-after, data within --quiet-after when declared, a spool lag under --late-after, and refused samples under 5% of the last hour (reason Refusing above it). nereus metrics source get journeys shows the condition, its reason and the two clocks; the series give the history the portal draws.

docs.title: Machine identities
docs.text:
A machine signs in on its own, with no browser and no shared secret, and the same way on every installation.

  • A Machine is a kind of core (core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1), beside User (ADR 0006): the platform generates its id, and no authentication Nereid owns it.
  • Its credential is a key pair made on the machine. nereus machine create owner-laptop generates the key locally (mode 0600, never sent anywhere) and registers only the public key on the Machine. Creating a machine needs a person's login, through the device flow of ADR 0006 on a server with no browser.
  • The Nereus API checks the machine, not a login Nereid (owner, 2026-11-14): the CLI signs a short assertion (jti used once, aud the API, exp of a minute) and the API verifies it against the Machine's public key, then answers with a short token of its own, valid only for the sources that name the machine. It is the model of a GitHub App's JWT, and it holds with Keycloak, Auth0 or any other login Nereid. This is the one exception to "every login is OIDC" of ADR 0006, which points here.
  • A machine can do only what it is bound to: sending as the sources that name it in --machine. It reads nothing and creates nothing else, until another ADR grants more.
  • Revoking is one command, nereus machine delete owner-laptop, and a new key is nereus machine rotate owner-laptop; a token already given stays valid until it expires, in minutes.
  • Pipelines, later: a private key in a pipeline's secret store is a shared secret in practice; a Machine that trusts the pipeline's own OIDC issuer and subject (federation, no stored key) is the next step, outside this ADR.

docs.title: The order of the work
docs.text:
A walking skeleton, the first data before the riskiest part (owner, 2026-11-14):

  1. The MetricSource kind, with its prefix and its clocks.
  2. The API route, with the person's token that exists today.
  3. nereus metrics send, with --heartbeat.
  4. status.lastSeenTime, status.lastReceivedTime and the conditions.
  5. The journeys' decision metrics script sending for real.
  6. The spool, one-shot, in a systemd timer.
  7. Machine: until then, a laptop sends with the refresh token of a device-flow login.
  8. OTLP on the same route, with histograms and delta conversion, after Machine, since a pipeline signs in as one.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Prometheus, When to use the Pushgateway: the push channel to avoid, since it keeps series of dead jobs forever and knows nothing of who pushed; the declared source and the late-send alert answer both.
  • OpenTelemetry, Metrics data model and OTLP/HTTP: the kinds this ADR uses and the entry for pipelines; the Collector's deltatocumulativeprocessor: the conversion the API does.
  • Datadog, Submit metrics: an HTTP intake with a key per source and the source stamped by the server.
  • Healthchecks.io and Cronitor: the dead man's switch, a job that pings within its period plus a grace time, with no data; Prometheus' absent_over_time is the same idea in a rule.
  • Maildir (D. J. Bernstein): write in tmp/, rename into place, so a reader never sees a partial file.
  • Fluent Bit's filesystem buffering and Promtail's positions file: a local spool with a checkpoint, so a restart resumes where it stopped.
  • GitHub, Authenticating as a GitHub App: a short JWT signed with a key the App keeps, exchanged for a short token.
  • RFC 7523 (JWT profile for OAuth 2.0 client authentication): the shape of the assertion (iss, aud, exp, jti).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The decision metrics of the journeys work become the first source; a later move of the decisions from GitHub to the Nereus API changes their script, not the channel.
  • The Nereus API gains the metrics route, the machine sign-in and an audit log; the metrics reef gains its first kind, and contracts.REEFS_WITHOUT_KINDS loses metrics.
  • The metrics Nereid gains a write endpoint reachable only from the API, with a credential.
  • Core gains Machine, and ADR 0006 points here for machines.
  • OWASP A01 (broken access control: a source writes only its prefix, a machine only its sources), A03 (injection: label values escaped where shown), A04 (insecure design: limits before parsing), A07 (identification and authentication failures: no shared secret, single-use assertions, short tokens) and A09 (logging failures: the audit log) are the categories this touches.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Where the API keeps the used jti values when it runs more than one replica.
  • The number of failed tries before the spool goes past a stuck file.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-11-14 in a session on per-agent journeys and decision envelopes (#1536), with a second opinion read before each. Raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-14/.

docs.title: 0026. The environment reef: an Environment is only the request, and the kept cluster is nereus
docs.text:
In short

The environment reef has one kind, Environment, which is only the request; the cluster kept for it is nereus. Status: Proposed (2026-11-14).

Status: Proposed (2026-11-14)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The Environment kind and the vcluster Nereid exist (#620), installed by the internal-developer-platform profile (#827), and a release Target with an environmentRef delivers into that Environment's cluster through the flux Nereid (#828). No ADR records the reef: what a person writes, what a Nereid writes, and how the release reef finds where to deliver. ADR 0010 (reefs at runtime) says only that the environment "knows the cluster and its credentials".

The kept k3d cluster, k3d-nereus, runs Triton and serves as production, but no Nereid knows it: #556 (two local k3d clusters at most) calls it production, and #159 and #160 (the always-on environment deployed from main) call it live. ADR 0017 (resource reefs) is Accepted and settles how a request picks its Mandate; this reef is its first user with two Nereids. #568 asked for the refinement, in the design session of 2026-10-30 on the catalog (#559), the tenancy (#21) and the resource reefs (#560).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
An Environment is only the request. The reef is environment.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, with one cluster-scoped kind, Environment. One writer per field (ADR 0005):

Field Writer What it holds spec.owner the person who it is for, {kind, name} in the tenancy tree (ADR 0015) spec.region the person optional, where it should run spec.expires the person optional, a duration after which it goes away spec.mandate the person optional, the Mandate to go through, by name status.nereid, status.mandate, status.phase the Nereid who made it, through which Mandate, and its state status.expiresAt the Nereid creationTimestamp plus spec.expires status.kubernetes.context, status.kubernetes.secretRef the Nereid how to reach a Kubernetes environment: a context name and a reference to the Secret holding its kubeconfig

spec names no technology (ADR 0002, the model): the person never names a cluster type, a provider or a Tool. A kept cluster, a vcluster, Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps or AWS Fargate are each a Nereid behind a Mandate, and each writes what it made in status. Credentials are never inline: secretRef points at a Kubernetes Secret today, and the secrets reef (#529) takes the kubeconfig over when it exists, without changing the field.

The Mandate is the one named, else the reef's default (ADR 0017's order, steps 3 and 4: no match key fits an environment's request today). The vcluster Nereid's Mandate is the reef's default, so every environment a person asks for, a PR's included, is a vcluster unless it names another Mandate. The kept cluster is the only environment that names one: nereus init creates it with --mandate local. match gets no expires key: ADR 0017 compares values, and "has an expiry" is a presence test (owner, 2026-11-14). Each Nereid acts only on the Environments whose Mandate names it, so the vcluster and k3d Nereids share the reef without touching each other's objects, as the vcluster Nereid already does.

The kept k3d cluster is the Environment nereus, the name of the k3d cluster itself (owner, 2026-11-23, #2150). The name is a disposable label like any other environment's, never prod: migrating data, restoring a backup, or swapping the cluster under a Workload changes the environment, not the Workload, all through the platform. It replaces production in #556 and live in #159 and #160 with one name.

A k3d Nereid registers nereus (a stand-in). It runs in the local-nereids image and knows only the cluster it runs in: it adopts that cluster for an Environment whose Mandate names it, writes status.kubernetes, refuses to make a second one, and never deletes the cluster; deleting nereus removes only the record. Only a Nereid writes its reef's status (ADR 0002), so nereus init asks for nereus like a person would and does not write its status, and the release reef reads nereus like any other environment (owner, 2026-11-14). It retires when a real environment Nereid makes clusters. #575 (the reef's first slice) builds it.

At expires, the Nereid that made the environment removes it, writes Expired in status.phase, and leaves the Environment until nereus environment delete, so the history stays visible. The vcluster Nereid already does it; nereus takes no expires.

The release reef finds its target in the Environment's status. A release Mandate's match on environment (ADR 0017) picks the Nereid that knows how to deliver there: flux for a Kubernetes environment, another Nereid for Cloud Run, with the same nereus release create. A Target with no environmentRef keeps meaning the cluster Nereus runs in, which is nereus on k3d; whether a Target may name a cluster directly stays ADR 0010's open question.

Hostnames per environment belong to the edge reef. Internal hostnames <workload>.<environment>.getnereus.dev (triton.nereus.getnereus.dev) behind the public <workload>.getnereus.dev are #470's (the edge reef), not this reef's.

# The admin, once (nereus init does it on k3d)
$ nereus mandate create vcluster \
    --reef environment \
    --nereid vcluster \
    --default
✓ core/mandates/vcluster created (reef: environment, nereid: vcluster, default)

$ nereus mandate create local \
    --reef environment \
    --nereid k3d
✓ core/mandates/local created (reef: environment, nereid: k3d)

# The kept cluster, registered by nereus init
$ nereus environment create nereus \
    --owner project/nereus \
    --mandate local
✓ environment/environments/nereus created (mandate: local, nereid: k3d)

# A PR environment: the default Mandate
$ nereus environment create pr-123 \
    --owner project/nereus \
    --expires 72h
✓ environment/environments/pr-123 created (mandate: vcluster, nereid: vcluster)

$ nereus environment list
ENVIRONMENT  OWNER           NEREID    STATUS  EXPIRES
nereus        Project/nereus  k3d       Ready   -
pr-123       Project/nereus  vcluster  Ready   2d

# A release into nereus: the release reef reads its status
$ nereus release create triton \
    --source triton \
    --target nereus
✓ release/releases/triton created (mandate: flux)

nereus environment create is nereus environment environment create (ADR 0013: a kind named after its reef takes the reef's verbs). The deck is docs/specs/cli/reefs/environment.yaml.

Stand-ins: the k3d Nereid, which knows only its own cluster, until a Nereid makes clusters; the kubeconfig in a Kubernetes Secret until the secrets reef (#529) holds it; owner has nothing behind it until the authorization reef (#897).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Crossplane's claims and compositions: the person's claim names no provider; the composition the admin chose makes it and writes back its connection details, here the Mandate and the Nereid's status.
  • Kubernetes StorageClass: a default class and a class named per request, the order ADR 0017 follows here.
  • Argo CD's cluster secrets and Flux's kubeConfig.secretRef: a delivery target reached through a referenced kubeconfig, never inline.
  • Preview environments removed at an expiry, as the vcluster Nereid already does (#620).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One shape for every environment, whatever makes it: the release reef, the delivery reef (ADR 0020) and the catalog read status, never a technology.
  • nereus init gets one more step: the local Mandate and the Environment nereus, through the k3d Nereid (#575).
  • The reef has two Nereids at once, which ADR 0017 allows; neither acts on the other's Environments.
  • A new provider (Cloud Run, Fargate) is a Nereid and a Mandate, with no change to spec or to a person's command.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether a Target may name a cluster directly (ADR 0010).
  • What status a non-Kubernetes environment publishes (Cloud Run, Fargate): decided with its first Nereid.
  • Whether region takes part in match (ADR 0017 lists only engine, environment and owner).

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-10-30 in the design session on the catalog, tenancy and resource reefs (#568), and of 2026-11-14 on its visual summary (the default Mandate and the stand-in for nereus). Raw data in Drive dump-mental-prompts/opinions/2026-10-30/ and #pontos/raw/2026-11-14/.

docs.title: 0027. Teams, roles and Users: a role is bound to a team, a position or a User on a node of the tenancy tree, and the Nereus API asks before it acts
docs.text:
In short

A role is bound to a team, a position or a User on a node of the tenancy tree, and the Nereus API asks before it acts. Access roles, teams and Users are kept apart. Status: Accepted (2026-11-16).

Status: Accepted (2026-11-16)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Today the Nereus API admits one group of people, the Keycloak group nereus-admins, and refuses everyone else: there is no way to say that a person may list Environments in one Project and create them in another. #897 (refine the authorization reef: an openfga Nereid answers who may do what) chose the tool; #1306 (decide how teams, roles and Users relate) asked for the model it serves, before the teams, hiring and university reefs are designed (#1307, #1308, #1309).

Three earlier decisions frame it. ADR 0006 (authentication) makes the person a User of core, not an identity provider's sub, and says teams and authorization are the platform's job, outside the identity provider. ADR 0015 (tenancy) gives the tree, Organizations and nested Projects, whose kinds come from each instance, and sketches the permissions as OpenFGA relations over it. ADR 0013 (command conventions) gives the verbs a rule can name.

The owner's concern (2026-11-10, #1306): a person who signs in and belongs to groups that grant access overlaps with the teams reef, a set of people who may or may not have a User. Keeping two lists, groups for access and teams for work, means keeping them in sync forever.

The first slice that builds this model is spec 0011 (the first slice of teams and authorization, the journey #1644); its decisions 1 to 19 are recorded here.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Three concepts, kept apart (owner, 2026-11-10, #1306):

Concept Answers Lives in Access role what may this person do on the platform? the authorization reef: Role and Binding, on the tenancy tree Team who does this person work with, in which position? the teams reef: Team and Member A person's skills and courses what does this person know? the teams reef's Member, read later by hiring and university

"Profile" stays ADR 0014's word (the set of reefs, Nereids and Mandates an instance installs); access is a role, and skills never go on core's User, since core is only the engine.

Team, not Group (owner, 2026-11-10). Team and Member live in the teams reef, Role and Binding in the authorization reef, User in core. There is one list of members, and access derives from it: a binding names a team, so joining the team grants its access and leaving removes it. An identity provider's groups are an output, never the source: a Nereid may later write Keycloak groups from the teams.

A person is one User with several identities (ADR 0006). The subject of every check is user:<User name>, never a sub or an e-mail, so the owner's Google, Microsoft and other accounts give the same access. A token whose identity is linked to no User has no permission: having a login is not having permission. An external candidate shows the split: they sign in, become a User and may apply to an opening, but belong to no team and hold no role.

A member points to a User when the person has one (owner, 2026-11-10), and the kind foresees members with none (an open position, a contractor, an agent). In the first slice a Member names a User and spec.kind takes only person; agent joins later with agents as subjects (docs/agent/ai-and-teams.md).

A binding names a team, a position in a team, or, as the exception, one User. The position is a free, lowercase name on the Member (tech-lead): when the person in the position changes, the access follows without touching a binding. #1307's Position kind (skills, level, places) takes the same name later, and neither the binding nor the tuples change.

A team sits on one node of the tenancy tree (spec.owner: {kind, name}, required, any node: an Organization or a Project), and teams do not nest: the tree already gives the hierarchy, and access flows down it.

Roles are registered, never a fixed list (owner, 2026-11-10). A Role is an object made of rules, and a rule is <reef>:<kinds>:<verbs>, each part a comma list or *, in the words the CLI already uses: the reef as the CLI names it (environment, core), the kinds as the plurals of the routes (environments), the verbs of ADR 0013 plus can-i. It is Kubernetes RBAC's apiGroups, resources and verbs in Nereus's words.

# A role from flags
$ nereus authorization role create release-manager \
    --rule release:releases:create,apply,delete
authorization/roles/release-manager created

# The developer role to a whole team, at a Project
$ nereus authorization binding create payments-developers \
    --role developer \
    --team payments \
    --owner project/payments
authorization/bindings/payments-developers created

# The team-lead role to whoever holds a position in the team
$ nereus authorization binding create payments-leads \
    --role team-lead \
    --team payments \
    --position tech-lead \
    --owner project/payments
authorization/bindings/payments-leads created

# The exception: one User, on the whole instance
$ nereus authorization binding create ana-admin \
    --role administrator \
    --user ana
authorization/bindings/ana-admin created

Where a role and a binding hold (#1306's first question). Both take an optional spec.owner: {kind, name}: a role with none serves the whole instance, and one with an owner serves that node and the nodes under it, as Kubernetes' ClusterRole and Role; a binding with none holds on the whole instance. A binding refuses a role whose owner is neither its own node nor an ancestor of it, and a role, team or User that does not exist.

The roles (#1306's fourth and fifth questions). administrator is built in: every verb on every kind of every reef, present and future (*:*:*, so a reef installed later is covered), never changed or deleted, so nobody locks the instance out by narrowing it. It is applied with the authorization reef, not by nereus init as #1306 first said: core checks nothing until that reef is installed, so the role arrives with the reef that reads it. viewer (*:*:list,get), developer and team-lead are editable examples a person applies from the reef's samples.

Managing members is a rule like any other (teams:members:create,delete), carried by a role: who may create a role, a binding or a member is itself a rule (#1306). A position that a binding names is assigned only by who may create bindings at that binding's node, so whoever manages members cannot give themselves more access than they hold.

The objects are the source of truth; the openfga Nereid writes the tuples. Role, Binding, Team, Member, User and the tenancy nodes are objects the Nereus API keeps, as it keeps tenancy; neither reef has a Nereid for its objects, and neither Role nor Binding names OpenFGA (the API never names a Nereid). The authorization reef's Nereid, openfga, reads the objects, computes the tuples and writes only the difference; deleting OpenFGA's store loses nothing, since one pass writes it again.

One fixed OpenFGA model, versioned with the Nereid and tested with fga model test. A new role becomes tuples, never a new model. One OpenFGA type, node, serves every tenancy kind: the kinds come from each instance (ADR 0015), and a fixed model cannot name them, so a node's id is its kind in lowercase, a slash and its name (node:project/payments), under one instance:nereus. A rule becomes a grant whose condition matches the request's reef, kind and verb, so * covers what does not exist yet:

type node
  relations
    define parent: [instance, node]
    define granted: [grant#subject with rule_matches]
    define can: granted or can from parent

The question is always one check, user:<name> can on the object's node (or on instance:nereus when it has no owner), with the context {reef, kind, verb}. The whole model, its tuples and its tests are in spec 0011, "The model".

OpenFGA runs from its official Helm chart through the release reef, with Postgres through the Database kind, as the keycloak Nereid does: open source first, nothing new to invent.

The Nereus API asks before every read and write, through the authorization reef's default Mandate, never OpenFGA by name: POST /v1/check to the Mandate's Nereid with {user, verb, reef, kinds, node}, answering {allowed, bindings}. A list keeps only the objects whose owner allows list. The routes that are always open (/healthz, /v1/me, /v1/status, /v1/doctor, /.well-known/nereus-configuration) are never asked. The check covers Environments and the tenancy tree too, which reach the platform through the Nereus API since #1638 and #1639.

Fail closed: with the Nereid down, every read and write is refused, except whoami, status and doctor. An outage must never become a way to read.

nereus-admins is the emergency exit. A token in that Keycloak group passes when the normal check does not (refused, no User, or the Nereid down), the API logs it, and nereus doctor warns that the exit was used. An instance with no default Mandate of the authorization reef keeps today's rule unchanged: only nereus-admins.

The instance's root (owner, 2026-11-10). The first administrator is the instance's root, as AWS's root user or Linux's root: nereus init creates it, bound to administrator, ends with the step to create a personal administrator, and the root is kept for recovery, its sign-ins audited, MFA required, nereus doctor warning when it signs in. It is not in the first slice: until it is built, the nereus-admins exit plays its part.

Commands use singular kinds (nereus authorization role create, nereus authorization binding list), as ADR 0013 and the built decks do; #1306's sketch used plurals. --owner takes <kind>/<name> in lowercase, as nereus environment does. The commands of the slice: nereus user, nereus teams (the default kind Team) and nereus teams member, nereus authorization role (the default kind Role) and nereus authorization binding, each with ADR 0013's five verbs.

can-i is a new verb, nereus authorization can-i <verb> <reef>/<kinds>, with the shortcut nereus can-i. It asks the question the Nereus API asks, and the answer names the binding that grants it; exit code 0 for yes and 1 for no. With no --user it answers for the caller; asking about another User is itself a permission (authorization:can-i:get at that node). ADR 0013 lists it.

# May bruno create Environments in the Project payments?
$ nereus authorization can-i create environment/environments \
    --owner project/payments \
    --user bruno
no: no binding gives bruno create on environment/environments at project/payments

docs.title: Stand-ins of the first slice
docs.text: Stand-in Why Replaced by The first identity is linked by the token's verified e-mail. An administrator creates the User with its e-mail; the first sign-in of a token with email_verified: true and that e-mail links {issuer, sub}. A second identity is not linked at all. ADR 0006 links a new sub only after an e-mail code, which needs a notification reef that does not exist. The stand-in trusts the email_verified claim of the instance's own issuer, also when that issuer brokered another identity provider. ADR 0006's e-mail code through a notification reef, and nereus user identity commands for a second identity. The User's id is the object's name (core/users/ana). ADR 0006 has the platform generate the id; the first slice keeps the name, which the CLI and the bindings already use. A generated id, with the name kept as a field. nereus-admins stands in for the instance's root. The exit exists already and does not depend on OpenFGA. The root User of nereus init, with MFA and audited sign-ins (#1306).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• GitHub teams (About teams): "Teams are groups of organization members that reflect your company or group's structure", and "Organization owners and team maintainers can give teams admin, read, or write access to organization repositories". A team as both the org chart and the subject of a permission is the shape taken here. GitHub's "Child teams inherit the parent's access permissions" is the nesting left out: the tenancy tree already nests.
  • Backstage's Group and User (Descriptor format of catalog entities): "A group describes an organizational entity, such as for example a team, a business unit, or a loose collection of people", and "A user describes a person, such as an employee, a contractor, or similar", whose spec.memberOf is "The list of groups that the user is a direct member of". Team and Member keep the person apart from the team as Backstage does, with the membership on its own object so a position can sit on it.
  • Kubernetes RBAC (Using RBAC Authorization): "A Role always sets permissions within a particular namespace" and "ClusterRole, by contrast, is a non-namespaced resource"; "Permissions are purely additive (there are no "deny" rules)"; "A role binding grants the permissions defined in a role to a user or set of users. It holds a list of subjects (users, groups, or service accounts), and a reference to the role being granted." The rule of reef, kinds and verbs, the optional owner of a role and the binding are taken from it. Its "You can only create/update a role binding if you already have all the permissions contained in the referenced role ... or if you have been authorized to perform the bind verb" is the later answer to escalation through bindings; the first slice guards only positions (decision 8 of spec 0011).
  • AWS's root user (Root user best practices for your AWS account): "We strongly recommend you don't access the AWS account root user unless you have a task that requires root user credentials", "Instead of accessing the root user, create an administrative user for everyday tasks", "it's crucial to add MFA for the root user", and "monitor, alert, and report the sign in and use of root user credentials". The instance's root, its personal administrator, its MFA and nereus doctor's warning follow it.
  • OpenFGA's modelling of roles (Roles and Permissions, Custom Roles, Conditions): "Roles are relations that are directly assigned to users" and "Permissions are relations that users get through other relations"; custom roles fit when "It is not known beforehand (at the time of Authorization Model creation) what the application roles are", so "we represent them in a new type instead of as relations on that same type"; and "Conditions allow you to model more complex authorization modeling scenarios involving attributes". Registered roles become tuples on a grant type, never relations of the model, and the condition rule_matches carries the reef, kind and verb.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The teams and authorization reefs gain their first kinds (Team, Member; Role, Binding), and core gains User; the openfga Nereid is the authorization reef's first. Spec 0011 builds them, task by task, under #1644.
  • Every route of the Nereus API declares its reef, its kinds and how to find the owner of the object it names; a route with no declaration refuses to register, so a new route cannot forget the check.
  • Nothing changes on an instance that has not installed the authorization reef with a default Mandate: nereus-admins stays the only door, as today.
  • The Team of the teams reef is not a tenancy node: a Mandate's match still names Projects (ADR 0006, ADR 0015), and quotas can attach to a team later.
  • ADR 0006 records the two stand-ins of the first identity and the User's id; ADR 0013 lists can-i; ADR 0015's sketch of one OpenFGA type per tenancy kind becomes one node type.
  • OWASP A01 (broken access control) is what the slice answers: every read and write is checked, it fails closed, and who may create a role, a binding or a member is itself a rule. OWASP A07 (identification and authentication failures) is the stand-in's risk: the first identity trusts email_verified, and the root's MFA and audit wait for the root User.

docs.title: 1307 (the Position kind), #1308 (the hiring reef) and #1309 (the university reef) build on Member, without changing a binding.
Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether the root can be disabled once a personal administrator exists, as AWS removes the root credentials of member accounts. Recommendation for the root's issue: yes, with the recovery path written down first.
  • Escalation through bindings: today whoever may create bindings at a node may grant any role there. Recommendation: only what they hold themselves, or an explicit bind, as Kubernetes RBAC does.
  • Bindings projected into Kubernetes RBAC, so kubectl is refused too, the layer below the Nereus API (ADR 0015, "the API projects them into the namespaces where a Project runs").
  • Agents as subjects: Member.spec.kind: agent, a token by OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) with the act claim, and a permission that is the intersection of the person's and the agent's.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-11-10 on #1306 (three concepts, teams as the one list, registered roles, the built-in administrator, the instance's root) and of 2026-11-15 refining #897 into spec 0011 (decisions 1 to 19, the stand-ins of the first identity); raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-10/ and #pontos/raw/2026-11-15/.

docs.title: 0028. The presentations reef: Nereus keeps the deck, a Session is each time it is given
docs.text:
In short

The presentations reef keeps the deck as a Presentation and each time it is given as a Session. Status: Accepted (2026-11-16).

Status: Accepted (2026-11-16)

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Decks live in the repository today: an outline in YAML (docs/presentations/*.yaml) rendered by docs/presentations/render-outline into one self-contained HTML file. Presenting from a phone while a projector and the room follow, with questions and feedback later, needs a home on the platform. #218 (refine the presentations reef) and its children held only recommendations; on 2026-10-19 the owner decided there that the deck's source lives in Git.

The review of 2026-11-16 (the deck docs/presentations/presentations-reef.yaml, PR #1685) took the decisions below and split the work into six journeys under #1687; the first, #1688 (J1, drive and follow), is the walking skeleton. Three measurements came first: #1689 (Server-Sent Events through the Nereus API), #1690 (the renderer under the portal's Content Security Policy) and #1691 (the database).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The reef is presentations.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, with two kinds.

Kind What it answers What it holds Presentation what is shown the deck and its revisions, each by digest Session each time it is shown, a rehearsal included the revision it shows, its public link and short code, its step, and later its event, room, speakers, times, staff, questions and feedback

Event (groups Sessions) and Workshop (has steps) come later; until then the event's name and venue live on the Session. One writer per field (ADR 0005): the person writes spec, the Nereid writes status.

Nereus is the source of the deck; Git is only an optional origin to import from. A deck is written anywhere, by any agent or editor, against a published JSON Schema versioned by outlineVersion, served on a public route and by the CLI, and named by the deck with $schema. What the schema cannot say (links, references, fitting the screen) is checked by the Nereid on a dry run. This replaces the owner's decision of 2026-10-19 on #218 (the source in Git), because nobody should need a repository to present.

One package per revision, never changed afterwards. The import takes the YAML and everything it points to: its assets, the files it cites from outside its folder and the shared references, each copy with its origin (path and commit), listed in a package.json manifest at the root with their hashes and the outlineVersion. The package is a deterministic tar whose sha256 is the revision; a Session points to the revision it showed. OCI comes later, only to share a package.

One database for the revisions and the live state: PostgreSQL through the Database kind (#1691). The reef asks the database reef for one Database (engine: postgres) per installation; the Nereid of its Mandate (cloudnative-pg today, a managed PostgreSQL later) makes it, and the reef's Nereid, leagore, reads the connection from the Service Binding Secret. The API holds no database connection: it writes spec and calls the Nereid, found through the reef's Mandate, over HTTP inside the cluster, as the ideas reef reads its notes from doris; the store and its driver stay behind the Nereid, so the API never names a tool.

  • Revisions: a table keyed by digest, behind a small put and get; a put of an existing digest changes nothing, and the API refuses a package over 1 MB.
  • Live state: a Session's row holds the step and a sequence; a step change is one statement, issued by leagore, that updates the row and calls pg_notify, so the state and its event commit together.
  • Fan-out: leagore holds the one dedicated LISTEN connection and streams each change to the API; each API replica holds one stream to leagore and writes each change to its own followers; a notification carries only the Session's name, step and sequence (its payload is at most 8000 bytes).
  • Reversible: put and get by digest hide the store, so object storage or OCI can take the revisions later without changing the package. NATS JetStream (a KV watch and an Object Store) is the measured alternative.

The follower is fed by the server and never runs the deck. The projector and the audience receive only the current state and redraw it. They show the revision as the deck engine renders it, fitted to each screen, with the engine's own font controls (A−, A+) per device; the engine's controls that change the step stay hidden, so the step comes only from the server (owner, 2026-11-16, #1760). A step is the engine's own: a slide and each item it reveals, so the room sees an item when the speaker reveals it (owner, 2026-11-16). The room sees what the speaker sees, animations included; each device can turn its animations off (an older phone), and then sees the same items in the same order, at once (owner, 2026-11-16). leagore renders each revision with the deck engine when it is stored, and refuses a deck that names a file, since a revision carries only its YAML. The speaker presents with the same engine and all its controls, in the Sessions tab; each move of it is the Session's step, the speaker's screen moving before the answer, and the notes and the talk's time are on the speaker's screen only (owner, 2026-11-16, #1761). The channel is Server-Sent Events on the Nereus API (#1689), through the entrance nereus init installs, with no change to it:

  • each event carries an id, the Session's sequence; a reconnect with Last-Event-ID gets the events it missed, and an unknown or old id, or a new follower, gets one state event with the whole current state first;
  • the API sends a heartbeat every 15 s, a fixed server setting, as a named event hb rather than a comment, since EventSource hides comments from the page, and a retry: delay; the page reopens the stream after about 35 s with no event, since neither TCP nor EventSource notices a dead network;
  • the stream's route has no request timeout, and each follower has a bounded queue, dropped when full, so a slow follower never holds the others back;
  • the API raises its open-files limit at start, and a cap of followers per pod answers 503: with the container's 1024, one pod failed every route at about 1000 followers;
  • driving is a plain POST that needs a token with the presentations reef in J1 and the right to present from J6 (#1725); following needs no token, only the Session's short code, and is read-only.

WebSocket was not chosen: it would also pass the entrance, but a follower only receives, and the API has no WebSocket library.

The deck fits the portal's policy with no exception. The portal keeps default-src 'self'; the renderer writes its script and its style as files of their own for the portal, and keeps one self-contained HTML file, everything inline, for the offline export (nereus presentations presentation get --output html). #1690 found 6 violations per deck (one inline script, one style block, four style attributes), so the split (#1693) is small.

The audience is anonymous; sign-up is a choice, later. A follower is a random id per device, with no login. Signing up (linking the device to a User, e-mails optional, deletion at any time) comes after the six journeys.

The reef's Nereid is leagore, the Nereid who gathers the people: Nereus's own code, so it takes a sea name, as doris, thetis and triton do. It is born with a new field, nameOrigin, that explains its name and is shown by the CLI and the portal; the field for every Nereid is its own issue. The name joins the reserved list, so no agent session gets it.

$ nereus presentations presentation create storytelling \
    --from talks/storytelling.yaml
✓ presentations/presentations/storytelling created, revision 1 (sha256:3f9c2a71)

$ nereus presentations session create platform-day \
    --presentation storytelling \
    --talk 30m
✓ presentations/sessions/platform-day created (revision sha256:3f9c2a71)
  follow: https://nereus.example.com/p/K7Q4

The import is create --from and the check is create --dry-run, the verbs of ADR 0013 (commands), so no new verb is needed.

Stand-ins, J1 only: one YAML stored as a blob, with no package (J2, #1699); only the talk time, with no rehearsal (J3, #1707); any token with the presentations reef drives (J6, #1725; retired by #1726, presenting a right of the authorization reef); one API replica.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Quiz platforms where the audience joins by a short code: a thin page fed by the server that redraws the state it receives.
  • Helm charts as packaged archives, with an OCI registry as only one way to move them: the package first, OCI later.
  • EPUB 3.3: one archive with a manifest at its root listing its files and the format's version, the idea of package.json.
  • JSON Schema: a published, versioned schema any editor or agent validates against.
  • The HTML EventSource and its Last-Event-ID reconnect; PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY as a fan-out across replicas.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A speaker needs no repository: any tool writes a deck against the schema, and Nereus keeps its history by digest.
  • The Nereus API gains its first long-lived stream: an open-files limit raised at start, a cap of followers per pod, and memory per follower (about 30 KB in the API and 55 KB in the gateway, #1689) to size for.
  • The presentations reef depends on the database reef: an installation without a Database Mandate cannot run it.
  • leagore is on the drive and follow path: while it is down, the steps stop and the followers wait; the API reopens its stream to leagore and sends each follower the current state.
  • The renderer gains a split output for the portal while the offline export stays one file.
  • cloudnative-pg configures no backup today, so a Session's live state and the revisions are not backed up until it does: a separate issue, outside J1.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• A second API replica or a second leagore: LISTEN/NOTIFY measured with two listeners, but more replicas, the stream relayed from leagore to the API, a failover and a pooler in front are not.
  • Whether cloudflared in front of the kept cluster buffers text/event-stream, and how phones behave with the screen locked: the owner's phone test in #1698.
  • The credential for a follower when following stops being public (sign-up, rights): EventSource sends no Authorization header, so a cookie or a short-lived query token, decided with that journey.
  • The name of the audience's identifier when sign-up comes, and how deletion keeps the statistics anonymized.

Origin: the owner's decisions of 2026-11-16 in the review of the presentations reef (the deck docs/presentations/presentations-reef.yaml, PR #1685, journeys #1687 and #1688), replacing the decision of 2026-10-19 on #218; the figures of the spikes #1689, #1690 and #1691 of the same day. Raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-11-16/.

docs.title: 0029. A reef declares its MCP tools in the Nereid contract, and the Nereus API serves them at /mcp
docs.text:
In short

MCP is a door of the Nereus API, not a reef: each reef declares its MCP tools in its Nereid contract, and the API serves them at /mcp. Status: Proposed.

Status: Proposed

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
nereus-mcp (#415) is the MCP server people and their agents reach the platform through: an entry point of the CLI's package (cli/src/nereus/nereus_mcp.py) that runs on the person's machine, reads the cluster with the kubeconfig, and serves one hand-written tool, status, on /mcp (Streamable HTTP). It serves the OAuth protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and proxies the realm nereus of the keycloak Nereid, and a cloudflared tunnel gives it a public HTTPS URL, which the claude.ai connector needs. Its tokens carry aud: nereus-mcp. The Nereus API (ADR 0018) checks tokens for aud: nereus-api (api/auth.py) and says nereus-mcp "becomes a client of the API, or a part of it, in a later issue".

Every feature planned "through MCP" (#350 the Claude app as a connector acting as the person, #137 the board, #214 ideas, #245 examples, #1196 presentations) would add tools to that one process by hand, so the tools would drift from the reefs installed in an instance. Reefs already extend the CLI with their commands (ADR 0004) and the portal with their screens (ADR 0022), each declared in the Nereid's contract; MCP has no such extension point.

Two kinds of client use MCP. A Claude Code session on the person's machine already runs the nereus CLI, with its login. claude.ai and the Claude app, the voice path, reach only a public URL with OAuth and never see the CLI's local token: they are the clients this decision is for.

The owner asked on 2026-11-17 whether the MCP tools should come from the reefs, staying in step with the platform and its authentication, and that the tools offered be chosen per instance, maybe per person (#1803).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
MCP is a door of the Nereus API, not a reef. A reef is an API group with kinds (ADR 0002); MCP holds none, it is a way in, as the portal is. The API serves /mcp (Streamable HTTP) and its protected resource metadata itself, behind the same public name. The options weighed:

Option What it is Against Keep nereus-mcp and add tools to it Today's process, on the person's machine Reads the cluster with the kubeconfig (ADR 0018, #1320); every reef's tools in one place, by hand A central mcp reef with hand-written tools One server in the cluster The "module of the portal" ADR 0022 refused: the server must know every reef Each reef declares its tools; the API serves them A tools list in the Nereid contract, read from status A contract to keep stable, and descriptions that are untrusted input Tools generated from the API's routes or the CRDs No declaration Many CRUD tools, badly described for a model

The contract gains a tools list, read with contractVersion 2; a Nereid on 1 (or none) publishes no tool. Each entry has exactly these fields; an unknown field makes the entry ignored:

{
  "name": "leagore",
  "commands": [],
  "contractVersion": 2,
  "screens": [],
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "presentations_list",
      "description": "List the presentations you can read: each one's name, deck and description.",
      "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}},
      "route": {"method": "GET", "path": "/v1/presentations/presentations"}
    }
  ]
}
  • name: <reef>_<verb>, by the reef, never by the Nereid, so two reefs never collide and swapping the Nereid keeps the names; lowercase letters, digits and _, at most 64 characters.
  • description: at most 300 characters, printable text with no markup. It reaches a model's context, so it is untrusted input (ADR 0004 already treats the contract as such; here it can steer a model, which MCP calls tool poisoning): the API drops an entry that breaks the rule and shows the reef next to each tool.
  • inputSchema: a JSON Schema object, as MCP's tools/list carries it, and as untrusted as the description, since it reaches the same context: only type, properties, required, items, enum of scalars, format (date, date-time, email, uri, uuid), description, title, default, additionalProperties as a boolean and the length and range bounds; every description and title under the description's rule, at most 5 levels and 4096 characters as JSON; anything else drops the tool.
  • route: the /v1 route that runs the tool, GET or POST, under the reef's own /v1/<reef>/, so a reef never routes a tool to another reef's API; a {name} of the path takes the argument of that name, the others go as the query of a GET or the body of a POST. No reef code runs in the API: the API carries data, as with screens.
  • No ceiling on the count (owner, 2026-11-18): every tool listed fills a model's context, but which tools are on is the instance's and the person's choice (below), not the reef's; how many are on and what they cost in tokens is measured later.

The SDK copies the list to the Nereid's status.tools, as it copies screens; the API reads the installed reefs' status and answers GET /v1/tools, as it answers GET /v1/screens. tools/list on /mcp is that list. Uninstalling a reef removes its tools with nothing to delete. /mcp is stateless, with JSON answers (owner, 2026-11-18): no session to keep, any replica answers, and so no notifications/tools/list_changed; a client lists the tools again on each connection. The platform's own status tool belongs to the core reef. When two Nereids publish tools for one reef, the first by name answers, as for screens.

The token. Only /mcp accepts aud: nereus-mcp; every other route keeps aud: nereus-api. A tools/call runs the declared route in process, as the person: the API's authorization and its audit log see the person's sub, as for the CLI. Its Principal says via: mcp (#1809): the log names it, and a route that must never run on a model's call refuses it (the instance's switch is one). No token goes on to another service (MCP forbids token passthrough) and no token exchange is needed, since the API is the MCP server.

Which tools a person gets. The client's own toggles (the claude.ai connector settings, Claude Code's permissions) stay; the platform filters before them, in this order:

  1. The instance: an enabled and a disabled list of tool names and <reef>_* patterns in the Installation's spec.mcp.tools (#1809: the instance's own object, validated by its CRD, kept across an upgrade of the chart, unlike a ConfigMap of the API), changed only by nereus-admins through the API (PUT /v1/tools/{name}), so the audit log records who turned what off. An exact name beats a pattern; within one, disabled wins. With no rule, a tool whose route is a GET is on and one whose route is a POST is off (owner, 2026-11-18, from the security review of #1808): a model steered by text it reads must not write as an admin until an admin chose that tool. A tool off is never listed nor called on /mcp; GET /v1/tools shows it with why.
  2. The person's permissions: a tool appears only when the person may call its route, so it never appears just to fail: the API asks the authorization reef for the route's verb (list, get, create or apply, read from the method and the path) on the instance; with no default Mandate of that reef, only nereus-admins get the reefs' tools, as the routes answer. A person whose bindings sit only on a Project does not see a listing tool yet. The route decides again on each call.
  3. The person's own choice, below what the instance allows: decided later (#1811).

The command, under mcp since a Nereid's Tool is the upstream program it runs (#1263), with ADR 0013's verbs:

$ nereus mcp tool list
REEF           TOOL                 STATE
core           status               on
presentations  presentations_list   on
presentations  presentations_share  off (write)

$ nereus mcp tool disable presentations_list
✓ tool presentations_list disabled for the instance

The cloudflared tunnel stays (owner, 2026-11-17): it exposes the authentication, the site and the claude.ai connector, now pointed at the API's /mcp. The nereus-mcp process retired once the API served /mcp (#1810).

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
• Backstage's Actions Registry and mcp-actions-backend (backstage.io): each plugin registers actions and one backend serves them as MCP tools; the same split of a declaration per extension and one server.
  • Kubernetes API aggregation and discovery (kubernetes.io): registration is data in the cluster and disappears with its object.
  • GitHub MCP server's toolsets (github.com/github/github-mcp-server): grouping and switching tools off, their answer to too many tools for a model.
  • MCP Authorization and Security Best Practices (modelcontextprotocol.io): the protected resource metadata (RFC 9728), tokens issued for the MCP server itself (RFC 8707), and no token passthrough.

A second opinion on this design came from an agent on another model, on 2026-11-17; its corrections (MCP as a door, not a reef; /mcp inside the API instead of a token exchange) are part of the decision above.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A reef offers tools with no release of the API or of an MCP server: install the reef, and its tools appear in claude.ai.
  • The Nereid SDK and templates/nereid learn the tools field and contractVersion 2 (#1807); leagore declares presentations_list first.
  • The API serves /mcp and GET /v1/tools, and nereus mcp tool list reads it (#1808); the instance's switch comes with nereus mcp tool enable | disable (#1809); nereus-mcp and its line in the kubeconfig allow-list went (#1810).
  • A reef's description reaches a model through the person's connector: installing a reef trusts its text as it trusts its screens' code (ADR 0022). The length, character and count limits narrow it; they do not make it trusted.
  • Triton, today a second MCP server, becomes the Nereid of the rooms reef behind the Nereus API, and its own connector goes (ADR 0030, #1812).
  • Until v1.0.0 this ADR is rewritten in place when the decision changes (ADR 0001).

docs.title: Origin
docs.text: Asked by the owner on 2026-11-17 in #1803, refined in the same session with a second opinion; the owner accepted the recommendations the same day. Raw data in #pontos/raw/2026-11-17/ (Drive).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• A person's own choice of tools (#1811).
  • Whether a tool may run a Nereid's command (POST /run) instead of a /v1 route, for reefs whose verbs live in their commands.

docs.title: 0030. Triton is the rooms reef's Nereid: Room and Peer, on a Topic of the messaging reef, reached only through the Nereus API
docs.text:
In short

The conversation between agents is a reef of its own, rooms (Room, Peer), looked after by Triton, which requires the messaging reef and asks it for a Topic per Room. Triton is an internal service reached only through the Nereus API. Status: Accepted.

Status: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The goal of Triton and NATS was always one thing: agents on different machines talk to each other as if they were on the same machine, with peers, rooms and Claude Code's cross-session messaging (owner, 2026-11-21; journey #1890 proves it for two people).

The first form of this ADR (2026-11-18) made Triton a second Nereid of the messaging reef, beside nats, and said that swapping the engine keeps the rooms. Checked on 2026-11-21, on the kept cluster and in the code:
