The rules for an agent that makes a deck or an HTML page for Nereus. They come from the deck engine of the first proof of concept (beach order 20261026-0030, its section 4), with the owner's decisions of 2026-10-26 (order 20261026-0035) where they differ.

The decks of the repository are rendered by docs/presentations/render-outline from an outline YAML (docs/presentations/README.md); a one-off page or companion screen follows the same rules. The CLI's specs are decks too, one per reef in docs/specs/cli/ (The CLI design, #477).

docs.title: Before writing
docs.text:
1. Gather the content first: what to show, to whom, for how long, and which commands. Ask one question at a time.
  2. Write the script before the slides: one line per moment. Show it, adjust it with the person, then build.
  3. Start from the engine, never from scratch. A deck is an outline rendered by render-outline: the CSS and the script are the same in every deck, so whoever learns one deck knows them all. A one-off page copies the page template of the engine and changes only the content.
  4. Plan from the commands: when a feature is involved, write the commands a person types and what they print before anything else.

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
1. One self-contained HTML file: CSS and scripts inline, system fonts, no external script, stylesheet, font or image. It opens from disk, from an attachment and on a phone. The portal takes the same deck rendered with --split (an HTML, deck.css and deck.js), since its policy refuses inline code (#1693); so no style attribute, event-handler attribute or eval goes into a deck: the script styles through the CSSOM.
  2. A title of two to four words in <title>, a name and not a sentence.
  3. Colours only as tokens on :root, with both themes and the manual toggle: the natural theme on :root (dark for a deck, light for a page), the other under prefers-color-scheme guarded by :not([data-theme]), and again under [data-theme]; an explicit body background. The terminal is the one exception: always dark.
  4. Phone first: 16px gutters, no horizontal page scroll, touch targets of 44px, then check it on a computer.
  5. Storage is a convenience: wrap every localStorage call in try/catch and render correctly without it.
  6. Respect reduced motion: turn off blinking, typing rises and pops under prefers-reduced-motion.

docs.title: Content
docs.text:
1. One moment per slide. A terminal of more than about 12 output lines, or one that mixes two moments, becomes two slides.
  2. A list stays on one slide while it fits. A list that does not fit continues on the next slide, repeats the message, and numbers the parts in the label (The model · Vocabulary · 1/2); render-outline splits a screen this way, estimating the height on a phone, the tightest screen. A diagram is measured by its viewBox, drawn on the last part, with the items that fit beside it (#1458); a slide with a terminal or a code frame keeps at most two items, since its height is not known from the text.
  3. Each slide has a label ("Part · topic"), a message of one sentence, at most 60 characters and with no full stop (? and ! stay) and at most one accent in amber (accent in the outline), an optional subtitle, which appears after the title as its own step and never with it, and the content. On a slide, Reef, Nereid and Mandate are capitalized and carry their color ({reef:Reef}); a command, a path and a terminal's output keep them literal. The subtitle and the items add to the message, never repeat it. A message with two parts splits: the second part becomes the subtitle, or goes when the items already say it; ; or : in a message with no subtitle is the sign.
  4. Every acronym carries its meaning the first time it appears. URLs and values are written in full, never cut with "…".
  5. One discreet colour per concept, kept from the first slide to the last, in the slide text, the terminals and the cards, only on the concept's own name: reef #1D9E75 (teal), Nereid #7F77DD (purple), Mandate #D85A30 (coral), secret #BA7517 (amber). In an outline: {reef:environment}, {nereid:vcluster}, {mandate:vcluster}, {secret:...}. The roles of the work have theirs too: order #BA7517, PR #1D9E75, agent #7F77DD, raw data #9aa0a6 (#6b7280 in light), human #D85A30, handoff #4FA3D9: {order:...}, {pr:...}, {agent:...}, {raw:...}, {human:...}, {handoff:...} (#1458).
  6. Notes say what to speak, with the first sentence of each paragraph in bold; external references go as links.
  7. Credit the sources: a deck ends with the references its ideas came from (the talk, book or tool, and who created it). The deck style follows "How to avoid death by PowerPoint" by David JP Phillips.
  8. Show, don't fill: fewer colours, fewer words, consistent sizes. Less is more.
  9. Every list item opens with a bold label: **Label:** short phrase, and the details go to the notes.

docs.title: Commands on screen
docs.text:
1. Always as a terminal with the fixed palette (docs/agent/owner.md), a comment line before each command and a blank line between commands; a reef, Nereid or Mandate takes its concept colour there too.
  2. The commands of the CLI design (docs/agent/cli.md, ADR 0013, command conventions): nereus <group> <verb> <name>, with the verbs create, apply, delete, get and list; never add. Full names only.
  3. Long options only, one per line: the command stays on the first line ending in \, each option with its value on its own line, indented 2 spaces from where nereus starts (4 with $). A terminal never scrolls sideways: long output lines wrap.
  4. Output reads kind/name verb in kubectl's words (core/reefs/environment created, configured, unchanged, deleted), success in green with ✓, and the Next steps: label with a blank line before and after, then the next commands indented two spaces; not the engine's yellow "next:" hint.
  5. Examples use today's model: the reef environment, its vcluster Nereid and its Mandate, on the local k3d. A command that does not exist yet is shown as its contract, and the notes say so.
  6. Messages are polite and actionable: what happened, who decided and what to do next; never a generic error (ADR 0012, error messages).

docs.title: Language and neutrality
docs.text:
1. Decks are bilingual, English first and Portuguese second, every slide in both (pt: in the outline; render-outline refuses a slide without it). A terminal, a code frame or a diagram whose text changes with the language has its Portuguese version in pt: too (pt.terminal, pt.code, pt.diagram, with the same parts), checked like the English one; without it, both languages share one (#1457). A page is in English unless asked otherwise.
  2. No real names: no company, client, person, account or tenant. Use example.com, maria@example.com, 123456789012 (docs/agent/rules.md).
  3. No secrets or personal data in a file meant to be shared.
  4. Search before delivering for names that should not leak (the old product name, company names, people), and remove them.

docs.title: Pages that browse data
docs.text:
The owner's feedback on Tide v4 (2026-10-30), read on a phone: a page that lets a person explore many items (notes, ideas, events) follows these rules too.

  1. The viewport meta lives in the file: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">. A hosted page gets one from its host, but the same file downloaded and opened in a phone browser renders at desktop width without it.
  2. The content travels inside the page: the in-app file viewer blocks external links, so the item's own text is embedded (capped, with a note that the rest is at the source), and the link to the source stays as a link plus a copy button that falls back to selectable text.
  3. Markdown is rendered, never shown as source, and the reading view has A− and A+ (12 to 26 px), remembered in localStorage. The renderer (marked) is inlined in the file, checked against its published hash, never loaded from a CDN.
  4. Filters fold behind one button that says how many are active; the search stays visible, so the items show on the first screen. The chips follow the search and the other filters: each one counts only the matching items, and a chip with no match disappears unless it is on.
  5. A group with no match disappears (a day with no matching note), with a short message when nothing matches; the summary chart keeps every group and shows matches/total, and each group's heading says shown of total.
  6. The selected item and its relations are all that stays: a tap hides every item with no link to the selected one (cites, cited by, close in topic), groups left empty disappear, the count says how many are related, and the selected item stays in view; clearing the selection brings everything back without losing the place.
  7. Navigation follows real links: the links between items come from a script (the notes' own citations, "file 150", file names), not from shared tags. The first tap draws the thread (cites, cited by, a few close in topic); the second opens the item, which lists the thread to walk and has earlier and later buttons.
  8. Tags are normalized by a script (case, plural folded into the singular) before they become filters.
  9. A timeline, not a grid: on a phone, many items read as a vertical timeline, one row per item (44 px, a touch target), in time order under each group's heading, with the title and a meta line (time, types) beside the mark; a grid of small dots is too dense to read or tap. The marks encode measures, as in a data poster: the length of a dashed stem from the axis is how many items it builds on (its citations followed back), the number in its circle is how many items cite it, and its colours are its types. Links are arcs in the margin beside the axis.
  10. A thread can be replayed, as in docs/presentations/doris-demo.html: the selected item has a "▶ Replay · N" button that rebuilds its thread (every item it comes from and every item that comes from it) one item at a time, in time order, about 1.3 s each, lighting the new item and drawing its new link while the rest stays faded. While it plays, its bar folds into a ball in a corner (a ring of progress and k/N); a tap pauses and unfolds it (resume, open, close), and the end offers "again". A tap elsewhere, a filter or Esc stops it; leaving the tab pauses it.
  11. The header is a title and a subtitle, nothing more: the name, with the version small and aligned to the top of the line (Tide v4), and a subtitle of a few words (Ideas ebb and flow). Where the data came from goes to the notes or the delivery message, not above the content.
  12. The legend sits in a box like the chart's: the colours first, then, below a rule, a sample of each encoding (a dashed stem, a numbered circle) with what it means.
  13. A link to an item off screen keeps its reference: when a replay step links to an item above or below the viewport, a bar slides in at the top for about 2 s with an arrow (↑ or ↓), the item's mark (its colours and number), its title and its date and time, at most two items at once; it goes away when the replay stops.

docs.title: Screens on a phone
docs.text:
The owner's feedback on the speaker's screen of the presentations reef (#1712, 2026-11-18, a Galaxy S23 Ultra): every screen a person uses from a phone (a deck, the portal's screens, a companion page) follows these rules.

  1. The top center is under the front camera: a phone's punch-hole hides what sits there, so live information (a clock, a pace, a status) goes to the bottom bar, beside the controls, never to the top center. The speaker's clock line lost its tail, the pace, until it moved to the deck engine's bottom bar.
  2. Check both languages, measured: English words are longer than Portuguese ones (Audience, Projector, Presentation against Plateia, Projetor, Apresentação), and a row that fit in one language ran past the screen's edge in the other. Check every row of controls in both languages at 340, 360, 390 and 412 px, and measure it (each control's right edge inside its bar, no horizontal scroll, no text cut), not only by eye in one screenshot.
  3. Controls share the row and shrink: a row of controls gives each one flex: 0 1 auto; min-width: 0, so the longest words never push the last one out; on a phone the primary control drops its icon first, since its fill already marks it.
  4. A short mark, the sentence behind it: on a phone a status is a short coloured mark (+0:40 amber behind, −0:40 green ahead, ±0 even), and the whole sentence is its title and aria-label, for a screen reader and a desktop's hover.
  5. The portal's language is the person's choice: the words of a widget inside a page (the clock, its labels) follow the language the person chose in the portal, never the language of the content it frames (owner, 2026-11-18, "Não força o idioma").
  6. Try it with data that means something: a measure checked on data made for something else is right but meaningless (a pace against a rehearsal skipped through in 50 s, a talk whose clock started half an hour before). Give the owner a small fixture made for the try (pace-check, a five-slide deck of about two minutes, then a fresh rehearsal and a fresh talk), and explain a new measure in one line when showing it.

docs.title: Check and deliver
docs.text:
1. Render: make decks re-renders every deck (the CLI reference, the walkthrough decks and the presentations), opens none and stops at the first that fails: run it after a change that crosses the docs, like a rename (#1962). make deck OUTLINE=<name> renders one presentation and opens it, for looking at it.
  2. Validate: make deck-test (the outline's validation, the terminal format, both languages, a fresh render equal to the committed deck); every <script> parses (node --check); every step, ⏎, A−/A+, button of the bar and of the navigation pad, and key works.
  3. Look at it: render it at phone width and at desktop width, in both themes and both languages, and check that every box fits its text (the measures of Screens on a phone).
  4. Deliver to where the person is: when they follow from a phone, send the file through the session, never a localhost link.
  5. Files to send keep their original: when you convert something (a GIF, a PDF), keep the source next to it.
  6. One question per screen when the page is used to decide: the recommended option first, its context, the options, and a "back" button; the chat only says the screen is up.
  7. Before finishing, show a few lines of what you are delivering, and say plainly what was checked and what was not.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text: The style guide of the docs site (make docs), from the docs restructure (#1985): one information architecture, one format per page type, one identity, AI affordances and a phone reader mode. scripts/docs/lint enforces every rule below that a script can check; the rest is judgement.

docs.title: The six tabs
docs.text:
Tab Directory Page type Reader Home docs/index.md landing everyone Start docs/start/ tutorial evaluator Concepts docs/concepts/ concept evaluator, author Guides docs/guides/<topic>/ howto, troubleshoot operator, author Reference docs/reference/ reference operator, author, AI agent Project docs/project/, docs/adr/, docs/specs/, docs/research/, docs/agent/... its own form contributor

A new page goes to the tab of its reader, never to a flat list; an old page rewritten into the tabs is deleted in the same change, with its line in scripts/docs/moves.yaml and scripts/docs/relink.

docs.title: Front matter
docs.text:
Every page of docs/index.md, docs/start/, docs/concepts/, docs/guides/, docs/reference/ and docs/project/ opens with:

---
type: howto            # landing | tutorial | concept | howto | troubleshoot | reference
goal: Keep a secret in the installation and read it from a Nereid   # at most 120 characters, no Markdown
audience: [operator]   # any of evaluator, operator, author, contributor
status: built          # built | planned | idea | stub
issue: 1234            # required when status is planned or stub: the issue that builds or writes it
proof: scene           # required on tutorial, howto and troubleshoot: the test whose run prints the outputs shown (a test/ scene or a test file's path), or none
---

goal feeds llms.txt, the prompts and the search; write it as the reader's goal ("Install the CLI"), not as the page's subject. proof: none means no scene runs those outputs: the page goes to the list of #1984 for a scene run on the owner's word.

A stub page holds the front matter, its H1 and one line, Being written in #<issue>.; the lint skips its template, and scripts/docs/lint --no-stubs (the final check of #1984) fails on any stub left.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
H1 once, ## for the blocks below, in this order, with these exact names; ### only inside Steps or Fix; no ####. Words count prose only: code blocks, tables, front matter and headings are not counted.

Type H1 ## blocks, in order (optional in italics) Caps tutorial a verb: "Install the CLI" Run, What you get, Next 250 words, at most 3 commands howto the goal: "Keep a secret" Before you start, Steps, Check it worked, Clean up, Next, Learn more 600 words, at most 7 steps (### in Steps) concept a noun: "Reef, Nereid and Mandate" Example, Overview, How it works, Not this, Next 400 words, at most 1 diagram, How it works at most 5 bullets troubleshoot the symptom as printed You see, Why, Fix, Check 200 words, Why at most 2 sentences reference the name: "Glossary" free; one example per entry paragraphs at most 40 words landing the product free 300 words

Every page: the first paragraph under the H1 says the goal or the definition in one sentence; prose paragraphs at most 60 words (40 on reference); at most 2 callouts, each at most 40 words.

docs.title: Commands and outputs
docs.text:
A command is a ```bash block with one command (a \ continuation counts as one); its output follows at once in a ``` { .text .output title="output" } block. Lines at most 80 characters.

A command exists in docs/specs/cli/**/*.yaml and its flags in uv run --project cli nereus <command> --help; link the first mention to its spec ([nereus init](../../specs/cli/core.html#init)). Outputs are real: printed by a command that needs no cluster, or kept from a page whose scene prints them (proof:). Never write an output by hand.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Graphite (owner, 2026-11-20): the page, header, tabs and footer in greys, links in the text color, underlined; the only color is inside a terminal (the prompt, option values, ✓ and ✗), on a neutral graphite panel. Color only through the tokens of docs/stylesheets/extra.css (--doc-page, --doc-text, --doc-muted, --doc-rule, --doc-ink* for the terminal, --doc-warn for a warning, the --t-* terminal ones); no raw hex outside :root and the scheme blocks; a token built from another goes in the [data-md-color-scheme] block.
  • Inter for text, JetBrains Mono for code; the terminal look is docs/javascripts/terminal.js.
  • Callouts: !!! note, !!! warning (something changes or is deleted), !!! tip; no other kind.
  • Status: a chip only on what does not run yet, after the H1's first paragraph or a command link: <span class="chip planned">planned #1234</span>, <span class="chip idea">idea</span> (grey, told apart by a dashed or dotted border). What runs today carries no chip (owner, 2026-11-20): the front matter's status says it; the one exception is the Status column of reference/what-is-built.md. Never free text such as · built on a new page.
  • Diagrams: an SVG drawn by scripts/docs/diagrams between the page's markers (<!-- diagram:<name>:start -->), a wide drawing and a narrow one for a phone, in the line of Red Hat's OpenShift diagrams (square boxes, grey zones, thin right-angle arrows), a caption line in italics right below; make docs-diagrams redraws them and make docs-lint fails on a stale one or on a ```mermaid block (#2021).
  • Icons: Material outline icons on Home's cards only; no emoji in prose.
  • Phone: tables at most 3 columns, no side-by-side layouts; a terminal runs edge to edge, square, as Material's own code blocks do. No $ before a command.

docs.title: AI affordances
docs.text:
scripts/docs/ai, run at the end of every build, writes into site/: <page>.md beside every page (the source without front matter), llms.txt (one line per nav page, [title](url.md): goal, Project under ## Optional), llms-full.txt (Start, Concepts, Guides, Reference in nav order) and ai.json (the prompts and each page's goal).

docs/javascripts/ai.js adds the row Copy page, Copy prompt, View as Markdown, and Open in Claude only when site_url is set (it is not while the repository is private); and an Ask AI button under each ```bash example (after its output), which copies a prompt about that example.

The prompts live only in scripts/docs/prompts.yaml; change the wording there, never in the JS.

docs.title: Reader mode
docs.text: The Reader button (and ?reader=1) sets data-reader="on" on <html>: header, tabs, sidebars, footer and the button row hide, the article fills the screen at 18px. Esc or the exit button leaves; the choice stays in localStorage["nereus.reader"], and ?reader=0|1 wins over it, so a link can open a page in reader mode.

docs.title: Text size
docs.text: A− and A+ at the end of the button row, and beside the exit button in reader mode, scale the article's text from 85% to 160% (docs/javascripts/font.js, owner, 2026-11-20); the choice stays in localStorage["nereus.font"] and is applied before the page is drawn.

docs.title: Writers of the restructure
docs.text:
Each package of #1985 writes and deletes only its file list, in its own worktree (git worktree add ../nereus-<issue>-<pkg> -b docs/<issue>-<pkg> <base>; scripts/worktree/new takes only origin/main), one commit per page (docs(<section>): <goal>), checks with make docs-build only.

A writer never edits mkdocs.yml, the CSS, the JS, scripts/ or a page of another package: it says what it needs in its report. Deleting an old page and fixing the links to it is the orchestrator's, at integration, with scripts/docs/relink and the map scripts/docs/moves.yaml.

docs.title: How we work
docs.text:
• Good enough first, then iterate: ship the thinnest slice that works end to end, get feedback, widen it. Polishing comes after something runs. "To require perfection is to invite paralysis" (David Bayles and Ted Orland, Art & Fear). "Most platform efforts fail not by starting too small, but by starting too broad": start from the Thinnest Viable Platform (Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante, Thinking in Platforms, p. 29-30; Thinking in platforms).
  • Open source first: before building, look for an open source tool that already does it (see "Open source first, native first, build last" in Rules).
  • Languages: conversation with the owner in Portuguese (pt-BR); everything versioned (files, code, comments, commits, issues, PRs) in English.
  • Small context: durable rules live in these guides and in the ADRs; CLAUDE.md only references them.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
• GitHub Issues are the backlog: what to do now and the next ideas. Nothing is tracked only in a chat, a local file or a Drive dump.
  • The order lives on the board (Project v2 #1 of getnereus); docs/agent/queue.md has the statuses and scripts/board/queue.
  • An idea that is not ready becomes an Idea issue in the Ideas column; it moves to Backlog only after the owner's triage.
  • Each issue carries what an agent needs to deliver it alone: context, decisions and who took them, dependencies, a checkable "Done when".
  • The issue holds the context, not the conversation (owner, 2026-10-29): before a context compact or a pause, everything the task needs is in its issue (the context, the decisions with who took them, the next step), in its body or a handoff comment. After the compact, the agent resumes by reading the issue (gh issue view <n> --comments), never from what it remembers of the conversation. A chain of work is opened as sub-issues first, each complete on its own, and done one at a time (#477, with #479 to #483).

docs.title: Journeys
docs.text: The owner's working agreement of 2026-11-14: to cut the owner's load of deciding across several anchored sessions, each session owns a journey, a clear goal it carries end to end inside a decision envelope agreed at the start. The first pilot is #1559 (the continuous deploy of Nereus on Nereus).

docs.title: What a journey is
docs.text:
• A parent issue with the journey label; its sub-issues are the steps, in order. An existing issue that already has another parent is named in the body instead (GitHub allows one parent per issue).
  • One owner: the session of one tmux window, named in a comment on the parent issue ("Owner session: "). Another session that touches a step asks the owner session first (docs/agent/peers.md).
  • At most about three active journeys: a soft limit; queue doctor warns above it, never refuses (#1566).

docs.title: The decision envelope
docs.text:
Written in the parent issue when the journey opens, agreed with the owner:

  • 🟢 Decide and record: what the session decides alone and writes down (scripts, tests, dry runs, the merge of what passed make checks).
  • 🟠 Decide and report in a batch: what the session decides and reports in one summary; the owner's silence accepts it (thresholds, new sub-issues, pages of docs/agent/).
  • 🔴 Wait for the owner: the one-way doors (a first real publish, a change to k3d-nereus, an ADR, anything irreversible); the session asks and waits.

A delegation of something the owner does by hand (#1559's click on ghcr.io) goes in the envelope with its limits and the event that ends it.

docs.title: Where a journey stands
docs.text:
When a session works on a journey, it opens with one line of the journey's progress, in pt-BR, e.g. "2/7 (28,6%) da jornada #1890 (os agentes de duas pessoas do time, em máquinas diferentes, se encontram numa sala do Triton)" (owner, 2026-11-18, #1916).

The count comes from scripts/board/queue journey <n> (the closed sub-issues over all of them), never from the agent's own count; the agent writes only the description. The detail per issue comes only when the owner asks for it.

docs.title: Measuring it
docs.text: Whether journeys cut the owner's decisions is measured by a script, never by an agent remembering: the 🔴 items asked and answered, the 🟠 items reported, how long a 🔴 waited, the steps closed, sent through nereus metrics send journeys (ADR 0025, #1566). The owner sees the open items and each journey's progress on the portal's decisions inbox (#1563).

docs.title: Where it comes from
docs.text: One-way and two-way doors (Jeff Bezos, Amazon's 2015 letter to shareholders); Delegation Poker's levels between "tell" and "delegate" (Jurgen Appelo, Management 3.0); limiting work in progress (Kanban).

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• cli/src/nereus/charts/nereus-reefs/: the chart nereus-reefs (#1050): the kinds, as templates kept on uninstall, inside the CLI's package; make chart writes its templates/ from cli/src/nereus/crds/.
  • cli/src/nereus/charts/nereus/: the chart nereus (#1043): the namespace and the API, inside the CLI's package, installed after nereus-reefs.
  • cli/: the CLI (ADR 0008); the nereus CLI, with the commands of The CLI design (#409; the legacy nereus system ... are deprecated aliases until #410). controllers/<name>/: one image per Controller (controllers/openbao/, the openbao-controller image, #612; controllers/flux/, the flux-controller image, #613; controllers/keycloak/, the keycloak-controller image, #614). api/: the Nereus API (nereus-api image, #607), the server nereus whoami asks and the MCP clients reach at /mcp (ADR 0029); nereus init installs it. lib/nereid/: nereid-sdk, the Nereids' shared library (#754), its own package and version, built by make nereid-sdk into the wheel a Nereid pins. templates/nereid/: the Copier template of a new Nereid (#752), included by the root copier.yml (Copier follows a template's history only from a repository's root); scripts/nereid/new renders it into controllers/<tool>/, and scripts/nereid/check (make nereid-check, run by make test) holds every Nereid's nereid-sdk pin to the library's version. test/scene: the end-to-end scene on a throwaway k3d cluster; it prints how long each part took when it ends, and test/scene-cache keeps the public images it pulls in pull-through caches (#563). docs/specs/, docs/adr/: designs and decisions.
  • scripts/deploy/live: takes main to the live cluster through the tailnet with helm upgrade --install from the published charts, then a read-only smoke test (#162, first slice; the push trigger waits for #914); test/deploy-live-test checks it with fakes, run by make test; the how-to is docs/guides/operate/deploy-live.md.
  • catalog/: what Nereus says it has (#902, ADR 0016): workload-types/, package-types/, workloads/ and packages/, one file per entry, registered by nereus catalog apply --from-file catalog/; the kinds are in reefs/catalog/, with no Nereid until #904.
  • images/: the images of third-party tools that publish none Nereus can pull, built from their source at a pinned tag: smokescreen/, the build egress proxy (#1142).
  • deploy/install/: the public repository getnereus/install's files (#1782): install.sh, the one command that installs the CLI on Linux, and its GitHub Pages (index.html, README.md); scripts/registry/cli-publish (make cli-publish) builds the wheel at a tag and publishes them with its release, test/cli-install-test (make cli-install-test) installs it in a clean container.
  • deploy/ingress/: the cluster's ingress (#728), the Gateway ingress (routes only from the namespaces it lists), one HTTPRoute per public hostname in its backend's namespace, and the istio-gateway release's values; linked into the CLI's package as nereus/ingress, whose entrance applies the Gateway and the values (#951), the routes applied by hand, a stand-in until the release reef installs manifests from git (#751) and the edge reef owns routes (#470).
  • docs/start/, docs/concepts/, docs/guides/ and docs/reference/: the pages a reader follows, one template per page type (docs/agent/docs.md, #1985). A new command, or a change to what one prints, updates the page that shows it in the same PR, with the output it really prints. docs/walkthrough/decks/ keeps the get-started, release and edge decks, unpublished.
  • docs/reference/what-is-built.md (what runs today), docs/project/roadmap.md (what comes next, the radar, the ideas being refined) and docs/project/stand-ins.md (the workarounds): a new capability, queued issue, idea or stand-in gets its line in the same PR.
  • docs/glossary.md: one line per term or uncommon acronym, added in the PR that introduces it. A term the project uses (in its docs, issues or the owner's sessions) and the glossary lacks is added without asking, by a background subagent in its own git worktree (isolation: "worktree"), so the session's checkout and the docs server it serves stay where they are: its own Docs issue, a docs/glossary-<term> branch from main, the line linked to the source it credits (#332), a PR that closes the issue, merged by the subagent once the local checks pass (CI is off and the repository has no auto-merge); it reports only the PR's number and title. In messages for the owner, the first mention of an ADR carries its title.
  • sessions/: the live sessions sketch (#223), a FastAPI server and one page, run on the owner's machine and shared with ngrok; make sessions runs it, make sessions-test tests it, and its README.md has the settings and the privacy rules. Its data stays outside the repository.
  • docs/presentations/: decks as outline YAML rendered by render-outline into HTML (generated, never edited by hand); make deck, make deck-test.
  • Generated assets are never edited by hand: docs/assets/logo/generate draws the logo; docs/assets/docs/generate-landscape draws landscape.svg, its planes and their capabilities under planes. (ported from the wasp-idp deck, #1490; a test keeps the committed file equal to its output); docs/assets/docs/generate-idp-profile draws idp-profile.svg.

docs.title: How the owner works
docs.text:
• By voice, from the terminal, the web and the phone: requests are often dictated in Portuguese; read them through transcription slips. Answer in pt-BR; everything committed (code, docs, issues, PRs) stays in English. A cloud session has no local files: whatever a session needs lives in this file or on GitHub, never only in CLAUDE.local.md.
  • Spoken summaries are off by default (owner, 2026-11-20): run speak "<text>" after each answer only once the owner asks for it in the current session, and stop when asked. When on: one to three sentences in pt-BR, ending with the turn's question, if any; numbers and issue references as words ("issue oitenta e um"), no code, paths or tables. Without speak (web, phone), skip it.
  • Every issue or PR number carries its short title, every time, in chat, spoken summaries, issues, comments and PR descriptions: #254 (events contract for Controllers); a title seen only in a tool result does not count as shown.
  • A background run can be followed: when running make scene, any test/scene* or anything else long in the background, show in the reply, before waiting, the complete tail --follow /absolute/path/of/the.log in a code block of its own, with no variable or shortened path, so the owner can paste it into another tmux pane of the same window (owner, 2026-10-31, 2026-11-03).
  • The owner is the only user for now, and for a good while (2026-11-03): a change of behaviour needs no migration or compatibility step, only a line in the PR.
  • Only the main session speaks aloud: subagents and background agents never call speak, and every prompt given to one says so.
  • End of session as buttons (owner, 2026-11-14): when proposing how a session ends (/next save, /wrap-up, /clear) or other next steps the agent can run itself, offer them as clickable options (AskUserQuestion), the recommended one first; on a click, run it (a skill through the Skill tool). /clear and other built-in commands only the owner types: say so in the option. The agent cannot write into the prompt box.
  • Flag a long side quest, once: when about an hour goes into one topic that does not move the MVP (issues labelled mvp), say so in one line ("we have spent about an hour on X, which is not on the MVP"); never push to leave it, the owner decides.
  • The visual companion's content stays out of the terminal: when a browser screen carries a diagram, names or options, the reply only says the screen is up and stops, with no question (the click answers it); never repeat the screen's content.
  • Decisions and spec reviews go through the visual companion: open questions, triage and spec reviews are one screen per question, with its context, the options and the recommendation first; the terminal only points to it. It is the default for refinements, whenever it fits.
  • Companion screens: buttons in one compact row fixed at the bottom left (no scrolling), each with a coloured icon, always a "back to the previous" one and never a "change" one (changes are asked in the terminal); a click moves on with no terminal message. Diagrams: boxes and arrows, a readable monospaced font, a comment line before each command and a blank line between commands; a diagram worth keeping goes to the docs, in English. One type scale per screen (body and diagram text the same size, only the title larger), and diagrams as HTML boxes rather than a scaled SVG, so the text keeps its size on a split screen.
  • CLI commands are shown as a terminal on every rendered surface (companion screens, decks, HTML pages), in the format of the wasp-idp deck (docs/presentations/diagrams/journey/build.py there, command_line): a dark window (#070b14, title bar #111827 with the three dots and the working directory), a monospaced font; $ in bold blue #4a9ef4; nereus (formerly platform) dim #9fb3c8, the command group in violet #c3a6ff, the verb in bold white, the names it acts on and option values in amber #e5c07b, options (--name) in light blue #7cc4ff; output in #9fb3c8, success lines (✓ ...) in green #7ee787; a comment line before each command and a blank line between commands; the Next steps: block of each output stays in it, with a blank line before and after its label. Long options only, one per line, indented 2 spaces from where nereus starts (4 with $). A reef, Nereid, Mandate or secret takes its concept colour in the terminal too (reef #1D9E75, Nereid #7F77DD, Mandate #D85A30, secret #BA7517; docs/agent/decks.md). Markdown keeps fenced code blocks.

docs.title: Peers
docs.text:
Several Claude Code sessions often work on this repository on the same machine, one per tmux window, each on its own issue and worktree. They talk through Claude Code's cross-session messaging by a protocol that holds in every repository of the owner, so it lives in the owner's linux repository since #1360 (the move to the owner's repository).

There: the protocol (the messages [claim], [ask], [ok], [wait], [note], [release], settling a conflict, what a message may never do), its rule (claude/rules/peers.md), the room skill (claude/skills/room/) and claude-peers, which tells a peer from a hook's helper session (#1340).

This is the walking skeleton of Triton's room (#618), with Claude Code as the transport until Triton carries the room across users and machines.

The two transports, local and Triton, and how a session reaches each peer once: Transports (#1418). A session started with nereus rooms join talks to the room nereus through Triton, and to more rooms with nereus rooms join <room> from inside it; a Room is a resource of the rooms reef (journey #2067, ADR 0030; controllers/triton/README.md, "The room" and "The ask"). The protocol's page and the room skill move to these commands with smsilva/linux#232.

This page holds only what is Nereus's own.

docs.title: Peers and helpers here
docs.text: A peer is a session whose working directory is the main clone or one of its worktrees (../nereus-*). A session named after a worktree plus a suffix (nereus-1271-publish-ghcr-70) is another session's helper, not a peer: claude-peers names its origin.

docs.title: A claim here
docs.text:
Before picking an item, read what the peers hold and are about to take (claude-peers, the Start of each peer's session prompt, the Triton room): reading sends nothing, and the next skill does it first (owner, 2026-11-14).

Right after scripts/board/queue claim <n> and scripts/worktree/new, before the first edit, send the [claim]: the issue with its short title, the worktree, the paths, the clusters it will use.

The room-announce hook (.claude/hooks/room-announce, #624) does the remembering: after a queue claim that succeeds it hands the session the [claim] line and the local peers from claude-peers; after scripts/worktree/remove, the [release]. Send the line exactly as given, with SendMessage, and to Triton's room only for a peer reachable only there.

The line carries the issue number, the session's name and the worktree, never the title: an issue's author can edit it into an instruction. Paths and clusters go in a [note] once known.

docs.title: The shared resources
docs.text:
Each needs an [ask] first (wait up to 2 minutes; silence counts as [ok]):

  • A throwaway cluster beyond your own: one per agent, named after its worktree, three at most (Rules, #626, #628). A scene never switches the shared current-context.
  • The kept cluster k3d-nereus and its registry localhost:5111: commands always name --context k3d-nereus (Kept cluster).
  • A file many branches touch: CLAUDE.md, docs/project/roadmap.md, docs/agent/index.md, README.md.
  • The board's order.
  • The machine's heavy runs (make checks, make scene-*): at most two at once (owner, 2026-11-18, #1867), held by scripts/checks/slot (#1871) with no [ask]: make checks runs through it, a scene goes through it by hand (scripts/checks/slot -- make scene-...), and a third run waits for a slot; a slot inside a slot takes no other, so scripts/checks/slot -- make checks runs at once instead of waiting on itself (#1989). The limit is for the machine (16 cores, 15 GB of memory), where tests with timeouts fail under pressure for no bug, and for docs/checks, which compares each run with the median of the last five.
  • Back to one at a time: a cautious first rule. When two at once put too much pressure on the machine (swap, a timeout that passes when run alone), say so in a [note] and tell the owner; on the owner's go, a PR sets the default of NEREUS_CHECK_SLOTS in scripts/checks/slot to 1 (the variable read by one run alone does not hold the others back).
  • Room for two: to free memory, a session may stop the kept cluster after an [ask] (k3d cluster stop nereus) and starts it again when the runs end (k3d cluster start nereus), then sends the [release]. While it is stopped, the portal, /mcp through the tunnel and the claude.ai connector are down (owner, 2026-11-18: acceptable for now).
  • A release (scripts/registry/release publish): it runs only on main's HEAD and tags that commit itself (#1350), so a peer's merge no longer makes it stale; a merge during a publish only makes the next one. On this machine a flock keeps two publishes apart; the [ask] names the version, so a session on another machine does not publish the same one (owner, 2026-11-14: 0.1.5 went stale on a release branch and was skipped).

docs.title: Publishing on ghcr.io
docs.text:
make promote (#850, #1271) copies the seed images and the charts to ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus by digest. A package it creates there starts private, and only a person can make it public, once, in GitHub's UI (#1338).

$ GHCR_USER=maria GHCR_TOKEN=... make promote
✓ ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/forgejo-controller@sha256:...
! 1 package(s) answer only with a credential: GHCR creates a new package private, and its API cannot
  make it public (#1338). Once per package, open its settings, Danger Zone, Change visibility, Public (irreversible):
  ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/forgejo-controller: https://github.com/orgs/getnereus/packages/container/nereus%2Fforgejo-controller/settings
  next: make promote CHECK=1 finds every one with no credential

Then check with no credential, as anyone pulling does: a private package fails with its settings link.

$ make promote CHECK=1
✗ ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/forgejo-controller:0.1.0 is private: make it public at https://github.com/orgs/getnereus/packages/container/nereus%2Fforgejo-controller/settings (Danger Zone, Change visibility, Public)

docs.title: Publishing a release
docs.text:
A release is published from main's HEAD and tagged there by one command (#1350), with no version-bump commit and no release branch: a merge to main is what gets published.

$ git switch main && git pull --ff-only
$ scripts/registry/release publish --dry-run
  would publish 0.1.7 from 3f1c2ab (main, after v0.1.6)
  ...
  flux-controller: :src-a17c9b3e01f2 exists, would reuse sha256:3c1e...
  doris-controller: inputs changed, would build :src-4f1e2d0c9a88
  nereus-api: platform image, would build at 0.1.7
  3 to build, 22 reused
$ GHCR_USER=maria GHCR_TOKEN=... make release
building at 0.1.7 from 3f1c2ab (main)
...
promoted the images and the charts to ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus (cli/src/nereus/charts/nereus/images.lock packaged into the chart nereus)
built 3 image(s), reused 22; tagged and pushed v0.1.7 on 3f1c2ab
ok: promote CHECK=1 finds every package with the same digest
  • The version: the next patch after the highest tag v*, reachable from main or not (v0.1.6 sits on its old release branch's commit); --version names another.
  • Git keeps no version and no digest (#186): the CLI reads its version from the tag (hatch-vcs: 0.1.7 on v0.1.7, 0.1.8.devN after it, nereus --version), and so do the images, so the publish tags HEAD locally before the build, checks the CLI reads it, and deletes the tag if it fails before the push. The charts say 0.0.0-dev in git: their version is set in the working tree for the packaging only and put back when it ends.
  • Every image by digest (#1351): make promote ONLY=images LOCK=<file> writes images.lock into the chart nereus, one line per image, <name>=<repository>:<tag>@sha256:<digest>, the digest the target answered after the copy; the release packages it with the chart and removes it at the end (git ignores it). The chart runs the API and thetis as <repository>@<digest>, with no tag, and writes each Nereid's image into the Profile the same way, so a tag moved on ghcr.io changes nothing that runs, and an unchanged image keeps its Pod spec (#1574). A chart from git has no lock: it needs image and thetis.image given, and images built by hand (nereids.registry=localhost:5111, or nereids.tag given) keep their tag. make scene-helm-ghcr fails on any Deployment that runs a ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus image with no digest.
  • Only what changed is built (#1574): one platform version for people, and each image tagged by its inputs too, :src-<hash> (make image-inputs, scripts/registry/image-inputs): a sha256 of git ls-tree of its folder (and lib/nereid/ when built with nereid-sdk) and its build arguments, at the committed tree. An image whose :src-<hash> the target already holds is reused: promote tags its digest with the new version too and the lock names that digest, so its Pod spec does not change and its Pod is not restarted. The API and thetis install the CLI at the release's version, so they are built every time. A reused image keeps the version label it was built at: the version in which it last changed. make release REBUILD=1 builds every one, for a base image's update (#1604).
  • It refuses another publish holding the lock (a flock in the clone's git dir), a working tree with changes, a branch other than main, a HEAD that is not the remote's main, a version already tagged, a CLI that does not read the new tag, and nothing to publish since the last tag (no change under api/, controllers/, lib/, cli/src/ or the Makefile).
  • The check again, later: make promote CHECK=1 on the tagged commit, with the IMAGES= and REUSE= the release printed (the reused images are not in the local registry), finds the images and the charts published at the tag by the digests the release pushed to the local registry (the charts say 0.0.0-dev in git, so their files cannot be compared there): a chart changed at the right version answers another digest and fails.
  • Plain git only: the remote is NEREUS_RELEASE_REMOTE (default origin) and the destination NEREUS_PROMOTE_TARGET; nothing in it calls gh.
  • The first real publish of each new way of publishing waits for the owner's go (#1559's envelope).

docs.title: Publishing the CLI
docs.text:
After make release, an optional step publishes the CLI to the public repository getnereus/install (#1782), where anyone on Linux installs it with curl -fsSL https://getnereus.github.io/install/install.sh | sh: one GitHub Release per version, v<x.y.z>, with the wheel, latest.json (version, wheel, sha256) and install.sh. make release does not run it.

$ make cli-publish
built nereus-0.1.22-py3-none-any.whl at v0.1.22 (9d0e886): 222 files, every file of cli/src/nereus/ inside
wrote /tmp/nereus-cli-publish.Ab12Cd/latest.json: {"version": "0.1.22", "wheel": "https://github.com/getnereus/install/releases/download/v0.1.22/nereus-0.1.22-py3-none-any.whl", "sha256": "627c..."}
dry run: nothing changes on GitHub (--publish runs it)
  would run: gh release create v0.1.22 ... --repo getnereus/install --title nereus\ 0.1.22 ... --latest
  would commit install.sh index.html README.md .nojekyll of deploy/install/ to getnereus/install's default branch when they changed, and push
$ make cli-publish PUBLISH=1
  • The wheel is built at the tag (VERSION=0.1.N, default the highest tag v*) in a throwaway git worktree, so hatch-vcs reads the version from the tag; the script refuses a wheel whose name or METADATA says another version, or that misses any file of cli/src/nereus/ (the charts, CRDs, manifests, assets and the reefs and tree it links).
  • The charts inside the wheel are git's (0.0.0-dev, no images.lock): only the charts make release pushes to ghcr.io carry the version and the digests.
  • Once, first: make cli-publish SETUP=1 says how it would create getnereus/install public, push deploy/install/ (install.sh, index.html, README.md) to its default branch and turn on GitHub Pages from its root; SETUP=1 PUBLISH=1 does it.
  • It refuses a tag that does not exist and a release that exists, unless FORCE=1, which replaces its files. The credential is the gh CLI's.
  • The check: make cli-install-test (about 30 seconds, docker and the network) builds the wheel from the working tree at a throwaway tag, serves it with python3 -m http.server, runs install.sh in a clean ubuntu:24.04 container and requires nereus --version to print that version; a wrong sha256 installs nothing.
  • The first real publish waits for the owner's go.

docs.title: Publishing the docs
docs.text:
The docs site is published to the public repository getnereus/docs (#2016), which holds only the built site, and GitHub Pages serves it from the root of its default branch at https://docs.getnereus.dev/. CI is off, so it is published from a workstation, the way the CLI is.

$ make docs-publish
built the docs at 879cc0e (240 pages, 632 files, 36M) into /tmp/nereus-docs-publish.Ab12Cd/site
wrote CNAME: docs.getnereus.dev
dry run: nothing changes on GitHub (--publish runs it)
  would commit 37 changed files of the site to getnereus/docs's main, and push
$ make docs-publish PUBLISH=1
pushed 879cc0e to getnereus/docs: https://docs.getnereus.dev/
  • When: after every merge, by itself (owner, 2026-11-23, #2161). The hook .claude/hooks/docs-publish-after-merge runs after a gh pr merge and starts scripts/docs/publish-main in the background, which checks out origin/main in a throwaway worktree and runs scripts/docs/publish --if-changed --publish there: it publishes only when docs/, mkdocs.yml or scripts/docs/ changed since the commit the last publish names. Its log is ~/.local/state/nereus/docs-publish.log; a session whose merge failed to publish reads it and fixes the cause. By hand: scripts/docs/publish-main, or --dry-run.
  • The build is make docs-build's (mkdocs --strict, so a warning fails it) into a temporary folder, never site/ in the checkout; CNAME and .nojekyll are written into it.
  • It refuses a working tree with changes on PUBLISH=1: each publish is one commit docs: <commit> naming the source commit, and the history is kept (a few MB per publish; revisit if the repository passes 1 GB). A page the docs drop leaves the repository too.
  • Once, first: make docs-publish SETUP=1 says how it would create getnereus/docs public, push the site, turn on GitHub Pages from main's root with the custom domain and enforce HTTPS; SETUP=1 PUBLISH=1 does it. HTTPS is enforced only once GitHub has issued the domain's certificate, minutes after the DNS record answers: run it again then.
  • The DNS record, by hand once in the Cloudflare zone of getnereus.dev: docs CNAME getnereus.github.io, DNS only (no proxy, so GitHub can issue the certificate). Made on 2026-11-21; the cloudflare Nereid takes it over with #577.
  • The check: test/docs-publish-test (in make test) runs the script against a fake gh and a bare repository; after a real publish, curl -sS https://docs.getnereus.dev/llms.txt answers 200.
  • repo_url and edit_uri in mkdocs.yml answer 404 to a reader until #9 opens getnereus/nereus.

Stand-in: the docs published from a workstation to GitHub Pages, until the platform builds and serves its own docs (#24, #577).

docs.title: The gh CLI's token as the credential
docs.text:
make release and make promote can take the gh CLI's token as GHCR_TOKEN, with no separate credential, when it holds the write:packages scope. Check it with gh auth status, which lists the Token scopes; when the scope is missing, add it with gh auth refresh --scopes write:packages.

$ GHCR_USER=maria GHCR_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)" make release

Never print the token: at most its first 3 characters (${GHCR_TOKEN:0:3}). Found while publishing 0.1.14 (#1755).

docs.title: The published release's check
docs.text:
Once every package answers with no credential, make scene-core FROM=ghcr (#1464) installs what was published, as a person does: a k3d cluster made by hand, the charts nereus-reefs and nereus from oci://ghcr.io/getnereus/nereus/charts at the highest tag's version (NEREUS_CHART_VERSION names another) with helm, and thetis pulling the reference Nereids from ghcr.io, then the core's checks of make scene-core, in a few minutes.

It is what a release names next, recorded in docs/checks/scene-core-ghcr.json. make scene-helm-ghcr, with every real tool (about 20 minutes), runs only on the owner's word (#1420's level 4).

docs.title: Why a click
docs.text:
• GitHub creates every new package private, and its REST API has no call to change a package's visibility (Configuring a package's access control and visibility).
  • A package linked to a repository "inherits the access permissions (but not the visibility) of the linked repository" (the same page), and getnereus/nereus is private until a first version (#9), so linking cannot make a package public.
  • Public is irreversible: "Once you make a package public, you cannot make it private again." Only the owner's go makes a package public.

docs.title: The link to the repository
docs.text:
Every published image carries org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/getnereus/nereus (the Makefile's IMAGE_SOURCE_LABEL), and each chart's sources in Chart.yaml, which Helm writes as the same OCI annotation. GHCR links the package to the repository, so it shows there and inherits the repository's access, which a publish with the repository's token (#1250) needs.

Stand-in: the click per new package, until GitHub exposes a package's visibility in its API or the repository is public.

docs.title: The queue
docs.text:
• The board is the queue: Project v2 #1 of getnereus (https://github.com/orgs/getnereus/projects/1), top first. The next task (/next) is one of your own In Progress items, else the top of Todo nobody holds; never an item assigned to someone else. Todo holds only what can start now; the rest waits in Backlog. Ideas (Refine issues) and agents' proposals wait in Ideas, out of the order, until the owner's triage moves one to Backlog; /next never takes from Ideas. There is no HANDOFF.md.
  • board-queue (global, smsilva/linux#203, configured by .claude/next.md) is what /next runs: next [--filter Track=<t>] [--filter Theme=<t>] [--new], claim, release, mine, team, list, status, move, doctor. Its claim also triggers the room's [claim] (.claude/hooks/room-announce).
  • scripts/board/queue: next [--track] [--theme], claim (refuses an item someone else holds or with an open dependency), release, mine, team, milestone, journey <n>, doctor, list [--status], metrics [--weeks <n>], move <n> --top | --after <m>, status <n> <status>. Needs a gh token with the project scope.
  • Milestones hold the golden path's order, under three rules (owner, 2026-11-03, #915):
  • A milestone closes only when the scene in its Done when passes, not when its issues end.
  • A new gap becomes an issue, and joins a milestone only on the owner's word.
  • Only the current milestone's issues are in Todo, in order of execution; the later ones wait in Backlog. The current milestone is the open one with the lowest number. An issue with no milestone may be in Todo.
  • queue milestone shows each open milestone's progress, and queue doctor checks what a script can: a later milestone's issue in Todo, and a description that does not start with Done when.
$ scripts/board/queue milestone
MILESTONE              DONE  OPEN  TODO  IN PROGRESS  BACKLOG
IDP 1: Deploy             5    10     9            1        0
IDP 2: Build              0     3     0            0        3
IDP 3: CI and install     0     4     0            0        4
  • An issue with an open dependency waits (owner, 2026-11-03, #915): next skips it; claim and status <n> "In Progress" refuse it.
$ scripts/board/queue claim 846
#846 depends on #845, #853, still open

A dependency is a #n in the list right after Depends on in the body (scripts/board/dependencies.jq), or an open issue in GitHub's native blockedBy. Prose never blocks, nor does a number in parentheses, a code block, a closed issue or the issue's own parent. To correct a wrong dependency, edit the issue's line. - queue metrics measures the flow from Backlog on, so ideas stay free (#813): registering an idea changes no figure; it counts once it leaves Ideas. Per ISO week (UTC), from the Status history in the issue timeline: - Arrived: the issue's first Status after its last move to Ideas, since the board adds every new issue in Backlog and triage moves an idea to Ideas seconds later; a return to Backlog from a later column does not count again. Closed straight from Ideas, it never arrived. An older issue's first recorded change stands in for its arrival, and with no history at all it arrived at createdAt, unless it is still in Ideas or has no status. - Completed: closed as completed in that week, among the issues that arrived. Not planned and duplicate closures are left out. - Net: arrived minus completed. - Backlog age: for each open issue in Backlog, the days since its latest entry to that column: p50, p85 and the oldest, never averages. - The calculation is scripts/board/metrics.jq, tested with fixtures in scripts/board/tests/. - Board ids (for gh project item-edit): project PVT_kwDOFAuFDM4BnccI. - Status PVTSSF_lADOFAuFDM4BnccIzhmBCzY: Ideas ffb2ebf8, Backlog 7bb2c7ea, Todo eed7cbe2, In Progress 45af3f21, Done 050281cc. - Track PVTSSF_lADOFAuFDM4BnccIzhmBC8A: Platform df08a980, Docs a1ad169c. - Theme PVTSSF_lADOFAuFDM4BnccIzhmBC9U: Workflow & Tooling 4409c391, First slice ccba8c7a, Controllers 1b157991, Security 40d2b056, Public release f70adc90. - Opening an issue follows the issue skill: search first, one issue per deliverable, sub-issues under a shared goal, a type (Feature, Bug, Idea, Proposal, Decision, Docs, Task) and labels on creation (enhancement/bug/documentation, one area: <name> per part, mvp, proposed-by-agent, dogfood on a feature that retires a stand-in, one reef, nereid or mandate per piece of the model it delivers or refines), Track and Theme set, placed in the order. Each issue carries every detail an agent needs to deliver it alone (the Definition of Ready, #25): context, decisions with who took them, dependencies, checked facts stated directly, a checkable "Done when". - Classified by the model (owner, 2026-10-29): reef, nereid and mandate say which piece of the model (ADR 0002, ADR 0011) an issue delivers or refines, so gh issue list --label nereid lists every Nereid planned or built. An issue may carry more than one (#470 (the edge reef with a cloudflare Nereid) carries reef and nereid); area: <name> still says which part of the repository it touches. - Agents' proposals keep proposed-by-agent and wait for the owner's triage: triage/accepted or closed as not planned; /next never takes one without triage/accepted. - Agents propose the state of the art, the owner decides (#332): a technique, practice or study that could improve the product, the code or the process becomes a Proposal issue with proposed-by-agent (named, credited, linked, its evidence, where it applies, a recommendation); an agent never adopts it on its own. - Before stopping mid-task, leave a handoff comment on the issue: last step, next step, open decision. - Closes #n in English. When an issue closes, move the next one to Todo. - Skills grow with use: when a request asks for something a skill in .claude/skills/ does not produce, ask whether to update it, in the same session. - A cloud session cannot reach the board (GraphQL is blocked) or delete branches; the owner runs scripts/board/queue locally.

docs.title: Raw data
docs.text:
The raw material of the project (voice sessions, transcripts, mental dumps, the agents' session logs, work orders) lives outside the repository, in the owner's Google Drive. Since 2026-11-08 the raw session data is in one place, and the work orders keep their own folder.

  • #pontos/raw/<YYYY-MM-DD>/: one raw folder per day, holding both origins side by side, told apart by the name: HHMM-voice-<slug>.<ext> for the owner's voice sessions (recordings, transcripts, the messages between the voice session and the local agent, and their classifications next to the notes), and HHMM-m15-... for the Claude Code session logs that Pontos saves. The time prefix orders the day.
  • #pontos/silver/classification/: the machinery of the daily classification by a Haiku model (classification-rules.md, topics.yaml, the watermarks, the grades, the worklists and the reports). The classification of a single note stays next to the note in raw/; the rules, the state and the reports of the run live here.
  • #pontos/beach/ (formerly the Drive folder dump-mental-prompts, removed on 2026-11-08): work orders sent by the voice session to the local agent (see Beach).
  • #pontos/beach/bridge/, opinions/, proposals/ and references/: unchanged (the bridge between the sessions, the opinions and research files of a design session, the agents' proposals, the reference notes).

The raw logs of the agents' own sessions are not this repository's concern: on the owner's machines, Pontos, a set of hooks in the owner's personal Claude Code settings, saves every session of the owner's repositories to #pontos/raw/<date>/. A contributor's sessions are saved nowhere; an agent writes nothing to Drive for it.

Rules:

  • Read it with rclone (rclone lsf gdrive:#pontos/raw/<date>, rclone cat ...); the FUSE mount is slow. Find a voice note of a day with rclone lsf gdrive:#pontos/raw/<date> --include '*-voice-*'.
  • Raw data is private. The repository is public by design (ADR 0007): copy into it only the decision or the method, never names, figures or personal data. An ADR or spec may cite the raw file by its path in the folder (#pontos/raw/<date>/HHMM-voice-<slug>.md).
  • When a session creates an idea or moves one on the idea radar, the summary of its raw log carries a Radar: <ring> line (In Nereus, Refining, Exploring or Parked), and the radar's row moves in the next pull request.

docs.title: Drive access: our own OAuth client
docs.text:
rclone reaches Drive through the gdrive remote, and Pontos, the beach and the bridge folder all depend on it. rclone's shared Google client_id is retired during 2026, so the remote runs on an OAuth client of the owner's own (smsilva/linux#89, done on 2026-10-31). On a new machine, or when the client changes, set it up once:

  1. Project: in the Google Cloud console, create a project (rclone-gdrive) and enable the Google Drive API in it.
  2. Consent screen (Google Auth Platform):
  3. Branding: app name rclone, the support and developer contact e-mails, and an application home page and privacy policy link (the repository's URL is enough). Without the two links, Publish app stays disabled.
  4. Audience: External, then Publish app. In Testing, the token expires every seven days and Pontos stops uploading.
  5. Data Access: the scope https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.
  6. The "requires verification" warning can stay: verification only matters for an app other people use.
  7. Client: Clients, Create client, type Desktop app, name rclone. Download the JSON before closing the dialog, since the secret is shown once. Keep it in a secret store (the owner keeps it in a key vault as rclone-gdrive-oauth-client), never in a repository or a session's transcript, and delete the downloaded file.
  8. Apply in a terminal of your own, outside any Claude Code session, since a session's log goes to Drive:
json="$(az keyvault secret show --vault-name <key vault> --name rclone-gdrive-oauth-client --query value --output tsv)"
GDRIVE_CLIENT_ID="$(jq --raw-output .installed.client_id <<< "${json}")" \
GDRIVE_CLIENT_SECRET="$(jq --raw-output .installed.client_secret <<< "${json}")" \
  ~/.scripts/gdrive-mount

gdrive-mount (smsilva/linux) switches the remote to the client, reconnects it in the browser (answer y; on "Google hasn't verified this app", choose Advanced, then Go to rclone) and restarts the mount. Its last line reads client_id...: own (...), and rclone lsf gdrive:#pontos no longer prints the shared client_id's NOTICE.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Public by design. Never commit e-mails, personal or company names, internal domains, tenant ids, account ids or tokens: the whole history becomes public. Examples use example.com, maria@example.com, 123456789012.
  • No personal data in a command or a log (owner's pillar, 2026-11-16, vision), a direction until Nereus has an audit trail: prefer the design below in new work, but do not stop a change or rewrite an existing command for it (owner, 2026-11-16). The direction: no command option, argument or path takes an e-mail, a phone number, a document or a person's name; a person is a User or a team, named by its name or id. A log line, an event, an error message or an audit record carries ids, never personal data. Personal data a feature needs goes in a request body, from a form, kept in one place the person can delete.
  • A check's exceptions live in a ratchet (owner, 2026-11-16, vision): when a new check finds what exists today, its exceptions go to an allowlist that only shrinks (the check fails on a new line or a higher count, compared with origin/main), and the change that fixes one lowers it in the same PR. Never add an exception to get a change through; fix it or ask the owner. The personal-data check (#1680) is the exception: its ratchet only warns until there is an audit trail (owner, 2026-11-16). Credit: Ratchets in software development (qntm, 2021).
  • A public doc never names where a secret file is saved (owner, 2026-11-07, #1143): a script that writes one (a password, a token) takes the path as an option, with an env var, keeps a default in its code and prints where it wrote it (#1145). The doc names the option, never the default path.
  • Sensitive data goes to the private repository (getnereus/internal): figures, contracts, investors, legal strategy, anything personal. Here, only the method (what is measured, how, where), never the values.
  • The names: the project is Nereus (repository getnereus/nereus), the CLI binary is nereus (formerly platform), and the MCP tools agents use to reach the platform (#137, #214) are served by the Nereus API at /mcp, its tokens for the audience nereus-mcp (formerly platform-mcp; ADR 0029). Each kept in one place (cli/src/nereus/names.py, one build setting) so renaming is cheap. Do not spend time on naming. Two things are never both called "catalog" (owner's backlog review, 2026-10-31, #699): the catalog is the catalog reef, Nereus's own Workloads and Packages (nereus catalog, ADR 0016); the public site listing Nereids and their install commands is the Nereid registry (#22), and a Nereid listed there reads status.source: registry (spec 0003).
  • The model's words, exactly (The CLI design, ADR 0002, ADR 0011): reef (the capability, an API group <reef>.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1; formerly Interface), Nereid (a controller installed, top-level, global name, may serve many reefs; formerly Implementation), Mandate (binds one reef to one Nereid; formerly Class), Instance, Tool, Vendor as an attribute. Controller is the mechanism (<reef>-<tool>-controller); people type the Nereid's name. Never "driver", "plugin" or "provider".
  • Reference and fake are different words (owner, 2026-11-13, #486, #1422): a reference Nereid (reference-release, reference-secrets, controllers/reference/) stands in for a reef with no tool and is the everyday check of the CLI, the API and their contracts; a fake stands in only for an external tool's API (test/fake-github, controllers/openbao/contract/fakebao.py), in a test of a real Nereid that runs on demand (make contract), never in make test or make checks. Never call a Nereid a fake.
  • One writer per field (ADR 0005): the API (or the CLI before it) writes spec; the Nereid (its controller) writes status.
  • A kind keeps a field while stored objects use it (owner, 2026-11-05, #1045): a chart upgrade replaces a kind's schema (Flux's crds: CreateReplace), and a field the new version drops no longer shows on a stored object, with no error. Add the new field, move the objects to it, then drop the old one. #1058 checks it in make test, #1059 in the cluster.
  • The API never names a Nereid: no if controller == "auth0", no Nereid's name or tool inside a reef's objects.
  • What a Nereid publishes is untrusted input: its commands description, image labels and /contract answer are validated before the CLI renders or routes them; no shell command built from them, no path out of the work directory.
  • Every command follows ADR 0013 (command conventions): the verbs are kubectl's: create builds from flags, fails when the thing exists and lists the commands to run; apply creates or updates (every former add) from files or folders of .yaml only (--from-file, --path; installing by name waits for #487); delete deletes (add and remove are not verbs); nereus <reef> <verb> is the reef's default kind; output lines name the object by its full path, <reef>/<kinds>/<name>[/<kinds>/<name>...] created|configured|unchanged|deleted (secrets/vaults/default/secrets/google-oauth created, core/reefs/secrets created); --dry-run on every command that changes something, no exception, --examples on every command; errors follow ADR 0012; every output ends with Next steps: (The CLI design); --reef and --nereid are the flags everywhere.
  • Names are validated with re.fullmatch, never re.match with $ (it accepts a trailing \n).
  • A CLI message says what is wrong and what to do in the person's terms, never a library exception's text ({error}, str(error), shown(error) in a ClusterError, AuthError, fail or other *Error); {error.status} is fine. cli/tests/test_messages.py enforces it with ast, and its OFFENDERS list only shrinks (#1301).
  • The CLI's code never imports click: Typer vendors its own copy (typer._click), so isinstance(command, click.Group) is false for every command of the CLI. Test TyperGroup and TyperCommand (typer.core) and build a context with typer.Context (#674).
  • Test runs never touch the person's own config: own XDG_CONFIG_HOME and cache, and the CLI of the checkout (as test/scene does).
  • The Nereus API is the one door between the platform and the world (owner's pillar, 2026-11-02, ADR 0018): whatever is new reaches the cluster through it, never through a kube context, and it cannot lie, as Nereus, who knows everything and never lies: a check that did not run says so, never pass. Commands not yet moved keep the kubeconfig, a stand-in ADR 0018 names; make kubeconfig-ban (one of make checks, #1529) refuses any kubeconfig access in the CLI outside nereus init, the bootstrap and the machine's own settings, and its allowlist (scripts/checks/kubeconfig-allowlist) only shrinks: a migration lowers its file's count in the same change. A new feature never adds a line to it: it reaches the platform through an API route from its first slice (ADR 0018, "For a new feature").
  • A person or an agent reaches the platform through the CLI, which calls the API; kubectl is the last resort (owner, 2026-11-03, #874): a new step, in a scene or by hand, uses nereus, or the CLI's own client when it has to skip a command on purpose; kubectl only when neither can do it. The kubectl lines scenes already have stay until they are rewritten.
  • What every client must do alike lives behind the API, in a Nereid, never in the CLI: the CLI is today's client and a portal will call the same API (owner, 2026-11-03, ADR 0020: the Nereid, not the CLI, resolves an image's tag to a digest).
  • Simple on the surface, consistent underneath (owner's pillar, 2026-11-03, first said 2026-10-25, spec 0007): when designing a command, give a person the familiar, welcoming form first, and let it reach the same verbs, output and errors as every other noun (ADR 0013).
  • The same quality for fewer tokens (owner's pillar, 2026-11-02, #809): before an activity, weigh whether it can be done as well for less, through smaller answers, the way subagents are called or the models chosen for them; do it that way, or suggest it when the choice is the owner's.
  • Production may break; when it does, stop the line (owner, 2026-11-04, #946): the owner is the only user of the kept cluster, so a deploy goes there on the owner's go even when it may break it. When it breaks, everything else stops until it is fixed and back; then what let it break becomes an issue, because the goal is a better deploy, with fewer and fewer incidents. The fix goes to the system, never to a person. This is about deploying: tests stay on the throwaway clusters (next rule). Learn more: jidoka (Sakichi Toyoda, Toyota) and andon, where any team member may stop the line; If it hurts, do it more often (Martin Fowler, 2011); the error budget policy (Steven Thurgood, Google), which halts changes until the service is back and is no punishment; blameless postmortems (John Lunney and Sue Lueder, Google).
  • One throwaway k3d cluster per agent, three at most (owner, 2026-10-30, #628; it was two clusters in all, #556): one kept cluster, k3d-nereus, runs Triton and is used as production, the dogfood and inception of Nereus (Nereus runs on Nereus): never delete it, recreate it or run a test in it (.claude/hooks/guard-kept-cluster refuses an agent's nereus init that would land on it, #822: --create-cluster with no --name, --name nereus, or the current context; the owner's own terminal has no hook). Beside it, each agent may hold one throwaway cluster for tests (make scene, make scene-release, make scene-environment), named by test/scene-cluster (#883) nereus-scn-<id>-<six characters of a UUID>, with the whole id of its worktree (nereus-scn-883-a3f9c2 from ../nereus-883-<slug>, nereus-scn-20261103-1450-a3f9c2 from an order's worktree, nereus-scn-main-a3f9c2 from the main clone); .scene-clusters/<scene>, which git ignores, keeps the name for a re-run and says which scene a cluster is for; --name overrides it. The scene deletes the cluster when it ends; three throwaway clusters at most at a time: before anything else, a scene that would make a fourth refuses with a line naming the three and exits non-zero. A scene exports a kubeconfig of its own, in a private folder (mktemp, mode 0700) deleted when it ends, and fails when the shared current-context moved (#626); any command on the kept cluster names it (--context k3d-nereus). Never delete a cluster you did not create; with three running, show them (k3d cluster list) and wait. The scenes' pull-through caches (test/scene-cache, #563) are k3d registries, not clusters: three containers (k3d-nereus-cache-docker, -quay, -ghcr) on 127.0.0.1 that the scenes keep between runs, so a second run pulls nothing from the internet.
  • Pillars (docs/vision.md holds the one full list and why they exist): know them, value them and register the ideas they suggest during your work. The working rules that follow from them:
  • Walking skeleton first: a thin end-to-end slice a person can run from the CLI, then widen it. A new slice gets its spec in docs/specs/.
  • CLI examples first: plan every new feature, Nereid or reef from the commands a person types and what they print: the contract and the experience, written as examples in the issue or spec before any implementation. Every command, built or imagined, goes first into its reef's deck in docs/specs/cli/ (#477, The CLI design).
  • Test-first, adjusted to agents (owner, 2026-11-07, #1153): what TDD gives an agent is a definition of done it cannot invent and proof that the test can fail; the micro-cycle that keeps a person on track costs an agent turns and tokens (#809). So:
    • The contract first: the behaviour is written before the code, as the scene, the CLI examples or a test of the behaviour.
    • Red proven: a bug is reproduced in a test that fails before the fix; a new test is seen failing once before the implementation, and the PR says so.
    • The test frozen during the implementation: once committed, the agent that implements does not change it without saying why in the PR. Better, one subagent writes the test from the issue and another implements without having written it, so the test does not mirror the code.
    • The micro-cycle is optional: once the behaviour's test exists and has failed, the unit may be written straight away; no red-green-refactor on every function, no triangulation, no "fake it till you make it".
    • Out of the rule: exploratory spikes, documentation only, configuration only.
    • Learn more: Kent Beck, Test-Driven Development: By Example (2002); Anthropic, Best practices for Claude Code, which asks the agent to "write a failing test that reproduces it, then fix it" and to know what done looks like through "a failing test it has to turn green". Freezing the test is the project's own choice.
  • Small: issues that close in hours, PRs merged as soon as the local checks and review pass; a long branch is a signal to cut again.
  • Every fix gets an issue, even a small one found mid-task: its own bug issue, closed by its PR. Left untracked, "workarounds multiply, exceptions harden, and over time the platform turns back into the accidental system it replaced" (Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante, Thinking in Platforms, p. 28; Thinking in platforms).
  • Eat your own dog food: what the project needs for itself is built as a capability of the platform as soon as it can be.
  • An experience that works becomes an exploration of a possible feature (owner, 2026-11-04, #957): when something done by hand works, open an issue asking whether it could be a Nereus feature, with what happened and what it taught; the owner's triage decides whether it goes on (#956 is the first).
  • Open source first, native first, build last: before designing any feature, look for a native resource or an existing tool that fulfills it while integrating with the model of reefs and Nereids (for example nereus-mcp as a connector of the Claude app, instead of an app of our own). Build only when none fits, and the issue says which ones were evaluated and why each falls short. Time, tokens and money are not spent rebuilding what a tool already does.
  • Courtesy and respect in every exchange; disagreement goes to the idea, and a review names what to change and why.
  • Security from the first slice: auditing, authorisation and secrets are designed into a feature from its first slice; every spec's security section names the OWASP categories its slice touches (#237), existing designs are reviewed against them (#235), and compliance (SOX, GDPR, LGPD) and DevSecOps are prepared the same way (#238).
  • Credit what we use (#332): every technique, practice or pattern the docs use is named, credited and linked: an ADR gets ## Prior art before Consequences (ADR 0012 is the model), a spec or page a "Learn more". A claim of effect cites its evidence or says it is the project's own observation; cite only what you opened, never guess an author or year. An accepted ADR may receive ## Prior art as an editorial addition, its Context, Decision and Consequences untouched.
  • What an attempt teaches is kept as an issue, a rule, an ADR or a measurement; a dropped idea closes with what it taught.
