  • Where a new pillar goes (#873), when the owner asks for one: a section and a bullet in docs/vision.md (with its source, when it is a known technique) and the announced count; the working rule here when it changes how an agent works; README.md when it is a highlight; CLAUDE.md when it holds in every session. No other page states a count. make docs-lint fails on a wrong count, a stray count or a README.md pillar with no section.
  • A phrase of the owner about practices or methodology does not pass by (#873): find the pillar or practice it belongs to, then propose where it goes: a line in that section of docs/vision.md, a working rule, a credit in docs/references.md when it quotes someone, or a new pillar when the owner says so.
  • Every workaround is a feature waiting for the platform (#269): every PR and issue says which stand-in it creates (and the feature that replaces it) or retires, or "none", in a "Stand-in" line (gh pr create --body-file skips the PR template, so write it in the body). The list lives in docs/project/stand-ins.md, updated in the same PR.
  • Conventional Commits: <type>(<scope>)!: <description>, type one of feat, fix, docs, chore, refactor, test, ci, build, perf, style, revert, bump; checked by scripts/check-commit-message in .githooks/commit-msg and in CI.
  • Decisions go to docs/adr/, Nygard format, NNNN-short-title.md, the number valid only once merged into main; until v1.0.0 a changed decision rewrites its ADR in place (ADR 0001); from v1.0.0 on an accepted ADR is immutable, superseded by a new one. ADRs stay Proposed until the owner reviews them.
  • Commit only on a branch, never on main; every change reaches main through a PR. Guards: .claude/hooks/guard-main and .githooks/ (make hooks, once per clone). Branches: feat/<issue>-<desc>, fix/<issue>-<desc>, docs/<topic>.
  • README.md follows the behaviour: a PR that changes what Nereus does (a command, a profile, a Nereid, a reef, how we work) updates README.md in the same PR; a new Nereid gets its row. No status badges while the repository is private (#438): they come back when it is public or a paid plan makes them render.
  • Docs go straight to the point (owner, 2026-10-31, #658): every doc (README.md, walkthroughs, guides, specs, docs/agent/) opens with the answer, keeps prose short and favours commands: what a person types and what it prints, in a code block, with one line of text only where the command does not say it. Cut background, history and repetition; link the issue or ADR instead. make docs-lint (run by make docs-build) checks what a script can: prose paragraphs of at most 80 words, a command in every walkthrough section (#680).
  • Which test level runs when (owner, 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13, #1420, #1424): installing the real tools makes a check slow, so the everyday checks use none.
Level What it proves Command When Unit functions, CLI parsing, the reference Nereids' code make checks before every PR Core the API, the reefs, the Mandates, thetis, the CLI, conformance, with a reference Nereid in place of every tool, and the reefs no tool serves (catalog, tenancy) make scene-core (about 6 minutes) before a PR that touches a cluster Contract a tool's Nereid against a fake of its tool's API, no cluster make contract NEREID=<name> (openbao today, #1422) only when the owner asks Integration the real tools together: make scene, make scene-idp, make scene-helm, each reef's scene (make help marks them) make scene-<name> only on the owner's word

A reef a tool serves joins the core once it has a reference Nereid (#1502); until then its scene stays whole as integration. A release branch runs make scene-core FROM=ghcr (#1464). - Before a PR: run what scripts/checks/which prints (#1378): make docs-build alone for a change of Markdown files only (owner, 2026-11-23: no test reads them), else make checks (lint, test, deck-test, docs-build, shellcheck and kubeconfig-ban; each check and scene writes docs/checks/<name>.json and renders the README's badges and table, so the PR carries its times: commit them, #1093), then the scenes its table scripts/checks/paths names for the changed paths (make scene-core, make catalog-check, make scene-presentations, the owner's standing word for the portal's and leagore's screens, 2026-11-18), with make scene-core for a path no row covers; a new folder gets its row in the same PR. All run locally. CI is off (owner, 2026-10-29, for cost): every workflow in .github/workflows/ (ci.yaml, fake-controller.yaml) is disabled on GitHub (re-enable one with gh workflow enable <name>), so a PR shows no checks and nobody waits for them; the PR's test plan says what ran locally. - Relay each test run's comparison (owner, 2026-11-14, #1513): every run through scripts/checks/checks record (each check of make checks, each scene) ends with two lines: checks: <name> <result> in <s>s (<m>), N passed, N failed, then how it compares with the earlier runs (the median of the last five passing runs, "slower" or "faster" only beyond 10% and 5 s, the failures against the run before). Relay both lines as printed; never compute or estimate a comparison yourself. The history lives outside git, one <name>.jsonl per check under ~/.local/state/nereus/checks/: scripts/checks/checks history <name> --last 5 shows it, scripts/checks/checks import seeds it from the records git holds. A run outside record (a contract) reports only its time. - Durable decisions of the owner: the repository stays private until a first version of the product exists (#9); CLI first, the portal after; at the end of each MVP wave, the panel skill convenes a stakeholder panel that proposes improvements as proposed-by-agent issues. - Every session records its metrics in the private repository before it ends (the log of #113), summed from its transcript by scripts/metrics/session, never by an agent. - Every order records its evaluation in the private repository, by scripts/metrics/order (#803): performance from the pull request, tokens and the estimated cost from ccusage. Its reply ends with the block of docs/agent/beach.md, and the agent never asks the owner for a rating.

docs.title: Session prompt
docs.text:
A session prompt is the instructions a session leaves so the next one, after /clear, resumes the same way of working (#1236, #1239). It carries no memory of what was done: the work itself is in the repository, the issues and the board.

Since #1953 the owner's global tools keep it (smsilva/linux#203): session-prompt and its global hook, driven by the global next skill; the cycle and the rules are in ~/git/linux/claude/session-prompt/README.md. Never write its path by hand: session-prompt path prints it.

docs.title: In Nereus
docs.text:
1. A session starts: the global hook (session-prompt hook, on every SessionStart and SessionEnd, in ~/.claude/settings.json) records its start. This repository's .claude/settings.json has no session hook of its own.
  2. Before /clear: the agent rewrites its prompt with /next save, without asking the owner to confirm (owner, 2026-11-09, #1284), shows what it saved, and only then tells the owner the session can be cleared. The prompt is .git/session-prompts/<agent name>.md in the main clone (inside the git folder, so no clone can bring one), with a ## Board at save block from board-queue team, so who holds what comes from the board, not from memory.
  3. After /clear: the hook puts the prompt in the session's context; one that was not rewritten says STALE.
  4. /next: with a prompt, follow it and skip the board; with none, the board (.claude/next.md).
  5. A session that ends for good (/exit, a closed window, not /clear): the hook archives the prompt to ~/.claude/prompts/nereus/<agent name>-<date>.md.
  6. /next clear: archives the prompt under a topic and goes back to the board.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• One prompt per agent, by its name (AGENT_NAME, else agent-name whoami): every worktree of that agent finds the same file, and two agents never overwrite each other.
  • STALE: say so to the owner before following it, check its state against the board and the repository, and rewrite it with /next save once checked.
  • A peer's item: the ## Board at save block is a snapshot; check the board again before acting on an item a peer holds.
  • If the branch or checkout path differs from the prompt's header, say so and ask before the first commit.
  • Before #1953 the prompts lived in .claude/prompts/ of the main clone, kept by scripts/session/prompt; the switch moved them to .git/session-prompts/.

docs.title: The status bar
docs.text:
The bar under Claude Code's prompt shows, in one line, where the session is working, how full its context is and how much of the plan's quota is left.

nereus  main  ≡ 13%  4h42m 4% ↻ 19:30  5d10h 16% ↻ Mon 01:00  today 69,6% of 23%  forecast 71,1% steady  ◔ 13m  ⇌ 14  ✦ Opus 5.5  ◈ 140k

docs.title: Each piece
docs.text:
Piece What it says Colors ⚠ pontos a raw log did not reach Drive (shown only then; run pontos-save status) red nereus the repository, and the subfolder when there is one blue main the branch and the git status ≡ 13% how full the context window is green, yellow from 50%, red from 70% 4h42m 4% ↻ 19:30 the 5-hour limit: time left, usage, reset green, amber from 50%, salmon from 80% 5d10h 16% ↻ Mon 01:00 the weekly limit: time left, usage, reset same as above today 69,6% of 23% 23% is where the weekly usage should be by the end of today; 69,6% is how much of that goal it has reached (16 of 23) white numbers forecast 71,1% steady the weekly usage at the reset if this pace goes on, and what to do about it the word, below ◔ 13m how long the session has been running green, amber from 15 minutes, orange from 25, bordeaux from 35 ⇌ 14 the owner's messages in this session ✦ Opus 5.5 the model ◈ 140k the session's tokens, input and output

/rc, on the right, is Claude Code's own: Remote Control is on.

docs.title: The forecast's word
docs.text:
forecast = weekly usage × 7 days / time gone in the window
Forecast Word What to do below 70% push (green) speed up: more subagents and parallel sessions from 70% to 95% steady (amber) keep the pace above 95% slow (salmon) hold back: one agent, no subagents, or a day off

The segment stays hidden in the first 6 hours of the window, while the forecast is unstable.

docs.title: Today's goal
docs.text:
The goal spreads what was left at the day's first reading evenly up to the reset, so it stays fixed all day. The share passes 100% once the goal is passed. A share above 100% does not mean the week is at risk: the forecast says that.

$ claude-usage-plan
  Weekly quota: 16% used, resets Mon 09/11 01:00, target 100%

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
The bar is the owner's own tooling, not part of Nereus: scripts/bin/claude-status-line, claude-usage-plan and claude-usage-forecast in the owner's dotfiles repository, set up by its statusline-setup skill.

To choose which limits appear:

$ claude-status-line-limits --show weekly

--show takes session, weekly, both or none.

docs.title: Saving tokens
docs.text: The owner's pillar (2026-11-02, #809): the same quality for fewer tokens. Before an activity, weigh whether it can be done as well for less, do the cheaper way, or suggest it when the choice is the owner's. Quality comes first: a saving that brings rework is no saving.

docs.title: The practices
docs.text:
1. One order per session. Every call reads the whole context again, so a long session is the main cost. Finish an order, then /clear or a new session. A UserPromptSubmit hook warns the owner and the agent once the context of a call passes 200k tokens, or CLAUDE_CONTEXT_TOKENS_REFERENCE when it is set.
  2. Filter tool output. Use --quiet, --json with --jq, tail, or Read with offset and limit: whatever enters the context is read again on every later call. A PostToolUse hook on Bash and Read warns when one output passes 10k characters.
  3. Subagents for mechanical work only, on a lighter model, with a short brief and a one-line report. What takes a few calls is done directly. A subagent that runs a scene waits for it to end and reports its verdict: its brief says so, since a subagent that stops while its scene still runs leaves the wait, the reading and the commit to the main session (owner, 2026-11-08).
  4. Shorter answers: the outcome and the next decision, with no recap of what the owner has already seen.

Both hooks are scripts/metrics/tokens, set in .claude/settings.json. They warn and never block, and whatever goes wrong in them, the session carries on.

docs.title: When the context warning fires
docs.text:
Situation Do Work finished or at a stopping point /wrap-up, then /clear Mid-task with little left (a few calls: a push, a PR, a merge) Finish it in this session, then /wrap-up and /clear Mid-task with much left (several steps, files or PRs) and the work has an issue /rollover: the handoff goes on the issue and a new session carries on Mid-task with much left and no issue /compact Nothing pending, all of it in a PR or an issue /clear

Suggest /rollover only when much is left (owner, 2026-11-03): it costs about a dozen calls on the long context plus a new session reading the issue again, so with a few calls left, finishing here is cheaper. /rollover is the owner's manual trigger while it is evaluated, compared with /compact on cost and rework. No /compact before /wrap-up: it spends tokens summarizing a conversation about to be cleared, and takes details the wrap-up needs.

docs.title: Knowing whether it worked
docs.text:
Compare one week with the one before, at the Friday summary. Figures go to getnereus/internal, never here.

scripts/metrics/order summary --file metrics/orders/2026-W45.csv
scripts/metrics/tokens report --file metrics/orders/2026-W45.csv
Practice Should go down or hold Read it in All of them, the result tokens and cost per order order summary 1, one order per session orders per session (to 1), mean and peak context tokens report 2, filter tool output big outputs, of all outputs tokens report 3, subagents tokens per agent in an order order summary 4, shorter answers output tokens per order the week's CSV The guard: quality holds review rounds order summary

Orders differ in size, so a few of them show a direction, not a proof. A week counts as better only when the cost per order falls and the review rounds hold.

docs.title: Worktrees
docs.text:
Every change on getnereus/nereus is made in its own git worktree (the owner, 2026-10-26, #447). A session may have its home in the main clone, one per tmux window, but the main clone is only read and pulled: it stays on main, for the owner, the docs server and the beach watcher (the owner, 2026-10-29). On the owner's machines a PreToolUse hook outside this repository, claude-guard-main-clone, refuses commits and file edits in the main clone, except files git ignores.

The session prompt follows the agent, not the worktree (#1239): the global session-prompt keeps one per agent name in the main clone's git folder, .git/session-prompts/<agent name>.md, loaded by the global SessionStart hook after /clear (#1953). The cycle: Session prompt.

  • One worktree per order or run, next to the main clone: ../nereus-<id>-<slug>, where <id> is the beach order id (20261026-1748) or, for a run without an order, the issue number (447), and <slug> says what the work is about. Example: ../nereus-20261026-1748-release-reef.
  • The branch carries the same name: <type>/<id>-<slug> (feat/20261026-1748-release-reef), from origin/main.
  • Create it: scripts/worktree/new <type> <id>-<slug> prints the path; work, commit and push from there.
  • Remove it after the merge, or when the order closes: scripts/worktree/remove <id>-<slug> refuses uncommitted changes and deletes the local branch once its pull request is merged or closed.
  • Do not move a worktree after a build: its .venv folders keep the old path, and make test fails with Failed to spawn: pytest. If you must, delete them and build again (#905).
  • A subagent gets its own worktree through isolation: "worktree" (as the glossary subagent does, Layout).
  • Say where the change lives (owner, 2026-11-18, #1868): in the first reply after creating a worktree, give its absolute path and say the main clone stays untouched. A session's shell returns to the main clone after each call ("Shell cwd was reset to ..."), which reads as if the change were made there, and changes another session's release leaves in the main clone look like yours.
  • Committing from a session that sits in the main clone: aim the whole command at the worktree, as one && chain of git -C <worktree> ... segments or cd <worktree> followed by git segments; .claude/hooks/guard-main checks the session's own branch otherwise (#346).
  • A push that names its branch passes from the main clone (#698): git -C <worktree> push --set-upstream origin <branch> 2>&1 | tail -2 is judged by <branch>, whatever pipe or chain surrounds it; it is refused only when it names main (origin main, HEAD:main). A push with no literal branch (git push, HEAD, --all, a $ in the name) is still checked against the session's branch, and quoted text (an issue or PR body that mentions a push) is not read as a command. Commits keep the plain-command rule below.
  • The guards read the command as text, so keep it plain: one line, the worktree as a literal absolute path (never "$w": neither guard expands a variable), and no $, ;, |, backticks, parentheses, redirections, heredoc or newline anywhere in it. Write the message to a file first: git -C /abs/worktree add --all && git -C /abs/worktree commit --file /abs/message.txt. The same applies to a commit in another repository's worktree (~/git/linux-...). Avoid the word commit in a worktree slug too: claude-guard-main-clone refused scripts/worktree/new docs <id>-...-commit-.... Four tries failed this way on 2026-10-29 before the plain form passed.
  • Text that names nereus init goes in a file, through the Write tool: in a heredoc, .claude/hooks/guard-kept-cluster cannot read the command and refuses it, even when nothing runs on a cluster (#827, twice).

docs.title: Reef, Nereid and Mandate
docs.text: A reef is a capability of the platform, a Nereid is the controller that looks after it, and a Mandate binds one reef to one Nereid.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
nereus --help lists each reef installed with the Nereid that looks after it:

output
Reefs:
  release         Reef release, looked after by nereid flux.
  secrets         Reef secrets, looked after by nereid openbao.

The secrets reef adds the kinds Vault and Secret and the commands nereus secrets ...; the Mandate default says that openbao keeps them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
nereus secrets createNereus installationReef secrets(an API group)Mandate default(binds the two)Nereid openbao(a controller)OpenBao(the tool) nereus secrets createNereus installationReef secrets(an API group)Mandate default(binds the two)Nereid openbao(a controller)OpenBao(the tool)

The CLI speaks to the reef; the Mandate names the Nereid that does the work with its tool.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A reef is an API group, <reef>.getnereus.dev, with its own kinds; nereus reef apply adds one at runtime.
  • A Nereid is a Kubernetes controller that reconciles the reef's objects and writes their status.
  • A Mandate binds one reef to one Nereid; one Mandate per reef is the default, and its commands go there.
  • Several Nereids can look after one reef (keycloak or auth0 for authentication): you pick one per Mandate.
  • Each reef adds its own commands to the CLI, so nereus --help grows with the installation.

docs.title: Not this
docs.text:
• A reef is not a Helm chart: it is the API; the Nereid brings the software behind it.
  • A Nereid is not the tool itself: openbao is the controller, OpenBao is what it drives.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Runtime install and profiles: how reefs and Nereids arrive in a running installation.

docs.title: The Nereus API
docs.text: The Nereus API is the platform's one door: the CLI, the portal, an IDE and agents talk to it with the person's token, and the Kubernetes API, the Nereids and their tools stay behind it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
nereus whoami asks the API's first route, GET /v1/me, instead of reading the local token:

nereus whoami --help
output
Usage: nereus whoami [OPTIONS]

  Who you are, as the Nereus API answers (GET /v1/me) for the token of nereus
  login, never what the local token says: the login, and the User of Nereus
  behind it (#1645), or that there is none yet.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
CLIPortalAgents, IDENereus API(api.<domain>, the person's token, one door)BEHIND THE DOORKubernetes API(the reefs' kinds)Nereids(they reconcile the kinds)Tools(OpenBao, GitHub, a cloud) CLIPortalAgents, IDENereus API(api.<domain>, the person's token, one door)BEHIND THE DOORKubernetes API(the reefs' kinds)Nereids(they reconcile the kinds)Tools(OpenBao, GitHub, a cloud)

Clients hold a token, never a kubeconfig; what is behind the door stays behind it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• It runs in the cluster as nereus-api in nereus-system, installed by nereus init with core; its public name is api.<domain>.
  • It alone validates the token: the issuer and keys come from the authentication reef's default Mandate, the audience is nereus-api, and the Kubernetes apiserver never sees a person's token.
  • It acts with its own identity, and decides what the person may do before acting (Tenancy and access).
  • It speaks of reefs and their kinds, never of tools, and reads what the Nereids publish in status; what it did not read, it says it did not.
  • Command groups move behind it one at a time; the rest keep the kubeconfig as a stand-in, and the check kubeconfig-ban refuses any new use outside nereus init and the bootstrap.

docs.title: Not this
docs.text:
• Not the Kubernetes API: the reefs' kinds live there, but no client reaches it directly.
  • Not a proxy to each tool's API: no route names Flux, Keycloak or OpenBao.
  • Not the portal: the portal is one client of the API, as the CLI is.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Install the CLI: try it on your own machine.

docs.title: Runtime install and profiles
docs.text: Nereus installs its capabilities at runtime: nereus init lays down the engine, core, and a profile is a named list of reefs, Nereids and Mandates applied on top of it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
nereus profile describe shows what a profile installs, in order, each Nereid with its reef and its Mandate:

nereus profile describe secrets
output
NEREID   REEF     MANDATE            REQUIRED BY
openbao  secrets  default (default)  -

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
nereus initNereus installationcore(the engine)Profile(picked at init)Nereid thetis(the installer)InstalledreefsNereidsMandatesnereus reef apply(and nereid apply, one at a time) nereus initNereus installationcore(the engine)Profile(picked at init)Nereid thetis(the installer)InstalledreefsNereidsMandatesnereus reef apply(and nereid apply, one at a time)

Init lays down core; a profile, or a person one command at a time, adds the rest.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• nereus init installs the kinds, the namespace, the Nereus API, core and the tenancy reef with Helm; the profile core, the default, installs nothing more.
  • nereus init --profile internal-developer-platform adds a profile: the Nereid thetis installs its reefs, Nereids and Mandates, and init waits until they are Ready.
  • A profile never writes the order: each Nereid comes after the Nereids of the reefs it requires, read from its image's label core.getnereus.dev/requires.
  • A profile adds nothing the commands cannot do: nereus reef apply, nereus nereid apply and nereus mandate create do the same by hand, on a running installation.
  • A profile never carries a secret: credentials reach a Nereid through the secrets reef, encrypted on the client, once the profile is installed.

docs.title: Not this
docs.text:
• Not a fixed install: reefs and Nereids come and go on a running installation, and init never has to run again for them.
  • Not a size: profiles are named by purpose, never minimal or full; core alone is the default, so a plain init stays fast.
  • Not access: who may do what is a role, in Tenancy and access.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Undercloud and overcloud: where an installation starts when its home is a cloud.

docs.title: Tenancy and access
docs.text: Tenancy says whose each thing is, a tree of Organizations and nested Projects; access says who may do what on a node of that tree, through roles bound to teams.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The tree is two kinds of the tenancy reef, applied with nereus tenancy apply:

apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Organization
metadata:
  name: example
---
apiVersion: tenancy.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Project
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  parent: {kind: Organization, name: example}

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Organization(example, the boundary)Project payments(a node of the tree)Team payments(its members)Binding(gives a Role)onRole developer(a list of rules)Nereus APImay this User? Organization(example)Project payments(a node of the tree)Team payments(its members)Binding(gives a Role on the Project)Role developerNereus APImay this User?

A binding gives a role to a team on one node; the API asks before it acts.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Tenancy is a reef, tenancy.getnereus.dev, whose kinds come from each instance: every kind is a node with an optional spec.parent, and one kind, the boundary, isolates people and billing (here Organization).
  • Whatever belongs somewhere names owner: {kind, name} in the tree: a Workload, an Environment, a team.
  • The authorization reef holds access: a Role is a list of rules, <reef>:<kinds>:<verbs>, and a Binding gives it to a team, a position in a team or, as the exception, one User, on one node; access flows down the tree.
  • The teams reef keeps one list of members: joining a team grants its access, leaving removes it. A person is one core User whatever the login, and a login with no User has no permission.
  • The Nereus API asks before it acts; nereus can-i asks the same question and names the binding that grants it.

docs.title: Not this
docs.text:
• A Project is not a Kubernetes namespace: it nests, and one Project runs in several environments, on several clusters.
  • A team is not an identity provider's group: groups are an output a Nereid may write, never the source.
  • A role is not a profile: a profile is what an installation installs.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The Nereus API: the door every client goes through.

docs.title: Undercloud and overcloud
docs.text:
The undercloud is the local k3d cluster that seeds an installation and bootstraps its cloud; the overcloud is the cloud cluster, AKS first, the platform then moves into, still as one installation.

planned #61

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A cloud in the settings file makes nereus init create the undercloud, tailwind-undercloud, instead of a plain local cluster:

apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: InitConfig
spec:
  cloud: azure
---
apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Installation
metadata:
  name: tailwind
spec:
  alias: tailwind

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
your az loginUndercloud(k3d, on your machine)Nereus installation(seeded here)bootstrap plan(issuer, identity)Overcloud(AKS)Nereus installation(the same one, moved)pivotAzure your az loginUndercloud(k3d, your machine)Nereus installation(seeded here)bootstrap plan(issuer, identity)pivotOvercloud(AKS)Nereus installation(the same one, moved)Azure

The undercloud gets the cloud to trust it, then hands the platform to the overcloud.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• nereus init --target azure computes the cluster's OIDC issuer from the installation's id before the cluster exists, then installs the cloud reef and its azure Nereid.
  • The Nereid plans the bootstrap (the names, the issuer storage, the issuer documents, the first identity); the CLI shows the plan and runs it with your own login once you approve.
  • From then on the cloud trusts the cluster's tokens through workload identity federation, so the platform keeps no secret.
  • The pivot moves the platform to the overcloud, as Cluster API's clusterctl move does, moves the federated credential to the overcloud's issuer, then deletes the undercloud planned #61.
  • Both are one installation: the same name, id and identities; only the cluster role label, core.getnereus.dev/cluster-role, stays with each cluster.

docs.title: Not this
docs.text:
• Not two installations, nor staging and production: one platform on two clusters, one after the other.
  • Not a management cluster kept forever: the undercloud is deleted after the pivot.
  • Not needed on a laptop: a plain nereus init with no cloud makes a cluster named nereus, with no undercloud role.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Tenancy and access: whose each thing is, and who may do what.

docs.title: What Nereus is
docs.text: Nereus is a composable API platform: reefs add the APIs, Nereids look after them, both installed at runtime, and one API and one CLI serve them all.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
nereus --help groups the commands: the platform's own, the model's, and one group per reef the installation knows:

nereus --help
output
Usage: nereus [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

  nereus: a composable API platform: reefs add the APIs, Nereids look after
  them, installed at runtime.

Model:
  mandate         Mandates: each binds one reef to one Nereid.
  nereid          Nereids: the controllers that look after reefs.
  reef            Reefs: the capabilities of the platform, each an API group.
  user            Users: one per person, whatever the login.

Reefs:
  authentication  Reef authentication, looked after by nereid keycloak.
  release         Reef release, looked after by nereid flux.
  secrets         Reef secrets, looked after by nereid openbao.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
IDE, CLI, Portal, AgentsNereus installationAskControl planeNereus APIreefs, one per planeNereidscluster stateEnvironmentsWorkloadsapps from a golden paththeir routesDatabasesMessage streamsreconcileImages and secrets(registry, vault)Outside(Cloudflare, GitHub, the cloud)LaptopVirtualPrivate cloudPublic cloudEdgeUnderlying infrastructure IDE, CLI, Portal, AgentsAskNereus installationControl planeNereus APIreefs, one per planeNereidsreconcileEnvironmentsapps from a golden paththeir routesDatabasesMessage streamsImages and secretsregistry, vaultOutsideCloudflare, GitHub, the cloudUNDERLYING INFRASTRUCTURELaptopVirtualPrivate cloudPublic cloudEdge

One installation: the control plane reconciles the environments, beside the services it uses, on any infrastructure.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The engine is core, the kinds Reef, Nereid, Mandate and Profile, and nothing else; the words are in Reef, Nereid and Mandate.
  • Every capability arrives at runtime as a reef, and a Nereid fills it with the tool you pick (Runtime install and profiles).
  • The CLI, the portal and agents go through one door, the Nereus API, and never name a tool.
  • Swapping a tool means adding another Nereid to the reef and moving its default Mandate: no command, client or app declaration changes.
  • Whose each thing is, and who may act on it, belongs to the platform itself (Tenancy and access).

docs.title: Not this
docs.text:
• Not only an Internal Developer Platform: that is one profile, internal-developer-platform; a reef can serve any recurring knowledge work.
  • Not a portal: the portal is one reef, portal, and one client of the API.
  • Not a wrapper around one tool: Flux, Keycloak or OpenBao stay behind a Nereid, and a reef outlives the tool.
  • Not a replacement for Kubernetes: it runs on a cluster, and each reef is an API group there.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Reef, Nereid and Mandate: the three words the rest of the docs use.

docs.title: Turn on authentication
docs.text: Turn on sign-in for an installation: the authentication reef and its Nereid keycloak run the realm nereus, and every person logs in with nereus login, never with a kubeconfig.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A cluster from Prepare the cluster. With --profile internal-developer-platform the reef and the Nereid are already there, and step 1 reports unchanged.
  • After a plain nereus init, Nereids for the secrets and release reefs, the release one with a default Mandate: Keycloak runs as a Release.
  • Tenancy and access explains who the initial admin is and what nereus-admins can do.

docs.title: 1. Install the reef and its Nereid
docs.text:
nereus reef apply adds the reef; nereus nereid apply runs Keycloak and makes the default Mandate keycloak.

nereus reef apply authentication
output
✓ core/reefs/authentication 0.1.0 created (authentication.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1: tokens)

Next steps:

  nereus authentication --help
  nereus nereid apply <nereid> --reef authentication

nereus nereid apply keycloak \
  --reef authentication
output
✓ core/nereids/keycloak created, Ready, pinned to sha256:e8731e3fb833: see 'nereus authentication --help'
  release/releases/keycloak created by core/nereids/keycloak, Ready (codecentric/keycloakx 7.0.1 in namespace nereus-system)
  core/mandates/keycloak created (reef: authentication, nereid: keycloak, default)
  issuer  http://localhost:8180/realms/nereus (dev mode, kept in the Database keycloak)
  client  claude (public, PKCE S256, redirect https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback)
  user    nereus (password: kubectl --namespace nereus-system get secret keycloak-user --output jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode)

Next steps:

  kubectl --namespace nereus-system port-forward service/keycloak-server-http 8180:8180

Until its Release is Ready the Nereid reports WaitingForRelease; with no default release Mandate it reports NoReleaseNereid. On a cluster with an ingress address the realm is served at http://auth.localhost:8080 and needs no port-forward.

docs.title: 2. Log in as the initial admin
docs.text:
The realm's user nereus is the instance's initial admin, in nereus-admins. nereus login --initial-admin reads its generated password with your kubeconfig and copies it to the clipboard, never printed. Paste it on the login page.

nereus login --initial-admin
output
The initial admin's password is in your clipboard (user nereus). Paste it on the login page.
Opening http://auth.localhost:8080/realms/nereus/protocol/openid-connect/auth?... in the browser.
logged in as nereus (nereus-admins), issuer http://auth.localhost:8080/realms/nereus

docs.title: 3. Give the realm a public host
docs.text:
nereus mandate apply replaces every param, so name them all. The API trusts one issuer at a time: after the change every person runs nereus login again.

nereus mandate apply keycloak \
  --reef authentication \
  --nereid keycloak \
  --default \
  --param publicUrl=https://auth.example.com

docs.title: 4. Log in from another machine
docs.text:
nereus login with the instance's address asks the instance for its identity provider, so no kubeconfig is needed. The address is kept for the next commands.

KUBECONFIG=/nonexistent nereus login https://nereus.example.com
output
Opening https://auth.example.com/realms/nereus/protocol/openid-connect/auth?... in the browser.
instance https://nereus.example.com saved in ~/.config/nereus/config.yaml
logged in as ana-silva (nereus-users), issuer https://auth.example.com/realms/nereus

On a machine with no browser, add --use-device-code and type the code on another device.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
nereus whoami asks the Nereus API who you are.

nereus whoami
output
ana-silva (nereus-admins, nereus-users)

nereus status now reads through the API with your token, and lists the reef:

nereus status
output
REEF            NEREID      VERSION  STATUS  AGE
authentication  keycloak    0.1.0    Ready   2m
core            nereus-api  0.1.0    Ready   4m
                thetis      0.1.0    Ready   4m
release         flux        0.1.0    Ready   3m
secrets         openbao     0.1.0    Ready   4m
tenancy         -           -        Ready   4m

Registry  localhost:5111

docs.title: Next
docs.text: • Grant access to the people of your team.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• The authentication reef: every command, and the realm's clients.
  • ADR 0006: the OIDC contract the default Mandate publishes.

docs.title: Authorize a team
docs.text: Give a team a role on a node of the tenancy tree: every member gets it by joining and loses it by leaving, and the Nereus API asks the authorization reef before every read and write.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A cluster from Prepare the cluster with --profile internal-developer-platform: it brings the teams reef, the authorization reef and its Nereid openfga with the default Mandate that turns the check on. Before that Mandate exists, only nereus-admins passes.
  • A Project to own the team, from Know whose each thing is: project/payments below.
  • Tenancy and access tells a User, a Team, a Role and a Binding apart.

docs.title: 1. Register the people
docs.text:
nereus user create records the e-mail the person's first sign-in is matched with. A login with no User may do nothing.

nereus user create ana --email ana@example.com
output
✓ core/users/ana created

nereus user create bruno --email bruno@example.com
output
✓ core/users/bruno created

Next steps:

  nereus teams create <team> --owner project/<project>

docs.title: 2. Make the team and name its tech lead
docs.text:
nereus teams create makes the team under its Project; nereus teams member create adds a member, here with the position tech-lead.

nereus teams create payments --owner project/payments
output
✓ teams/teams/payments created

Next steps:

  nereus teams member create <user> --team payments

nereus teams member create ana \
  --team payments \
  --position tech-lead
output
✓ teams/teams/payments/members/ana created

Next steps:

  nereus teams get payments

docs.title: 3. Give the team a role
docs.text:
nereus authorization role list shows the roles: administrator is built in and cannot change; viewer, developer and team-lead are examples to edit. nereus authorization binding create makes every member a developer of the Project.

nereus authorization binding create payments-developers \
  --role developer \
  --team payments \
  --owner project/payments
output
✓ authorization/bindings/payments-developers created

Next steps:

  nereus authorization binding list --owner project/payments

docs.title: 4. Give one position a role
docs.text:
With --position, only the team's tech lead gets team-lead, which may create Environments.

nereus authorization binding create payments-leads \
  --role team-lead \
  --team payments \
  --position tech-lead \
  --owner project/payments
output
✓ authorization/bindings/payments-leads created

Next steps:

  nereus authorization binding list --owner project/payments

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
nereus authorization binding list shows who holds what on the Project.

nereus authorization binding list --owner project/payments
output
NAME                 SUBJECT                         ROLE       OWNER
mobile-leads         team/payments-mobile/tech-lead  team-lead  project/payments
payments-developers  team/payments                   developer  project/payments
payments-leads       team/payments/tech-lead         team-lead  project/payments

nereus authorization can-i answers with the binding that allows it. With no --user it asks about you.

nereus authorization can-i create environment/environments \
  --owner project/payments \
  --user ana
output
yes: authorization/bindings/payments-leads gives team-lead to team/payments/tech-lead at project/payments

Signed in as Bruno, creating an Environment there is refused, and nothing changes:

nereus environment create staging --owner project/payments
output
✗ environment/environments/staging: bruno may not create environment/environments at project/payments. To see who may, run:
  nereus authorization binding list --owner project/payments
  Nothing was changed.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: • Know whose each thing is: the tree a binding reaches down.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• The authorization reef and the teams reef: every command, presenting rights included.
  • ADR 0027: users, teams, roles and bindings.

docs.title: Connect a GitHub App
docs.text: Connect a GitHub App as a Mandate of the authentication reef's Nereid github: its status proves where the App is installed and what it may do, and consumers ask it for one-hour tokens, never for its key.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A cluster with the secrets reef and its vault default, from Keep a secret.
  • An App you already have: its id, and its private key (a .pem file). With no App yet, nereus authentication app-register creates one in the browser, and only the Nereid ever holds its key; skip to step 4.
  • Reef, Nereid and Mandate: the App is a Mandate, its id and key its params.

docs.title: 1. Keep the App's private key as a secret
docs.text:
nereus secrets create encrypts it on your machine before it leaves it.

GITHUB_APP_KEY="$(cat app.pem)" nereus secrets create github-app-key --from-env GITHUB_APP_KEY
output
✓ secrets/vaults/default/secrets/github-app-key created (key SHA256:l0jt+UOKUmA72jydN0DSpTzFJIdO6wP/xUvdAKryBe4)
Stored encrypted; a Kubernetes Secret is made only when a binding asks for it (#532).

docs.title: 2. Apply the Nereid
docs.text:
The Nereid is opt-in, outside every profile. nereus nereid apply gives it one namespace, nereus-system-github, the only one where it reads Secrets.

nereus nereid apply github --reef authentication
output
✓ core/nereids/github created, Ready, pinned to sha256:021dd70640d0: see 'nereus authentication --help'
  namespaces/nereus-system-github applied (the github Nereid's Role there, where vault default delivers the App keys)

Next steps:

  nereus mandate create github --reef authentication --nereid github --param appId=<id> --param privateKey=<secret> --param allow=<namespace>:<repository>:<permission>=<level> --default

docs.title: 3. Create the App's Mandate
docs.text:
nereus mandate create names the App, its key's secret and who may ask a token. Each allow is <namespace>:<repository or *>:<permission>=<level>; with none, no token is ever made.

nereus mandate create github \
  --reef authentication \
  --nereid github \
  --param appId=123456 \
  --param privateKey=github-app-key \
  --param allow=nereus-system:*:contents=read \
  --param allow=example:example/app:metadata=read \
  --default
output
✓ core/mandates/github created (reef: authentication, nereid: github, default)
  clusterrole/controller-github configured (nereid github writes the status of mandate github)

docs.title: 4. Lend a repository for an hour
docs.text:
nereus authentication token create asks the Mandate for a token of one repository. The Nereid writes it to the Secret token-<name> of the Token's namespace; no command prints it.

nereus authentication token create catalog \
  --repository example/app \
  --permission contents=read
output
✓ authentication/tokens/catalog created (expires in 1h, mandate github)

Next steps:

  nereus authentication token get catalog

A namespace the Mandate does not allow gets no token, and the line names the allow to add.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
nereus mandate get shows the App as GitHub answered, and the allowlist as the Nereid read it.

nereus mandate get github
output
Name:           github
Reef:           authentication
Nereid:         github
Default:        true
Params:         allow=nereus-system:*:contents=read;example:example/app:metadata=read, appId=123456, privateKey=github-app-key
Status:         Ready
App:            example-nereus
Installations:  example (all repositories)
Permissions:    contents=read, metadata=read
Age:            10s
Allowed:
  NAMESPACE      REPOSITORY   PERMISSIONS
  nereus-system  *            contents=read
  example        example/app  metadata=read

Another status names what is wrong: NotInstalled with the URL to install the App, InvalidCredentials for a key of no App, MissingParam for a secret that does not exist.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
nereus authentication token delete catalog
output
✓ authentication/tokens/catalog deleted

Next steps:

  nereus authentication token list

docs.title: Next
docs.text: • Connect a repository host that builds and mirrors through the App.

docs.text:
• The authentication reef: app-register, tokens and every command.
  • ADR 0006: the platform's identity towards an outside system is a Mandate.

docs.title: Grant access
docs.text: Grant a Nereid that reaches the cloud the roles it asks for: the Nereid acts as its reef's identity, <installation>-<reef>-<role>, with no secret of its own; it asks, and you approve with your own login.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• An installation connected to the cloud: the cloud reef with its Nereid azure.
  • A Nereid whose image declares requires: cloud (spec 0005), here keyvault for the secrets reef.
  • A cloud login that can create identities and role assignments. A role it cannot write is printed as the command an administrator runs.

Recorded against fakes

The outputs below come from the CLI's tests, against a fake cloud Nereid and a fake cloud. test/scene-azure runs a real subscription.

docs.title: 1. Apply the Nereid
docs.text:
nereus nereid apply gives the Nereid a short-lived token for the cloud, writes its reef's access entry and shows the plan that creates its identity.

nereus nereid apply keyvault \
  --reef secrets
output
✓ image            0.0s  secrets-keyvault-controller:0.1.0 implements secrets, requires cloud
✓ login            0.0s  az, account 00000000-…
✓ mandate          0.0s  core/mandates/keyvault created (reef: secrets, nereid: keyvault, default)
✓ plan             0.1s  2 requests for secrets (r-01m5bk)
  1  create  managed identity      tailwind-secrets-reader  in westeurope
  2  create  federated credential  tailwind-undercloud-keyvault
  tagged with the installation and who asked
  --show-requests for the why, URLs and tags
  log: ~/.local/state/nereus/logs/20261019T221500Z-install.log
Approve 2 requests? [y/N]: y
✓ requests         0.0s  2 applied
✓ ready            0.0s  keyvault reports Ready
  total            0.1s
✓ keyvault added to secrets · acts as tailwind-secrets-reader

Another Nereid of the same reef later keeps the identity and its grants: the plan only swaps the federated credential.

docs.title: 2. See what is asked
docs.text:
nereus system access list shows each reef's access entries and the roles its Nereid asks for but nobody approved yet.

nereus system access list
output
REEF       REQUEST        WHAT                                                                                                              STATE
cloud      r-01jaq3…m2n3  identity tailwind-cloud-provisioner                                                                               Applied
secrets    r-01m59t…zejf  identity tailwind-secrets-reader                                                                                  Applied
secrets    -              grant Key Vault Secrets User on key vault vault-0123456789abcdef in resource group tailwind-platform              Asked
terraform  -              grant Storage Blob Data Contributor on storage account state0123456789abcdef in resource group tailwind-platform  Asked

An ask for Owner, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator shows Refused and is never copied into a plan.

docs.title: 3. Approve
docs.text:
nereus system access approve --all turns every reef's asks into plans, shows them and runs them after one question; --dry-run shows them and runs none.

nereus system access approve --all
output
1/2 secrets  r-01m5bk…5563  2 requests
  1  check   managed identity  tailwind-secrets-reader
  2  access  Key Vault Secrets User on vault-0123456789abcdef to tailwind-secrets-reader
2/2 terraform  r-01m5bk…dh0a  3 requests
  1  create  managed identity      tailwind-terraform-runner  in westeurope
  2  create  federated credential  tailwind-undercloud-stacks
  3  access  Storage Blob Data Contributor on state0123456789abcdef to tailwind-terraform-runner
  tagged with the installation and who asked
  --show-requests for the why, URLs and tags
  log: ~/.local/state/nereus/logs/20261019T221500Z-approve.log
Approve 2 plans (5 requests)? [y/N]: y
✗ 1/2 secrets  r-01m5bk…5563  grant Key Vault Secrets User on vault-0123456789abcdef to tailwind-secrets-reader refused: AuthorizationFailed: The client cannot write role assignments on the account.
    ${0.properties.principalId} = 33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333
An administrator can grant Key Vault Secrets User to tailwind-secrets-reader:
  az role assignment create --assignee-object-id 33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333 --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope /subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/tailwind-platform/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/vault-0123456789abcdef
✓ 2/2 terraform  r-01m5bk…dh0a  3 applied
    ${0.properties.principalId} = 33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333
✗ 1 of 2 plans applied: run 'nereus system access approve --all' again to apply what is missing
  log: ~/.local/state/nereus/logs/20261019T221500Z-approve.log

A failed plan undoes none of the others. Hand the printed az line to an administrator, or approve with a login that holds the right.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
Run the approval again: it plans only what is still missing, and ends with every plan applied.

nereus system access approve --all
output
1/1 secrets  r-01m5bk…satf  2 requests
  1  check   managed identity  tailwind-secrets-reader
  2  access  Key Vault Secrets User on vault-0123456789abcdef to tailwind-secrets-reader
  --show-requests for the why, URLs and tags
  log: ~/.local/state/nereus/logs/20261019T221500Z-approve.log
Approve 2 requests? [y/N]: y
✓ 1/1 secrets  r-01m5bk…satf  2 applied
    ${0.properties.principalId} = 33333333-3333-4333-8333-333333333333
✓ 1 plan applied

  • Spec 0005: the cloud reef, its plans and what a Nereid may ask.

docs.title: Know whose each thing is
docs.text: Build the installation's tenancy tree, Organizations with Projects under them, so every Workload, Environment and database names who it belongs to.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A cluster from Prepare the cluster, in any profile: nereus init installs the tenancy reef, its admission policy and the tree in tenancy/. The reef has no Nereid.
  • Tenancy and access explains the tree and what an owner points at.

docs.title: 1. Create an Organization
docs.text:
nereus tenancy organization create makes the top of a tree, its boundary.

nereus tenancy organization create example
output
✓ tenancy/organizations/example created

Next steps:

  nereus tenancy organization list

docs.title: 2. Add a Project under it
docs.text:
nereus tenancy project create needs a parent that exists; the line shows the full path. --dry-run --output yaml prints the object as apply takes it.

nereus tenancy project create shop \
  --parent organization/example \
  --repository https://github.com/example/shop
output
✓ tenancy/organizations/example/projects/shop created

Next steps:

  nereus tenancy project list

docs.title: 3. Nest a Project
docs.text:
A Project can sit under another Project. A parent that does not exist is refused, and nothing is written.

nereus tenancy project create checkout --parent project/shop
output
✓ tenancy/organizations/example/projects/shop/projects/checkout created

Next steps:

  nereus tenancy project list

docs.title: 4. Make a Project your default owner
docs.text:
nereus config set owner names the owner the next commands use when you give none.

nereus config set owner project/checkout

The kinds come from the installation, not the CLI: an installation whose reefs/tenancy/ adds Department and Squad gets nereus tenancy squad create the same way. To keep the tree in files, nereus tenancy apply --from-file tenancy/ writes parents before children.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
nereus tenancy project get shows the full path and the boundary Organization.

nereus tenancy project get checkout
output
Name:        checkout
Kind:        Project
Path:        tenancy/organizations/example/projects/shop/projects/checkout
Parent:      Project/shop
Boundary:    Organization/example
Repository:  -

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Deletes everything under it

--cascade deletes every node under the Project, deepest first. Preview it with --dry-run.

nereus tenancy project delete shop --cascade

docs.title: Next
docs.text: • Authorize a team on a Project of the tree.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• The tenancy reef: every command.
  • ADR 0015: one tree of a fixed shape, with kinds from each installation.

docs.title: Run the CLI from a checkout
docs.text: Put nereus on the PATH from a checkout of the repository, editable: a change in cli/ takes effect at the next run.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • A checkout of github.com/getnereus/nereus and uv.

docs.title: 1. Install it editable
docs.text:
make cli

It also installs nrs, the same program under a short name for typing (#606). It replaces any other nereus installed with uv tool.

docs.title: 2. Turn on Tab completion
docs.text:
From bash or zsh, for nereus and nrs, then open a new terminal:

nereus --install-completion

nrs <Tab> lists the commands, nrs nereid apply --<Tab> the options, and nrs reef get <Tab> the reefs the CLI last saw on the cluster, with no call to it (#795).

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text: nereus --help lists the command groups. git pull updates the CLI; nereus upgrade refuses an editable install.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text: make cli-uninstall removes nereus and nrs.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Prepare the cluster: a checkout's init installs the Nereids from the local registry, after make nereids.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Start a new Nereid from the template.
  • Keep the CLI up to date, for a CLI installed from a release.

docs.title: Pass the conformance tests
docs.text: Prove that a Nereid serves every verb of every kind of its reef, with the status its contract declares, before anyone else relies on it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A throwaway k3d cluster, never the kept cluster k3d-nereus: the check creates and deletes objects, and refuses any other context.
  • The Nereid applied and Ready (Build a Nereid's image), and named by the reef's default Mandate.

docs.title: 1. Ship a sample per kind
docs.text: Each kind of the reef has a sample in its contract, cli/src/nereus/interfaces/<reef>/samples/<kind>.yaml: the objects the kind needs first, the object as created, then the same object with a change to its spec. The release reef ships release.yaml, repository.yaml, source.yaml and target.yaml.

docs.title: 2. Write the status the contract declares
docs.text: Every object the Nereid answers gets a Ready condition whose reason the contract declares, status.observedGeneration, and the finalizer <reef>.getnereus.dev/cleanup, removed only once what it made is gone. A kind the Nereid does nothing with still answers, with the reason NotApplicable.

docs.title: 3. Run the check
docs.text:
test/conformance drives nereus and kubectl kind by kind: apply with --dry-run then for real, the status checked against the kind's schema, the finalizer, a change, get, list, then delete.

test/conformance release --nereid reference-release
output
✓ reference-release serves every verb of every kind of the release reef and honours its contract: Release Repository Source Target

--timeout sets the seconds each wait lasts, 120 by default.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
The last line of the run names every kind it proved; any FAIL: line before it names the object, the field and the rule it breaks.

make scene-release runs the same check against the reference Nereid, then against flux.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• See what happened when a step of the check fails.
  • Require a reef.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Spec 0003: what every Nereid answers, and the check kind by kind.
  • ADR 0013: the verbs every kind serves.

docs.title: Build a Nereid's image
docs.text: Build a Nereid's image whose labels name its reef, push it to the local registry and apply it: the CLI reads the labels before anything runs in the cluster.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A cluster from Prepare the cluster: nereus init creates the local registry localhost:5111.
  • The reef applied, here release: Apply your first reef.
  • Docker, to build and push. The example is the reference Nereid of controllers/reference, whose commands only simulate output.

docs.title: 1. Declare the reef in labels
docs.text:
The Dockerfile names the reef the Nereid looks after, the reefs it requires, its name and its version:

LABEL ${API_GROUP}/reef=${REEF} \
      ${API_GROUP}/requires=${REQUIRES} \
      ${API_GROUP}/nereid=${NEREID} \
      ${API_GROUP}/reference=${REFERENCE} \
      org.opencontainers.image.version=${VERSION} \
      org.opencontainers.image.title=${TITLE}

${API_GROUP} is core.getnereus.dev. The reference Nereid's commands are data, in commands.yaml, each with its help and an example:

- path: [repo, add]
  help: Add a chart repository.
  arguments:
    - name: name
      help: Name of the repository.
    - name: url
      help: URL of the repository.

docs.title: 2. Build and push
docs.text:
make reference builds the image for the release reef and pushes it; a Nereid from the template builds with make nereids.

make reference
output
✓ localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0 pushed: nereus nereid apply --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0

docs.title: 3. Apply it
docs.text:
nereus nereid apply reads the labels, pins the image to its digest and waits for Ready.

nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --reef release \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0
output
✓ core/nereids/reference-release created, Ready, pinned to sha256:ffb8e8957c6e: see 'nereus release --help'

Next steps:

  nereus nereid list

docs.title: 4. Move it to a new image
docs.text:
Applied again with another image, the Nereid is updated in place; --dry-run shows what would change and writes nothing.

nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.1 \
  --dry-run
output
Would configure core/nereids/reference-release for reef release: image sha256:ffb8e8957c6e → sha256:3f2a9c1d7e4b.
Nothing changed (--dry-run).

Without --dry-run, the apply waits for the new pod and says what the image was:

nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.1
output
✓ core/nereids/reference-release configured, Ready, pinned to sha256:3f2a9c1d7e4b (was sha256:ffb8e8957c6e): see 'nereus release --help'

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
nereus nereid list shows the Nereid Ready on its reef:

nereus nereid list
output
NEREID             REEFS    IMAGE                                                 STATUS  AGE
reference-release  release  localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0     Ready   10s
openbao            secrets  localhost:5111/openbao-controller:0.1.0               Ready   1m

The commands it published are under its reef: nereus release --help.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
nereus nereid delete removes it; its reef stays.

nereus nereid delete reference-release
output
✓ core/nereids/reference-release deleted

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Require a reef: a label that makes one Nereid depend on another reef.
  • Pass the conformance tests.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Reef, Nereid and Mandate.
  • Spec 0003: the labels read at install, and what Ready means.

docs.title: Start a new Nereid
docs.text: Render a new Nereid from the template: a skeleton that already reports Ready, serves its metrics and passes its tests, so you only write the Tool's work.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A checkout of Nereus, with uv on the PATH: the template runs through Copier, pinned and run by uvx, so there is nothing else to install.
  • The reef the Nereid looks after, and the Tool it drives: here the edge reef and Caddy.

docs.title: 1. Render the skeleton
docs.text:
scripts/nereid/new renders templates/nereid into controllers/<tool>/ and refuses a folder that exists.

scripts/nereid/new --reef edge --tool caddy
output
✓ controllers/caddy/ created from templates/nereid (copier 9.19.1)
  server.py            the reconcile loop on nereid-sdk, Ready, status.kinds, GET /metrics, the commands' HTTP server
  kube.py              the Kubernetes API, standard library
  requirements.txt     nereid-sdk==0.5.0 (#754), pinned
  Dockerfile           edge-caddy-controller, nereid-sdk from the build context (#741)
  README.md            what the Nereid does, and what every Nereid must do
  test_server.py       the loop's tests, a failing pass counted with its reason
  .copier-answers.yml  the answers, for copier update
Next steps:
  add caddy to NEREIDS in the Makefile, its tests and lint to make test and make lint
  make nereids
  nereus nereid apply caddy --reef edge --image localhost:5111/caddy-controller:0.1.0

By default it serves the kind <reef>s; --kinds hostnames,certificates names the reef's kinds it serves instead.

docs.title: 2. Write the Tool's work
docs.text: The Tool's work goes in reconcile() of server.py. The generated README.md lists what every Nereid must do: serve every verb of every kind of its reef, with the status its contract declares.

docs.title: 3. Wire it into the build
docs.text: Add caddy to NEREIDS in the Makefile, and its tests and lint to make test and make lint, as the skeleton's next steps say.

docs.title: 4. Take a later change of the template
docs.text:
From the root of a clean checkout, Copier brings a change of the template as a diff that keeps the Nereid's own changes:

uvx copier==9.19.1 update \
  --defaults \
  --vcs-ref HEAD \
  controllers/caddy

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
The skeleton's tests run on the library of the checkout, as the other Nereids' do in make test:

uv run --project cli --with lib/nereid pytest -q controllers/caddy
output
.............                                                            [100%]
13 passed in 0.18s

make nereid-check, part of make test, fails when a Nereid does not pin nereid-sdk at the version of lib/nereid/pyproject.toml, in requirements.txt and in its Dockerfile.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Build a Nereid's image, with the labels that name its reef, and apply it.
  • Require a reef when the Nereid needs another reef's work.
  • Pass the conformance tests: every verb of every kind of its reef.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Reef, Nereid and Mandate: what a Nereid looks after.
  • Spec 0003: the contract a Nereid honours.

docs.title: Require a reef
docs.text:
Make a Nereid require another reef through a label of its image: the CLI refuses to apply it until that reef has a Nereid, and refuses to delete that reef's last Nereid while it is needed.

A Nereid requires reefs, never Nereids (spec 0003): any Nereid of the reef will do.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The release reef with its Nereid reference-release, from Build a Nereid's image.
  • An image whose label core.getnereus.dev/requires lists the reefs it needs, comma-separated. Build the reference Nereid as a Nereid of a docs reef that requires release: docker build --build-arg API_GROUP=core.getnereus.dev --build-arg REEF=docs --build-arg REQUIRES=release --tag localhost:5111/reference-docs-controller:0.1.0 controllers/reference, then docker push it.

docs.title: 1. Create the reef
docs.text:
nereus reef create adds the docs reef the new Nereid looks after.

nereus reef create docs

docs.title: 2. Apply the Nereid that requires a reef
docs.text:
nereus nereid apply reads requires from the image's labels and records it in the Nereid's spec.requires.

nereus nereid apply reference-docs \
  --reef docs \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-docs-controller:0.1.0

release has a Nereid, so the apply goes ahead. Without one, it is refused before anything runs, with reference-docs requires reefs with no Nereid: release. and the command that applies one. When the required reef's Nereid is there but not Ready, the apply warns and goes ahead.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text:
nereus nereid list shows both Nereids Ready: reference-docs on docs, reference-release on release.

nereus nereid list

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
reference-release is the last Nereid of release, which docs requires, so nereus nereid delete refuses it first:

nereus nereid delete reference-release
output
✗ reference-release is the last Nereid of reef release, which added Nereids require: reference-docs.
  Remove them first, or go ahead with: nereus nereid delete reference-release --force

Delete reference-docs first, then the docs reef with nereus reef delete; reference-release stays:

nereus nereid delete reference-docs

nereus reef delete docs

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Pass the conformance tests.
  • When the Nereid stops: what a required reef's Nereid does to its commands.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Reef, Nereid and Mandate.
  • Spec 0003: the labels read at install, requires among them.

docs.title: Keep the CLI up to date
docs.text: Keep a nereus installed from a release up to date: it upgrades itself in the background, and you choose how (#1782).

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: • nereus installed from a release, as in Install the CLI. An editable install from a checkout updates with git pull instead: Run the CLI from a checkout.

docs.title: 1. Let it upgrade itself
docs.text:
At most once a day, a call starts nereus upgrade --background on its own, detached, and the next call says so on stderr:

output
nereus upgraded 0.1.22 → 0.1.23

The worker reads the release manifest (latest.json of the getnereus/install releases), refuses a wheel whose sha256 differs, and installs it with uv tool install --force. It logs to ~/.local/state/nereus/upgrade.log ($XDG_STATE_HOME).

docs.title: 2. Upgrade now, or only look
docs.text:
nereus upgrade

nereus upgrade --check only says which release is the latest.

docs.title: 3. Choose how it upgrades
docs.text:
The CLI's config, ~/.config/nereus/config.yaml, holds the mode: background installs (the default), notify only says that a release is available, off never looks.

nereus config set auto_upgrade notify

nereus config set check_interval 7d looks once a week. For one shell, NEREUS_AUTO_UPGRADE=off wins over the config.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text: nereus --version prints the release you upgraded to. It never upgrades on its own an editable install, a dev version (0.1.23.dev4), a run with CI set, or shell completion.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Write the settings of an installation, or prepare a cluster for Nereus.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• NEREUS_VERSION=0.1.23 pins a version at install time; sh -s -- --help lists the installer's options.
  • The settings file holds the settings of nereus init, not the CLI's own config.

docs.title: Connect to the cloud
docs.text:
Apply the Nereid azure of the cloud reef: it plans the cloud requests, and the CLI shows them in plain words, asks, and runs them on your machine with your short-lived token, which never leaves it.

Recorded against fakes

The outputs are what the CLI prints in its tests, against a fake Nereid, az and cloud. A real subscription is checked by hand with test/scene-azure (#266).

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A cluster whose issuer Azure can reach: Prepare the undercloud runs these steps for you; run them by hand on an existing cluster or for another subscription.
  • az login done, and a default location (az config set defaults.location=westeurope) or --param location=<region> below.
  • The cloud reef applied: nereus reef apply cloud --from-file ./reefs/cloud/.

docs.title: 1. See the plan, run nothing
docs.text:
nereus nereid apply reads your login, writes the Mandate and the Cloud Instance default, waits for the Nereid's plan and shows it. With --dry-run, no cloud request is sent.

nereus nereid apply azure \
  --reef cloud \
  --dry-run \
  --param location=northeurope
output
✓ image            0.0s  cloud-azure-controller:0.1.0 implements cloud, login az
✓ login            0.0s  az, account 00000000-…, organization from the login
✓ plan             0.0s  3 requests for cloud (r-01m5bk)

Plan for Azure · northeurope · 3 requests · not run (--dry-run)
  1  create  resource group        tailwind-platform
  2  create  managed identity      tailwind-cloud-provisioner
  3  create  federated credential  tailwind-undercloud-azure
  tagged with the installation and who asked
  --show-requests for the why, URLs and tags

Nothing ran in Azure. To run it:
$ nereus nereid apply azure --reef cloud --param location=northeurope --approve-access

The CLI derives each line's words from the request's method, URL and body, never from text the Nereid sends, so what you read is what runs. --show-requests adds each step's why, method, URL and tags.

docs.title: 2. Approve and run it
docs.text:
Without --approve-access, the CLI asks Approve 3 requests? [y/N]; a non-interactive run prints the plan and stops. Each line then gets ✓ and its time, and the run ends with the proof: the Nereid exchanging its token.

nereus nereid apply azure \
  --reef cloud \
  --param location=northeurope \
  --approve-access

docs.title: 3. Pick another subscription or location
docs.text: --param account=<subscription id> uses another subscription of the same login; --param location=<region> writes the location, which a later run keeps.

docs.title: 4. Use an identity an administrator created
docs.text: When you may not create identities, --param identity=<client-id> names one an administrator created. A first plan checks it is in the account; only once its client id matches does the Nereid plan its federated credential, so another identity is never trusted.

docs.title: Check it worked
docs.text: The run ends with ✓ azure exchanged its token as tailwind-cloud-provisioner. Every resource carries tags naming the installation, who asked and why it exists; the CLI shows no plan with a resource that lacks them.

docs.text:
