docs.title: O vigia da praia sinaliza as ordens que não consegue atribuir
Adoption metrics
docs.text: Backstage adoption and success metrics published by Spotify. Use: a reference for measuring the adoption of the platform (not only of the portal).

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Official Backstage doc, "Strategies for adopting", section "KPIs and metrics": https://backstage.io/docs/overview/adopting/: the part of the documentation that lists the metrics (source in docs/overview/adopting.md in the backstage/backstage repository).
  • Spotify blog, "How we measure Backstage success at Spotify": Helen Greul, 2021-10-18 (updated 2026-06-30). https://backstage.spotify.com/discover/blog/measuring-backstage-success-at-spotify
  • InfoQ, "Spotify Reveals Metrics for Success of Developer Portal Backstage": Matt Saunders, 2023-04-24. https://www.infoq.com/news/2023/04/spotify-success-backstage/
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: North-star metric: onboarding time
docs.text:
• Official doc: "Onboarding time — Time until new engineers are productive. At Spotify we measure this as the time until the employee has merged their 10th PR (this metric was down 55% two years after deploying Backstage)."
  • Spotify blog: the "time-to-merge your 10th pull request" had reached 60 days and dropped to "less than 20 days for a new joiner to merge their 10th PR". The blog also says the metric is a good proxy for the overall complexity of the ecosystem, even for those who do not hire at Spotify's pace.
  • The numbers do not add up with each other: 60 to under 20 days is a drop of more than 66%; the doc says 55% "two years after deploying". They are probably measurements from different moments. Always cite the source and the date of the number used.
  • Caveat from Pia Nilsson herself (former head of Platform Developer Experience at Spotify), in an InfoQ talk: it is not a fantastic metric and lacks nuance; it was copied from Meta. Use it as a direction.

docs.title: Other KPIs in the official doc
docs.text:
• Number of merges per developer/day (less tool switching, more time coding).
  • Deploys to production (frequency as a proxy for productivity).
  • MTTR (finding the root cause faster with the integrated tools).
  • Context switching: "the number of different tools an engineer has to interact with" to complete a task.
  • T-shapedness: the ability to contribute in different domains thanks to consistent infrastructure.
  • eNPS: a satisfaction survey about productivity and tools.
  • Fragmentation: variance of technology choices across components, as a measure of standardization.

docs.title: Proxy metrics (adoption of the portal itself)
docs.text:
• Official doc (numbers may be out of date): 63 teams contributed at least one plugin; 135 plugins in total; 85% of contributions from outside the core team; about 50% of all employees use Backstage monthly.
  • Spotify blog (updated): "86% of internal users are satisfied with Backstage"; "80% of contributions are from outside the core team"; "150+ plugins contributed from 100+ squads"; "Most Spotify engineers visit Backstage on a daily basis"; search measured by "search success rates, click-through rates, and search results relevance".
  • The blog also warns: "there is no universal answer on how to measure Backstage success"; choose metrics aligned with each organization's goals.
  • InfoQ: Spotify measures developer productivity, efficiency and effectiveness; engagement by unique users, visit frequency and time in the portal; satisfaction by surveys in the Pulse plugin.

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• "Frequent users 2.3x more active on GitHub, deploy twice as often, changes 17% faster": appears in search summaries attributed to InfoQ (2023), but was not found in the text of the article. Do not use until the primary source is found.
  • "Average Backstage adoption outside Spotify around 10%": attributed to Spotify talks in a TechTarget report; not checked.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• The platform's north-star metric: "how many days a new dev takes to get a change into production": a measure of the ecosystem's complexity, not of portal usage.
  • Contrasts with vanity metrics (Platform as a Product, p. 35: services in the catalog, page views) and fits with the same report's scorecard (MTTFD, mean time to first deploy) and with the Stone case (NPS + funnels).
  • Natural candidate: the time from the request of an Environment to Claude Code's first use of LiteLLM.

docs.title: Agent evals and validation loops
docs.text:
Foundation for the claim in State of AI in Platform Engineering Vol. 2 (p. 29-30) that, in probabilistic paths, "Evals become the test suite", and for the recommendation of validation loops and deterministic gates on irreversible effects (see state-of-ai-in-platform-engineering.md).

  • Source (all read on 2026-10-07):
  • Anthropic (vendor), "Demystifying evals for AI agents", 2026-01-09: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
  • Anthropic (vendor), "Building effective agents", 2024-12-19: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
  • Anthropic (vendor), "Writing effective tools for agents — with agents", 2025-09-11: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
  • Anthropic (vendor), Claude Code docs, "Best practices" (undated page): https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
  • OpenAI (vendor), "A practical guide to building agents" (PDF, April 2025): https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf
  • SWE-bench (academic benchmark, Princeton): https://www.swebench.com/original.html; paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770
  • HashiCorp (vendor, official doc), terraform plan: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan
  • Kubernetes (official doc), "API Concepts": https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/
  • Crossplane (official doc), CLI command reference: https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/cli/command-reference/
  • Open Policy Agent (official doc), "Terraform": https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/terraform
  • Kyverno (official doc), "Validate Rules": https://kyverno.io/docs/policy-types/cluster-policy/validate/
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open in a browser (the site refuses scripts).

docs.title: (a) Evals as a test suite for agents
docs.text:
• Evals give you regression for free: "Once evals exist, you get baselines and regression tests for free: latency, token usage, cost per task, and error rates can be tracked on a static bank of tasks." (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)
  • A regression eval is a regression suite in the classic sense: "Regression evals ask, “Does the agent still handle all the tasks it used to?” and should have a nearly 100% pass rate. They protect against backsliding, as a decline in score signals that something is broken and needs to be improved." (same URL)
  • A capability eval becomes a regression suite: "After an agent is launched and optimized, capability evals with high pass rates can “graduate” to become a regression suite that is run continuously to catch any drift." (same URL)
  • What is evaluated is the final state, not the agent's words: "A flight-booking agent might say “Your flight has been booked” at the end of the transcript, but the outcome is whether a reservation exists in the environment’s SQL database." (same URL) — a direct infrastructure analogue: the agent saying "cluster created" does not count; what counts is the resource existing and the echo answering 200.
  • Deterministic grader for a coding agent: "Deterministic graders are natural for coding agents because software is generally straightforward to evaluate: does the code run and do the tests pass? Two widely used coding agent benchmarks, SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench, follow this approach." (same URL)
  • Each eval task needs verification: "Each evaluation prompt should be paired with a verifiable response or outcome." (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)
  • OpenAI puts evals as the first principle for choosing a model: "Set up evals to establish a performance baseline" (OpenAI PDF, section on model selection).

docs.title: SWE-bench: real tests as verification
docs.text:
• Definition of the original benchmark: "Without the Pull Request's changes, a number of test(s) fail. After the Pull Request is merged, the same set of test(s) pass. These "Fail-to-Pass" tests are the primary signal for evaluation." (https://www.swebench.com/original.html)
  • How it runs: "Per task instance, an AI system is given the issue text. The AI system should then modify the codebase in order to resolve the described issues. When the AI system is finished, we run the aforementioned Fail-to-Pass tests to check if the issue was successfully resolved." (same URL)
  • The Verified version, described by Anthropic: "SWE-bench Verified gives agents GitHub issues from popular Python repositories and grades solutions by running the test suite; a solution passes only if it fixes the failing tests without breaking existing ones." (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

docs.title: (b) Validation loop: deterministic feedback returned to the agent
docs.text:
• Ground truth at every step: "During execution, it's crucial for the agents to gain “ground truth” from the environment at each step (such as tool call results or code execution) to assess its progress." (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
  • Why coding agents work: "Code solutions are verifiable through automated tests; Agents can iterate on solutions using test results as feedback; The problem space is well-defined and structured; and Output quality can be measured objectively." (same URL)
  • The closed loop, in the words of the Claude Code docs: "Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop: every mistake waits for you to notice it. Give Claude something that produces a pass or fail, and the loop closes on its own. Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and iterates until the check passes." (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)
  • What counts as a check: "The check is anything that returns a signal Claude can read in the conversation: a test suite, a build exit code, a linter, a script that diffs output against a fixture, or a browser screenshot compared against a design." (same URL)
  • The failure must come back with the reason, not as an opaque code: "if a tool call raises an error (for example, during input validation), you can prompt-engineer your error responses to clearly communicate specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks." (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) — this is exactly the report's "the failure goes back to the agent with the reason".
  • Limit of the loop: "it's also common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control." (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents); OpenAI calls it "Exceeding failure thresholds: Set limits on agent retries or actions. If the agent exceeds these limits (e.g., fails to understand customer intent after multiple attempts), escalate to human intervention." (OpenAI PDF)

docs.title: Deterministic platform/IaC checks that serve as feedback
docs.text:
• Kubernetes rejects an unknown field with a message that lists the error: "Strict: The API server rejects the request with a 400 Bad Request error when it detects any unknown or duplicate fields. The response message from the API server specifies all the unknown or duplicate fields that the API server has detected." And: "The default validation setting for kubectl is --validate=true, which means strict server-side field validation." (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/)
  • Server-side dry-run runs all validation without persisting: "When you set ?dryRun=All, any relevant admission controllers are run, validating admission controllers check the request post-mutation, merge is performed on PATCH, fields are defaulted, and schema validation occurs. The changes are not persisted to the underlying storage, but the final object which would have been persisted is still returned to the user, along with the normal status code." (same URL)
  • Crossplane validates offline against XRDs: "The resource validate command validates the provided Crossplane resources against the schemas of the provided extensions (XRDs, CRDs, Providers, Functions, and Configurations)." and "All validation happens offline using the Kubernetes API server’s validation library, without requiring a Crossplane instance or control plane." (https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/cli/command-reference/, beta command)
  • Crossplane shows what the Composition would do before applying: composition render "runs the Crossplane render engine (either in a Docker container or via a local binary) to produce high-fidelity output that matches what the real reconciler would produce." (same URL)
  • Kyverno as an admission gate: with failureAction: Enforce, "resource creation or updates are blocked when the resource does not comply"; with Audit, the violation is recorded "but the resource creation or update is allowed." (https://kyverno.io/docs/policy-types/cluster-policy/validate/)

docs.title: (c) Deterministic guardrails on irreversible actions
docs.text:
• OpenAI, risk per tool (including reversibility): "Assess the risk of each tool available to your agent by assigning a rating—low, medium, or high—based on factors like read-only vs. write access, reversibility, required account permissions, and financial impact. Use these risk ratings to trigger automated actions, such as pausing for guardrail checks before executing high-risk functions or escalating to a human if needed." (OpenAI PDF, "Tool safeguards")
  • OpenAI, human on an irreversible action: "High-risk actions: Actions that are sensitive, irreversible, or have high stakes should trigger human oversight until confidence in the agent’s reliability grows. Examples include canceling user orders, authorizing large refunds, or making payments." (OpenAI PDF)
  • OpenAI, layered guardrails and deterministic rules: "Think of guardrails as a layered defense mechanism. While a single one is unlikely to provide sufficient protection, using multiple, specialized guardrails together creates more resilient agents." and "Rules-based protections: Simple deterministic measures (blocklists, input length limits, regex filters) to prevent known threats like prohibited terms or SQL injections." (OpenAI PDF)
  • Anthropic: "We recommend extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along with the appropriate guardrails." (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
  • Terraform plan as a preview before apply: "The terraform plan command creates an execution plan, which lets you preview the changes that Terraform plans to make to your infrastructure." -detailed-exitcode gives a binary signal for automation: "0 = Succeeded with empty diff (no changes)", "1 = Error", "2 = Succeeded with non-empty diff (changes present)". (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan, checked by rendering the page)
  • OPA over the plan: "OPA makes it possible to write policies that check the changes Terraform is about to make before it makes them." Example rule from the doc: "Authorization holds if score for the plan is acceptable and no changes are made to IAM". Benefit cited: "Giving individual developers a first pass review of their Terraform changes". (https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/terraform)

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• The exact page number of the quotes from the OpenAI PDF (the text was extracted with pdftotext; "Tool safeguards" and "Rules-based protections" appear on p. 25-26, "High-risk actions" at the end of the document). Check in the PDF before putting a page on screen.
  • OpenAI's platform "Evals guide" (https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/evals) was not read in this session.
  • The phrase "Evals become the test suite" is from the platformengineering.org report (see state-of-ai-in-platform-engineering.md); no primary vendor source uses this literal phrase. Anthropic says the equivalent ("regression suite", "regression tests for free").
  • No primary source read deals specifically with an agent-generated change going through Terraform plan/OPA/Kyverno; the link "IaC gate = agent gate" is our inference from docs that deal with change in general.
  • The literal sentence "The plan command alone does not actually carry out the proposed changes" was not verified (a WebFetch summary, not confirmed in the raw text).
  • Medium posts/secondary blogs were not consulted (403 and outside the primary-source criterion).

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Slide on deterministic / probabilistic / hybrid paths: in the probabilistic path, the eval is the test suite (Anthropic: regression evals "should have a nearly 100% pass rate"); in the hybrid, the agent generates and the deterministic gate decides.
  • Example from the first proof of concept (wasp-idp), deterministic gate: the Crossplane XRD rejects an unknown field (unknown field) — the claim with domain.parentZoneId removed fails loudly at the API server. It is Kubernetes Strict field validation applied to the XRD, and the error message that lists the field is the feedback that goes back to the agent in the validation loop.
  • Example from the first proof of concept (wasp-idp), gate on an irreversible effect: aws/eks/scripts/decommission-environment requires --yes-destroy (and offers --dry-run, analogous to terraform plan). It matches OpenAI's "High-risk actions ... should trigger human oversight"; the flag is the explicit confirmation, not the agent deciding alone.
  • Link with fitness-functions.md: the fitness function is the deterministic check that returns pass/fail; inside the validation loop it becomes the feedback the agent reads until it passes ("iterates until the check passes"). The HTTP 200 echo on both NLB IPs is the "outcome" in Anthropic's sense (the final state in the environment, not what the agent says).
  • One-line message for the slide: "The agent proposes, the deterministic check decides; irreversible asks for confirmation."

docs.title: AGENTS.md
docs.text: Context declared next to the code for agents, in the same role that catalog-info.yaml plays for humans and the portal. Covers AGENTS.md (open standard), CLAUDE.md (Claude Code's equivalent) and Agent Skills (open standard for packaged capabilities), plus the studies that measure the effect of these files.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
All read on 2026-10-07.

  • The standard's official site: https://agents.md/ (maintained by the Agentic AI Foundation; originated by OpenAI and other vendors).
  • Linux Foundation, press release of 2025-12-09: https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation (neutral foundation).
  • Anthropic, official Claude Code doc "How Claude remembers your project": https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory (vendor: Anthropic).
  • Agent Skills, the standard's site: https://agentskills.io/ (originated by Anthropic).
  • Anthropic, engineering blog "Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills", 2025-10-16, with an update note of 2025-12-18: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills (vendor: Anthropic).
  • Anthropic, "Introducing Agent Skills", 2025-10-16: https://claude.com/blog/skills (vendor: Anthropic).
  • Gloaguen et al. (ETH Zurich / LogicStar.ai), arXiv:2602.11988, v1 2026-02-12, v3 2026-09-29: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988 (academic, vendor-independent).
  • Lulla et al., arXiv:2601.20404, v1 2026-01-28, v2 2026-03-30: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20404 (academic).
  • Khatri, arXiv:2607.27250, 2026-07-28: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27250 (academic, single author).

  • OpenAI's post on the AAIF (https://openai.com/index/agentic-ai-foundation/): not read, 403.

  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open in a browser (the site refuses scripts).

docs.title: AGENTS.md: what it is
docs.text:
• Literal definition: "a simple, open format for guiding coding agents", "a dedicated, predictable place to provide the context and instructions to help AI coding agents work on your project" (https://agents.md/).
  • In the Linux Foundation's voice: "a simple, universal standard that gives AI coding agents a consistent source of project-specific guidance needed to operate reliably across different repositories and toolchains" (LF press release).
  • Origin: launched by OpenAI in August 2025 (LF press release). The site credits the joint creation to OpenAI Codex, Amp, Jules (Google), Cursor and Factory.
  • Governance: "AGENTS.md is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation" (https://agents.md/). The AAIF was announced on 2025-12-09 with three founding projects: MCP (Anthropic), goose (Block) and AGENTS.md (OpenAI) (LF press release).
  • Adoption: "used by over 60k open-source projects" (https://agents.md/); the LF says "more than 60,000 open source projects and agent frameworks" (December 2025). The site lists more than 25 compatible tools, among them GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Zed, Jules, Gemini CLI, Codex, Aider, Devin, Junie and Warp.
  • Same umbrella as MCP: the press release describes MCP as "the universal standard protocol for connecting AI models to tools, data and applications", with more than 10,000 published servers. AGENTS.md (static context in the repo) and MCP (dynamic context via tools) are under the same foundation.

docs.title: AGENTS.md: recommended structure
docs.text:
• Sections suggested by the site: project overview, build and test commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, security considerations, commit message or pull request guidelines (https://agents.md/).
  • Monorepo: "For large monorepos, use nested AGENTS.md files for subprojects. Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence." The example cited is OpenAI's repository, with 88 AGENTS.md files (https://agents.md/).
  • It is free Markdown, with no schema: unlike catalog-info.yaml, there is no required field and no validation.

docs.title: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code)
docs.text:
• Definition: "CLAUDE.md files are markdown files that give Claude persistent instructions for a project, your personal workflow, or your entire organization." (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory).
  • Hierarchy, from the broadest to the most specific: Managed policy (/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md on Linux; "Organization-wide instructions managed by IT/DevOps"), User (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), Project (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md; "Team-shared instructions for the project", shared via source control) and Local (./CLAUDE.local.md, personal, in .gitignore).
  • Loading: files in the directories above the working directory load at startup; those in subdirectories load on demand. "All discovered files are concatenated into context rather than overriding each other." Different from AGENTS.md's "nearest wins" rule.
  • Compatibility with AGENTS.md: "Claude Code can read AGENTS.md as your project instructions, so a repository already set up for other coding agents works without adding a CLAUDE.md". If both exist, by default it reads only CLAUDE.md; CLAUDE.md can import AGENTS.md with @AGENTS.md.
  • Size guidance: "target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence."
  • It is not enforcement: "Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead."
  • What goes in: "Treat CLAUDE.md as the place you write down what you'd otherwise re-explain"; multi-step procedures go to a skill or a path-scoped rule.

docs.title: Agent Skills
docs.text:
• The standard's definition: "Agent Skills are a lightweight, open format for extending AI agent capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows." "At its core, a skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file", with metadata (name and description, at minimum), instructions and, optionally, scripts/, references/ and assets/ (https://agentskills.io/).
  • Anthropic's definition: "Organized folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that agents can discover and load dynamically to perform better at specific tasks" (engineering blog, 2025-10-16).
  • Progressive disclosure in three stages: discovery (only name and description at startup), activation (reads SKILL.md when the task matches the description), execution (scripts and files on demand). "Full instructions load only when a task calls for them, so agents can keep many skills on hand with only a small context footprint." (https://agentskills.io/).
  • Dates: launched by Anthropic on 2025-10-16; published as an open standard on 2025-12-18 ("We've published Agent Skills as an open standard for cross-platform portability. (December 18, 2025)", note in the engineering blog). The standard's site says: "originally developed by Anthropic, released as an open standard".
  • Platform argument: skills package "procedural knowledge and company-, team-, and user-specific context into portable, version-controlled folders" (https://agentskills.io/). The clients showcase lists, among others, Claude Code, ChatGPT & Codex, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Junie, Kiro, Goose and Pulumi Neo.
  • Unlike AGENTS.md, Agent Skills do not appear as an AAIF project in the sources read.

docs.title: Effect on agent quality (studies)
docs.text:
Three papers on arXiv, with conclusions that do not match each other. None shows an increase in success rate.

  • Gloaguen et al., arXiv:2602.11988 (SWE-bench with LLM-generated context files and a new dataset, AGENTbench, with context files written by devs): "providing context files does not generally improve task success rates, while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average". The agents follow the instructions, but "repository overviews", although widely recommended, did not help. The authors' conclusion: context files serve for non-standard coding practices; any attempt at a gain must be evaluated before going to production.
  • Lulla et al., arXiv:2601.20404 (Codex, 10 repositories, 124 PRs, with and without AGENTS.md): "the presence of AGENTS.md is associated with a lower median runtime (Δ28.64%) and reduced output token consumption (Δ16.58%), while maintaining a comparable task completion behavior". Measures efficiency, not correctness.
  • Khatri, arXiv:2607.27250 (Claude Code and Codex, 17 tasks, 3 repositories, 288 runs): "Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing)". The agents fail because of "implementation skill" (design, pattern choice, exact wiring), not "missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply". Small sample, a single author.
  • Joint reading: the file changes behavior (the agent follows the instructions) and can reduce cost/time, but does not replace capability. It holds for non-obvious conventions and project commands, not for a generic overview. This matches Anthropic's guidance to keep CLAUDE.md short.

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• The exact launch date of AGENTS.md (the LF says only "August 2025").
  • The current adoption count beyond the site's "over 60k", which carries no date. There is no primary source for a more recent number.
  • The text of OpenAI's post on the AAIF (403).
  • That v1 of 2602.11988 said context files "tend to reduce" the success rate: it came from a search summary, not from the v1 text. Cite only the current abstract (v3).
  • That the design of 2602.11988 is biased toward Python: a critique from a secondary blog (ArXivIQ), not from the authors.
  • A2A's (Google) entry into the AAIF in August 2026 and the count of AAIF members: only secondary sources (Forbes and others).
  • Whether Agent Skills were donated to any foundation: nothing in the sources read.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Direct parallel with the declare-next-to-code slide (catalog-info.yaml): the same repo declares what the app is for humans and the portal (catalog-info.yaml) and how to work on it for agents (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). Both are versioned and reviewed in a PR together with the code. Difference to cite: the catalog has a schema and the portal validates it; AGENTS.md is free Markdown.
  • The golden path generates the agent's context: the template that creates the repo already creates catalog-info.yaml and AGENTS.md with build/test commands, conventions and the platform's guardrails. The platform's skills (e.g., "provision an Environment", "register a route") are distributed as Agent Skills, in the role of the portal templates.
  • The CLAUDE.md hierarchy maps onto the division of responsibility: managed policy = platform/security, project = the team that owns the app, local = the dev. The platform owns the org-wide layer.
  • "Catalog as context": the file is static; MCP (same foundation, AAIF) is the dynamic channel through which the agent queries the catalog, ownership and live state. The file says how, MCP answers what, right now.
  • Honest caveat for the slide's note: the studies do not show a gain in correctness (Gloaguen: cost +20%; Khatri: no measurable effect); the measured gain is in efficiency (Lulla: -28.64% median runtime). Message: short, specific content (commands, non-obvious conventions), not a repo overview. This reinforces generating it through the golden path instead of letting each team write a long text.

docs.title: System model
docs.text:
Source: https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/system-model#ecosystem-modeling

  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

  • Component: a piece of software (service, website, data pipeline); it provides and consumes APIs and depends on Resources.

  • API: the boundary between Components, in a machine-readable format; public, restricted or private.
  • Resource: infrastructure a Component needs at runtime (database, queue, bucket).
  • System: a collection of Components and Resources that exposes one or more public APIs, hiding the implementation from consumers.
  • Domain: groups Systems that share terminology, model and business purpose — a bounded context.
  • User / Group: people and teams; every Component, API, Resource and System has an owner.

docs.title: Why the catalog does not hold versions
docs.text:
Source: https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/faq/#can-i-represent-versions-of-apis-services-etc-in-the-catalog

  • "We do not recommend trying to represent fine grained versions in the catalog."
  • The catalog holds "the human concept of a thing": a service with several versions running at the same time is one Component.
  • It is data that is "rarely changing, human curated", maintained by the owner.
  • Fine-grained versions come from external systems (CI/CD, registry, deploy) and show up in the portal through plugins.
  • Exception: a major breaking change that is in practice a new thing (customerinfo → customerinfo2), at the cost of duplicated search results.

Role in the narrative: it is the bridge between the Developer Control Plane and the Integration & Delivery Plane — the catalog holds the stable concept, and what changes (version, environment) lives in the registry, GitOps and the orchestrator.

docs.title: How a file enters the catalog
docs.text:
Sources: https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/life-of-an-entity, https://backstage.io/docs/integrations/github/discovery (read on 2026-10-07).

  • Registered locations: "URLs to yaml files that you register using either the Create button or add to your app-config, are both handled by entity providers."
  • Discovery on GitHub: "The provider will crawl the GitHub organization or App and register entities matching the configured path." The configuration example runs every 30 minutes (frequency: { minutes: 30 }).
  • The processing loop reprocesses each entity periodically: "Every unprocessed entity comes with a timestamp, which tells at what time that the processing loop should next try to process it." The doc does not fix the interval.

docs.title: Role in the presentation: how the dev declares the app
docs.text:
The Backstage model is used to teach the dev to declare their application in the catalog — not as the model of the presentation itself. The sequence in the Developer Control Plane:

  1. Two levels: business (Domain, System) and implementation (Component, API, Resource).
  2. One entity per slide, each with an example from a well-known system.
  3. The full tree in a well-known example; then the same tree in the repo's real catalog.
  4. How to declare: catalog-info.yaml next to the code, shown as an IDE-style frame in parts (same format as Score): whole file → identity (kind, type, lifecycle) → owner + system → providesApis → dependsOn. File: snippets/catalog-info.yaml (greeting-api with its dependencies). Then, automatic discovery by the portal.
  5. What is not declared there (version, environment) — a bridge to the next act.

docs.title: Well-known example: the Tailwind Air catalog
docs.text:
Source: idp/catalog/airline/tailwind/catalog-info.yaml — a fictional airline (Tailwind Air), one of the example catalogs of fictional companies (#528). It replaces the Backstage demo catalog (packages/catalog-model/examples, a Spotify), whose names the audience does not recognize. scripts/demo/backstage-tailwind shows each entity in Backstage.

Domain tailwind                          owner team-tailwind-architecture
├─ Domain airport   (subdomainOf: tailwind)   owner team-airport
│  ├─ System seat-map                    web-checkin, seat-selection, seats
│  │  ├─ Component seat-selection     type service   providesApis seats   dependsOn resource:passengers-db
│  │  ├─ Component web-checkin  type website   consumesApis seats
│  │  └─ API seats              type openapi
│  ├─ System boarding-pass
│  └─ System bag-tracking
├─ Domain booking   (subdomainOf: tailwind)   owner team-booking
│  ├─ System flight-search
│  ├─ System reservations                Resource passengers-db (type database, shared)
│  └─ System fares
├─ Domain flight-ops (subdomainOf: tailwind)  Resource flight-events (type topic, shared)
├─ Domain loyalty   (subdomainOf: tailwind)
└─ Domain crew      (subdomainOf: tailwind)

docs.title: The real catalog of this repo
docs.text:
Source: idp/catalog/communication/catalog-info.yaml (vanilla Backstage validated locally).

Domain communication                 owner platform-team
├─ System greeter                    owner team-alpha         greeting-api, greeting-http, greeting-db, greeting-events, greeting-avatars
└─ System notifier                   owner platform-team
  • Built from each application's Crossplane compositions, only to know what the app needs to run. Provisioning (network, cluster, LB, firewall, add-ons) stays outside the catalog.
  • Resources are described by role (relational database, queue, topic, object storage), not by cloud service — this is what makes it possible to link the catalog to the Resource Plane ("in the catalog it is a relational database; in the Resource Plane it is Azure SQL").

docs.title: Base deck
docs.text:
• Original 2-slide deck (not published); its content is reproduced in this file.
  • Slide 1: map of the 5 planes and their categories. Source stated in the notes: https://platformengineering.org/platform-tooling.
  • Slide 2: reference architecture — one or more tools per category, mostly Azure.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: Source of the planes
docs.text: The page https://platformengineering.org/platform-tooling lists the 5 planes — Developer Control, Integration & Delivery, Resource, Observability, Security — as parallel layers of a tool landscape, not as a sequence. Any slide that claims "a platform is organized into five planes" cites this source. The order in which the presentation walks through the planes (the journey of a request) is our own narrative choice and must be presented as such.

docs.text:
