docs.title: configure8: portal vs. platform
docs.text:
• Source: configure8, "Internal developer portal vs. internal developer platform: what's the difference and why both matter", 2023-03-29, no author stated. https://configure8.io/blog/internal-developer-portal-vs-internal-developer-platform-whats-the-difference-and-why-both-matter
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.
  • Vendor material: configure8 sells a portal (catalog, self-serve actions, scorecards, cost management). Same caveat as the Port guide (port-portal-guide.md): it is the view of someone who sells the interface.

docs.title: Definitions (literal)
docs.text:
• Internal Developer Platform: "The collection of tooling built by platform engineers and used by developers. It is often a heterogeneous tool chain stitched together in a way to minimize cognitive load for developers without abstracting away important meaning."
  • Internal Developer Portal: "The singular interface to your developer platform. It discovers every aspect of your architecture, organizes it into a knowledge graph, and exposes information as well as actions developers can take."

docs.title: Argument
docs.text:
• "You need both to tame sprawl": the platform is a heterogeneous set of tools; the portal unifies the knowledge scattered across them.
  • Recommendations: have both; scorecards to define standards ("it's only what gets measured that gets managed"); a universal catalog to reduce metadata drift; self-serve actions with approval as a guardrail (golden paths).
  • The only number: "over 40 metrics you can use to define a scorecard", a product figure, not an industry one.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Reinforces portal-is-not-platform with a short, citable definition of the two terms.
  • Disagreement with the presentation's thesis: "the singular interface" makes the portal the single door; here the portal is one of the interfaces, next to the CLI and agents (many-clients, formae-cli.md). A good contrast to say out loud.

docs.title: Nobody owns the data
docs.text:
• Source: Tharun Mathew, "Platform teams own the pipeline. Nobody owns the data", platformengineering.com, 2026-09-23. https://platformengineering.com/features/platform-teams-own-the-pipeline-nobody-owns-the-data/
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open in a browser (the site refuses scripts).
  • The author's account of his experience: the numbers come from his implementation, not from research; cite as "a case", never as a trend.

docs.title: Argument
docs.text:
• Platform engineering solved ownership of infrastructure and runtime, but the data still has no responsible owner.
  • A pipeline failure triggers an alert; a data quality failure happens silently inside a "healthy" system.
  • Way out: treat data contracts as declarative infrastructure, enforced by CI/CD, not as a policy document.

docs.title: Quotes (literal)
docs.text:
• "A service fails loudly and syntactically...A data system fails quietly and semantically."
  • "No stated contract means every change is potentially breaking and none is officially breaking."
  • "Kubernetes does not ask politely for resource limits...An internal data platform needs the same posture."

docs.title: Numbers (from the author's case)
docs.text:
• Median time to find the responsible owner of a dataset: from about three days of asking around to under an hour.
  • About a third of the cataloged datasets had no live consumer; they were retired within two quarters.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
1. A named owner at scale (a route), not a team mailbox.
  2. Explicit interfaces and schemas.
  3. Known consumers, by registration or query attribution.
  4. A deprecation path with a migration window.
  5. CI/CD rejects the pull request of an incomplete pipeline: it requires a schema, an alert routing key and a TTL/retention manifest.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Extends catalog ownership beyond code: Resource and API also need an owner, a contract and known consumers (slides catalog-ownership, entity-api, entity-resource).
  • "A broken contract becomes a new entity" (major-breaking) is the same principle applied to data.
  • A third with no consumer and retired = the same reasoning as Fury's idle environment (mercadolibre-fury.md).
  • A contract enforced by CI/CD, not by a document: an executable guardrail, as in the Security Plane.

docs.title: DORA AI report
docs.text:
• Source: DORA / Google Cloud, "State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025", v. 2025.2, public PDF at https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf (read on 2026-10-07; presentation page at https://dora.dev/dora-report-2025/). Pages below = the number printed in the PDF footer.
  • Source: DORA / Google Cloud, "DORA AI Capabilities Model", v. 2025.1, public PDF at https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_dora_ai_capabilities_model.pdf (read on 2026-10-07). Companion to the 2025 report.
  • Source: DORA / Google Cloud, "Accelerate State of DevOps 2024", v. 2024.3, public PDF at https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2024_final_dora_report.pdf (read on 2026-10-07; page at https://dora.dev/research/2024/).
  • Source: Nathen Harvey and Derek DeBellis, "Announcing the 2025 DORA Report", Google Cloud Blog, 2025-09-23, https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report (read on 2026-10-07).
  • Source: Jessica Baolin and Nathen Harvey, "Balancing AI tensions: Moving from AI adoption to effective SDLC use", dora.dev, 2026-03-10, https://dora.dev/insights/balancing-ai-tensions/ (read on 2026-10-07).
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: Methodology (2025)
docs.text:
• Survey: "a global survey conducted between June 13 and July 21, 2025" (2025 report, p. 4, Key findings).
  • Sample: "This year, a total of 4,867 respondents answered our survey" (p. 103, Demographics and firmographics). In the executive summary: "more than 100 hours of qualitative data and survey responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals" (p. 3).
  • Interviews: "In total, we interviewed 78 participants", continuously "from July 2024–July 2025" (p. 115, Methodology).
  • Survey in four randomly assigned streams: "AI", "Platform engineering", "Sociocognitive aspects", "AI capabilities" (p. 114). Each respondent saw only one stream, so not every question has all 4,867.
  • The effects are standardized Bayesian estimates "with 89% credible intervals" (Figure 1, p. 4; Figure 28, p. 38): the 2025 report gives direction and standardized size, not percentages like the 2024 one.
  • Instability in 2025 = "Change fail rate" + "Rework rate"; throughput = "Lead time for changes", "Deployment frequency", "Failed deployment recovery time" (p. 13, Software delivery performance factors).

docs.title: Methodology (2024)
docs.text: • "This year, nearly 3,000 working professionals from a variety of industries around the world shared their experiences" (2024 report, p. 91, Demographics and firmographics). History: "roughly 39,000 professionals" over the course of the program.

docs.title: AI, throughput and instability (2025) — the slide's primary source
docs.text:
• "AI adoption now improves software delivery throughput, a key shift from last year. However, it still increases delivery instability. This suggests that while teams are adapting for speed, their underlying systems have not yet evolved to safely manage AI-accelerated development." (p. 4, Key findings).
  • The person with higher AI adoption reports "Higher levels of software delivery instability" and "Higher levels of software delivery throughput" (p. 38, The results this year).
  • "AI's relationship with software delivery throughput has turned from negative to positive" (p. 42, Changes in last year's patterns suggest adaptation).
  • "it continues its detrimental relationship with software delivery stability" (p. 43, Conclusion).
  • Blog: "AI accelerates software development, but that acceleration can expose weaknesses downstream. Without robust control systems, like strong automated testing, mature version control practices, and fast feedback loops, an increase in change volume leads to instability." (Google Cloud Blog, 2025-09-23, section "Key findings from the 2025 report").
  • dora.dev (2026-03-10): "higher AI adoption is associated with an increase in both software delivery throughput and software delivery instability"; proposed mechanism: "the time saved in creation is frequently re-allocated to auditing and verification".

docs.title: AI and delivery in 2024 (literal numbers)
docs.text:
• Section "AI is hurting delivery performance", Figure 10 (2024 report, p. 39): "If AI adoption increases by 25%…" → "Delivery throughput -1.5%", "Delivery stability -7.2%".
  • "We see that the effect on delivery throughput is small, but likely negative (an estimated 1.5% reduction for every 25% increase in AI adoption). The negative impact on delivery stability is larger (an estimated 7.2% reduction for every 25% increase in AI adoption)." (p. 40).
  • DORA's hypothesis: "since AI allows respondents to produce a much greater amount of code in the same amount of time, it is possible, even likely, that changelists are growing in size. DORA has consistently shown that larger changes are slower and more prone to creating instability." (p. 40).

docs.title: AI as amplifier
docs.text:
• "AI's primary role in software development is that of an amplifier. It magnifies the strengths of high-performing organizations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones." (2025 report, p. 3, Key takeaway).
  • "Without this foundation, AI creates localized pockets of productivity that are often lost to downstream chaos." (p. 3).
  • Blog: "AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there." (Google Cloud Blog, section "AI, the great amplifier").
  • Adoption: "The majority of survey respondents (90%) use AI as part of their work and believe (more than 80%) it has increased their productivity. Yet a notable portion (30%) currently report little to no trust in the code generated by AI" (p. 4).

docs.title: DORA AI Capabilities Model (7 capabilities)
docs.text:
Literal list (AI Capabilities Model, p. 4, Executive summary):

  1. "Clear and communicated AI stance" — "Ambiguity creates risk. A clear policy provides the psychological safety needed for effective experimentation."
  2. "Healthy data ecosystems" — "The benefits of AI are significantly amplified by high-quality, accessible, and unified internal data."
  3. "AI-accessible internal data" — "Connecting AI to your internal documentation and codebases moves it from a generic assistant to a specialized expert."
  4. "Strong version control practices" — "As AI increases the velocity of change, version control becomes the critical safety net that enables confident experimentation."
  5. "Working in small batches" — "This discipline counteracts the risk of AI generating large, unstable changes, ensuring that speed translates to better product performance."
  6. "User-centric focus" — "A focus on user needs is essential to ensure that AI-accelerated teams are moving quickly in the right direction."
  7. "Quality internal platforms" — "A platform provides the automated, secure pathways that allow AI's benefits to scale across the organization."

docs.title: Platform as a precondition for AI (2025)
docs.text:
• "90% of organizations have adopted platform engineering, making a high-quality internal platform the essential foundation for AI success." (2025 report, p. 4).
  • "Our data shows that 90% of organizations have adopted at least one platform, with 29% of organizations now using a multi-platform environment." and "76% of organizations have at least one dedicated platform team" (p. 67, The platform landscape).
  • "AI adoption has a negligible effect on organizational performance when platform quality is low, but when platform quality is high, the effect is strong and positive." (p. 71, The strategic imperative; Figure 49).
  • "With a high degree of certainty, we found that AI adoption's impacts depend on organizations having quality internal platforms." (p. 62, Quality internal platforms). But also: "respondents experience more friction in organizations with quality internal platforms" (p. 62).
  • Platform quality = "a single score, indicating how many of 12 characteristics a respondent indicates their internal platforms have" (p. 62).
  • "An investment in AI without a corresponding investment in high-quality platforms is unlikely to yield significant returns at the organizational level." (p. 72).
  • Individual productivity gains "are often lost to downstream disorder, swallowed by bottlenecks in testing, security reviews, and complex deployment processes." (AI Capabilities Model, p. 59, Quality internal platforms).
  • The platform also increases instability: "a better platform is associated with a small but credible increase in software delivery instability, meaning a higher change failure rate and increased rework." DORA's reading: "a manageable trade-off for the significant gains in performance" (2025 report, p. 70).
  • "Experience gap": technical capabilities (reliability, security) are rated well; "acting on feedback" and "how well tasks are automated" lag behind (p. 67). "the capability most correlated with a positive user experience is providing clear feedback to tasks" (p. 69).
  • Named antipatterns: "Build it and they will come", "The ticket-ops trap", "The ivory tower platform" (p. 68).

docs.title: Platform engineering in 2024 (literal numbers)
docs.text:
• "we found that 89% of respondents are using an internal developer platform" (2024 report, p. 50).
  • "Internal developer platform users had 8% higher levels of individual productivity and 10% higher levels of team performance. Additionally, an organization's software delivery and operations performance increases 6% when using a platform. However, these gains do not come without some drawbacks. Throughput and change stability saw decreases of 8% and 14%, respectively" (p. 49).
  • Developer independence: "a 5% improvement in productivity when users of the platform are able to complete their tasks without involving an enabling team" (p. 51). Mandatory platform: "there was a 6% decrease in throughput" for those who must "exclusively use the platform" (p. 53).

docs.title: Value stream management (2025)
docs.text:
• "Value stream management (VSM), the practice of visualizing, analyzing, and improving the flow of work from idea to customer, acts as a force multiplier for AI, ensuring that local productivity gains translate into measurable improvements in team and product performance." (2025 report, p. 4).
  • "Without VSM, AI risks creating localized efficiencies that are simply absorbed by downstream bottlenecks, delivering no real value to the organization as a whole." (p. 77). Stated findings: "VSM drives team performance", "VSM leads to more valuable work", "VSM improves product performance" (p. 77).
  • Note: p. 77 phrases "VSM moderates the relationship between AI adoption and organizational performance" as a hypothesis ("We hypothesize"); the executive summary (p. 4-5) treats it as a finding.

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• 2026 edition of State of AI-assisted Software Development: not found; dora.dev/research/ lists up to 2025 (read on 2026-10-07).
  • "ROI of AI-assisted Software Development" (2026): read in full on 2026-10-07 — see dora-roi-ai.md. The numbers cited by third parties (J-curve, CFR from 5% to 6%, 39% ROI) are there, but they are illustrative assumptions of the calculator, not findings.
  • The size of the AI effect on instability in 2025 exists only in a chart (Figure 28, standardized scale ~-0.05 to 0.20); there is no literal number in the text — do not cite a percentage for 2025.
  • List of the 12 characteristics of a quality platform (Appendix of the 2025 report): not read.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Slide ci-bottleneck: replace the secondary source (Signadot's sponsored article, sandbox-routing.md) with the 2025 report, p. 4 ("improves software delivery throughput… still increases delivery instability") and, as the mechanism, the blog ("an increase in change volume leads to instability") and the AI Capabilities Model p. 59 ("swallowed by bottlenecks in testing, security reviews"). 2024→2025 contrast: throughput went from -1.5% to positive; stability stayed negative (-7.2% in 2024).
  • Platform-as-a-precondition-for-AI slides (platform-readiness, rebuild-platform): p. 71 ("negligible effect… when platform quality is low"), p. 72 ("An investment in AI without a corresponding investment in high-quality platforms…"), 90% / 76% / 29% (p. 67) and the 7th capability of the AI Capabilities Model. Honest caveat for the notes: the platform also brings more friction (p. 62) and slightly more instability (p. 70; 2024: -8% throughput, -14% change stability).
  • dora-metrics: in 2025 DORA measures instability by "Change fail rate" + "Rework rate" and moved "Failed deployment recovery time" to throughput (p. 13) — check against dora-metrics.md.

docs.title: DORA metrics
docs.text:
• Source: DORA, "DORA's software delivery performance metrics", https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics/ (page dated 2026-01-05).
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: The five metrics (literal)
docs.text:
Throughput:

  • Change lead time: "The amount of time it takes for a change to go from committed to version control to deployed in production."
  • Deployment frequency: "The number of deployments over a given period or the time between deployments."
  • Failed deployment recovery time: "The time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention."

Instability:

  • Change fail rate: "The ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment."

  • Deployment rework rate: "The ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production."

  • The model started with four metrics ("four keys"); today there are five. Failed deployment recovery time replaced the old MTTR, and deployment rework rate is the fifth. When you hear "four keys" in presentations, that is the old version.

docs.title: How not to use them (DORA guide)
docs.text:
• Do not turn the metric into a target (it becomes a game).
  • Do not measure a complex system by a single metric.
  • Do not compare very different applications.
  • Do not leave the metric in a single silo: dev, ops and release share it.
  • Do not make teams compete; each one compares itself with itself.
  • Do not invest more in measuring precisely than in improving.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• DORA measures the delivery of the teams that use the platform; the platform can collect them and return them to the portal through an integration.
  • They also measure the platform itself (the platform team delivers changes to the hub and to the Compositions).
  • They complement time to 10th PR (adoption-metrics.md, onboarding) and the Platform as a Product scorecard (MTTFD etc.).
  • "Measure developer sentiment alongside DORA" (empathy-gap.md).

docs.title: DORA ROI of AI-assisted Software Development
docs.text:
• Source: DORA and Google Cloud (delta team), The ROI of AI-assisted Software Development, v. 2026.1, https://dora.dev/ai/roi/report/ (60 pp., license CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; report quotes retrieved in February 2026). Authors: Eva Dong, Andre Ellis Jr., Nathen Harvey, Vivian Hu, Ursula Löbbert-Passing, Eric Maxwell, Aaron Wanjala (p. 51-52). Page below = printed numbering, which matches the PDF's. Read in full on 2026-10-07.
  • Interactive calculator: https://dora.dev/ai/roi/calculator. Landing page: https://dora.dev/ai/roi/report/.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.
  • Nature: it is not a new survey. It is an ROI calculation framework backed by the DORA 2025 findings (dora-ai-report.md) and by a calculator with example assumptions. The example numbers (39% ROI, 8-month payback, CFR from 5% to 6%) are illustrative assumptions, not findings — the report itself asks that they be treated as a "high-uncertainty estimate meant to spark a conversation" (p. 23, p. 54).
  • Bias: co-authored by the delta consulting team at Google Cloud, which offers the service at the end (p. 27, p. 38, p. 53). The market numbers on p. 12 and 36 (78%, 88%, 727%, average payback of 8 months) come from Google Cloud commercial material, not from DORA research — do not put them on screen.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The report's thesis: AI is an amplifier; the return comes from the system around it (internal platform, workflows, team alignment), not from the tool (p. 3, p. 13).
  • It explicitly states the IDP's role in the agentic era: context provider and risk mitigator for agents, which are also users of the platform (p. 40). It is the most direct source, and not sponsored by a platform vendor, for the "IDP for humans and agents" thesis.
  • Adoption follows a J-Curve: a temporary productivity drop (learning curve, verification tax, pipeline adaptation) before the gain (p. 4, p. 8-9).
  • The investment roadmap starts with the context layer: a quality internal platform and a healthy data ecosystem, with "machine readable" documentation and a "standardized map" of the technical landscape (p. 44).

docs.title: Quotes on platform and agents
docs.text:
• "In the agentic era, an IDP is no longer just a portal for infrastructure, it is the risk mitigator and the context provider for AI agents." (p. 40, Treat your Internal Developer Platform (IDP) as a product)
  • "The 2025 research confirms that a quality internal platform is the primary connective tissue for AI value." (p. 40)
  • "When AI agents can navigate a well-defined platform, they spend less time hallucinating architectural patterns and more time delivering valuable code." (p. 40)
  • "The goal is a platform that treats the developer—or any builder—as the user, minimizing the cognitive load required to move code from an agent's prompt to a production environment. Simultaneously, the platform provides the guardrails for the agents who are also users of the platform." (p. 40)
  • "If your organization possesses mature internal developer platforms and streamlined deployment pipelines, AI will rapidly scale your capacity to deliver user value and drive revenue." With manual-testing bottlenecks, bureaucracy or fragmented data, "injecting AI into that system will simply accelerate the accumulation of technical debt and maintenance costs." (p. 7)
  • "Without a solid foundation built on quality internal platforms and clear workflows, AI merely generates isolated pockets of productivity. For example, a developer might write code significantly faster using an automated assistant, but that code simply piles up in front of manual security reviews or brittle deployment pipelines." (p. 13)

docs.title: Context layer (first investment)
docs.text:
• "Build the context layer (CapEx). Primary capabilities: quality internal developer platforms and healthy data ecosystems. The first investment must be in the environment in which AI operates. In an agentic world, garbage in, garbage out refers to the context provided to the agent." (p. 44)
  • "This involves centralizing architectural standards and ensuring documentation is high fidelity and machine readable. The goal: Minimize friction by ensuring agents have a clear, standardized map of the organization's technical landscape." (p. 44)
  • "AI agents are only as effective as the data they can access." It includes "high-quality documentation, clean APIs, and a healthy data ecosystem"; with fragmented or outdated knowledge, "AI generates bloat, duplicated or irrelevant code". Agents need the "ground truth needed to make accurate decisions within the specific context of your code base." (p. 41)
  • After the context layer, the investment goes to people: "Empower the human in the loop (OpEx)", with training in "context engineering and verification"; devs "equipped to act as high-level orchestrators" (p. 44).

docs.title: Automated guardrails
docs.text:
• "This involves shifting from manual checkpoints to automated nonoptional security and quality gates. In an agentic world, these guardrails act as the brakes that allow the engineering engine to go faster safely." (p. 42)
  • Against the verification tax: "technical guardrails, such as nonoptional checkpoints and pre-commit hooks paired with static analysis", "investing heavily in automated testing, leveraging AI to assist with code reviews, and providing better context to the AI to improve initial code quality." (p. 33)
  • The five keys to adoption: "trust, platform, data, users, and guardrails" (p. 42).

docs.title: J-Curve and verification tax
docs.text:
• "We anticipate that most organizations will encounter a J-Curve: a temporary productivity dip and period of instability associated with early adoption. Think of this dip as the tuition cost of transformation." (p. 4)
  • Three factors in the dip (p. 9): learning curve (including moving "from users prompting AI to systems built on context, intent, and specification"), verification tax (reviewing generated code and the larger volume of code) and pipeline adaptation ("testing and change approval must scale to handle the increased volume").
  • The depth and duration of the curve depend on technical maturity, learning culture and "the baseline health of its internal developer platforms" (p. 10).
  • The same pattern already seen in "continuous delivery and platform engineering" (p. 8): leadership cuts investment during the dip by mistaking learning for failure.
  • "For an individual developer, AI does not necessarily make friction vanish; rather, the friction moves." The effort saved on boilerplate becomes "a verification tax—the cognitive load required to iterate on prompts and rigorously audit AI-generated code that looks remarkably similar to correct code." (p. 20)
  • "If trust is low, the J-Curve deepens as developers second guess every line of code" (p. 40).

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
• "We don't measure AI by the code it writes but by the bottlenecks it clears." (p. 7)
  • Indicators: DORA metrics as an "operational early warning system" — lead time to measure the impact of agents on speed, change failure rate for effectiveness (p. 10); "experiment frequency" (how often teams use agents to explore solutions) and deployment frequency as leading metrics; change failure rate and rework as a "stability gauge" (p. 45).
  • Experiment frequency as a financial option: AI lowers the "premium" of each experiment; the organization only "exercises the option" (keep, scale, protect the code) when the experiment proves value (p. 46).
  • Leading indicators (productivity, developer experience, user experience) vs. lagging (cost and revenue) (p. 22-23).
  • Explicit recommendation: do not use the gain to reduce headcount; reinvest the capacity (p. 25, p. 48).

docs.title: Numbers (with their origin)
docs.text:
Data point Value Page Origin Respondents who perceive a productivity increase with AI more than 80% 18 DORA 2025, p. 30 Largest effect of AI: individual effectiveness; second largest: instability — 25 DORA 2025, p. 38 Inference cost of advanced models fell by a factor of 280 (Nov/2022 to Oct/2024) 36 Stanford AI Index 2025 (secondary) Productivity gain: simple greenfield vs. complex brownfield 35-40% vs. 10% or less 36 Stanford Software Engineering Productivity Research (secondary) Replacing a dev costs 1.5 to 2x the annual salary 28 no source cited Calculator example: ROI / payback / CFR 39% / 0.7 year / 5% to 6% 35-36, 57 illustrative assumptions
  • The consequence the report draws from the inference cost: "the true financial burden of adoption has shifted to governance cost: managing the verification tax, adjusting workflows, and upskilling talent." (p. 36)

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• The Stanford numbers (280x, 35-40% vs. 10%) were not checked against the original source.
  • The Google Cloud market numbers (78% of executives with ROI, 88% of agentic early adopters with a return, 727% over three years, average payback of 8 months) are commercial material — do not use.
  • The "5 strategic priorities" (p. 13) come from "an internal research study conducted by Google in 2025", unpublished.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Thesis slide of the final act (aep-evolution or equivalent): the quote on p. 40 — "risk mitigator and the context provider for AI agents" — closes the "IDP for humans and agents" arc with a source neutral toward Kratix/Syntasso.
  • catalog-as-context: "clear, standardized map of the organization's technical landscape" (p. 44) is the description of the catalog; combine it with Backstage's mcp-actions-backend (mcp-platform-interface.md).
  • platform-readiness / rebuild-platform: "code simply piles up in front of manual security reviews or brittle deployment pipelines" (p. 13) gives the concrete image of the bottleneck; it complements DORA 2025 (p. 71).
  • ci-bottleneck and deterministic paths: "guardrails act as the brakes that allow the engineering engine to go faster safely" (p. 42).
  • token-finops: cost moved from inference to governance (p. 36); it matches "cost per accepted output" from State of AI.
  • mvp1 / where-we-are: the J-Curve explains to the executive audience why MVP 1 measures cost and does not promise an immediate gain; experiment frequency links to the on-demand Environment and to a sandbox per request.
  • Caveats in the notes: co-authored by the Google Cloud consulting team; the calculator example is an assumption, not data.

docs.title: The empathy gap
docs.text:
• Source: Tatiana Mikhaleva (founder of DevOps.Pink), "The empathy gap: Why your platform needs UX, not just APIs", platformengineering.org, 2026-03-23. https://platformengineering.org/blog/the-empathy-gap-why-your-platform-needs-ux-not-just-apis
  • Opinion article, not research: the numbers cited in the text ("most engineers report not knowing where to start"; platform engineer salary "up to 27% more than DevOps") do not give the original source — do not use on screen.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open in a browser (the site refuses scripts).

docs.title: Argument
docs.text:
• IDPs fail by prioritizing technical capability over the experience of use: a lot of investment in infrastructure, little in the human who uses it. The result is low adoption — the empathy gap.
  • Cognitive friction: switching tools and deciphering a cryptic error breaks the dev's flow state.
  • Golden paths must remove barriers, not add steps.
  • Visual engineering: dashboards, graphs and clear statuses instead of raw logs.

docs.title: Quotes (literal)
docs.text:
• "We forget the most critical component in the stack. We forget the human being trying to use it."
  • "A backend engineer should not need deep Kubernetes knowledge to get a URL for their service."
  • "Clarity brings confidence. Confidence brings speed."
  • "Ask: 'How does it feel?' If it feels like a struggle, nobody will use it."

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Invest in visual engineering and dashboard interfaces.
  2. Measure dev sentiment alongside the DORA metrics.
  3. Have product designers and frontend engineers on the platform team.
  4. Treat error messages and CLI design as UX.
  5. Prioritize the dev experience over feature complexity.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Reinforces "platform as a product" and the cognitive load of the "problem" act.
  • The URL quote fits the first proof of concept (wasp-idp): a request becomes a URL without the dev knowing Kubernetes.
  • "The CLI and the error message are UX" applies to the many-clients slide: the CLI is not a second-class citizen.
  • "Measure sentiment alongside DORA" fits the Stone case (NPS and funnels — stone-caravela.md).

docs.title: Fitness functions
docs.text: Foundation for saying that the platform and each environment it generates (with its resources) have fitness functions that answer "is the current state the desired one?".

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Mark Richards and Neal Ford, Fundamentals of Software Architecture (O'Reilly, 2020; 2nd ed. 2025). https://fundamentalsofsoftwarearchitecture.com/
  • Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua (and Pramod Sadalage in the 2nd ed.), Building Evolutionary Architectures (O'Reilly, 2017; 2nd ed. 2023). Ch. 2, "Fitness Functions": https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/building-evolutionary-architectures/9781491986356/ch02.html. The authors' katas: https://evolutionaryarchitecture.com/ffkatas/
  • Thoughtworks Technology Radar, "Architectural fitness function" (Trial → Adopt): https://www.thoughtworks.com/radar/techniques/architectural-fitness-function

  • Books not read in this session: the excerpts below come from the user's summary, the official pages and secondary summaries. Check the book's text and page before putting a quote on screen.

  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open in a browser (the site refuses scripts).

docs.title: How the two books divide up (the user's framing)
docs.text:
• Fundamentals gives the vocabulary and taxonomy — descriptive and static, the "what": architecture characteristics (operational, structural, cross-cutting), how to choose them, explicit trade-offs ("least worst architecture"), ADRs, architectural styles.
  • Building Evolutionary Architectures gives the governance mechanism — operational and dynamic, the "how to keep it over time": fitness functions, cadence, guarded evolution.

docs.title: Fundamentals: characteristics
docs.text:
• Three groups: operational (e.g., scalability, performance, availability), structural (e.g., configurability, extensibility, maintainability, portability), cross-cutting (e.g., security, accessibility, legality).
  • Choose the minimum of characteristics: each one adds complexity and affects the others. When identifying them with stakeholders, ask them to choose the three most important (in any order), instead of ranking the whole list. The book itself warns not to obsess over the number; the goal is to keep the design simple. (The user's summary calls it the "less than three" rule; the book's text speaks of "top three".)
  • Explicit trade-off: there is no best architecture, only the "least worst"; the decision becomes an ADR.

docs.title: Building Evolutionary Architectures: fitness functions
docs.text:
• Definition (1st ed., ch. 2): "An architectural fitness function provides an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristic(s)." The 2nd ed. appears quoted as "any mechanism that provides an objective integrity assessment…" (InfoQ). Check the edition before quoting.
  • The term comes from evolutionary computing: it measures how close a solution is to the goal.
  • Any objective, repeatable check counts: tests, metrics, monitors, alerts, architecture rules, chaos experiments.
  • Dimensions cited from ch. 2 (via summaries): atomic vs. holistic, triggered vs. continual, static vs. dynamic, automated vs. manual, temporal.
  • Guarded evolution: the architecture can change freely as long as the fitness functions keep passing.

docs.title: Application to the platform (the user's thesis)
docs.text:
The platform and each Environment declare the desired state; fitness functions continuously check whether the real one matches it. Examples that already exist in the first proof of concept (wasp-idp):

Fitness function Type What it guarantees Ready/Synced conditions of the XR and of the Crossplane MRs continual, automated the real resource converges to the declared one Echo HTTP 200 on all the NLB IPs holistic, triggered the environment is available end to end ACME staging issuer in a test environment static does not burn the shared quota

Candidates: the golden signals (golden-signals.md) per environment as runtime fitness functions; DORA (dora-metrics.md) as the fitness function of delivery; idle environment (mercadolibre-fury.md) as the cost fitness function.

docs.title: formae CLI
docs.text: An example of a CLI that exposes the platform's entities (resources, stacks, targets, policies) to humans, pipelines and agents. Use: a reference for the platform's CLI.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Post indicated by the user: "formae 0.88 is out", Platform Engineering Labs blog on Medium, https://blog.platform.engineering/formae-0-88-is-out-e98579c48e73. Not read: Medium blocks automated access (Cloudflare 403). The content below comes from the official documentation and the release.
  • Release 0.88 announcement (2026-08-03, PRWeb): https://www.prweb.com/releases/platform-engineering-labs-advances-human-ai-infrastructure-engineering-with-the-new-formae-release-302840059.html: "completely redesigned interactive CLI", typed authoring and restructured docs.
  • Official documentation (read on 2026-10-07): CLI reference https://docs.formae.ai/documentation/reference/cli, formae inventory https://docs.formae.ai/documentation/reference/cli/inventory, Properties https://docs.formae.ai/documentation/concepts/properties, Architecture https://docs.formae.ai/documentation/concepts/architecture, AI assistants https://docs.formae.ai/documentation/guides/ai-coding-assistants.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open in a browser (the site refuses scripts).
  • formae is an open source IaC tool (FSL-1.1-ALv2 license) from Platform Engineering Labs, written in Pkl. It is an IaC tool, not a portal or an orchestrator: the parallel here is in CLI design.

docs.title: What is worth taking as an example
docs.text:
• CLI and API are the platform's front end: "a consistent interface for people and applications to drive the platform" (Architecture). The CLI only talks to the agent through the REST API; the agent executes and keeps state. Several team members point the CLI at the same agent: one source of truth.
  • CLI and MCP side by side: the architecture diagram shows CLI and MCP as sibling clients of the same API. formae publishes a plugin for Claude Code/Codex with MCP tools (inventory, command history, schema, simulation, deploy) and skills (simulate before applying, confirm before destroying).
  • Inventory queryable by entity: formae inventory <resources|stacks|targets|policies>, with a --query filter in key:value terms and the * wildcard:
formae inventory resources --query 'type:AWS::S3::Bucket stack:prod'
formae inventory resources --query 'target:eu target:us managed:false'
formae inventory targets --query 'namespace:AWS label:prod-*'
formae command list --query 'status:InProgress'
  • Output for human or machine: --output-consumer <human|machine> and --output-schema <json|yaml>. In the terminal, a table and a live progress view; in a pipe/CI, JSON and an immediate return with the command ID (follow it with formae command status).
  • Managed and discovered: the inventory includes resources that exist in the cloud and are not yet under management (managed:false); formae extract brings them into code. 0.88 started cleaning discovered inventory after a configurable period, without touching managed resources (release).
  • Typed properties become flags: the platform hides the detail behind a small, typed interface; the consumer only passes values, validated before any cloud call.
formae apply --help database.pkl     # shows --team [required], --size [default: "xs"]
formae apply --mode reconcile --team team-a --size s database.pkl
  • Simulate before applying: apply in human mode always simulates and asks for confirmation; --simulate stops at the dry run; --yes for automation.
  • Profiles (--profile) switch environments without editing config.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Slide many-clients: the CLI is a first-class client, not a portal shortcut; CLI and agent (MCP) consume the same API.
  • Design of a platform CLI: inventory by catalog entity type (Environment, Component, Resource), --query by owner/system/lifecycle, human or JSON output, simulation before applying, typed flags derived from the contract (like the Environment XRD).
  • "Managed vs. discovered" ties into ownership and into Fury's idle environment (mercadolibre-fury.md).

docs.title: Four golden signals
docs.text:
• Source: Site Reliability Engineering (Google), ch. 6 "Monitoring Distributed Systems", written by Rob Ewaschuk, edited by Betsy Beyer. https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: The four signals
docs.text:
• "The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation."
  • Latency: "The time it takes to service a request" — separate the latency of successful requests from that of failed ones (a fast error distorts the average).
  • Traffic: the demand on the system, measured in a way suited to each type of system (e.g., HTTP requests per second).
  • Errors: "The rate of requests that fail, either explicitly (e.g., HTTP 500s), implicitly … or by policy".
  • Saturation: how "full" the system is, in its most constrained resources.
  • "If you measure all four golden signals and page a human when one signal is problematic … your service will be at least decently covered."

docs.title: Symptom vs. cause
docs.text: • Symptom = what broke; cause = why. Alert on symptoms; use causes to debug. Reduces alert noise.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• The minimum observability contract that the platform delivers ready for every environment and resource it generates, without the team configuring it.
  • In MVP 1: latency, traffic (requests and tokens), errors and saturation of the LiteLLM proxy — links to token-finops.
  • They are the runtime fitness functions of an environment (fitness-functions.md).

docs.title: Internal Products (IP)
docs.text:
The platform's goal beyond MVP 1, in the user's view (2026-10-08): to stimulate creativity and make it easier to create new products inside the organization, as happens with products that are born as ideas. IP = Internal Product: an application or solution created internally.

  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: An idea's journey
docs.text:
Anyone in the company has an idea and:

  1. Registers it in the platform (it becomes a catalog entity, with an owner).
  2. Provisions resources and deploys.
  3. Tests and monitors.
  4. Refines.
  5. Shares it with the rest of the organization.

docs.title: Sharing = changing lifecycle
docs.text:
Backstage already has the spec.lifecycle field in Component, API, Resource and System, with three well-known values: experimental, production and deprecated (doc). Today the whole catalog of the repo is experimental.

Proposal (the user's idea, not decided):

Lifecycle Meaning for an IP experimental Idea under construction: the owner provisions, tests and refines production Validated and shared with the organization: other teams may depend on it deprecated Being discontinued: those who depend on it get a warning and a deadline

The lifecycle change can become a platform gate: moving up to production requires what the organization asks of a shared product (owner, observability, attributed cost, security).

docs.title: Relation to the idp-cloud shaping
docs.text: The shaping's segment is squads that build IPs or want to start a POC/MVP, teams of 3–4 people without dedicated operations; the North Star is the time from request to first working deploy.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• problem act: the goal is not just to provision environments faster; it is to take an idea to a product.
  • Developer Control (declare-identity): the file's lifecycle: experimental becomes the hook for the IP lifecycle.

docs.title: internaldeveloperplatform.org
docs.text:
• Source: https://internaldeveloperplatform.org/ (read on 2026-10-07). Pages used: "What is an IDP" https://internaldeveloperplatform.org/what-is-an-internal-developer-platform/, "Core components" https://internaldeveloperplatform.org/core-components/, "Environment management" https://internaldeveloperplatform.org/core-components/environment-management/.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.
  • A community curation site about IDPs ("Everything the WWW has around Internal Developer Platforms in one curated space"). Some of the contributors work at Humanitec, which the site itself calls "the market leader in IDPs"; Humanitec sells a platform orchestrator. Same caution as for vendor material: the framing favors the orchestrator category.

docs.title: Definitions (literal)
docs.text:
• IDP: "An Internal Developer Platform (IDP) is built by a platform team to build golden paths and enable developer self-service." The platform integrates several technologies to reduce cognitive load without removing access to the technologies underneath.
  • Portal (citing Gartner): "Internal developer portals serve as the interface through which developers can discover and access internal developer platform capabilities." The portal is one UI-based interface to the IDP; the platform is the whole layer underneath.
  • Platform team: builds and maintains the IDP as a product for the devs (internal customers), listening to infra/ops, security, architecture and executives.
  • The name matters: Internal (not external), Developer (the main user is the application dev), Platform (a product category). The site rejects "internal platform" and "developer portal/platform".

docs.title: Five core components (literal)
docs.text:
1. Application Configuration Management: "Manage application configuration in a dynamic, scalable and reliable way."
  2. Infrastructure Orchestration: "Orchestrate your infrastructure in a dynamic and intelligent way depending on the context."
  3. Environment Management: "Enable developers to create new and fully provisioned environments whenever needed."
  4. Deployment Management: "Implement a delivery pipeline for Continuous Delivery or even Continuous Deployment (CD)."
  5. Role-Based Access Control: "Manage who can do what in a scalable way."

docs.title: Environment management (detail)
docs.text:
• "With Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) developers can self-serve fully provisioned environments on demand."
  • "Each new environment is provisioned as defined by the platform team."
  • Creation through "a user interface (UI), a command-line interface (CLI), or an API".
  • Environment types defined by the platform (smaller machines in dev, larger ones in production).
  • "automated teardown or pausing of environments if they are not needed to avoid unnecessary costs".

docs.title: Quote
docs.text: • "I'm convinced the majority of people managing infrastructure just want a PaaS. The only requirement: it has to be built by them." — Kelsey Hightower, 2017-04-11 (cited on the site).

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Environment Management is literally MVP 1: the dev asks for an Environment provisioned as the platform defined it, through UI, CLI or API. It gives an external source to say "MVP 1 delivers one of the five core components of an IDP".
  • Automatic teardown/pausing to avoid cost = the same idea as Fury (mercadolibre-fury.md).
  • UI, CLI or API as ways to create = many-clients.
  • RBAC as a core component = single-sign-on/who-decides.
  • The Gartner definition of portal reinforces portal-is-not-platform, with a less biased source than Port/configure8 (still through a site tied to Humanitec).
  • The five components are another cut, by capability, different from the five planes (by layer, base-deck.md). Do not mix the two "fives" on the same screen.

docs.title: MCP as platform interface
docs.text:
Thesis tested: the platform catalog (Backstage: Domain/System/Component/API/Resource, ownership, dependencies) serves as context for AI agents through MCP: the same catalog serves the portal (human) and MCP (agent). Result: confirmed by a primary source in upstream Backstage (catalog-backend registers catalog read actions that mcp-actions-backend exposes as MCP tools) and, as vendors, in Port, Spotify Portal and Red Hat Developer Hub.

  • Source (all read on 2026-10-07):
  • MCP spec, current revision 2026-07-28, overview: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest
  • MCP spec, versioning: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/versioning
  • MCP spec, Tools: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools
