docs.title: What MCP is (spec)
docs.text:
• Literal definition: "Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that enables seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools." — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest
  • Architecture: "The protocol uses JSON-RPC 2.0 messages to establish communication between: Hosts: LLM applications that initiate connections; Clients: Connectors within the host application; Servers: Services that provide context and capabilities." — same URL.
  • Official analogy with LSP: "In a similar way, MCP standardizes how to integrate additional context and tools into the ecosystem of AI applications." — same URL. Useful for the talk: just as LSP decoupled the editor from the language, MCP decouples the agent from the system.
  • Version: "The current protocol version is 2026-07-28." Format YYYY-MM-DD, "to indicate the last date backwards incompatible changes were made." — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/versioning
  • Revision 2026-07-28 declares the protocol stateless: "Stateless, self-contained requests" and "Per-request capability negotiation"; negotiation by handshake applies only to "2025-11-25 and earlier". — overview and versioning above.

docs.title: Server primitives: who controls each one
docs.text:
• Literal list: "Resources: Context and data, for the user or the AI model to use"; "Prompts: Templated messages and workflows for users"; "Tools: Functions for the AI model to execute". From client to server: "Elicitation: Server-initiated requests for additional information from users". — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest
  • Tools are "model-controlled, meaning that the language model can discover and invoke tools automatically based on its contextual understanding and the user's prompts." — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools
  • Resources are "application-driven, with host applications determining how to incorporate context based on their needs" and serve to "share data that provides context to language models, such as files, database schemas, or application-specific information." — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/resources
  • Prompts are "user-controlled, meaning they are exposed from servers to clients with the intention of the user being able to explicitly select them for use." — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/prompts
  • Optional extensions in the current revision: Tasks ("Asynchronous execution of long-running operations"), Skills over MCP and MCP Apps ("Interactive UI elements ... rendered inline within conversations"). — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest
  • Reading for the presentation: the catalog fits naturally in resources (context, read) and the platform's actions in tools (execution). In Backstage, however, everything comes out as a tool (see below), including reading the catalog.

docs.title: Governance: Linux Foundation / Agentic AI Foundation
docs.text:
• "Anthropic is donating MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation." — official MCP blog, 2025-12-09: https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025-12-09-mcp-joins-agentic-ai-foundation/
  • Technical governance unchanged: "The people making decisions about the protocol are still the maintainers who have been stewarding it, guided by community input through our SEP process." — same URL.
  • The AAIF was born with three founding projects: MCP (Anthropic), goose (Block) and AGENTS.md (OpenAI). — https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation

docs.title: Backstage: catalog exposed as MCP (upstream, not vendor)
docs.text:
• Mechanism in two pieces. Actions Registry: "The Actions Registry Service is a core service designed to provide a distributed registry for actions that can be executed within Backstage backend plugins." Status (alpha). — https://backstage.io/docs/backend-system/core-services/actions-registry/
  • MCP Actions Backend: "The MCP Actions Backend exposes actions registered with the Actions Registry as MCP tools." Package @backstage/plugin-mcp-actions-backend; default Streamable HTTP endpoint http://localhost:7007/api/mcp-actions/v1; plugins exposed through backend.actions.pluginSources (e.g. 'catalog'). — https://backstage.io/docs/ai/mcp-actions/
  • Landed in v1.40.0 (tag of 2025-06-17): "A new mcp-actions backend plugin, which will surface these actions as tools as an MCP server. This can be used to expose plugin Actions with your favourite AI tools, such as Cursor, Claude or ChatGPT." With the warning: "it's currently highly experimental and could be subject to breaking changes in future releases." — https://backstage.io/docs/releases/v1.40.0/
  • Actions that catalog-backend itself registers (source code on master, checked on 2026-10-07; latest Backstage release v1.55.3, 2026-09-29): get-catalog-entity, query-catalog-entities, get-catalog-model-description, register-entity, unregister-entity, refresh-catalog-entity, validate-entity. — https://github.com/backstage/backstage/tree/master/plugins/catalog-backend/src/actions
  • get-catalog-entity: "This allows you to get a single entity from the software catalog. ... Each entity is identified by a unique entity reference, which is a string of the form "kind:namespace/name"." Attributes readOnly: true, destructive: false, idempotent: true.
  • query-catalog-entities documents ownership-relation queries for the LLM: "Querying relations - find all entities owned by a specific group: { query: { "relations.ownedby": "group:default/team-alpha" } }". It is direct proof of the thesis: the catalog's ownership and relations reach the agent as a tool filter.
  • get-catalog-model-description: comment in the code: "Lets users fetch a markdown formatted description of the catalog model. This is useful for informing LLMs how to properly work with it." Tool description: "Returns a markdown formatted description of the current catalog model, including all registered entity kinds, annotations, labels, tags, and relations."
  • Controls: destructive/readOnly/idempotent attributes per action, and visibilityPermission, which filters the action out of the listing and returns 404 on invocation for those without permission; it reuses the portal's permission framework. — https://backstage.io/docs/backend-system/core-services/actions-registry/
  • MCP auth in Backstage: static token ("temporary workaround"), CIMD (recommended, aligned with the spec) and DCR (deprecated). — https://backstage.io/docs/ai/mcp-actions/

docs.title: Other platform products with MCP (vendor)
docs.text:
• Spotify Portal (vendor): "Portal exposes its plugin capabilities as MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools that any compatible AI agent can discover and use." Plugins in the diagram: Catalog, Soundcheck, Scaffolder. — https://backstage.spotify.com/docs/portal/core-features-and-plugins/mcp/overview
  • Red Hat Developer Hub (vendor, Backstage distro): "Starting in version 1.8, you can install plug-ins from the Extensions Marketplace that provide an MCP server in Developer Hub". Tools: software-catalog-mcp-tool and techdocs-mcp-tool. — https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/11/10/mcp-red-hat-developer-hub-chat-your-catalog
  • Port (vendor): "The Port Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server acts as a bridge, enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) - like those powering Claude, Cursor, or GitHub Copilot - to interact directly with your Port.io developer portal." — https://docs.port.io/agent-management/port-mcp-server/overview/
  • Humanitec (vendor): the MCP is about product knowledge, not about the customer's platform: the assistant "does not have access to any data within your Orchestrator organization". A useful counterexample: not every "platform MCP" exposes the platform's state. — https://humanitec.com/blog/feature-announcement-mcp-knowledge-server (the quoted sentence came from the former docs page, which now answers 404)
  • Upbound Crossplane (vendor): "MCP servers, packaged as Add-Ons...install on your control plane. They deliver tools that the language model can use." Intelligent Control Planes "bring LLM-driven logic into your control plane's reconcile loop." Note: in Upbound's docs "MCP" also means managed control plane. — https://docs.upbound.io/manuals/uxp/features/intelligent-control-planes
  • Argo CD (argoproj-labs project, Argo community, donated by Akuity): "An implementation of Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Argo CD." Has an MCP_READ_ONLY mode that turns off create/update/delete/sync. — https://github.com/argoproj-labs/mcp-for-argocd

docs.title: Risks and auth (spec)
docs.text:
• Tool Safety principle: "Tools represent arbitrary code execution and must be treated with appropriate caution." and "descriptions of tool behavior such as annotations should be considered untrusted, unless obtained from a trusted server." and "Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool". The protocol admits the limit: "MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level". — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest
  • Human in the loop: "For trust & safety and security, there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations." Servers "MUST: Validate all tool inputs; Implement proper access controls; Rate limit tool invocations; Sanitize tool outputs". — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools
  • Tool poisoning, prompt injection and rug pull (official tutorial, non-normative): "Tool names and descriptions are instructions your model reads. A server can hide directives in them that steer the agent — including how it uses other servers' tools — without the poisoned tool ever being invoked (often called tool poisoning, or tool shadowing when it targets another server's tools)." and "a server can quietly change them after you approved it (a rug pull)". Also: "Prompt injection in untrusted content can steer an honest server into the same overreach". And the principle: "no check proves what a server will do." — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/local-server-security
  • Auth in the spec: "Authorization is OPTIONAL for MCP implementations." When present, it is based on "OAuth 2.1 IETF DRAFT (draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-13)" + RFC 8414, RFC 7591, RFC 8707, RFC 9728, RFC 9207, CIMD. "A protected MCP server acts as an OAuth 2.1 resource server". "MCP servers MUST implement OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC9728)." DCR "is deprecated" in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents. — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization
  • Audience binding: "MCP servers MUST validate that access tokens were issued specifically for them as the intended audience" and "MCP servers MUST NOT accept or transit any other tokens." — same URL.
  • Security Best Practices lists: Confused Deputy, Token Passthrough ("explicitly forbidden"), SSRF, State Handle Hijacking, Local MCP Server Compromise, OAuth Authorization URL Validation, stdio in proxy, Mix-Up, Localhost Redirect URI Impersonation, CIMD Trust Policies, Scope Minimization ("Poor scope design increases token compromise impact, elevates user friction, and obscures audit trails."). The normative page does not cover prompt injection/tool poisoning; those are in the local server tutorial. — https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/security_best_practices

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
• MCP adoption numbers in the first year (e.g. "97 million monthly SDK downloads", "10,000 active servers") appeared in a search summary attributed to the AAIF announcement; the literal sentence was not checked on the Linux Foundation/Anthropic page. Do not use on a slide without rereading.
  • AAIF supporting members beyond the three founders (Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare, Bloomberg): only via a search summary.
  • Current maturity status of mcp-actions-backend ("highly experimental" is from v1.40.0; the package is still 0.x, 0.2.3-next.1 in package.json on master). No GA declaration was found.
  • Spotify Portal: the MCP's beta/GA status is not stated on the page.
  • Red Hat Developer Hub: whether the MCP plugins are Tech/Developer Preview: the article does not say; Red Hat's product documentation was not read.
  • Port: the exact list of tools and the permission model ("runs with the signed-in user's permissions") came from a search summary; the page read does not have the literal text.
  • Kubernetes MCP: containers/kubernetes-mcp-server exists ("Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Kubernetes and OpenShift"), but no official documentation from the Kubernetes project adopting an MCP server was found; do not cite it as "official Kubernetes".
  • Upstream Crossplane (not Upbound): no official MCP server documentation was found on crossplane.io.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Candidate slide catalog-as-context (catalog: portal for humans, MCP for agents): the proof is upstream Backstage's query-catalog-entities filtering by relations.ownedby, plus get-catalog-model-description made explicitly "for informing LLMs". Message: one catalog, two consumers; the portal's permission framework (visibilityPermission) is the same one that filters the agent's tools.
  • Link with many-clients (CLI + MCP already cited through formae): Backstage's CLI (catalog module) and MCP consume the same Actions Registry actions: same surface, different clients.
  • Link with agent-identity (MCP auth): MCP server = OAuth 2.1 resource server, mandatory audience binding, token passthrough forbidden, CIMD in place of DCR; Backstage already follows this (CIMD recommended, DCR deprecated).
  • Risk note for the slide (a sentence in the notes, not on screen): a tool description is an instruction the model reads: tool poisoning/rug pull; that is why the exposed catalog should be read-only by default (readOnly: true) and destructive actions go through a human in the loop.
  • Optional counterexample: Humanitec exposes an MCP for documentation only: "having an MCP" does not imply exposing the platform's state.

docs.title: Mercado Libre Fury
docs.text:
A real IDP case that looks after the lifecycle of what it provisions. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aFJTxKak6sM. Summary provided by the user on 2026-10-07; check against the video (and note the timestamp) before citing a detail on screen.

  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

  • Mercado Libre's IDP: Fury.

  • The platform monitors whether a provisioned environment is not being used and suggests deletion to the environment's owner.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• A practical answer to the "puppy for Christmas" (Platform as a Product, p. 16): the resource is not abandoned after the click: the platform remembers who the owner is and asks whether it is still needed.
  • Depends on ownership in the catalog: the owner can only be notified if the catalog knows who they are.
  • Ties into cost (FinOps): an idle environment is cost without value. In a platform environment, each Environment is an EKS cluster with the cost running.
  • The platform suggests, the owner decides: a guardrail, not a gate.

docs.title: Platform as a Product (O'Reilly / Syntasso)
docs.text:
• Source: Platform as a Product (https://www.syntasso.io/platform-as-a-product-oreilly-report) — Abby Bangser, Daniel Bryant, Colin Humphreys and Cat Morris, O'Reilly Media, first edition, October 2025 (copyright 2026). All four authors are from Syntasso (the company behind Kratix): the report is vendor-sponsored and advocates orchestration, but it does not mention Kratix or Promise in the text, only in the bio of Abby Bangser (a Kratix core contributor).
  • Pages cited below are the ones printed in the book (chapter 1 starts on p. 1); the PDF has an offset of about 6 pages of front matter.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A platform must be treated as a product, not as an infrastructure project: it has users, a value proposition, a feedback loop, iteration and a focus on adoption (pp. 3-4, 9-11).
  • Portal + pipeline/workflow engine form a "platform façade": they look like a platform, but without orchestration (persistent state, policy, ownership, lifecycle) the platform decays (pp. 15-18).
  • Orchestration is the persistent control layer that coordinates capabilities, keeps state, enforces policy and enables safe evolution; portals are where the user interacts, pipelines are execution tools (pp. 16, 19).
  • Success is measured on four pillars (speed, safety, efficiency, scalability) with a scorecard and one key metric per pillar, avoiding vanity metrics (pp. 4-5, 31-36).
  • The platform scales through contribution (platform democracy / multiplayer mode), fleet management and versioning, and the future includes AI inside the platform, always on top of contracts, policy and audit (pp. 21-29, 37-40).

docs.title: Argument by chapter
docs.text:
• Ch. 1, pp. 1-7 — The Platform Imperative: cloud native complexity creates the need for an IDP; two-layer DevOps; trends; four pillars of value; a 4-stage maturity model.
  • Ch. 2, pp. 9-14 — Platform as a Product: a platform is more than a stack of tools; product mindset (feasibility, viability, usability, value); optional, composable abstractions; involve stakeholders early; brownfield; think in years.
  • Ch. 3, pp. 15-19 — Orchestrate, Don't Just Automate: platform façade, limits of pipelines and portals, "puppy for Christmas", automation vs. orchestration, user observability, platform decay.
  • Ch. 4, pp. 21-24 — Fleet Thinking: manage services/environments/infrastructure as a fleet, lessons from automotive OTA, versioning, composable and upgradable services.
  • Ch. 5, pp. 25-29 — Platform Team Dynamics: three personas (platform engineers, app developers, vendors/producers), platform democracy, multiplayer mode, sustainable contributions.
  • Ch. 6, pp. 31-36 — Internal Platform Scorecard: four pillars with metrics, baselines, scorecards per maturity stage, measurement pitfalls.
  • Ch. 7, pp. 37-40 — The Future of Internal Platforms: open source vs. enterprise, "making the mix work", preparing for the AI-native era.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
The report has almost no statistics; only one case and the structural numbers below.

Data point Value Page Suggested use Insurance company (a client of Colin Humphreys): deploy cycle from "up to two years" to daily releases 12, 28 Impact slide: platform as a collaborative product and stakeholders (security, compliance) involved early Pillars of platform value 4 (speed, safety, efficiency, scalability) 4 Structure of the IDP scorecard Stages of the maturity model (CNCF Platforms WG) 4 (ad hoc automation, catalog and portal, orchestrated product, federated ecosystem) 5-6 "Where we are" slide: the portal alone is stage 2 Key scorecard metrics 4: MTTFD, SRPC, MTTUSI, MTTASP 33 Proposed metrics for the IDP Platform personas 3 25 Developer, platform team, contributors/producers Cases cited without detail NatWest, USwitch, Adidas, The Home Depot 14 Reference only; the report gives no numbers for them Diverging versions (example) example v1.2, v1.4 and a fork 23 Illustration of "invisible divergence" Time metaphor "day two thousand" 13, 33 Longevity of the platform

docs.title: Quotes
docs.text:
• "A platform is not just a collection of tools, templates, or workflows. It is an evolving system that must continuously respond to user needs." (p. 9)
  • "an evolving set of reusable services, integrated with your existing systems, that creates valuable outcomes for your business." — Colin Humphreys's definition of a platform product (p. 10)
  • "The model is based on enablement rather than enforcement and self-service rather than ticket queues." (p. 3)
  • "abstractions should be composable and optional. They should guide without constraining. They should reduce complexity without hiding critical details." (p. 11)
  • "Your platform should 'float above' what is already available off the shelf" (p. 11, credited to Gregor Hohpe)
  • "everything is brownfield and complex" (p. 12)
  • "Portals are where users interact. Pipelines and workflow engines are execution tools. Orchestration is the system that ties it all together, delivering value across the lifecycle." (p. 19)
  • "a polished UI for running fragile automation." — about a portal without orchestration (p. 16)
  • "Who feeds the puppy?" — the "puppy for Christmas" problem (p. 16)
  • "That is not empowerment. That is abandonment." (p. 16)
  • "Developers request capabilities, and the platform team governs how those requests are fulfilled." (p. 17)
  • "This is not a guide to spinning up a portal or building a golden path." (p. 7)

docs.title: Concepts and frameworks
docs.text:
• Four pillars of platform value: speed, safety, efficiency, scalability, defined as the "legs of a table" (pp. 4-5).
  • Platform maturity model (CNCF Platforms WG): Stage 1 ad hoc automation, Stage 2 catalog and portal, Stage 3 orchestrated product, Stage 4 federated ecosystem; "not a race to the top but a self-assessment tool"; two acceleration principles: contracts/APIs at the center and a baseline on the four pillars before optimizing one (pp. 5-6).
  • Two-layer DevOps: an application layer and a platform layer, consumed through well-defined contracts/APIs; the platform does not replace DevOps (pp. 2-3).
  • Product mindset: balance between feasibility, viability, usability and value; it requires product management, UX design and user research (p. 10). Practices: collaborate directly with users, feedback loops with small, frequent improvements, internal brand (p. 11).
  • Golden cage: a rigid, top-down golden path generates shadow platforms; "there is no universal golden path" (p. 11).
  • Platform façade: portal + workflow engine/CI without coordination, governance and lifecycle (p. 15).
  • Orchestration: "persistent control layer that coordinates capabilities across the platform, manages state, enforces policy, and enables safe evolution over time" (p. 16). Table 3-1 compares automation (pipelines + portals) and orchestration across the four pillars (p. 17). Attributes of an orchestrated platform: clear APIs and contracts, declarative requests with automated fulfillment, shared governance and policy, lifecycle awareness and upgrade paths, a persistent record of what was created, by whom and why (p. 19).
  • User observability (Fournier and Nowland): visibility into how developers interact with the platform and how their requests progress; it answers "What happens when I request a new service? Why is my upgrade delayed? Who owns this resource?" (pp. 17-18).
  • Platform decay and its symptoms (p. 18).
  • Fleet thinking / fleet management: manage a collection of similar but not identical things, each with a lifecycle; analogy with OTA updates of cars (staged, paused, rolled back); version capabilities and track what runs where (pp. 21-23).
  • Invisible divergence: v1.2, v1.4 and a fork outside the platform's control (p. 23).
  • Three personas: platform engineers, app developers, vendors/producers (internal or external) (pp. 25-26). "Platform democracy" (Ted Newman, NatWest) and "multiplayer mode" (Paula Kennedy) (p. 27). Sustainable contribution: a clear process, frameworks for contributing, governance of ownership/lifecycle/deprecation (p. 28).
  • Internal Platform Scorecard, Table 6-1 (p. 33): Speed = MTTFD (mean time to first deploy, from the request to the running service); Safety = SRPC (% of services running in compliance with the current policy); Efficiency = MTTUSI (mean time to upgrade service instances, time to propagate a change to all live instances); Scalability = MTTASP (mean time to add a service to the platform, from defining the requirement to offering it on the platform). Indicators: API-first, golden paths with composable abstractions, internal marketplace, policy-driven workflows, one-click/one-API upgrades, drift detection and continuous convergence, multiplayer contribution, inner sourcing.
  • Scorecards by stage: early-stage, mid-stage with growing adoption, mature/regulated (p. 35).
  • Build / buy / borrow as a product decision; "treat integration code as part of the platform product" (p. 38). Three changes with AI: natural-language/chat UIs over existing APIs, orchestration assistants that propose fixes within the guardrails, data and model governance; plan: strengthen contracts and metadata, invest in policy and audit, instrument everything, keep humans in the loop, treat models and prompts as versioned artifacts (p. 39).

docs.title: Roles: portal vs. orchestrator vs. IaC
docs.text:
The report covers the split at a conceptual level, without naming Kratix or Promises (the only link to Kratix is Abby Bangser's bio, p. 41). Backstage, Crossplane, Argo Workflows and GitHub Actions appear only as examples.

  • Portal (e.g. Backstage, p. 15): improves discoverability and offers a friendly entry point; with no orchestration behind it, it becomes a "polished UI for running fragile automation" (p. 16). "Portals are where users interact" (p. 19). A click that provisions without later management enables drift and risk (p. 16).
  • Pipelines and workflow engines (Argo Workflows, GitHub Actions, p. 15): "execution tools" (p. 19); excellent for deploys, retries and parallelism, but they are transient systems that keep no persistent state, no policy over time and no ownership (pp. 15-16).
  • Orchestration: a persistent control layer (state, policy, ownership, lifecycle); it creates a separation of concerns between who requests and who governs the fulfillment (pp. 16-17, 19).
  • IaC: appears only as an example of an interchangeable component. "run a commercial orchestration engine and integrate it with an open source infrastructure-as-code tool" (p. 38). Terraform modules, cloud APIs and bash scripts should sit behind a consistent interface (p. 13). Crossplane and Backstage are cited as CNCF projects, "proven foundations" (p. 38).
  • Contracts and APIs make it possible to swap implementations without breaking developers' workflows (pp. 6, 38).
  • The report does not describe an end-to-end flow (portal calls orchestrator, which calls IaC), nor does it cover Argo CD/GitOps, nor observability/security planes as architecture; that design has to come from other sources.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
• Treating the platform as a project with a final milestone and a "vague hope" of adoption (p. 9).
  • The platform team as an internal service provider chasing feature requests instead of a strategic enabler (p. 9).
  • Golden cage / rigid, top-down abstractions: it generates shadow platforms, unapproved tools and workarounds (p. 11).
  • Rebuilding what already exists on the market instead of "floating above" the off-the-shelf; lock-in to a tool or workflow (pp. 11-12).
  • Involving security, compliance and networking late, retrofitting compliance at the end (p. 12).
  • Ignoring brownfield: a platform that supports only Kubernetes and not cloud APIs, Terraform, scripts and legacy (pp. 12-13).
  • One-off exceptions, permanent workarounds and bolted-on features; sharing only code, not services (p. 13).
  • Platform façade: portal + pipeline without orchestration (p. 15).
  • "Puppy for Christmas": provisioning by click and abandoning the resource, with no upgrade, policy or lifecycle (p. 16).
  • Sealed box: no user observability, "buttons are clicked, pipelines run, and then... silence", devs go back to tickets (p. 17).
  • Platform decay: obscure ownership and upgrade paths, workflows that only work in certain environments, snowflakes, fragmented compliance, a backlog of "quick fixes" (p. 18).
  • Invisible divergence and silent updates with no communication or rollback (p. 23).
  • The platform as a bottleneck: platform engineers own all capabilities, with no vendors/producers (p. 26).
  • One-off integrations and undocumented hacks (p. 28).
  • Measuring a single pillar before having a baseline on all four (p. 34).
  • Vanity metrics: number of services in the catalog, clicks/page views in the portal, lines of YAML (p. 35).
  • Only quantitative metrics, with no surveys and conversations; the scorecard as a one-off exercise (p. 35).
  • AI as a bolt-on experiment (p. 39).

docs.title: The platform engineering illusion
docs.text:
• Source: David Iyanu Jonathan, "The Platform Engineering Illusion: Why Most Internal Developer Platforms Fail Before Developers Ever Use Them", platformengineering.com, 2026-07-31. https://platformengineering.com/features/the-platform-engineering-illusion-why-most-internal-developer-platforms-fail-before-developers-ever-use-them/
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open in a browser (the site refuses scripts).
  • platformengineering.com belongs to Techstrong Group (the same as "Nobody owns the data", data-ownership.md); do not confuse it with platformengineering.org (a community tied to Humanitec, source of empathy-gap.md).
  • Opinion article, no sourced data. The numbers (14 months, adoption below 20%, 43 services with 12 out of date, three teams disbanded within 18 months) are the author's personal observation: cite them as "an account", never as a trend, and never on screen.

docs.title: Thesis
docs.text: IDPs fail because the organization treats platform engineering as a tooling initiative, when it is structurally a product discipline, with the accountability mechanisms a product has (user research, retention, churn) that most platform teams never install.

docs.title: Quotes (literal)
docs.text:
• "the team built a platform the way you build a bridge, and developers experienced it the way you experience a toll booth."
  • "the platform was correct and nobody wanted it."
  • "Why would a developer, mid-deadline, exhausted, half paying attention, choose your paved road over the goat trail they already know?"
  • "A technology platform is infrastructure with an API. A developer platform is a product with users, and users have preferences, workarounds, trust thresholds, and memory of every time the tool embarrassed them in front of their team."
  • On the Backstage + Kubernetes + Terraform + Crossplane + Argo CD stack: "Every one of those tools is legitimate. None of them, combined, constitutes a platform, any more than a stack of good ingredients constitutes a meal."
  • "you build it, you run it, you secure it, you monitor it, you cost-optimize it, and you keep current on eleven CVE feeds."
  • "reduce unnecessary complexity while preserving necessary complexity — not to eliminate complexity, which is impossible, and not to hide it so thoroughly that debugging becomes archaeology."
  • "Developers don't experience your architecture. They experience the fifteen minutes." (a 15-minute CI queue that nobody on the platform team owned)
  • "mandated usage generates resentment rather than advocacy, and resentment metastasizes into shadow infrastructure"
  • "A platform that adds security friction after launch teaches developers that the platform is where good ideas go to get slower"
  • "the best platform teams I've worked with measure themselves partly by what they refuse to expose to developers"
  • "every manual step in a 'self-service' system is really just a support queue wearing a costume."
  • "infrastructure outputs are the platform team congratulating itself."
  • On AI: "adoption was never a tooling problem to begin with — it was a trust and design problem, and trust doesn't move faster because the tool generating the config got smarter." And on Kubernetes and operational complexity: "It didn't. It relocated it."

docs.title: Five failure modes
docs.text:
1. Building for the infrastructure, not for the dev: it measures uptime and provisioning speed; it never follows a real deploy.
  2. No product mindset: with no owner, the roadmap becomes "a list of things a VP saw at KubeCon".
  3. Wrong metrics: number of clusters, deployment frequency in isolation, CPU.
  4. Adoption by mandate, not by earned trust: usage goes up, and with it the shadow infrastructure.
  5. Governance arrives after the party: security comes in at the end, becomes obstruction and is patched in, worsening the experience.

docs.title: Metrics the author proposes
docs.text:
• Time-to-first-deploy for a newcomer.
  • Self-reported cognitive load (a survey of the dev).
  • Ratio of deploys through the golden path to deploys through the escape hatch.
  • Bypass rate: how often the dev works around the platform — "the platform's real adoption curve", almost never on the dashboard shown to leadership.
  • Business outcome: lead time, incident rate, onboarding speed.

docs.title: What surviving platforms have in common
docs.text:
• A product with a named owner who can say no.
  • A focus on reducing cognitive load, not on adding capability.
  • Opinionated golden paths with an escape hatch, not infinite configurability ("a tax paid in decision fatigue").
  • Real self-service: no Slack message and waiting.
  • Continuous feedback, with the change visible to whoever complained.
  • Documentation before launch.
  • Security in the design phase, not in the audit phase: policy-as-code, security in the template, a guardrail that prevents instead of only detecting.
  • Start with the smallest platform that solves a real, named problem; automate the repetitive flow that generates tickets, not the one that makes a good talk.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
It reinforces theses already in the deck with a second voice, and adds three new ideas: bypass rate, tool stack ≠ platform (the stack cited is ours) and security in the design.

Slide Use empathy-gap A second voice for the same thesis: "the platform was correct and nobody wanted it"; bridge vs. toll booth cognitive-load Expansion of "you build it, you run it"; absorb the unnecessary complexity and preserve the necessary one platform-as-product "infrastructure with an API" vs. "product with users"; the manual step as a "support queue wearing a costume" golden-paths, golden-paths-shape The question of the tired dev in the middle of a deadline (paved road vs. goat trail); mandate generates shadow infrastructure (a source independent of Syntasso) catalog-ownership 43 services, 12 out of date: a catalog with no owner becomes a dead list (an account) score-what-not Good teams measure themselves by what they refuse to expose to the dev platform-amplifier AI does not solve adoption: the problem is trust and design platform-as-product-signals Bypass rate as a new item; feedback with a visible change guardrails Security in the design phase reference-architecture Caveat: the drawn stack (Backstage, Crossplane, Argo CD) is an ingredient, not a platform mvp1 The smallest platform that solves a real, named problem (Claude Code with managed cost) ask Pilot teams and earned adoption, not mandate

docs.title: First proof of concept (wasp-idp)
docs.text:
• Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

Concrete examples the presentation can use, all verifiable in the first proof of concept (wasp-idp) repo. The reference architecture of the base deck is Azure; the first proof of concept (wasp-idp) ran on AWS.

  • Environment as a claim: 1 Environment claim becomes an entire EKS cluster (~28-30 min) with network, DNS in a delegated sub-zone in Route 53, certificate, Gateway, identity and GitOps (Argo CD). Abstractions (XRDs and compositions) in aws/eks/resources/; timings per step in aws/eks/README.md (the EKS control plane dominates, ~12-15 min).
  • Gate on an irreversible action: destroying the environment requires --yes-destroy (aws/eks/scripts/teardown); make clean refuses without CONFIRM=1.
  • Hub-and-spoke: the AWS topology (a network account with the hub, cells per region, centralized ingress) is in the ADRs in docs/adr/ and in aws/docs/.
  • Product decision: the Environment is "the entry of the IDP catalog", consumed by different clients (Backstage, CLI, agent).
  • Portal: Backstage in idp/ (runs locally), with a python-service template that creates a repo and a PR in the central GitOps repo, a catalog discovered from the GitHub org (ADR 0020) and complete catalog examples (Domain communication, Domain bookstore). Deployed to two environments (development, production) by the central Argo CD (ADR 0019).
  • Map to the planes: Claude Code and Backstage = Developer Control; Crossplane = IaC; Argo CD = Delivery; Route 53 = Networking; Secrets Manager + ESO = Secrets.
  • Framing in the presentation: the platform's MVP 1 is this path — a control plane (today a local k3d) runs Crossplane and Argo CD and provisions Environments on AWS.

docs.title: Port practical guide to internal developer portals
docs.text:
• Source: "The practical guide to internal developer portals", published by Port (https://www.port.io/guide; PDF at https://info.port.io/hubfs/The%20Practical%20Guide%20to%20Internal%20Developer%20Portals.pdf), created in March 2024. 40 pages; the printed numbering matches the PDF (cover = p. 1). The guide names no individual authors.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.
  • Vendor material. Port is a commercial internal developer portal and a direct competitor of Backstage; the guide says it "isn't a plug for our technology" (p. 4), but it ends with a product promotion (p. 40) and cites Port as an example throughout the text. Every claim that favors a commercial portal (un-opinionated, blueprints, real-time sync, open-source extensibility) is the vendor's opinion, not independent evidence. The guide has no research of its own: the only external numeric data point is the one from Puppet Labs (p. 3).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Platform (IDP) and portal are distinct things: the platform is the set of tools for build, deploy and operation; the portal is the interface with the right abstractions for the developer. The platform is "necessary but not sufficient" (pp. 6-7).
  • The portal rests on four pillars: self-service actions, software catalog, scorecards and automations, all defined on top of blueprints (metadata schemas) and relations (pp. 7-10, 14-15).
  • The data model must be defined by the organization (un-opinionated), guided by personas and by the questions one wants to answer, and must include runtime data ("running service"), not just static metadata (pp. 11, 15-18, 20).
  • Design best practices: extensible, loosely coupled, API-first, portal-as-code and customizable with RBAC per persona; self-service must stay decoupled from the underlying infrastructure and GitOps (pp. 11-13, 21).
  • Reporting and executive views are treated as underrated value, and adoption is the central risk: integrate into the developer's workflow, start with an MVP, adopt a product mindset and roll out incrementally (pp. 31-34, 38-40).

docs.title: Argument by chapter
docs.text:
• Introduction, pp. 3-4: the platform era: platform engineering replaces traditional DevOps, with developers as "customers"; the complexity of Kubernetes, the migration to SaaS and tool fragmentation motivate golden paths and guardrails; the portal is presented as a new product category.
  • Ch. 1, pp. 5-13: Overview: difference between IDP and portal, the four pillars and six design considerations (un-opinionated, extensible and open, loosely coupled, API-first, portal-as-code, customizable).
  • Ch. 2, pp. 14-16: Blueprints: the metadata schema of each entity type, linked by relations (graph); they define the catalog, actions and scorecards; adjustable over time; they include runtime context.
  • Ch. 3, pp. 17-20: Software catalog: not a static inventory; persona-driven data model; base models (Classic/SDLC and C4) and extensions (K8s, API catalog, cloud resources, CI/CD, packages, vulnerabilities, incidents, alerts, tests, feature flags, misconfigurations, FinOps); stateful, real-time catalog.
  • Ch. 4, pp. 21-23: Developer self-service actions: autonomy with guardrails and golden paths; actions reflected in the catalog; examples by domain; asynchronous actions, manual approval and run logs.
  • Ch. 5, pp. 24-28: Scorecards: measure the health and maturity of each catalog entity; types (readiness, maturity, DORA, migration, health, code quality, cloud cost, security); initiatives group scorecards; uses such as periodic review and as an alert/CI/CD gate; four-step process.
  • Ch. 6, pp. 29-30: Automations: trigger + action over the portal's API (escalate an incident, remediate security, clean up resources, block a deploy).
  • Ch. 7, pp. 31-34: Reporting and executive views: reports by persona (developer, product manager, executive, CIO); usage, health, productivity and business impact types; scorecards and initiatives as input.
  • Ch. 8, pp. 35-37: Extensibility: value grows with the data; requirements of real-time sync, bi-directional sync, reconciliation, secure by design and flexible protocols; defense of an open source integration framework.
  • Ch. 9, pp. 38-40: Adoption strategy: pitfalls (not integrating into the workflow, too many features, lack of sponsorship), product mindset, Team Topologies to map teams, focused and iterative rollout; conclusion and presentation of Port (p. 40).

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
The guide has very few numbers. Values marked as "example" are illustrative parameters from the text, not research data.

Data point Value Page Original source cited by the guide Suggested use Organizations that adopted platform engineering or plan to adopt it in the next year 51% 3 Puppet Labs (no title, year or link to the report) Adoption of platform engineering; use with caution, cite Puppet Labs and not Port, and check the original report (State of DevOps) before putting it on a slide Scorecard cycle: example check "code coverage > 70%" and yellow below 80% 70% / 80% 27 (diagram) no source (illustrative example) Do not use as data; at most illustrate the mechanics of thresholds Scorecard alert example: uptime below 99% 99% 24 no source (illustrative example) Do not use as data Self-service example: development environment for 5 days; extend TTL by 3 days 5 days / 3 days 9, 22 no source (illustrative example) Illustrate an ephemeral environment with a TTL Number of portal pillars / design considerations / team types (Team Topologies) / scorecard steps 4 / 6 / 4 / 4 8, 11, 39, 27 Team Topologies (Skelton and Pais, 2019) for the four team types (p. 39); the rest have no source (the guide's own framework) Structure of the argument, not evidence

The guide has no adoption metrics, ROI, time saved or comparison with Backstage. There is no adoption number to set against the Backstage adoption material already in backstage-catalog.md/earlier references.

docs.title: Quotes
docs.text:
• "An internal developer platform is necessary but not sufficient. It centralizes everything DevOps – but still requires an interface that provides the right abstractions for developers and promotes golden paths." (p. 6)
  • "Internal developer portals are the answer. They act as a user-friendly interface to the platform – abstracting the complexity of the software development environment by providing a single user interface that's built for the questions and needs of different dev teams." (p. 7)
  • "It can't be the other way around. In other words, the portal can't dictate the organization's use cases and priorities." (p. 7)
  • "A blueprint is a metadata schema definition – each blueprint defines the assets that the portal can manage and track" (p. 7)
  • "when you order a ticket from an airline you don't want to choose the pilot and other flight staff. The same applies for developer self-service actions: the form should only include what developers care about" (p. 9, attributed to Kostis Kapelonis)
  • "An internal developer portal isn't a static list of microservices; it's a dynamic graph of all your entities in context." (p. 18)
  • "Your code is not your app." (pp. 16, 20)
  • "Self-service actions should be loosely coupled (deliberately segregated) from the underlying infrastructure of the platform." (p. 21, text extracted with noise; the idea is also on p. 12)
  • "it's considered best practice for the portal to remain loosely coupled from underlying GitOps platforms." (p. 21)
  • "An API-first portal will have a generic interface to model the software catalog, ingest data, invoke actions, query scorecards and more – providing an optimized experience for both humans and machines." (p. 12)
  • "Reporting is almost always treated as an afterthought in conversations about internal developer portals." (p. 31)
  • "even the most advanced portal will fail without a sound adoption strategy." (p. 38)
  • "Developers reject the portal if it doesn't integrate into their workflows." (p. 38)
  • "Executive sponsorship is necessary – but far from sufficient – to ensure adoption." (p. 38)
  • "Low usage may indicate poor marketing rather than a bad product." (p. 32)
  • "low utilization of a new tool may indicate UX issues rather than inherent low value." (p. 39)
  • "In their rush to implement scorecards, too many teams rush through the critical phase of discussing quality and standards with teams." (p. 27)
  • "An effective internal developer portal requires more than just technical buildout – it demands cultivating users." (p. 40)

docs.title: Concepts and frameworks
docs.text:
• Internal developer platform vs. portal: platform = hub of tools (CLI, CI/CD, provisioning); portal = interface with abstractions for the developer, which triggers actions in tools such as Jenkins instead of using them directly (pp. 6-7).
  • Golden path: "single supported approach" for tasks such as creating a backend service or a data pipeline (pp. 3, 6).
  • Blueprint: metadata schema of an entity type (microservices, environments, packages, clusters, databases, third-party data); accepts any number of properties, which can be changed; it is also where self-service actions and scorecards are defined (pp. 7-8, 14-15).
  • Relation: connection between blueprints (one-to-one, one-to-many); makes the catalog a graph (pp. 7, 14).
  • Software catalog: central repository of software metadata and underlying resources, continuously updated, "single pane of glass", a source of truth that pipelines can query (environment TTL, ownership, feature flags) (pp. 9, 17); syncs with the identity provider to reflect ownership (p. 17).
  • Base data models: Classic/SDLC (Service, Environment, Running Service) and C4 (an adaptation of Backstage's C4 model: Context, Containers, Components, Code) (p. 18). Extensions for DevOps (K8s, API catalog, cloud resources, CI/CD) and for all devs (packages, vulnerabilities, incidents, alerts, tests, feature flags, misconfigurations, FinOps) (pp. 19-20).
  • Running service / stateful catalog: an entity that represents the live version of a service in an environment; the guide insists that the catalog must include runtime data and sync in real time with CI/CD (pp. 16, 18, 20).
  • Self-service actions: forms curated by the platform team; they cover provisioning, day-2 operations, ephemeral environments with a TTL, manual approval; every action creates, changes or removes catalog entities; run logs give a curated view instead of the full pipeline log (pp. 9, 21-23). Examples by domain: SDLC, developer environments, cloud resources, SRE, Data & ML (p. 22).
  • Scorecards: benchmarks per catalog entity; types: operational readiness, service maturity, operational maturity, DORA, migrations, health, code quality, cloud cost, security (pp. 10, 24-25). Three reasons to use them: organizational alignment, alerting and prioritization, quality improvement (pp. 24-25).
  • Initiatives: groups of scorecards tied to a strategic area (e.g. "Improve Reliability"); they align workflows with business KPIs (pp. 25-26).
  • Use of scorecards: periodic review by managers and as an alert/trigger for automation, including CI/CD that stops a deploy if the scorecard tier is low (pp. 26-27).
  • Four-step scorecard: discuss quality and standards with the teams, define checks, define thresholds (red/yellow/green and alerts), adopt and evaluate (p. 27, diagram; the extracted text does not include these steps, they were read from the image).
  • Automations: a trigger + action pair; triggers: entity matches a condition, form submitted, entity created or updated, scheduled time, scorecard degrades; actions: e-mail, Slack, weekly digest, job, API call, block a deploy (pp. 29-30). Enabled by the portal's API (p. 29).
  • Six design considerations: un-opinionated vs. opinionated, extensible and open, loosely coupled, API-first, portal-as-code (configure the portal through code, e.g. Terraform), customizable with fine-grained RBAC per persona (pp. 11-13).
  • RBAC: cited as a requirement for customization per persona and as reinforcement of the golden path in the UI (pp. 13, 21).
  • Reporting: reports by persona (developers, product managers, executives, CIOs) and by type (usage, health, productivity/DORA, business impact); customization of metric definitions, visualization, frequency and documentation (pp. 31-33).
  • Extensibility: real-time continuous sync, bi-directional sync, reconciliation with the source as ground truth, secure by design (no credential sharing or IP whitelist), flexible protocols (webhooks, APIs, message queues) (p. 36); defense of an open source integration framework (pp. 36-37).
  • Adoption: pitfalls: not integrating into the workflow, starting with too many features, lack of executive sponsorship (p. 38); two-step rollout: map the team structure via Team Topologies (stream-aligned, enabling, complicated subsystem, platform) and adapt the rollout (interviews and surveys, focused use case, monitor usage, feedback, champions, expansion on demand) (p. 39). It cites "platform-as-product" as the portal's approach of choice (p. 5).

docs.title: Relevance by plane
docs.text:
• Developer Control Plane: this is the guide's central plane: portal, self-service actions, catalog and scorecards are all interfaces for the developer (pp. 6-10). The guide treats the portal as the single interface ("single user interface", p. 7), although it also says the API-first portal serves "humans and machines" (p. 12) and that pipelines query the catalog (p. 9).
  • Integration & Delivery Plane: self-service actions trigger CI/CD and GitOps (pp. 6, 21); scorecards block deploys (p. 27); CI/CD feeds the catalog in real time (p. 20); the guide recommends keeping the portal decoupled from GitOps (p. 21), which matches an orchestration role outside the portal.
  • Resource Plane: provisioning cloud resources through self-service with guardrails, and extending the data model with cloud resources and K8s (pp. 9, 19, 22); automatic cleanup by TTL (pp. 10, 29).
  • Observability Plane: alerts, incident management and FinOps as catalog extensions (pp. 19-20, 35); reporting on usage, health, DORA and business impact (pp. 32-33).
  • Security Plane: security scorecards, vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in the catalog (pp. 19-20, 25); RBAC (pp. 13, 21); secure by design in the integrations (p. 36); auto-remediation (p. 29). The guide does not address agent identity or AI.

docs.title: Relation to the presentation
docs.text:
• Catalog as a human concept, not just a tool. Reinforces: the guide says the data model must be born from the questions the organization wants to answer and from personas (pp. 15, 17), and that the portal "can't dictate" the use cases (p. 7). Partly contradicts the idea of a catalog as a static versioned file: the guide requires a stateful catalog, updated in real time, with "running service" (pp. 16, 20). backstage-catalog.md already records that the Backstage catalog does not keep versions, and that is exactly the point where the guide positions the blueprint model as superior (vendor opinion).
  • Portal as one client among CLI and agents. The guide partly contradicts this thesis: it treats the portal as the abstraction layer and source of truth for the developer, and a platform "without a portal" as insufficient (p. 6). However, it admits that the portal is API-first, serves "humans and machines" and that the API serves scripts, CI/CD and automations (pp. 12-13, 29), which supports the idea that the catalog and actions can be consumed by other clients. The guide mentions neither AI agents nor the CLI as a first-class client of the platform.
  • "Platform façade" in the O'Reilly report (platform-as-a-product.md). The O'Reilly/Syntasso report criticizes "portal + pipeline" without orchestration as a façade. The Port guide is an example of what the report criticizes: the portal is the center, the pipelines (Jenkins, GitOps, CI/CD) sit behind it, and the guide itself recommends that the portal remain "loosely coupled" from the underlying systems (pp. 6, 12, 21). There is no concept of orchestration, persistent desired state or resource reconciliation (the guide's "reconciliation", p. 36, is about syncing catalog data with the source, not resource control). Useful as a counterpoint: it shows the portal-centric argument that the O'Reilly report and the presentation (an orchestrator behind the portal: Kratix under evaluation, Crossplane for IaC) rebut.
  • Adoption metrics. The guide treats adoption as the main risk (p. 38), recommends monitoring usage to detect obstacles (p. 39) and suggests platform adoption reports (p. 31), but gives no adoption number. The only number is Puppet Labs' 51% (p. 3). For Backstage adoption metrics, the basis remains the material already recorded in earlier references, not this guide.
  • Scorecards vs. the Platform as a Product scorecard. O'Reilly uses a platform scorecard (four pillars, one key metric per pillar, pp. 4-5 of the report) to measure the platform as a product. Port's guide uses scorecards to measure each service (catalog entity): readiness, maturity, DORA, security, cost (pp. 24-25). They are different scopes: Port's evaluates the teams' services; O'Reilly's evaluates the platform. Initiatives (pp. 25-26) come closer to a platform scorecard, but they still group service scorecards. It is the guide's usage and adoption reports (pp. 31-33) that touch on measuring the platform itself.
  • Port (blueprints) vs. Backstage (entity model). Port is portal-centric and un-opinionated: each organization defines its blueprints and relations as a free schema, and the catalog is a dynamic graph (pp. 11, 14-15, 18). Backstage has an opinionated entity model (Component, API, Resource, System, Domain, User/Group, see backstage-catalog.md) with owner on all of them. The guide admits the contrast by describing C4 as an "adaptation of the Backstage C4 Model" (p. 18) and cites a Backstage-to-Port migration guide (p. 18, title only, not read), but it does not discuss Backstage's limitations beyond the "opinionated" label (p. 11), which is a commercial argument. Make the comparison carefully: "opinionated is rigid" is the vendor's opinion; Backstage's fixed model can also be read as an advantage of consistency across organizations.
  • Points of use in the presentation. (1) Definition of IDP vs. portal (pp. 6-7), useful to separate "platform" from "interface" in the slides on the planes. (2) The four pillars as portal vocabulary (p. 8). (3) Runtime data ("your code is not your app", pp. 16, 20) as an argument for live state in the catalog. (4) Adoption pitfalls (p. 38), useful as a warning, always citing them as the vendor's view.

docs.title: Reading anomalies
docs.text:
• All 40 pages have extractable text. On p. 27 the diagram of the 4 scorecard steps was an image; it was read rendered.
  • Some passages have extraction noise (p. 21, p. 36 "Rapid innovation"); the quotes above were reconstructed with care.
  • The guide points to several Port blog articles ("Further Reading") that were not read: do not treat their content as part of this reference.

docs.title: Sandbox routing
docs.text: Verify changes (above all those made by agents) before the PR, against the real system, with lightweight per-request sandboxes in a shared cluster. Origin: consolidation of a conversation with claude.ai (2026-10-06); article and docs checked on 2026-10-07.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Arjun Iyer (CEO of Signadot), "Agents have made CI the bottleneck. Faster pipelines are the wrong fix.", The New Stack, 2026-10-04. https://thenewstack.io/ci-bottleneck-agent-verification/ — a post sponsored by Signadot (tag sponsored), which sells exactly this solution.
  • Istio: request routing https://istio.io/latest/docs/tasks/traffic-management/request-routing/; supported versions https://istio.io/latest/docs/releases/supported-releases/ (in 2026-10: 1.31 current, EOL ~Feb/2027; 1.30 EOL ~Dec/2026; 1.29 EOL 2026-10-12 — recheck close to the presentation).

  • OpenTelemetry Baggage: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/baggage/

  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: The article's thesis
docs.text:
1. Agents turned CI inside out: "Agents pushed CI job volume up 25x at Anthropic." At Linear, the test suite "has nearly quadrupled since January, and agents now write most of their tests".
  2. Wrong position: CI runs after the PR; the agent that waits minutes for a red check has lost its context.
  3. Green ≠ works: a repo is one service among dozens, and the tests mock the rest; the real failures live at the boundaries (a renamed field, a timeout with cascading retries, a migration that locks a table). "Making the gate faster does not change what it checks." DORA associates higher AI adoption with higher throughput and more instability.
  4. Verify against the system, before the PR: in a shared cluster only the changed service comes up; "every other hop resolves to the shared stable versions". "A test environment costs roughly the price of one pod, and it comes up in seconds. Fifty agents working in parallel share one stable environment instead of cloning it fifty times."
  5. Verification governed by the platform: "the platform team writes those steps once, as a sequence of approved actions that exercises a change against the live system and records what happened. Agents invoke them through the skills and hooks that Claude Code, Cursor, and similar tools already support". The record becomes evidence for review and merge gates; CI becomes confirmation.

docs.title: Mechanics: request-level isolation
docs.text:
• Pattern used by Lyft, Uber and Signadot (according to the conversation; not checked against the Lyft/Uber sources).
  • The version under test comes up next to the stable one with its own label; a DestinationRule defines the subsets and a VirtualService sends to the test subset only the requests carrying the sandbox header; the rest goes to the stable one.
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: orders
spec:
  hosts: [orders]
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        baggage:
          regex: ".*sandbox=pr123.*"
    route:
    - destination: {host: orders, subset: test-pr123}
  - route:
    - destination: {host: orders, subset: stable}
  • Context propagation is the critical point: Envoy does not link the incoming request to the outgoing one, so every service must pass the header on. With OpenTelemetry Baggage (baggage: sandbox=pr123) the instrumented SDKs propagate it along with the traceparent. Just one service that does not propagate is enough to break the routing silently from there on → a candidate for a fitness function / "good citizen" requirement of the platform (fitness-functions.md).

docs.title: Cautions and limits
docs.text: Topic Caution Ambient mode L7 routing by header needs a waypoint for the service under test; ztunnel alone is not enough Messaging (Kafka/SQS) the mesh does not help: carry the baggage in the message header and filter at the consumer, or use a topic/consumer group per sandbox Data the version under test writes to the same databases; a schema change or side effect calls for an isolated database/schema Entry the gateway injects or validates the header, so external traffic does not land in a sandbox Traffic mirroring mirror: copies real traffic and discards the response; passive validation, safe only without writes

docs.title: Full environment × per-request sandbox
docs.text:
• Full ephemeral environment (the Environment of MVP 1 is a whole EKS cluster): total isolation, expensive, ~28-30 min to come up; still needed for infrastructure changes and for the platform's own changes.
  • Per-request sandbox: ~one pod, comes up in seconds, tests the real boundaries; requires context propagation and care with data and messaging.
  • The platform should offer both, not just "environment per PR".

docs.title: Relation to other references
docs.text:
• State of AI Vol. 2 (state-of-ai-in-platform-engineering.md): only 17% run automated validation loops and 35% validate only by human reading (p. 26); validation loop and sandboxed environments are among the four prerequisites of Level 3 (p. 10, p. 50).
  • Progressive rollout in production based on metrics is the natural continuation of the same routing (golden signals as the criterion — golden-signals.md).
  • Build vs. buy: Signadot (commercial, author of the article) × in-house Istio + OTel. Not decided.

docs.title: Open questions (from the conversation)
docs.text:
• Do the services already have OpenTelemetry? In which languages?
  • Mesh in sidecar or ambient mode?
  • Which services use messaging, and which broker?
  • Sandbox data strategy: shared database, schema per sandbox or synthetic data?
  • Build with Istio + OTel or evaluate Signadot and alternatives?
  • Which agents do the teams use (defines the format of the skills and hooks)?

docs.title: SSO with Dex
docs.text:
• Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

Concepts for the identity slides (Security Plane). Source: four proposed ADRs (2026-10-04) of a reference proof of concept of the team, written with the support of claude.ai — they are not decisions of this repo. Org, CLI and cluster names were neutralized here.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
• Several clients need the same identity and the same groups: portal (Backstage), the platform CLI, Argo CD and the clusters' RBAC (EKS through an OIDC identity provider). LiteLLM comes in too.
  • GitHub OAuth is not OIDC for users: EKS does not accept GitHub directly. A direct GitHub login through the portal solves only the portal.

docs.title: Proposed decision: Dex as the single OIDC issuer
docs.text:
• A standalone Dex issues the tokens for the whole platform; the identity source is a connector (in the reference proof of concept, the org's GitHub, with the teams becoming the groups claim).
  • One static client per consumer: portal (confidential), CLI (public, with PKCE and a redirect on localhost), Argo CD (oidc.config pointing to Dex), clusters (EKS registers Dex as an OIDC identity provider, groupsClaim: groups).
  • Changing the source means changing the connector (GitHub → Google Workspace, Entra ID, LDAP, SAML); portal, CLI, Argo CD and clusters do not change. Caveat: Google Workspace does not send groups in the OIDC login — it requires a service account and the Admin SDK.
  • Changing the issuer later is expensive (all clients and clusters): the production IdP must be chosen before multiplying clusters.

Alternatives discarded in the ADR:

  • Direct GitHub login through the portal: it covers neither the CLI nor the clusters.
  • Amazon Cognito: it does not federate GitHub; external groups only with a Pre Token Generation Lambda; an issuer tied to AWS even with part of the infrastructure on Azure.
  • Argo CD's embedded Dex: coupled to Argo CD's configuration and lifecycle.

docs.title: Who decides what
docs.text:
• In the portal, ownership comes from the catalog: the login matches the User entity, whose memberOf comes from the ingested GitHub teams. Whoever does not exist in the catalog does not get in.
  • In Kubernetes, the token's groups claim decides — the API server does not know the catalog.
  • Catalog and claim diverge only during the sync interval. Accepted.
  • User/Group in the catalog is the contract; the origin (GitHub Teams in the proof of concept) is just a swappable adapter.

docs.title: Identity and audit
docs.text:
• Immutable key = the numeric GitHub ID; the login is a label (it can be renamed and reused by another person).
  • On every login, the login ↔ user_id pair goes to an audit sink.
  • The catalog is not an audit trail. The trail lives in Git (every Environment/claim/deploy is a commit or PR), in Backstage's auditor, in the API server's audit logs, in Argo CD's and Crossplane's events — all in a central sink in the Observability Plane.

docs.title: Where Dex runs
docs.text:
• On the platform cluster (hub), as a Security Plane component, not a portal accessory: its own namespace and Argo CD Application, secrets through External Secrets, NetworkPolicy, storage: kubernetes (keys survive a restart), two replicas.
  • A stable issuer independent of where Dex runs (https://id.<base-domain>): moving Dex means changing the Application's destination.
  • Break-glass: every cluster, including the hub, keeps administrative access through IAM (EKS access entries). Access to the cluster that runs Dex never depends on Dex.
  • If the hub goes down, no new token is issued; the clusters keep running, and break-glass covers the interval.
  • EKS requires a publicly accessible issuer (discovery + JWKS).

docs.title: Relation to the first proof of concept (wasp-idp)
docs.text:
• The base deck's reference architecture has Auth0 under ID Management. In the first proof of concept (wasp-idp), the evaluation with Dex was replaced by Keycloak as an identity broker (ADR 0021, proposed): Google authenticates, Keycloak holds users and groups (platform-admins, platform-users) and issues the JWT that the Platform API validates.
  • Why not Dex: with a personal Google account (outside Workspace) Google does not provide groups, and Dex does not store users or groups — the groups claim would have no origin. Keycloak stores the groups and natively supports Authorization Code + PKCE and Device Authorization Grant, so Dex would become a second broker with no function.
  • The principles in this file still hold with Keycloak in place of Dex: a single issuer, the identity origin as a swappable connector, break-glass outside SSO and an immutable identity as the key.

docs.title: State of AI in Platform Engineering Vol. 2
docs.text:
• Source: State of AI in Platform Engineering, Volume 2 (https://weaveintelligence.io/research/state-of-ai-in-platform-engineering-2026) (Weave Intelligence, 2026; authors Sam Barlien, Luca Galante, Florian Lipp; partners Thoughtworks, Vultr, Syntasso, env zero, Microsoft). Methodology (p. 55): 350 global practitioners, data collected from April to August 2026, 24 questions; profile: individual contributors 31%, team leads 27%, heads of function 19%, VP/director/C-level 23%. The maturity levels and the gains are self-reported (p. 18, p. 21). Page numbering below = the PDF's printed numbering.
  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The report's central finding: 38% of organizations ship at least twice as much since adopting AI, but only 8% describe the return as transformative. The whole report explores this gap (p. 8, p. 54).
  • The bottleneck is not the model, it is the platform: "platform readiness" leads the obstacles to scaling AI (27%), "model capability" is fourth (11%) (p. 24).
  • Maturity pays off in steps, not in a gradient: adding agents without rebuilding the platform adds 6 percentage points of throughput; rebuilding the platform adds 24 (p. 21).
  • Code generation has industrialized, absorption has not: 35% still validate AI-generated changes by human reading alone and only 17% run automated validation loops (p. 26).
  • Governance is the weakest point: a quarter run agents with borrowed human credentials, 12% with a shared service account and 18% do not know how agent identity is managed (p. 38). The Agentic Engineering Platform (AEP) is presented as the evolution of the IDP, not its replacement (p. 28-30).
