docs.title: Quotes
docs.text:
• "The Agentic Engineering Platform is the evolution of the IDP, not the replacement of it." (Kaspar von Grünberg, p. 28)
  • "an agent without specially designed controls and validation checkpoints does not fail gracefully; instead, it generates chaos at machine speed." (p. 28)
  • "Nobody is waiting for a better model." (p. 7; reinforced on p. 54)
  • "Generation industrialized. Absorption did not." (p. 7)
  • "An agent that cannot be identified cannot be audited, scoped, or switched off without switching off a person" (p. 7)
  • "tighter governance actually raises the autonomy ceiling instead of lowering it." (p. 41)
  • "Organizations that throw agents at a Level 1 substrate will find their agents moving faster than their guardrails." (p. 30)
  • "AI has made code cheap and judgment expensive." (Irina Gontcharova, Microsoft, p. 26)
  • "It's because they have the platform around the model." (Rickey Zachary, Thoughtworks, p. 24)
  • "the discipline exists because recurring work in software development, when done by humans, was being relentlessly ad hoc ... Define the path once, govern it, and let everyone run it." (p. 16, abridged excerpt: "Define the path once, govern it, and let everyone run it")

docs.title: Concepts and frameworks
docs.text:
• Four levels of agentic development (p. 18): Level 0 Human is the loop (no agents; the IDP baseline), Level 1 Human in the loop (AI suggests, human executes), Level 2 Human on the loop (agents generate PRs in parallel), Level 3 Humans as orchestrators (agents work continuously from observed signals, review by exception), Level 4 Fully autonomous (systems of agents inside guardrails designed by humans).
  • Agentic Engineering Platform (AEP) (p. 27-30, glossary p. 56): what the IDP becomes when agents are its users; an evolution of the IDP, not a replacement.
  • Three layers of the AEP (p. 29): tooling layer (the five planes: developer control, integration and delivery, resource, security, observability; marked as the IDP), paths layer (repeatable, governed, machine-executable routes) and agent infrastructure layer (identity, context, capability, execution, evaluation, security, observability, all as code).
  • Path types (p. 29): Deterministic (pipeline, same output for the same input), Probabilistic (agent, "Evals become the test suite"), Hybrid (probabilistic generation with deterministic gates in a loop). Recommendation: name the type of each path and require deterministic gates on irreversible effects.
  • The four prerequisites of Level 3 (p. 10, p. 50): dispatch path, validation loop, scoped identity, sandboxed environments, which only pay off together.
  • Validation gate vs. validation loop (p. 30, glossary p. 58): a gate is a binary checkpoint; a loop returns the failure to the agent with the reason until the deterministic checks pass ("first-pass failure is convergence, not defect").
  • Six return vectors (p. 34): delivery velocity, outcome predictability, operational resiliency, maintenance overhead, organizational learning, structural incentives.
  • Metric "cost per accepted output" instead of cost per token (p. 36, p. 51); four functions of token FinOps: attribute every call, watch spend velocity, enforce hard limits in the platform, produce an audit trail (p. 36).
  • Six coverage questions (p. 50): is there a governed, machine-executable path in Plan, Code, Review, Test, Deploy, Monitor? 0-2 yes = the substrate is the work; 3-4 = "expensive middle"; 5-6 = the constraint has already moved to cost and architecture.
  • Five recommendations (p. 50-51): build the four Level 3 prerequisites together; close the validation loop before adding agent capability; fix attribution (no borrowed human credentials); gate by consequence, not by category (possible damage and speed of detection); measure value, not output.
  • Governance patterns of the leaders (p. 41): policy, identity and network inherited from the workspace; human/agent privilege separation (least privilege, writes only through pull request); ephemeral workspaces; controlled, recorded failure instead of a silent incident.
  • AI implementation plateau (p. 12, glossary p. 56) and "Platform as a product, golden paths, standardization" as differentiators of those who got past the plateau (p. 12).
  • Thinking in Platforms and the "Paths to Outcome" model (p. 47); IDP defined in the glossary as a platform that standardizes paths, enables self-service and reduces cognitive load (p. 57).

docs.title: Relevance by plane
docs.text:
• Developer Control Plane: agents are already platform customers in 29% of organizations and 43% expect the role to shift to governance and guardrails (rows "Platform customers" and "Expectation of the role"); the dispatch path as the first new path of Level 2 (p. 56); maturity in steps (the throughput-by-level rows and 6 vs. 24 p.p.).
  • Integration & Delivery Plane: absorption bottleneck (35% human reading only vs. 17% loops; review bandwidth from 12% to 23% from Level 1 to 2); validation loop as the engine (p. 30); AI code does not degrade stability (39% improves, 12% worsens); Plan/Code/Review/Test/Deploy/Monitor coverage (p. 50).
  • Resource Plane: 65% use AI to generate IaC and 66% for error and log analysis (p. 15, p. 39); current controls inspect code, not the effect on the provisioned environment; policy-as-code and sandboxed execution are still a minority (p. 39); gate by consequence (p. 51).
  • Observability Plane: token FinOps (13% do not track, 14% do not know, 15% in Levels 1 and 2; attribution by team, path and model; "cost per accepted output"); shadow AI (47% minimal, 27% significant, 8% no visibility; "observability has to precede restriction", p. 41); 66% use AI in log analysis.
  • Security Plane: agent identity (25% human credentials, 12% service account, 18% do not know, 19% dynamic by policy); 37% govern by policy vs. 13% block; risks (64% data exposure, 52% hallucinations, 47% unmanaged use, 43% control bypass, 37% prompt injection); leaders' patterns (workspace-level, least privilege, ephemeral workspaces, p. 41).
  • Portal/catalog: the report does not address portals directly (no mention of Backstage or a catalog in the pages read); use only the concept of a path as a "repeatable route from intent to usable output" (p. 29), golden paths as a differentiator (p. 12) and the expansion of customers (business users 48%, data/ML 49%, p. 43) to justify a single portal for humans and agents. Kratix appears only as a product of the partner Syntasso (p. 5-6), not as a research finding.

  • Agents/AI: maturity (41/31/14/4/9%), throughput by level (30/36/60/79%), 6 vs. 24 p.p., the four Level 3 prerequisites, path types, tooling vs. agent infrastructure, the forecast of more than 30% at Level 3 or above, investment priorities (31% SDLC automation); why "platform readiness" (27%) beats "model capability" (11%).

  • Definition of the levels (Figure 5, p. 18): Level 0 "Human is the loop" (no agents; the IDP baseline); Level 1 "Human in the loop" (AI suggests, humans execute); Level 2 "Human on the loop" (agents generate PRs in parallel; humans trigger and verify behavior); Level 3 "Humans as orchestrators" (agents work continuously from observed signals; review by exception); Level 4 "Fully autonomous" (systems of agents start and finish work inside guardrails designed by humans).

docs.title: Stone Caravela
docs.text:
A real case of an IDP treated as a product: Stone measures the platform's satisfaction and usage and controls feature rollout with product tools. Source: YouTube live, https://www.youtube.com/live/xACNR0cBzTQ (timestamps below). Summary provided by the user on 2026-10-07; check the video before citing any detail on screen.

  • Checked on 2026-10-29: the links open.

  • Stone's IDP: Caravela.

docs.title: Satisfaction and usage (product analytics)
docs.text:
• Hotjar (31:05–35:00): qualitative and quantitative feedback. NPS with surveys triggered at key moments; session recordings to find friction and frustration in the dev's journey; click analysis to improve usability.
  • Amplitude (35:30–43:00): quantitative data. Conversion funnels of the "offers" (provisioning templates) to find where the dev gives up and optimize the flow.

docs.title: Feature toggles
docs.text: • Amplitude Experiment (59:00–1:03:00): feature flags and A/B tests. SDK integrated into the IDP; hooks in the frontend condition the feature's behavior. Gradual rollout without holding up a release in the development flow.

docs.title: Use in the presentation
docs.text:
• Concrete example of "platform as a product": a product has users, measures satisfaction and conversion, and launches features gradually.
  • Links to user observability (Platform as a Product, pp. 17-18: "What happens when I request a new service?") and to the vanity-metrics trap (p. 35: counting services in the catalog or portal page views does not measure value). An offer's funnel measures the path from request to use, not the click.

docs.title: Hipotese
docs.text: Acreditamos que [mudança] para [público] vai resultar em [efeito]. Saberemos quando [métrica] ≥ [valor]

docs.title: Hypothesis
docs.text: We believe that [change] for [audience] will result in [effect]. We'll know when [metric] ≥ [value]

docs.title: Agile
docs.text:
The beat "Agile", with the predictable questions answered in the open: XP's founding project was cancelled, and Agile became a ceremony in many places. Checked on 2026-10-18 (#190).

  • Source: the Manifesto for Agile Software Development and its twelve principles, 2001, https://agilemanifesto.org/ and https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html.
  • Source: Chrysler Comprehensive Compensation System, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Comprehensive_Compensation_System.
  • Source: Martin Fowler, "C3", https://martinfowler.com/bliki/C3.html.
  • Source: ACCU review of Extreme Programming Refactored (Stephens and Rosenberg, 2003), https://accu.org/bookreviews/2003/glassborow_1734.
  • Source: InfoQ, 2014, on Dave Thomas's "Agile is Dead (Long Live Agility)", https://www.infoq.com/news/2014/10/pragmatic-dave-agility.

docs.title: The manifesto
docs.text:
• Four values, "Working software over comprehensive documentation" among them.
  • The seventh principle: "Working software is the primary measure of progress."
  • The eighth principle: sustainable development; sponsors, developers and users "should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely".

docs.title: C3, XP's founding project
docs.text:
• Started in 1993 (Smalltalk from 1994). Kent Beck joined in 1996 because the system had not printed a single paycheck.
  • Live in 1997, paying about 10,000 people of the 87,000 it was meant to pay by 1999.
  • After Daimler-Benz bought Chrysler (1998), development stopped in 1999 and the project ended in February 2000; the live system went back to COBOL.
  • Fowler: "C3's cancellation, however, also proves that XP is no guarantee of success." He says no well-informed analysis of the cancellation exists.
  • The customer representative, a key XP role, left from burnout months after launch and was not replaced.
  • How it is told: say it first, then turn it. A project stuck for three years without a paycheck was paying 10,000 people within a year of changing how it worked, and when the business decided it was not worth going on, it stopped: a failure that shows early is cheaper than one that shows after 800 pages of requirements (references/failures.md).

docs.title: Agile as a ceremony
docs.text: • Dave Thomas, a signatory, in 2014: the word "agile" had been "devalued", consultants "started to circle", and agility "cannot be imposed from the top".

docs.title: AI and delivery
docs.text:
The beat "AI": the jargon, and the uncomfortable question of what faster delivery delivers.

  • Source: DORA / Google Cloud, "State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025", https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf (read on 2026-10-07 for the wasp-idp deck, its references/dora-ai-report.md; page numbers are the printed ones).
  • Source: Google Cloud, "Announcing the 2024 DORA report", https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/announcing-the-2024-dora-report (checked on 2026-10-18, #190).
  • Source: METR, "Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity", July 2025, https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/ (checked on 2026-10-18).
  • Source: Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, AI section, https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai (checked on 2026-10-18).

docs.title: DORA 2025: faster, and less stable
docs.text:
• "AI adoption now improves software delivery throughput, a key shift from last year. However, it still increases delivery instability." (2025 report, p. 4, Key findings).
  • Caveat: the 2025 report gives direction and standardized size (Bayesian estimates), not percentages. The 2024 report gave percentages: as AI adoption increased, throughput fell an estimated 1.5% and stability fell 7.2%; 39% had little or no trust in AI-generated code. Correlational, from a survey.

docs.title: METR (2025): believing is not measuring
docs.text:
• 16 experienced developers, 246 real issues in their own repositories: 19% slower with AI, while they expected to be 24% faster and still believed they had been 20% faster afterwards.
  • Caveat: a small sample and early-2025 tools; METR marks the study as outdated and points to follow-up data from February 2026, not read yet. The point told is the gap between belief and measurement, not "AI is slow".

docs.title: Stack Overflow (2025)
docs.text: • 84% use or plan to use AI tools; 46% distrust their accuracy against 33% who trust it; the top frustration, cited by 66%: answers that are "almost right, but not quite".

docs.title: Change approval
docs.text:
The turn of the story: required controls integrated into the flow, not queued beside it. The owner's reframing (#190): "isn't it one more heavy process?" applies to every company's software development life cycle (SDLC). Checked on 2026-10-18.

  • Source: DORA, "Streamlining change approval", https://dora.dev/capabilities/streamlining-change-approval/.

docs.title: What DORA found
docs.text:
• Heavyweight external approval (a change advisory board, a senior manager's sign-off) has "a negative impact on software delivery performance", and "no evidence was found" that it lowers the change failure rate; slower, larger releases tend to carry more risk.
  • DORA recommends peer review recorded in the team's platform (which still satisfies segregation of duties), continuous testing and integration, and a CAB focused on coordination rather than code review.

docs.title: Required controls that never became automation
docs.text:
Examples from different areas, so the point is not read as a criticism of security teams: security belongs in the SDLC from the first step.

A necessary control How it often runs Integrated into the flow A firewall rule A ticket, days in a queue Declared next to the application, approved in review A security review Scheduled weeks ahead, at the end Static analysis on every PR, the human review for what changed A new database A request to the database team An Instance of a database Interface, with an agreed Class Access to production A ticket per person, revoked by hand Short-lived access by role, recorded A change approval board A weekly meeting Peer review in the PR and automated checks A TLS certificate or DNS entry Renewed by hand, expiring in production Issued and renewed by the platform Audit evidence Screenshots and spreadsheets Produced by the pipeline: who approved, what ran A dependency's license An e-mail to legal A license check in CI with an allow-list

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
A few failures that made history, for rhythm, not a catalogue. Checked on 2026-10-18 (#190).

  • Source: Ariane 5 flight 501, report of the inquiry board, https://www.csm.ornl.gov/~sheldon/cs422/ariane5fr.html.
  • Source: IEEE Spectrum, "Who Killed the Virtual Case File?", https://spectrum.ieee.org/who-killed-the-virtual-case-file.
  • Source: The Register, 2013, on the NHS National Programme for IT, https://www.theregister.com/2013/08/22/nhs_national_programme_for_it_10_billion_pounds/.
  • Source: SEC, press release 2013-222 on Knight Capital, https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2013-222.
  • Source: Nextgov on the GAO report on HealthCare.gov, 2014, https://nextgov.com/people/2014/07/gao-blasts-planning-oversight-and-cost-overruns-for-healthcaregov/255400.
  • Source: TechCrunch, 2024, on the CrowdStrike outage, https://techcrunch.com/2024/07/20/microsoft-says-8.5m-windows-devices-were-affected-by-crowdstrike-outage/.

docs.title: Therac-25 (1985-1987)
docs.text: • Six known massive radiation overdoses, with deaths. Reused software, hardware interlocks removed in favour of software, and overconfidence. Caveat: people died; tell it with care.

docs.title: Ariane 5 flight 501 (1996)
docs.text: • Destroyed about 30 seconds after lift-off. A 64-bit to 16-bit conversion overflowed in code reused from Ariane 4, in a function that served no purpose after lift-off but kept running "for commonality".

docs.title: FBI Virtual Case File (2005)
docs.text: • Scrapped after US$170 million, US$105 million of it in unusable code; an 800-page requirements document; about 400 change requests in 2003; a flash cutover with no fallback. A textbook case of heavy up-front process.

docs.title: NHS National Programme for IT (2002-2011)
docs.text: • Dismantled in 2011 after £7.3 billion spent; projected total £10.1 billion. Caveat: estimates vary (the NAO said £12.7 billion in 2008, £9.6 billion in 2012).

docs.title: Knight Capital (2012)
docs.text: • More than 4 million orders in 45 minutes and a loss of more than US$460 million, from a deployment that left old code active. Caveat: often quoted as US$440 million; the SEC says over US$460 million.

docs.title: HealthCare.gov (2013)
docs.text: • Launched on 1 October 2013 and failed. The federal exchange went from US$56 million to over US$209 million; GAO cited weak oversight, unclear and shifting requirements, and deadline pressure.

docs.title: CrowdStrike (2024)
docs.text: • One faulty update affected 8.5 million Windows devices (Microsoft's estimate): delivery speed without safe rollout.

docs.title: GDS
docs.text:
A counterexample worth telling: the UK's Government Digital Service delivered at scale, and discarded what did not work in the open. Checked on 2026-10-18 (#190).

  • Source: Government Digital Service, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Digital_Service.
  • Source: Mike Bracken, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Bracken.
  • Source: GDS blog, "GOV.UK Pay at 10", September 2026, https://gds.blog.gov.uk/2026/09/02/gov-uk-pay-at-10-how-it-started-and-how-its-going/.
  • Source: Think Digital Partners, October 2026, on GOV.UK One Login, https://www.thinkdigitalpartners.com/news/2026/10/08/one-login-could-cover-every-central-government-service-within-18-months-says-gds/.
  • Source: UKAuthority on the closing of GOV.UK Verify, https://www.ukauthority.com/articles/gds-closes-govuk-verify-service/.
  • Source: UKAuthority on the decommissioning of GOV.UK PaaS, https://ukauthority.com/articles/gds-to-decommission-platform-as-a-service/.
  • Source: PublicTechnology, August 2025, on One Login's amber rating, https://www.publictechnology.net/2025/08/14/society-and-welfare/one-login-needs-to-manage-risk-of-complex-roadmap-and-dependency-on-departments-annual-report-finds/.

docs.title: Where it came from
docs.text: • Martha Lane Fox's 2010 report led to GDS in 2011; GOV.UK replaced Directgov on 17 October 2012. The 2012 design principles start with "Start with user needs", and include "Do less" and "Make things open". "The strategy is delivery" became the title of Mike Bracken's 2018 book.

docs.title: It delivers
docs.text:
• GOV.UK Pay (2016): more than 600 organisations, almost 1,800 services, nearly £10 billion processed.
  • GOV.UK One Login: more than 23 million accounts and 256 services (October 2026).

docs.title: It discarded what did not work
docs.text:
• GOV.UK Verify: take-up was "disappointing", identity providers shrank from nine to two, and it closed in April 2023, replaced by One Login.
  • GOV.UK PaaS: in July 2022 GDS decided to decommission it, because commercial clouds had improved and departments had built their own Kubernetes-based platforms. A warning for this project: a platform survives by being adopted, not by being mandated.
  • Caveat: One Login is not finished; the 2025 major projects report kept it at amber.

docs.title: gov.br
docs.text:
A Brazilian example, close to every Brazilian audience: delivered at scale, measured in the open, agile even in public contracting. Checked on 2026-10-18 (#190).

  • Source: Mobile Time, March 2026, figures from the Ministry of Management (MGI), https://www.mobiletime.com.br/noticias/24/03/2026/govbr-175-milhoes/.
  • Source: Tecnoblog, July 2026, on the gov.br signature, https://tecnoblog.net/noticias/assinatura-digital-via-gov-br-ultrapassa-548-milhoes-de-usos/.
  • Source: Canaltech on the World Bank's GovTech Maturity Index 2022, https://canaltech.com.br/governo/brasil-e-o-segundo-pais-com-mais-servicos-publicos-digitalizados-230253/.
  • Source: Secretaria de Governo Digital, the 2022 model for contracting software development, https://www.gov.br/governodigital/pt-br/contratacoes-de-tic/apresentacao-do-modelo-de-desenvolvimento-de-software.pdf.
  • Source: Contábeis on Startup GOV.BR, https://www.contabeis.com.br/noticias/46310/startup-gov-br-governo-impulsiona-inovacao-e-transformacao-digital/.
  • Source: TCU, July 2026, audit of security and identification on gov.br, https://portal.tcu.gov.br/imprensa/noticias/auditoria-avalia-seguranca-e-identificacao-de-usuarios-no-portal-govbr.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text:
• 175 million gov.br accounts (March 2026), 83.4 million at the gold level; more than 4,600 federal services.
  • The gov.br electronic signature passed 548 million uses.
  • 2nd of 198 countries in the World Bank's GovTech Maturity Index 2022.

docs.title: Agile, even in public contracting
docs.text:
• Startup GOV.BR (2021): multidisciplinary teams that take one digital solution "from start to finish", in rapid cycles of tests and adjustments with users.
  • The 2022 contracting model (Portaria SGD/ME 5.651/2022) adopts agile methods, with payment per sprint tied to delivered increments.
  • Since 19 January 2018, servicos.gov.br/painel publishes, per service, the average time to serve, users' satisfaction and the share of digital steps.

docs.title: The honest side
docs.text: • TCU (Acórdão 2019/2026): weak and reused passwords, phishing of verification codes, and facial biometrics that blocks legitimate users; it recommended phishing-resistant multifactor authentication. Controls are needed, and they must be part of the flow and fair to every user.

docs.title: Measuring failure
docs.text:
The beat "the same mistakes, measured", and the turn approved by the owner: measuring success by the forecast is part of the problem. Checked on 2026-10-18 (#190).

  • Source: Standish Group CHAOS figures, summarized at https://opencommons.org/CHAOS_Report_on_IT_Project_Outcomes.
  • Source: J. Laurenz Eveleens and Chris Verhoef, "The Rise and Fall of the Chaos Report Figures", IEEE Software, 2010, https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-chaos-report-figures/.
  • Source: McKinsey and the University of Oxford, "Delivering large-scale IT projects on time, on budget, and on value", 2012, https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/tech-and-ai/our-insights/delivering-large-scale-it-projects-on-time-on-budget-and-on-value.
  • Source: CISQ, "The Cost of Poor Software Quality in the US: A 2022 Report", https://www.it-cisq.org/the-cost-of-poor-quality-software-in-the-us-a-2022-report/.

docs.title: McKinsey and Oxford (2012): the size of the problem
docs.text: • More than 5,400 IT projects. Large projects ran 45% over budget and 7% over time, and delivered 56% less value than predicted; 17% went so badly they could threaten the company.

docs.title: CHAOS (1994), only with its critique
docs.text:
• 1994: 16.2% of projects on time and on budget, 31.1% cancelled, 52.7% over budget by 189% on average. 2020: 31% successful, 50% challenged, 19% failed.
  • Critique: Eveleens and Verhoef (2010) show the definitions judge only how well a project hit its forecast of time, cost and scope, not the value it delivered, and that this distorts the figures.
  • The turn: the industry's most quoted measure of failure judges projects by how well they predicted themselves. A project that delivered great value but missed its first estimate counts as a failure. It rewards the plan, not the working software.
  • On the slide: the CHAOS figure appears only with the critique next to it; McKinsey and Oxford carries the size of the problem.

docs.title: CISQ (2022)
docs.text: • The cost of poor software quality in the US is at least US$2.41 trillion; accumulated technical debt about US$1.52 trillion. Caveat: US only, and an estimate.

docs.title: Software crisis
docs.text:
The beat "before it had a name": the field was named in 1968, and its first problems are the ones it still has. Checked on 2026-10-18 (#190).

  • Source: Brian Randell, "Fifty Years of Software Engineering, or The View from Garmisch", 2018, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.02742.
  • Source: the report of the 1968 NATO conference in Garmisch, https://www.scrummanager.com/files/nato1968e.pdf.
  • Source: Melvin Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, April 1968, summarized at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway%27s_law.
  • Source: David A. Wheeler on Winston Royce's 1970 paper, https://dwheeler.com/essays/waterfall.html.
  • Source: The Mythical Man-Month, Fred Brooks, 1975, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mythical_Man-Month.

docs.title: 1968: the name as a provocation
docs.text:
• NATO's conference in Garmisch named the field "software engineering", a title chosen as a provocation: a requirement, not a reality (Randell, 2018).
  • Participants recognized a shared concern some called the "software crisis" (Randell, 2018; the 1968 report).
  • Caveat: Randell also notes that many projects then were successful.
  • Licklider described large projects as marked by "underestimates and overexpectations"; Randell says it still happens (Randell, 2018).

docs.title: 1968: Conway's law
docs.text: • "Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations" (Conway, 1968). It connects to the bridge metaphor: each side builds its half.

docs.title: 1970: Royce warned against the waterfall
docs.text: • The paper credited with the waterfall called the simple sequential approach "risky and invites failure", and recommended iterating (Wheeler on Royce). The industry adopted the diagram Royce warned against.

docs.title: 1975: Brooks's law
docs.text: • "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." From IBM's OS/360; the book was republished in 1995 with "No Silver Bullet".

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
The architecture decisions (ADRs) of Nereus, one file per decision, each opening with an "In short" block. The format and the rule for numbers are in ADR 0001.

Decision Status In short 0001. Record architecture decisions Accepted Every architecture decision is recorded in docs/adr/, one file per decision in Nygard's format. A number is valid only once its ADR is merged into main. 0002. Conceptual model: reef, Instance, Mandate, Nereid, Tool Proposed The platform is five layers plus Vendor: reef, Instance, Mandate, Nereid and Tool. A reef is a capability, an API group, and may exist with no Nereid. 0003. nereus init prepares the platform; reefs and Nereids are added at runtime Accepted nereus init prepares a cluster with the built-in core reef, the tenancy reef and a profile's reefs; every other capability arrives later as a reef, with Nereids added at runtime. What init installs is revised by ADR 0014. 0004. Reefs and their Nereids extend the CLI with their own commands Proposed Each reef describes its commands as data published in status, and the CLI builds them at runtime, grouped by reef, never by Nereid or Tool. 0005. One writer per field Proposed The API writes spec; each Nereid writes only its own part of status. A field that needs two writers is split. 0006. Authentication is a reef Proposed authentication is a reef: logins are always OIDC, the platform proves itself outwards through a Mandate per identity, and the User belongs to core. 0007. Public by design Accepted The project is Apache-2.0 and public by design: no identifying data in any commit, and public names chosen as if already public. 0008. The CLI is written in Python, with uv and typer Accepted The CLI is written in Python, managed with uv, with typer for commands and the official kubernetes client. 0009. Each reef is an API group <reef>.getnereus.dev Proposed Each reef is its own API group <reef>.getnereus.dev, starting at v1alpha1; the platform's own kinds live in core.getnereus.dev. 0010. Reefs are added at runtime; commands are grouped by reef Proposed A reef is added at runtime from its contract, and a Nereid is added on its own and looks after one or more reefs. The release reef has four kinds. 0011. Reefs, Nereids and Mandates, managed with top-level commands Proposed Reefs, Nereids and Mandates are managed with top-level commands, with --reef and --nereid as the flags everywhere; a Mandate binds one reef to one Nereid. 0012. Every error message says what happened and how to fix it Proposed Every error message, from the CLI or a Nereid, follows eight rules: what happened, the cause, how to check, how to fix, what changed, no traceback, and a fitness function. 0013. Command conventions Proposed Commands share one shape, nereus <noun> <verb> <name>, with kubectl's verbs, dry runs, examples, and refusals that list the commands to run. 0014. Profiles Proposed Core is only the engine; a profile lists the reefs, Nereids and Mandates to install, run as the commands a person would type. It revises what nereus init installs (ADR 0003). 0015. Tenancy Proposed Tenancy is a reef whose kinds come from each instance, with one fixed shape: every kind is a tree node with an optional parent, and one kind is the boundary. 0016. The catalog reef Proposed A catalog reef holds two kinds split by lifecycle, Workload for what runs and Package for what is published, with three characteristics and configurable types. 0017. Resource reefs Accepted Five resource reefs, each a small contract kind per family, with the provider chosen in the Mandate and a Mandate selected by its match. 0018. The Nereus API is the one door Proposed The Nereus API is the one door of the platform: clients talk to it with the person's token, and the Kubernetes API stays behind it. 0019. The messaging reef Proposed The conversation joins the messaging reef as records (Thread, Order, Claim, Message), with a bus behind a Nereid. 0020. The delivery reef Proposed A delivery reef with one kind, Delivery, takes a Workload to an Environment; the Nereid, never the client, resolves an image tag to a digest. 0021. The registry reef Proposed A registry reef with Registry and Repository kinds; images are read with one read-only credential per Registry, over TLS, and published through the platform. 0022. A reef adds a screen to the portal as a Web Component its Nereid serves Accepted A reef adds a screen to the portal as a Web Component its Nereid serves, named in its contract, loaded at runtime. 0023. An external registry's push credential is the Repository's secret Proposed An external registry's push credential is the Repository's secretRef, read by the Nereid through a SecretBinding, never on the person's machine. 0024. The scm reef Proposed An scm reef holds what a source host is to Nereus: a Connection names an organisation, reached through the App its scm Mandate names, and a Mirror copies a repository. 0025. The platform receives metrics from anywhere through the CLI and the Nereus API Accepted Metrics enter only through the Nereus API, with the CLI as the official client: declared sources, a spool, late-send alerts with a heartbeat, and machine identities. 0026. The environment reef Proposed The environment reef has one kind, Environment, which is only the request; the cluster kept for it is nereus. 0027. Teams Accepted A role is bound to a team, a position or a User on a node of the tenancy tree, and the Nereus API asks before it acts. Access roles, teams and Users are kept apart. 0028. The presentations reef Accepted The presentations reef keeps the deck as a Presentation and each time it is given as a Session. 0029. A reef declares its MCP tools in the Nereid contract Proposed MCP is a door of the Nereus API, not a reef: each reef declares its MCP tools in its Nereid contract, and the API serves them at /mcp. 0030. Triton is the rooms reef's Nereid: Room and Peer, on a Topic of the messaging reef Accepted The conversation between agents is a reef of its own, rooms (Room, Peer), looked after by Triton, which requires the messaging reef and asks it for a Topic per Room. 0031. Gates and approvals native to Nereus Accepted A hard gate refuses; under a soft gate the object is written held Pending until an approver approves or rejects it through the API: Gate and Approval in the authorization reef, one hold, one admission policy, no flow per kind.

docs.title: Decks
docs.text:
Each deck is rendered from one outline, one slide at a time, in English and Portuguese. The renderer and its keys are in the deck README; the rules for writing one are in docs/agent/decks.md.

Deck What it is for Nereus The idea, the model, the first slice and where it is heading More than an IDP The pitch: a composable platform API, ending with a pilot of the comparator Faster than ever. Toward what? The talk before the platform: software delivery from 1968 to the AI era How we work How the work happens in this repository, with AI agents How I use AI One real night told in eight acts, the reference style of the decks The release reef A chart repository to a running release, step by step Implementation comparator Two Nereids of one reef measured side by side to decide with data The presentations reef The journey to present from the phone Triton's roadmap From a room that says hello to a Nereid that carries messages Why a platform Building an Internal Developer Platform as a shared journey Developer Control Plane The catalog, the app declaration and the golden paths Where we're heading From an idea to a shared product, through five planes Doris demo The replay of a thread of notes, built by hand

docs.title: Inception
docs.text:
How Nereus started: a Lean Inception (Paulo Caroli's method) run with an agent as facilitator, which fixed the vision, the goals and the sequence of the MVP.

The words are the model's: reef, Nereid and Mandate. The work that followed is on the roadmap and in What is built.

docs.title: Product vision
docs.text:
For platform teams whose IDP is a fixed set of tools glued by hand, where swapping one means rewriting the platform, Nereus is a composable platform API and CLI built out of Nereids added at runtime.

Unlike Humanitec (commercial, with its own resource model) and Kratix (each Promise bundles contract and implementation), Nereus separates the contract, the reef, from what implements it, the Nereid, and swaps one for another without changing the API.

docs.title: Is, is not
docs.text: Is Is not A composable API and CLI, the CLI first A portal, for now Built out of Nereids added at runtime A fork of Backstage Compatible with the Backstage catalog A secrets vault Open source An installer of a fixed stack of tools Does Does not Comes up from zero from the CLI Keep copies of secrets Logs in with Google through Keycloak, swappable for Auth0 Tie anyone to a tool: the API never names a Nereid Reads secrets where they are already kept Require a kubeconfig from people Helps to build itself In the MVP: several tenants or a cloud other than Azure

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
The MVP served the first five; the last three wait for later waves.

Goal In the MVP Prove the swap: replace Keycloak with Auth0 without changing the contract or the API yes From zero through the CLI, in a guided sequence with progress yes Build itself: add and configure its own first Nereids yes Reuse what exists: Terraform as Stacks, secrets where they are, the Backstage catalog yes Secure by default: no copy of a secret, federated identity in the cloud yes Run its own lifecycle after the pivot, with recovery and destroy tested no Tell its own story in docs, talks and courses no Attract the community with "bring your Terraform" no

docs.title: Persona
docs.text: The platform engineer betting on the idea. Wants to run it first, end to end, and show the result to other platform engineers. The only persona of the MVP, so the MVP had to be demonstrable, live or recorded.

docs.title: The journey
docs.text:
1. Already there: the CLI, an Azure CLI login and a Key Vault holding the Google OAuth client.
  2. Bring up the undercloud: nereus init --target azure creates a local k3d cluster and the installation's identity.
  3. Connect to Azure: the cloud reef and its Nereid azure.
  4. Secrets: the secrets reef and the Key Vault Nereid, which adopts the vault with no copy.
  5. Authentication: the authentication reef and the Keycloak Nereid, with Google keys read from secrets.
  6. Auth0 alongside, then nereus mandate create makes it the default: the same commands, the same API.
  7. Show it: record the session or run it live.

docs.title: Undercloud and overcloud
docs.text:
Names from OpenStack TripleO, behaviour from Cluster API. See Undercloud and overcloud.

  • Undercloud: a local k3d that bootstraps a cloud; it publishes its OIDC issuer so Azure can verify service-account tokens, and the signing key never leaves the cluster.
  • Identities: one managed identity per reef and per installation, trusted through a federated credential; no client secret or certificate is kept.
  • Overcloud: AKS, created by running Stacks; after the pivot it takes over its own lifecycle and the k3d is deleted.
  • First wave: stays on k3d and proves the handshake with Azure; AKS and the pivot come second.

docs.title: Sequence of the MVP
docs.text:
Waves respect the dependencies; the biggest risk, the connection to Azure, comes early on purpose.

Wave What can be seen at its end 1. The base nereus reef apply and nereus nereid apply, with the reference Nereid 2. Ready for agents Agents work in parallel; init with progress 3. Azure answers The handshake with the Key Vault 4. Secrets with no copy The first real Nereid 5. First login Login with Google through Keycloak 6. The swap Auth0 alongside, then active 7. The demo The walkthrough as the talk's script

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text: Block Content Proposal Prove that a platform of swappable Nereids works end to end from the CLI Result The demo runs end to end with no change to the CLI or the API across the swap Metrics Time from init to first login; zero changes across the swap; flow of the work (#95)

docs.title: Specs
docs.text:
The specs of Nereus: the plan or the design of one slice, written before its code. The command specs, one file per reef, are the CLI reference.

Spec Status What it settles 0001. First slice Done init, a Nereid list and a fake Nereid that publishes commands 0002. Reef at runtime Done A reef added from the CLI and a Nereid installed into it from its image label 0003. Nereid conformance Proposed What a Nereid image declares and how the platform checks it 0004. Init time SLO Proposed A fitness function caps how long nereus init takes 0005. Cloud reef Accepted How the platform presents itself to a cloud, with no credential kept 0006. Installation identity Proposed A name, an id and an alias for each installation 0007. Invitation Proposed A link and a QR code that let one person in, for a while 0008. Portal first slice Proposed A PWA that says who you are 0009. Build security Accepted What a hostile Dockerfile can reach in the build reef 0010. Build trigger Proposed A new commit on a Mirror builds a Workload 0011. Authorization first slice Proposed The first slice of teams and authorization 0012. Presentations first slice Not stated Drive and follow: a phone drives a Session, others follow

Every workaround is a feature waiting for the platform (#113): what the project does by hand until the platform offers it (#269).

Every pull request and issue says which stand-in it creates or retires; a feature that retires one carries the dogfood label.

docs.title: The checks
docs.text:
make checks runs six checks locally, because CI is off, and records each result in docs/checks/<name>.json.

Run one check alone with make <name>. Its record holds the result, the time, how many checks passed, the first failure and the commit.

docs.title: make checks
docs.text: Check What it checks Record lint ruff on the CLI, the Python scripts, the sessions sketch and nereid-sdk: pycodestyle, pyflakes, complexity at most 10 lint.json test the unit tests of the CLI, the Nereids, the API, the hooks and the scripts, after nereid-check and cli-check test.json deck-test the deck renderer and the follow page, in headless Chromium deck-test.json docs-build the docs lint, then a strict build of the site docs-build.json shellcheck shellcheck on every bash script of the repository shellcheck.json kubeconfig-ban no kubeconfig access in the CLI outside nereus init, against an allowlist that only shrinks kubeconfig-ban.json

docs.title: Before a pull request
docs.text: Run make checks always. Add make scene-core when the change touches a cluster, and make catalog-check when it touches catalog/, reefs/catalog/ or the tenancy.

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
A scene runs a reef end to end on a throwaway k3d cluster, and make scene-<name> records scene-<name>.json beside the checks. Scenes with the real tools run only on the owner's word.

Scene Runs When scene-core the core with a reference Nereid in place of every tool the change touches a cluster scene the platform end to end, with the real tools the owner's word scene-idp the profile internal-developer-platform the owner's word scene-helm Nereus from the charts alone, no nereus init the owner's word scene-<reef> one reef with its tool: release, environment, messaging, delivery, build the owner's word
