docs.title: Infrastructure governance in the agentic era
docs.text:
Notes on a report, not decisions

The topics of one industry report and how they map to Nereus. The gaps became ideas to refine (#2042 to #2044) and comments on #2035 and #2036, in Ideas until the owner's triage.

Credit: Infrastructure governance for platform teams in the agentic era, an "Enterprise in Practice" report of 28 pages by Sam Barlien (researcher at Weave Intelligence, the research arm of platformengineering.org, and co-host of PlatformCon), published by Weave Intelligence in 2026 (the PDF is dated 2026-11-06) and commissioned by env zero, the company formed by the merger of env zero and CloudQuery in March 2026. env zero supplied briefings and reviewed the report for accuracy about its own products; the conclusions are Weave Intelligence's. The survey figures come from Weave Intelligence's own State of AI in Platform Engineering 2026 (Volume 2), 350 respondents. Read from the PDF the owner downloaded on 2026-11-21; no public URL of the report was found that day.

The four capabilities the report proposes match what its sponsor sells (a store of every cloud resource, IaC governance and a knowledge graph on top): read them as one vendor-backed view, useful for its framing.

docs.title: The topics
docs.text:
The estate stopped matching the code

  • The 2 a.m. database: an on-call engineer resizes it in the console, the fix never reaches the code, and the next terraform apply puts the old size back three weeks later. It happened at Razorpay (an Auto Scaling Group's image, rolled back by an unrelated apply).
  • With agents, the same story lands on day two: an agent asked to cut costs finds an instance bigger than its code says, with no owner and no note, and shrinks it.
  • The dangerous problems are the silent ones: a bucket left open, a server in an unapproved region, a forgotten test cluster, a deleted backup.

What practitioners report (the survey)

  • 65% use AI to generate infrastructure as code; 43% name agents bypassing security controls as a major threat.
  • 35% validate AI-generated changes by human review alone, against 17% with automated validation loops. Validation has to become a loop: an agent proposes, a deterministic gate verifies, and the system that produces a change is not the one that validates it.
  • An agent on a borrowed human login "cannot be audited, scoped, or switched off without switching off the person it borrowed from". Caroline Wong (PlatformCon 2026): "You can't govern agents that you don't know exist", the shadow-agent problem. Agent identities and scopes belong in declarative definitions, so an unknown agent shows up as a mismatch, as drift does.

What deploy-time policy never promised

  • A deploy-time check governs the pipeline, not every route into the cloud: console fixes, scripts and agents holding credentials never meet it. An old example: Salesforce, May 2021, a global DNS change through the emergency break-fix process and about five hours of unreliable logins.
  • Three things are missing: the implication (a drift report weighs a struggling database like a retagged test bucket), the owner (an unowned divergence waits in a ticket queue, the TicketOps anti-pattern) and the context (an agent fills the gaps with whatever the reachable APIs show).
  • "The platform supplies the determinism": probabilistic reasoning inside deterministic guardrails, the question moved from model quality to system structure.

Shift down, and the four levels

  • Shift down: the step past shift left, where a capability is embedded in the platform instead of pushed earlier onto its users.
  • At Level 2 (human on the loop) every agent pull request waits for a person; at Level 3 (human as orchestrator) the platform's gates check and people handle the exceptions. The survey places the return on agents at Level 3.
  • The path is gradual: low-risk classes of change are promoted by codified rules, consequential ones (blast radius, cost, policy class) keep human verification. Two decisions stay with people on purpose: granting or widening a non-human actor's scope, and owning the exceptions. Oleg Danilyuk (VP, env zero): what matters is the scope an actor has, not whether it is a person or an agent.

Four things the platform has to provide

  • One view of declared and running state, held as current, queryable data: an agent and an engineer asking the same question get the same answer.
  • Ownership and relationships as platform data (a service catalog, an ownership file), not tags: "A tag records what someone typed, while ownership records what teams agreed."
  • Attributable, scoped actors: each agent with its own identity, its scope declared as code, no borrowed credential.
  • Every change goes through code: fixes land as pull requests against the owning code; a change made outside is reverted or codified back, and a resource created outside is brought into code or removed.

Next steps and readouts

  • Five steps in order: see what is running, record ownership, scope each agent before write access, route fixes through code, start agents on low-risk work. Each human override is data about where the rules stop being trustworthy.
  • Three readouts from the first month: the share of running resources with a declared counterpart, the share of the highest-risk resources with a recorded owner, and the count of agents holding write access without an identity of their own.

docs.title: How it maps to Nereus
docs.text:
What Nereus already does the same way

  • One route in: ADR 0018 (the Nereus API is the one door; CLI, portal and agents talk to it, the Kubernetes API stays behind it); MCP is a door of the same API, ADR 0029 (each reef declares its MCP tools, served at /mcp). An agent and a person get the same answer.
  • Declared and running state in one object: ADR 0005 (spec written by the API, status by the Nereid), with continuous reconciliation.
  • Ownership as data, not tags: owner: {kind, name} points to the tenancy tree, ADR 0015 (a tenancy reef with one fixed shape), on the catalog's Workloads and Packages, ADR 0016 (each Workload with its owner and its audience, which may include agents), on Environments and Instances.
  • The credential stays with the platform: ADR 0017 (the provider is named in the Mandate) and ADR 0023 (an external registry's push credential is read by the Nereid, never on the person's machine); the platform proves itself through a Mandate, ADR 0006.
  • Attribution: ADR 0030 (Triton behind the Nereus API) adds Principal.agent, so the audit log says "person X, agent Y, via mcp".
  • Generation kept apart from validation: the project's deterministic pillar (guards, hooks, make checks), and the journeys' decision envelope (🟢 decide, 🟠 report, 🔴 wait for the owner), an exception-based review of the agents' own work.

Gaps the report points at

  • A comment on #2035 (fleet rollout and drift): a drift's implication, its route to the owner, and revert-or-adopt decided per kind.
  • A comment on #2036 (the platform's business metrics): the report's three readouts.

docs.title: 2042 (agents as subjects of their own: each agent declared with an identity and a scope, and an unknown agent reported). Today an agent acts on the person's token and only names itself in a header; ADR 0027 leaves Member.spec.kind: agent and token exchange for later.
2043 (resources outside Nereus: a reef lists what its tool runs without an Instance, and a person adopts or ignores it).
2044 (change classes: a rule decides which requests pass on the gates alone and which wait for a person, and each override is recorded).
Learn more
docs.text:
• Weave Intelligence, the publisher, and its State of AI in Platform Engineering 2026, the survey behind the figures, already in References.
  • The report's sources: Saijal Shrivastava, "The Dark Side of Terraform: Drifts, Chaos, and the Headaches They Bring" (Razorpay Engineering, 2025); Caroline Wong, "Security by design for agentic AI" (PlatformCon 2026); "That Salesforce outage" (The Register, 2021). The report's footnote numbers do not match its text from note 3 on; the list above follows the sources, not the numbers.
  • Thinking in Platforms, by Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante (Weave Intelligence), already in References.

docs.title: kagent for Amphitrite
docs.text: Amphitrite is the Nereid that will give the platform its AI agents: a reef whose kind is Agent (plural agents), used by other Nereids for the tasks where AI does better than a deterministic step (summarise, catalogue, classify). The Agent does not name its engine: it points at a mandate that says which gateway and model to use, as a PersistentVolumeClaim points at a StorageClass, so swapping LiteLLM for OpenRouter is swapping the mandate. Triton, the coordinator of the agents, is the first Agent. "Native first, build last" (vision) asks whether an open-source tool already does this; this page evaluates kagent, compares it briefly with the alternatives, and records a first end-to-end run of Triton on k3d with a tiny local model through Ollama. It answers the beach order 20261028-1708-evaluate-kagent-for-amphitrite-resend. Facts come from pages opened on 2026-10-28, linked inline and in Learn more; repository figures were read from the GitHub API that day; what the run on k3d showed is marked as our own observation.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Adopt kagent as the Tool of the Amphitrite Nereid, behind a thin Nereus reef: wrap it, do not build our own runtime and do not expose kagent's CRDs as the platform's API.

  • Adopt the runtime: kagent already does what we would build: a Kubernetes controller that turns an Agent resource into a Deployment serving the agent over A2A, a ModelConfig that is exactly the StorageClass-style engine object of the design, OpenAI-compatible endpoints (LiteLLM, OpenRouter) and Ollama as providers, MCP tools, memory, a UI and a CLI. It is Apache-2.0, a CNCF Sandbox project, and very active. It ran Triton end to end on k3d in minutes (below).
  • Wrap it in a reef: kagent's API is kagent.dev/v1alpha2 and moving fast towards 1.0 (17 alphas in five weeks, and the chart on main already differs from the 0.10 docs), so other Nereids should depend on a Nereus contract, not on kagent's. The rule "the API never names a Nereid" (rules) says the same: the reef's Agent carries what an agent is (description, instructions, the engine's mandate, tools), and Amphitrite renders it into kagent's Agent and ModelConfig. Swapping kagent later (for Ark, say) changes the Nereid, not the Nereids that use agents.
  • Do not build our own CR runtime: the alternatives either are not an agent definition (Agent Sandbox, Dapr Agents) or are younger and smaller than kagent (Ark, Kagenti).

docs.title: kagent
docs.text: Question Answer What it is Kubernetes-native framework for AI agents: an agent is a resource the controller reconciles into a pod serving the agent over A2A (repo) Started by Solo.io; CNCF Sandbox since 2025-05-22 (CNCF) Licence Apache-2.0 (repo) Activity (2026-10-28) about 4.1k stars, about 213 contributors, repository created 2025-01-21; releases v0.10.4 and v1.0.0-alpha17, both 2026-10-21; 17 v1.0 alphas between 2026-09-18 and 2026-10-21; 100+ commits on the default branch in the last month (releases) API kagent.dev/v1alpha2 (also serves v1alpha1) (API reference) CRDs installed by chart 0.10.4 Agent, ModelConfig, ModelProviderConfig, RemoteMCPServer, MCPServer, ToolServer, Memory, SandboxAgent, AgentHarness (our observation, kubectl get crd); the API reference documents the first four plus SandboxAgent and AgentHarness, memory as declarative.memory (API reference) Agent types Declarative (model, system message, tools, on kagent's runtime, go by default or python) or BYO (your own image serving A2A on port 8080) (API reference; kubectl explain agent.spec) Tools MCP servers (RemoteMCPServer, up to 20 tools per agent) and other Agents as tools (API reference) Invocation A2A on the controller, port 8083: /api/a2a/<namespace>/<agent>/; kagent invoke --agent <name> --task "..." (A2A example)

docs.title: Model providers: LiteLLM and OpenRouter
docs.text:
ModelConfig.spec.provider is one of Anthropic, OpenAI, AzureOpenAI, Ollama, Gemini, GeminiVertexAI, AnthropicVertexAI, Bedrock, SAPAICore, Foundry (API reference).

  • LiteLLM: yes. provider: OpenAI with openAI.baseUrl takes any OpenAI-compatible endpoint; the "BYO OpenAI-compatible model" page shows kagent in front of a LiteLLM proxy (BYO OpenAI-compatible).
  • OpenRouter: yes by the same field, not documented. OpenRouter has no page among the supported providers (providers); its API is OpenAI-compatible at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 (OpenRouter quickstart), so it is the same openAI.baseUrl case. Not run yet: it needs a key.
  • The path is proven: the Triton run below uses provider: OpenAI with baseUrl pointing at Ollama's OpenAI-compatible /v1 (Ollama docs), the same mechanism LiteLLM and OpenRouter would use (our observation).
  • Ollama natively: provider: Ollama with ollama.host (Ollama provider).
  • Caveat: the agent sends tool definitions; a backend without automatic tool choice (vLLM without it) fails every turn with a 400 (BYO OpenAI-compatible).

docs.title: Install footprint on k3d
docs.text:
Chart 0.10.4, with the ten built-in agents, kagent-tools, kmcp and grafana-mcp turned off (values below), our observation:

Pod Image Requests kagent-controller ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/controller:0.10.4, 42 MB 100m, 128Mi kagent-ui ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/ui:0.10.4, 136 MB 100m, 256Mi kagent-postgresql (bundled, "for development and evaluation only") postgres:18.6-alpine3.23, 120 MB 250m, 256Mi one per Agent (triton) ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/golang-adk:0.10.4, 38 MB 100m, 384Mi

The whole k3d node used about 970 MiB of memory with Triton running. The UI has no enabled flag in the chart. The default install (installation) adds ten agents and the tool servers; kagent install --profile minimal installs none.

docs.title: What to watch
docs.text:
• Security: the controller's auth.mode defaults to unsecure: a caller who reaches port 8083 acts as admin@kagent.dev (chart values, controller.auth). Amphitrite must install it with trusted-proxy (oauth2-proxy in front) or keep the controller unreachable outside the cluster; the authentication reef is the natural front. This is OWASP A01 (Broken Access Control) and A07 (Identification and Authentication Failures).
  • The bundled Postgres is for evaluation only; a real install points database.postgres.url at a database of the platform.
  • API churn: v1alpha2 and a 1.0 in alpha; the reef shields the other Nereids from it.
  • Unknown: how the 1.0 Substrate runtime changes the footprint.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
Project Licence and status What it is Why not first Ark (McKinsey) Apache-2.0, about 432 stars, v0.1.72 on 2026-10-21 Kubernetes CRDs Agent, Model, Team, Query, Tool, MCPServer, A2AServer, Memory (docs) Closest model (a Model the Agent references, Team for coordination); younger and ten times smaller; the second candidate if kagent stalls Kagenti Apache-2.0, about 302 stars, docs at v0.7.0; the repository now redirects to rossoctl/rossoctl Framework-neutral platform for agent identity, authorisation, tools and sandboxes, A2A and MCP Its CRDs are not documented in the README; in transition Agent Sandbox (kubernetes-sigs, SIG Apps) Apache-2.0, about 4.4k stars, v1.0.8 on 2026-10-22 Sandbox, SandboxClaim, SandboxTemplate, SandboxWarmPool (agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1) Runtime isolation, not an agent definition: a possible layer under Amphitrite for agents that run code Dapr Agents Apache-2.0, under the CNCF Dapr project, about 767 stars, v1.1.0 on 2026-10-27 Python framework for durable agents on Dapr A library, no agent CRD

LangGraph Platform and Kubeflow were not evaluated.

docs.title: Triton under the recommendation
docs.text:
The reef's Agent, what other Nereids and the CLI write. The reef's name and the shape of the mandate are open questions (below); this draft assumes a reef agent and a second reef model whose mandates are the engines (Nereids ollama, litellm, openrouter):

apiVersion: agent.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: triton
spec:
  description: Triton, the coordinator (mediator) of the platform's agents.
  instructions: |
    You are Triton, the coordinator of the Nereus platform's agents.
    Answer in one short sentence.
  model:
    mandate: local        # model reef mandate: Nereid ollama, model qwen2.5:0.5b
  tools: []

Moving Triton to the Anthropic API later changes only mandate: (for example anthropic), never the Agent's other fields. Amphitrite renders it into kagent's objects, the ones applied by hand in the run below.

docs.title: The first end-to-end run
docs.text:
Agent → ModelConfig → Ollama → answer, on 2026-10-28 (our observation). The quality of the answer does not matter; the flow does.

  • Model: qwen2.5:0.5b (about 400 MB), pulled into the Ollama already installed on the machine (0.20.7, systemd service on 127.0.0.1:11434).
  • Wiring: Ollama listens only on loopback, so a socat container on the host network forwards the k3d network's gateway (host.k3d.internal, here 192.168.240.1) to it; Ollama's own config stays untouched. The ModelConfig uses provider: OpenAI with baseUrl: http://host.k3d.internal:11434/v1, the path LiteLLM and OpenRouter would take.
  • Result: Triton answered "I am an agent designed to help users smoothly interact with Nereus, the platform for coordinating AI research." The first call took about 50 s (the model loading), the second about 5.5 s.

To reproduce:

ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b

k3d cluster create amphitrite \
  --no-lb \
  --k3s-arg '--disable=traefik@server:0' \
  --wait

gateway="$(docker network inspect k3d-amphitrite --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}')"

docker run \
  --detach \
  --name amphitrite-ollama-bridge \
  --network host \
  alpine/socat \
  "TCP-LISTEN:11434,bind=${gateway},fork,reuseaddr" \
  TCP:127.0.0.1:11434

cat > minimal-values.yaml <<'EOF'
providers:
  default: ollama
  ollama:
    provider: Ollama
    model: "qwen2.5:0.5b"
    config:
      host: host.k3d.internal:11434
kmcp: {enabled: false}
kagent-tools: {enabled: false}
grafana-mcp: {enabled: false}
k8s-agent: {enabled: false}
kgateway-agent: {enabled: false}
istio-agent: {enabled: false}
promql-agent: {enabled: false}
observability-agent: {enabled: false}
argo-rollouts-agent: {enabled: false}
helm-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-policy-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-manager-agent: {enabled: false}
cilium-debug-agent: {enabled: false}
EOF

helm install kagent-crds oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent-crds \
  --kube-context k3d-amphitrite \
  --version 0.10.4 \
  --namespace kagent \
  --create-namespace

helm install kagent oci://ghcr.io/kagent-dev/kagent/helm/kagent \
  --kube-context k3d-amphitrite \
  --version 0.10.4 \
  --namespace kagent \
  --values minimal-values.yaml \
  --wait

kubectl --context k3d-amphitrite apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: triton-local-engine
  namespace: kagent
stringData:
  OPENAI_API_KEY: ollama # Ollama ignores the key; LiteLLM or OpenRouter need a real one
---
apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2
kind: ModelConfig
metadata:
  name: triton-local-engine
  namespace: kagent
spec:
  provider: OpenAI
  model: qwen2.5:0.5b
  apiKeySecret: triton-local-engine
  apiKeySecretKey: OPENAI_API_KEY
  openAI:
    baseUrl: http://host.k3d.internal:11434/v1
---
apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2
kind: Agent
metadata:
  name: triton
  namespace: kagent
spec:
  description: Triton, the coordinator (mediator) of the platform's agents.
  type: Declarative
  declarative:
    modelConfig: triton-local-engine
    systemMessage: |
      You are Triton, the coordinator of the Nereus platform's agents.
      Answer in one short sentence.
EOF

kubectl --context k3d-amphitrite --namespace kagent wait \
  --for=condition=Ready agent/triton \
  --timeout=300s

kubectl --context k3d-amphitrite --namespace kagent port-forward svc/kagent-controller 8083:8083 &

curl --silent http://localhost:8083/api/a2a/kagent/triton/ \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"message/send","params":{"message":{"kind":"message","role":"user","messageId":"m1","parts":[{"kind":"text","text":"Who are you?"}]}}}' \
  | jq --raw-output '.result.artifacts[0].parts[0].text'

To clean up: k3d cluster delete amphitrite and docker rm --force amphitrite-ollama-bridge.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The reef's name and group: agent.getnereus.dev (kind Agent, plural agents) is a draft.
  • Where the model lives: a second reef model (Nereids ollama, litellm, openrouter, its mandates naming gateway and model) or the model as a parameter of Amphitrite's own mandate. ADR 0011 (a Mandate binds one reef to one Nereid) fits the first: the Agent references a mandate of the model reef.
  • Does Amphitrite expose kagent's tools and memory in the first slice, or only description, instructions and model?
  • The UI and Postgres: keep kagent's UI (no flag to turn it off) and point it at a database of the platform, or wait for the 1.0 chart.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• kagent and its repository, releases, API reference, installation, supported providers, BYO OpenAI-compatible model, Ollama, A2A agents, Helm reference.
  • kagent at the CNCF.
  • OpenRouter quickstart (the OpenAI-compatible base URL).
  • Ark and its docs, Kagenti, Agent Sandbox, Dapr Agents.
  • Ollama's OpenAI compatibility.

docs.title: Kamaji or vCluster for the environment reef
docs.text: Keep vCluster as the Nereid of today's Environments; register Kamaji as the candidate Nereid for an Environment, or a cluster, with nodes of its own. The owner asked on 2026-11-07 whether Kamaji should replace vCluster. Facts come from Kamaji's README and versioning page, opened on GitHub that day; kamaji.clastix.io was not reachable from the session.

docs.title: What each one gives
docs.text: Question vCluster (the vcluster Nereid) Kamaji What it makes A virtual cluster: control plane in a pod, tenant pods synced into a host namespace A hosted control plane: kube-apiserver, scheduler and controller manager in pods (TenantControlPlane), state in a Datastore Where the tenant's pods run On the host cluster's own nodes On worker nodes that join the control plane (kubeadm, Konnectivity); Kamaji does not create them, Cluster API does What an Environment needs A Helm release in env-vcluster-<name>: one chart, no machine A control plane plus at least one node: a VM or a machine per Environment Datastore Embedded, in an emptyDir today etcd, or MySQL, PostgreSQL or NATS through kine, one store shared by many control planes Cluster API A control plane provider Licence and releases Apache-2.0; the chart 0.37.5 pinned by SHA-256 Apache-2.0; monthly -edge releases only; stable, semantically versioned artifacts only by subscription to CLASTIX since July 2024

docs.title: Why not swap
docs.text:
• The use case is an Environment per agent on one k3d cluster (#620, #568). vCluster runs it with no new machine; Kamaji would need a node per Environment, a VM or a kubeadm container, for the same result, with more to delete at expiry.
  • The scenes stay small: make scene-environment makes two vclusters at once on the throwaway cluster; with Kamaji each would also need node containers of its own beside the throwaway cluster.
  • Releases: only edge versions are open; Nereus pins what it installs, and pinning an edge release means following one every month.

docs.title: Where Kamaji fits
docs.text:
• An Environment with its own nodes, isolated at the node level: a second Nereid of the environment reef, chosen by Mandate, without changing the reef (ADR 0002).
  • Bootstrapping from a local seed (#61): the clusters the platform creates in a cloud, with Cluster API, could get their control planes from Kamaji, many on one management cluster and one shared datastore (CloudNativePG, already a Nereid).

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Kamaji README and releases and versions (CLASTIX).
  • The vcluster Nereid (#620, #633).

docs.title: Nereid SDK controller metrics: assessment and proposal
docs.text: Asked by the owner (2026-11-17), from a voice session. Assessment and proposal only; nothing implemented.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The SDK exists and is custom: lib/nereid (nereid-sdk 0.2.0, #754), no Kopf, no work queue. Each Nereid runs one thread with a periodic, level-triggered pass over everything it owns (passes.forever + passes.Pace).
  • Metrics already exist, under Nereus names: six nereus_nereid_* series on every Nereid's GET /metrics, through OpenTelemetry's Prometheus exporter. 19 Nereids pin nereid-sdk==0.2.0; all 21 with a loop use telemetry/passes.
  • Scraping already works: the victoriametrics Nereid's VMPodScrape nereids picks every pod labelled core.<domain>/metrics: "true" in nereus-system, which the CLI sets on every Nereid it deploys. A new Nereid is discovered with zero effort.
  • The gap is the names: none of the controller-runtime / client-go workqueue names exist, so community dashboards do not work. Several workqueue metrics have no honest meaning in a queue-less, one-worker loop and must be mapped with care.
  • The portal view is already designed: #744 (each Nereid's golden signals, with sparklines on the phone), on top of #740 (home screen, one row per reef and Nereid) and #746 (baselines). No reef has an icon today.

docs.title: Decisions (owner, 2026-11-17)
docs.text:
• SDK design accepted: nereid-sdk 0.3.0 emits the controller-runtime and workqueue names alongside nereus_nereid_*, both kept.
  • #744 is adjusted, not replaced: its queries move to the standard names.
  • Reef icon: an icon field on the Nereid's GET / contract (an amendment to ADR 0022), naming an icon of an open-source set vendored in the portal, honeycomb.svg when missing.
  • Dashboards: only the portal for now; a Grafana Nereid in the metrics reef stays an idea for later.

docs.title: 1. The SDK
docs.text:
Location: lib/nereid/src/nereid/ — telemetry.py, passes.py, logs.py, screens.py, addresses.py.

Question Finding Framework None. Plain Python, threading, urllib against the Kubernetes API (each Nereid has its own kube.py). Kopf is not used anywhere. Reconciliation A pass: one call that reconciles the Nereid's whole world (all its objects), level-triggered, no watches (no ?watch= anywhere in controllers/). Work queue None. No per-object keys, no dedup, no rate limiter. Retries Implicit: a failed pass sets Ready=False with a reason and the next lap runs again. passes.publish retries a failed status write on the next lap. passes.forever never dies (#932). Concurrency One reconcile thread per Nereid (17× threading.Thread(target=loop, …)), so max concurrency is 1. The HTTP server runs in a separate daemon thread. Pace passes.Pace (#1297): idle seconds between laps, busy (1 s) for 30 s after a pass reported work. Existing metrics telemetry.py, OpenTelemetry SDK + PrometheusMetricReader on a private CollectorRegistry, text format 0.0.4. No process_* collector.

The six metrics today (lib/nereid/README.md, pinned by tests/test_telemetry.py):

Metric Type Labels nereus_nereid_reconcile_total counter nereid nereus_nereid_reconcile_errors_total counter nereid, reason nereus_nereid_reconcile_duration_seconds histogram, 5 ms – 60 s nereid nereus_nereid_reconcile_period_seconds gauge nereid nereus_nereid_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge nereid nereus_nereid_ready gauge 1/0 nereid, reason

docs.title: 2. The metrics reef and the VictoriaMetrics Nereid
docs.text:
controllers/victoriametrics/ (reef metrics), objects in nereus-system:

  • VMSingle nereus (14 d retention), VMAgent nereus with selectAllByDefault: false (only its own scrape objects).
  • VMPodScrape nereids: selector core.<domain>/metrics: "true", namespace nereus-system only, port http, path /metrics, label nereid from the pod's app.kubernetes.io/name, honorLabels: false (a series cannot fake its nereid). Built in cli/src/nereus/local_nereids.py:426; the label is put on every Nereid pod in cli/src/nereus/cluster.py:2683 (METRICS_LABEL).
  • VMNodeScrape kubelet-cadvisor for CPU and memory per container.
  • ADR 0025 (metrics enter from outside only through the Nereus API, with declared sources) reserves the nereus_ prefix and the nereid label for the platform; scraped Nereid metrics are unaffected.

Discovery of a new Nereid: automatic. Deployed by nereus nereid apply → labelled → scraped. Nothing for the author to do.

docs.title: 3. Open source first
docs.text:
• controller-runtime (kubebuilder metrics reference, checked 2026-11-17) defines: controller_runtime_reconcile_total, controller_runtime_reconcile_errors_total, controller_runtime_terminal_reconcile_errors_total, controller_runtime_reconcile_time_seconds, controller_runtime_max_concurrent_reconciles, controller_runtime_active_workers, the webhook metrics, rest_client_requests_total, and the client-go workqueue set (workqueue_depth, workqueue_adds_total, workqueue_queue_duration_seconds, workqueue_work_duration_seconds, workqueue_unfinished_work_seconds, workqueue_longest_running_processor_seconds, workqueue_retries_total). Labels (from controller-runtime's source, not the reference page, which lists none): controller on all controller_runtime_*, plus result (success, error, requeue, requeue_after) on reconcile_total; name (and controller in recent versions) on workqueue_*. To pin against the vendored version before implementing.
  • Kopf: exposes only a liveness/health endpoint; no Prometheus metrics (docs.kopf.dev, "Health-checks"). Adopting Kopf would bring watches and per-object handlers but not the metrics, and would mean rewriting 21 Nereids: out of scope.
  • No Python library found that emits the controller-runtime names. prometheus_client (already a dependency) is the right building block; the SDK already owns the registry.

Conclusion: adopt the names and labels (the standard), build the thin emitter in the SDK, where it already is.

docs.title: 4. Proposed metrics layer in the SDK
Principles
docs.text:
• Zero effort: emitted from telemetry.reconcile_pass() and passes.forever/Pace, which every Nereid already calls. Bump nereid-sdk to 0.3.0, bump the pin in the 19 requirements.txt; no Nereid code changes.
  • Deterministic: pure counters/gauges from the loop; no AI anywhere.
  • Honest: a metric with no meaning in this model is emitted with its truthful constant value (or not at all), never faked to look like a busy queue.
  • controller label = the Nereid's name (the value of setup(nereid=…)); the scrape still adds nereid.

docs.title: Mapping
docs.text: Standard metric Meaning in a Nereid Source in the SDK controller_runtime_reconcile_total{controller,result} one per pass; result="error" on failure, "requeue" when the pass called Pace.busy(), else "success" reconcile_pass() controller_runtime_reconcile_errors_total{controller} failed passes reconcile_pass() (keeps the Nereus reason only on nereus_nereid_reconcile_errors_total) controller_runtime_terminal_reconcile_errors_total{controller} passes failing with one of known (a refusal the Nereid raises on purpose) passes.run controller_runtime_reconcile_time_seconds{controller} pass duration same histogram data, controller-runtime buckets controller_runtime_max_concurrent_reconciles{controller} constant 1 setup() controller_runtime_active_workers{controller} 1 while a pass runs, else 0 reconcile_pass() workqueue_depth{name,controller} 1 when a lap is due and not started, else 0 (practically 0) forever workqueue_adds_total{name,controller} laps scheduled forever workqueue_queue_duration_seconds{name,controller} lateness of a lap: actual start minus scheduled start forever workqueue_work_duration_seconds{name,controller} pass duration reconcile_pass() workqueue_unfinished_work_seconds{name,controller} seconds the current pass has been running callback gauge workqueue_longest_running_processor_seconds{name,controller} same as above (one worker) — the most useful one: a stuck pass shows up callback gauge workqueue_retries_total{name,controller} passes started right after a failed pass forever process_* (CPU, RSS, fds, start time) prometheus_client.ProcessCollector on the SDK registry setup(); used by the community dashboards rest_client_requests_total{code,method,host} optional, later: needs a hook in each Nereid's kube.py; candidate for moving Kube into the SDK out of this step

docs.title: Migration of the Nereus names
docs.text:
The nereus_nereid_* set stays (it carries what the standard lacks: reason, period, last_success, ready). Emit both sets in 0.3.0. Then either keep both (cardinality is tiny: ~20 Nereids × ~15 series) or drop the two duplicated ones (reconcile_total, reconcile_duration_seconds) after #744's queries move to the standard names. Recommendation: keep both; drop nothing until the portal is on the standard names.

Rejected alternative: VMRule recording rules that rename nereus_* to controller_runtime_* in the store. Deterministic and no SDK change, but cannot produce active_workers, unfinished_work_seconds or process_*, and dashboards querying a raw /metrics would not see them.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text: The Kubebuilder Grafana plugin (grafana/v1-alpha) generates controller-runtime-metrics.json and controller-resources-metrics.json that query these names (and process_*, job). Nereus ships no Grafana; VictoriaMetrics' vmui can import Grafana-style queries but not the dashboards. Worth a follow-up decision: a Grafana Nereid in the metrics reef, or only the portal view below.

docs.title: 5. Portal view (RED per Nereid)
docs.text:
Already specified by #744 (each Nereid's golden signals from the metrics reef, with sparklines on the phone), on the rows of #740 (portal home screen, one row per reef and Nereid) and #746 (baseline thresholds, then 7-day baselines). #744 defines signals on each GET /v1/status row: rate, errorRatio, p95Seconds, saturation, CPU and memory, with 1 h series for sparklines, one query per signal for all Nereids (by (nereid)).

Proposed adjustments to #744, not a new issue:

  • Rate: sum by (nereid) (rate(controller_runtime_reconcile_total[5m])).
  • Errors: sum by (nereid) (rate(controller_runtime_reconcile_errors_total[5m])) / R.
  • Duration: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (nereid, le) (rate(controller_runtime_reconcile_time_seconds_bucket[5m]))).
  • Keep saturation (mean pass time over period) and add workqueue_longest_running_processor_seconds as the "stuck" flag.
  • Layout: one compact row per Nereid (icon, name, state chip, R · E% · p95, one sparkline) on the phone; a table with all sparklines on desktop.

Reef icons: no reef has one. Only ADR 0022 screens carry an icon name (validated by /^[a-z0-9-]{1,40}$/ in static/screens.js, used today only by leagore), and the portal only sets it as data-icon with no icon set behind it. Proposal: an icon field on the Nereid's GET / contract (ADR 0022's contractVersion: 1 allows new fields), merged into its status like the screens, from one shared, open-source icon set vendored in the portal (e.g. Lucide, ISC); fallback honeycomb.svg.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
1. No controller-runtime / workqueue names or labels: community dashboards do not work.
  2. No active_workers / in-flight gauge: a stuck pass is invisible until last_success ages.
  3. No process_* metrics on the SDK registry (CPU/memory come only from cAdvisor).
  4. No result dimension (requeue vs success).
  5. No API client metrics (rest_client_requests_total): each Nereid has its own kube.py.
  7. No reef icon anywhere; no icon set in the portal.

docs.title: 744's queries use the Nereus names; no portal signals implemented yet.
Next steps
docs.text:
1. Pin the exact labels from the controller-runtime version to follow (source, not the reference page), and write the mapping table into lib/nereid/README.md as the contract.
  2. nereid-sdk 0.3.0: emit the standard set alongside nereus_nereid_*, ProcessCollector, tests in tests/test_telemetry.py pinning the exposition; bump the 19 pins.
  3. Check make scene-metrics (test/scene-metrics) sees the new series through the VMPodScrape.
  4. Update #744's queries to the standard names; then deliver #739/#740/#744.
  5. ADR 0022 amendment: the reef icon field and the portal's icon set (decided).
  6. Later: move Kube into the SDK and add rest_client_requests_total; a Grafana Nereid only if the portal falls short.

docs.title: Platform in an era of AI agents
docs.text:
Notes on a podcast, not decisions

The topics of one podcast episode and how they map to Nereus. The gaps became ideas to refine (#2033 to #2037), in Ideas until the owner's triage.

Credit: What does the concept of the platform mean in an era of AI agents?, Thoughtworks Technology Podcast, published 2026-11-12, 47 min. Host: Ken Mugrage (Thoughtworks). Guest: Abby Bangser, Principal Founding Engineer at Syntasso, where she builds Kratix, a framework for building platforms, and leads a CNCF white paper on platforms. The page, with its transcript, was opened on 2026-11-21; the topics below are a summary in our own words, and the quotes are short. The owner brought the episode; an agent summarised it and mapped it to Nereus.

docs.title: The topics
docs.text:
Platforms are not new

  • The industry swings between decentralising and centralising; after DevOps, the common tooling comes back to a central team.
  • The difference from the days of Heroku and Cloud Foundry: then the platform was a third party's, now it is built inside the company.

A puppy for Christmas

  • A new, polished Terraform module is the tip of the iceberg; patches, upgrades and drift follow.
  • Handing templates to the teams hands them every Day 2.
  • The answer is a managed service behind an API: the team that knows the tool controls the supply chain.

The builders' experience

  • When the tools of the platform team are poor, the poor experience rolls downhill to the application developers.

From golden paths to golden bricks

  • Say why the path meets the organisation's expectations, and give a checklist, automated where possible, to whoever leaves it.
  • Build the path from composable bricks: replace one brick instead of rebuilding the path. The episode credits the phrase "golden bricks" to an unnamed source.

Agents

  • Agents work inside the structures teams already have (stream-aligned and platform teams); they need no new interaction model (a talk by a Meta engineer at Fast Flow Conf, London, as quoted in the episode).
  • They are faster consumers, without empathy: at a barrier, they go around it.
  • What matters is a safe environment: clear boundaries and least-privilege permissions. A job that must be deterministic is a script, which AI can help write.

The platform as a marketplace, not a gatekeeper

  • Specialists (security, databases) contribute capabilities without learning the central tooling, as sellers do on Etsy or the App Store.
  • To contribute: an API (OpenAPI v3), documentation of who owns it, and the automation that serves a request.
  • A low barrier into an experimental zone, then alpha, beta and GA deciding who can see and use a capability: shadow IT comes into the light. The episode cites the old blog post "Let a 1,000 flowers bloom and pull out 999 of them".

A three-tier architecture

  • On top the interfaces (portal, CLI, MCP); at the bottom infrastructure as code, cloud providers, SaaS; in the middle the business process, which is the platform.
  • Several platforms (control planes) per compliance zone, as a small and trim PCI zone in a cloud estate.

The floating platform

  • Gregor Hohpe's floating platform: the platform rises as the layers below become commodity.
  • When the API speaks of jobs to be done (deploy, a test environment, scale), what sits behind it can change from handcrafted infrastructure as code to an agent with clear boundaries.
  • "That is their platform now, the harness": the shared harness of a team's agents is a platform.

What breaks first with more consumers

  • Maintenance: an upgrade that becomes a ticket on every team's backlog does not scale.
  • An ambiguous contract: more users mean more edge cases; start from the smallest API.

The platform is a product

  • Its domain is what is unique to the business but common to the teams; what can be bought off the shelf, buy.

Monday morning

  • Measure how long it takes to get a capability, and how long and how much work it takes to maintain it (a security patch, for example).

Interfaces

  • There is no one right interface: the logic stays in the API, and CLI, portal and MCP are doors on it.

docs.title: How it maps to Nereus
docs.text:
What Nereus already does the same way

  • "Your platform, your way" is Nereus: Kratix is a framework to build platforms, and so is Nereus; an Internal Developer Platform is one profile, ADR 0014 (a profile is a YAML file that installs a set of reefs).
  • Golden bricks are the reefs: each capability is an API group installed at runtime, ADR 0010 (reefs at runtime); a profile assembles the path from them.
  • A managed service instead of a puppy: a resource reef, ADR 0017 (resource reefs), keeps the tool behind the API; database with the Nereid cloudnative-pg writes the connection Secret in status.binding and stays the owner of Day 2.
  • The marketplace's contribution model is the Nereid contract with a Mandate, ADR 0011 (reefs, Nereids and Mandates): a specialist writes a Nereid and binds it to a reef, without touching the core.
  • Three tiers, interfaces as doors: everything comes from the Nereus API, ADR 0018; the portal gets a screen per reef, ADR 0022 (a reef's screen is a Web Component its Nereid serves); MCP is a door of the API, ADR 0029 (each reef declares its MCP tools, served at /mcp).
  • Agents as one more kind of consumer: Triton, ADR 0030 (the messaging Nereid for agents), and the project's own work with agent sessions inside boundaries (journeys, guards).
  • Owner and audience: the catalog records each Workload's owner and audience, ADR 0016 (the reef that says what Nereus has).

Gaps the episode points at

docs.title: 2033 (reef maturity at runtime: an alpha reef is offered only to its audience), a sub-issue of #28 (how every feature is born: alpha, beta, stable).
2034 (profile guarantees: a profile states the expectations it meets as runnable checks, for those who leave the golden path).
2035 (fleet rollout and drift: one Mandate change reaches every Instance in waves, and an Instance changed by hand is reported).
2036 (the platform's two business metrics: time to get a resource, and time for a change to reach every Instance).
2037 (one installation per compliance zone: how several Nereus installations of one organisation relate).
Learn more
docs.text:
• The episode and its transcript (Thoughtworks, 2026-11-12).
  • Kratix documentation (Syntasso).
  • Platform as a Product, the O'Reilly report by Abby Bangser, Daniel Bryant, Colin Humphreys and Cat Morris, already in References.

docs.title: Platform orchestrators
docs.text:
Historical page (2026-10-19): it uses the model's words of that time (Interface, Implementation, platform); today's are reef, Nereid and nereus (The CLI design).

Are we reinventing the wheel? "Native first, build last" (vision) asks, before building more of Nereus, whether an existing tool already does what it proposes. The page Platform Orchestrators of internaldeveloperplatform.org calls the orchestrator the centrepiece of an Internal Developer Platform and, after Thoughtworks, describes these tools as offering published contracts between developers and platform teams, with variations self-served through configuration. That is close to what Nereus proposes, so this page compares the four orchestrators it lists (Humanitec, Kratix, KusionStack, Massdriver) and the open-source tools closest to the model (Crossplane, Radius, KubeVela, kro, and Score as a workload specification), as asked in #363 (evaluate the platform orchestrators). Every fact below comes from a page opened on 2026-10-19 and linked in Learn more; what could not be verified is said so. Repository figures (licence, stars, last push, last release) were read from the GitHub API on that day.

docs.title: What Nereus proposes
docs.text:
The rows every tool is measured against, with where each is decided:

# Our proposal Where it is decided 1 Interface, Instance, Class, Implementation, Tool; the API never names an Implementation ADR 0002, ADR 0011 2 The platform starts empty; capabilities are Implementations installed at runtime ADR 0003, ADR 0010 3 Each installed Implementation adds its own commands to the CLI ADR 0004, ADR 0013 4 One writer per field: the API writes spec, the Controller writes status ADR 0005 5 Swapping an Implementation (Keycloak for Auth0) keeps the same commands and API ADR 0002, Inception 6 Cloud access as plans the person approves, no secret stored spec 0005 7 CLI first, the portal after, platform-mcp for agents CLAUDE.md

docs.title: The comparison
docs.text:
Tool Licence and governance Activity (2026-10-19) Closest to our Could Nereus be built on it? Humanitec Platform Orchestrator Commercial, "a SaaS solution operated by Humanitec", with a self-hosted option; Score and resource definitions are its open-source building blocks No public repository of the Orchestrator to read; two documentation sets (v1 and a newer one) are live Resource Type ≈ Interface, Resource Definition with a Driver ≈ Implementation, matching criteria ≈ Class No: closed, hosted, and it would own the API Kratix Apache-2.0, created and hosted by Syntasso; Syntasso Kratix Enterprise adds support and a Backstage integration 780 stars; pushed and released on 2026-10-19 Promise = Interface and Implementation in one object Partly, at the cost of fusing Interface and Implementation and of a GitOps state store KusionStack (Kusion) Apache-2.0, CNCF Sandbox (accepted 2024-09-12) 1,323 stars; last push 2026-10-15; last release v0.15.0 on 2025-06-30; its docs call it an early project Module ≈ Implementation, AppConfiguration ≈ an app declaration No: client-side, application-centric, slow releases Massdriver Commercial; Business plan at $999/month for 15 seats, self-hosted only in Enterprise; its CLI mass is Apache-2.0 mass: 112 stars, release 2.4.1 on 2026-10-14; the platform's own code is not in the public repositories seen Bundle with typed connections ≈ Implementation with a contract No: closed and paid Crossplane Apache-2.0, CNCF Graduated (2025-10-28) 12,180 stars; release v2.4.2 on 2026-09-22 XRD = Interface, Composition ≈ Implementation Possible for the contract, rejected by ADR 0010; best as a Tool behind an Implementation Radius Apache-2.0, CNCF Sandbox (accepted 2024-04-16) 1,667 stars; release v0.61.1 on 2026-09-30 Resource Type = Interface, Recipe Pack = Implementation, Environment selects it Possible for the contract; Recipes are templates, not Controllers with commands KubeVela Apache-2.0, CNCF Incubating (2023-02-27) 7,915 stars; release v1.11.0 on 2026-07-20 X-Definitions and addons ≈ Interfaces added at runtime No: its centre is the Application (OAM), not a capability kro Apache-2.0, a subproject of Kubernetes SIG Cloud Provider; API at v1alpha1 3,077 stars; release v0.9.4 on 2026-09-04 ResourceGraphDefinition = an Interface and its composition No as a base; a good Tool for an Implementation that composes Kubernetes resources Score Apache-2.0, CNCF Sandbox score-spec/spec: 8,092 stars, 0.4.1 on 2026-05-25; score-compose 0.48.0 and score-k8s 0.21.0 on 2026-10-17 A workload specification, the "app declaration" of the vision Not a platform; a candidate input format for the Platform API

How each covers the rows above, from the pages opened (✓ covers, ◐ covers in part, — not found in the pages opened). In row 4, ✓ marks a tool whose API is made of Kubernetes custom resources, so it inherits the spec and status convention ADR 0005 takes; none of the pages opened states a writer rule of its own.

Tool 1 Model 2 Starts empty 3 CLI grows 4 One writer 5 Swap 6 Approved plans 7 CLI, portal, MCP Humanitec ◐ — — — ✓ — ◐ Kratix ◐ ✓ — ✓ ◐ — ◐ KusionStack ◐ — — — ◐ — ◐ Massdriver ◐ — — — ◐ — ◐ Crossplane ✓ ✓ — ✓ ✓ — — Radius ✓ ◐ — ◐ ✓ — ◐ KubeVela ◐ ✓ — ✓ ◐ — ◐ kro ◐ ✓ — ✓ — — — Score — — — — ◐ — ◐

No tool covers rows 3 and 6: an installed capability that adds its own commands to the CLI as data (ADR 0004), and cloud access the person approves as a plan run with their own short-lived login, with nothing stored (spec 0005). Those two, with the strict split of Interface and Implementation that lets a whole running Controller be swapped, are what Nereus adds.

docs.title: Humanitec
docs.text:
What it is. The product page calls the Platform Orchestrator a "graph-based backend for your IDP" that unifies infrastructure management "for humans and AI agents", reached through a portal, a CLI, Terraform, Score and an API ("One API for every agent, developer, and pipeline"). The documentation's overview says "The Platform Orchestrator is a SaaS solution operated by Humanitec"; the product page also offers a self-hosted option. It does not say the Orchestrator itself is open source; it lists Score and Resource Definitions as "OSS building blocks".

How it maps. A developer describes a workload once (Dynamic Configuration Management), and the platform builds its configuration per environment. A Resource Definition "defines how and when a Resource should be provisioned": a Resource Type (our Interface), a Driver (Terraform, Template, or a custom one, our Implementation) and matching criteria by environment type, application, environment, resource id or Resource Class (our Class, resolved from the scope as ADR 0002 asks). Swapping the Driver behind a Resource Type keeps what the developer wrote: row 5 is covered. Its MCP knowledge server answers questions about the product and "cannot see data in your Orchestrator organization".

What it lacks for us. The Orchestrator owns the API and the model; an Implementation does not add commands to its CLI; the pages opened describe no plan the person approves with their own cloud login. Its activity could not be measured: there is no public repository of the Orchestrator.

Built on it? No. Adopting it would make a closed, hosted product the centre of an Apache-2.0 platform (ADR 0007, public by design), and its open parts (Score, Resource Definitions) are useful without it.

docs.title: Kratix
docs.text:
What it is. "Created by Syntasso, Kratix is an open-source platform framework", Apache-2.0 (repository). Its documentation calls the Promise its core: a contract between the platform and application teams that bundles self-service APIs, embedded workflows and fleet management; Syntasso Kratix Enterprise adds support and a Backstage integration.

How it maps. A Promise has an API ("Promise APIs are Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) under the hood", namespace-scoped only), dependencies installed on every matching Destination, configure and delete workflows (chains of containers) at Promise and at resource level, and destination selectors. A Promise is installed at runtime, so the platform grows one capability at a time (row 2), and the workflows write the result, keeping requests and their fulfilment apart (row 4). A Destination is "the representation of a system that Kratix can write documents to": Kratix writes into a Git or bucket State Store, and a GitOps tool on the target cluster, "such as Flux or ArgoCD", applies them.

What it lacks for us. The Promise fuses our Interface and our Implementation: the API and the workflows that fulfil it ship together, so swapping Keycloak for Auth0 means editing or replacing the Promise, not installing a second Implementation into the same Interface and switching (row 5 only in part). Promises add no commands to a CLI; the pages opened describe no approved cloud plans.

Built on it? Partly possible: each Interface a Promise whose workflow calls the active Implementation. It would add a GitOps state store to every installation and a second, Syntasso-led framework under ours, for little the CRDs of ADR 0010 do not already give.

docs.title: KusionStack
docs.text:
What it is. Kusion is "an intent-driven Platform Orchestrator, which sits at the core of an Internal Developer Platform" (repository, Apache-2.0), a CNCF Sandbox project since 2024-09-12. Its documentation says it is still early and iterating quickly; the docs shown are for v0.14, and the last release on GitHub is v0.15.0 of 2025-06-30.

How it maps. Developers write one AppConfiguration, "without needing to supply environment-specific values"; platform engineers build Modules that "abstract the complexity of underlying infrastructure tooling" and Workspaces per landing zone. The documentation calls it a "Pure client-side solution"; since v0.14 a Kusion Server offers the same as the CLI with a Developer Portal and REST APIs. Projects are folders with a project.yaml, usually kept in Git.

What it lacks for us. The centre is the application, not a capability with its own lifecycle; Modules are not running Controllers and add no commands; the pages opened describe no swap of an active Module across running Instances, nor approved cloud plans.

Built on it? No. Its slow release pace and application-first model make it a reference for the app declaration, not a base.

docs.title: Massdriver
docs.text:
What it is. "An internal developer platform that turns infrastructure-as-code into reusable, self-service components" (documentation). Its pricing page lists a Business plan at $999/month billed annually for 15 seats and an Enterprise plan with custom pricing and self-hosted support. Of its public repositories, the CLI mass is Apache-2.0; none of the repositories seen is the platform itself.

How it maps. A bundle is "a reusable, versioned definition of cloud infrastructure or application components": IaC (Terraform, OpenTofu, Helm, Bicep), its inputs (parameters and connections), its outputs, and policies. Typed contracts make sure "You can't connect a PostgreSQL database to a component expecting a Redis connection". The platform is "API-first", and developers wire bundles on a visual canvas.

What it lacks for us. Closed and paid; the portal comes first, not the CLI; a bundle is a template run by a pipeline, not a Controller that keeps running and serves commands; the pages opened describe no approved cloud plans.

Built on it? No.

docs.title: Crossplane
docs.text:
What it is. "Crossplane is a control plane framework for platform engineering" (what's Crossplane), Apache-2.0, CNCF Graduated since 2025-10-28, the most mature tool here (v2.4.2, repository).

How it maps. A composite resource definition "define[s] the schema for a custom API" (our Interface; namespaced by default in v2), and Compositions, pipelines of functions in YAML, KCL, Python or Go, fulfil it without writing a controller. "If more than one Composition references the same XRD, the composite resource must select which Composition to use"; an XRD sets a defaultCompositionRef or an enforcedCompositionRef: the swap of row 5, done in the cluster. Managed resources reach external systems, and the package manager installs providers, functions and shared configurations at runtime (row 2). ADR 0010 already took the shape of an XRD for an Interface.

What it lacks for us. A Composition renders resources; it is not a long-running Implementation (Keycloak, a helm Controller) that also serves commands. Crossplane has no CLI that grows with what is installed, no portal and no MCP of its own in the pages opened, and no plan the person approves with their own login: it acts with the credentials its providers hold.

Built on it? Possible: every Interface an XRD, every Implementation a Composition. ADR 0010 (Interfaces are objects added at runtime) rejected it because Crossplane would then be the platform and one of its Implementations at once, and an Implementation that is a running Controller (row 3, the commands) does not fit a Composition. This research finds no reason to reverse that: Crossplane is the strongest Tool for a database or cloud Implementation, not the base.

docs.title: Radius
docs.text:
What it is. An application platform with a rad CLI, "the primary means of interacting with Radius for both developers and platform engineers" (concepts), Apache-2.0, a CNCF Sandbox project since 2024-04-16 (v0.61.1, repository). Its dashboard is built on Backstage.

How it maps. It is the closest match to our split. Resource Types are defined by platform engineers as the contract between developers and the platform, each with an OpenAPI schema, "cloud provider agnostic". Recipe Packs supply the implementation: "While a Resource Type defines the interface used to request a resource, a Recipe Pack defines the implementation", one Bicep or Terraform recipe per type, and "An Environment lists the Recipe Packs it uses". "Changing the Recipe Pack changes how resources are deployed without changing the applications that use them" is our row 5. Read-only properties (host, port) are "set by the recipe after the resource has been deployed", close to our status.

What it lacks for us. A Recipe is a Bicep or Terraform template run at deploy time, not a running Controller; installing a Recipe Pack adds no commands to rad; the pages opened describe no approved cloud plans; and it is pre-1.0. Its centre is the application, with the Environment selecting the implementation, where ours is the capability, with an active Implementation per Interface.

Built on it? Possible for the contract (an Interface as a Resource Type, an Implementation as a Recipe Pack), but it would leave out what makes an Implementation here: a Controller with its own lifecycle and commands. Worth following, and worth a conversation with its maintainers on the vocabulary.

docs.title: KubeVela
docs.text:
What it is. An application delivery platform built on the Open Application Model (documentation), Apache-2.0, CNCF Incubating since 2023-02-27 (v1.11.0, repository), with native multi-cluster delivery.

How it maps. An Application bundles Components, Traits, Policies and Workflow steps (core concepts); each is backed by "programmable configurations called Definitions" that the platform team maintains, written in CUE, and "A package of OAM Definitions and Kubernetes CRD Controller is called an Addon": capabilities installed at runtime (row 2).

What it lacks for us. Everything is shaped around delivering one application; a capability like authentication or a cloud connection is not a first-class contract with swappable Implementations; addons add no CLI commands of their own in the pages opened; no approved cloud plans.

Built on it? No: it would make the application model the centre, where ours is the capability.

docs.title: kro
docs.text:
What it is. "Kube Resource Orchestrator (kro) is a subproject of Kubernetes SIG Cloud Provider" (repository, Apache-2.0), whose API "is currently at v1alpha1" and may break.

How it maps. A ResourceGraphDefinition "is the blueprint for a custom API": kro "turns that definition into a CRD, watches for instances of that API", and infers the order of the resources it creates from CEL expressions ("You never declare resource order"). It is the lightest way to give an Interface a CRD whose Instances become several Kubernetes resources.

What it lacks for us. One RGD is one fixed composition: there is no second Implementation of the same API to switch to, no CLI, no portal.

Built on it? No as a base. A good Tool for an Implementation whose job is to compose Kubernetes resources (ACK, ASO, Config Connector, or plain Deployments), as an alternative to writing that Controller by hand.

docs.title: Score
docs.text:
What it is. "Score is a developer-centric and platform-agnostic workload specification" (score.dev), Apache-2.0, a CNCF Sandbox project, with reference implementations score-compose and score-k8s (specification); Humanitec builds on it.

How it maps. One score.yaml says what a workload needs; an implementation turns it into Docker Compose or Kubernetes configuration per environment. It is not a platform; it is the shape of the "app declaration" the vision says the Platform API will compose into several Instances.

Built on it? Not a base, but a candidate input: the Platform API could read a score.yaml and turn each resource it requests into an Instance of an Interface, instead of inventing its own app file.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Build as now; do not adopt or build on any orchestrator as the base; use them as Tools behind Implementations, and consider Score for the app declaration.

  • The model is not new, and that is good news. Crossplane (XRD and Compositions), Radius (Resource Types and Recipe Packs) and Humanitec (Resource Types, Drivers and matching criteria) all split a contract from what fulfils it and let the fulfilment change without touching the request. Rows 1, 2, 4 and 5 are well-trodden; ADR 0002 and ADR 0010 already credit the same precedents. The docs should say so plainly, citing these tools, rather than present the split as an invention.
  • What no tool does is what Nereus is for. None lets an installed capability add its own commands to the CLI (ADR 0004), none treats an Implementation as a whole running Controller swappable inside one Interface (ADR 0011), and none asks the person to approve the cloud plan and runs it with their own short-lived login (spec 0005). Building on Crossplane, Radius or Kratix would keep the contract and lose these, and would put a second framework, with its own vocabulary and release pace, under ours.
  • Adopting is ruled out by licence or maturity. Humanitec and Massdriver are closed and paid, against ADR 0007 (public by design, Apache-2.0). KusionStack's releases have slowed, Radius is pre-1.0, kro is v1alpha1.
  • Native first still applies inside Implementations. An Implementation that provisions cloud resources should use Crossplane or kro as its Tool rather than call cloud APIs by hand; a database Interface could have a Crossplane Implementation and a Radius-style Terraform one side by side. That is ADR 0010's position, and this research confirms it.
  • One idea worth taking. Score is an open, CNCF workload specification for exactly the app declaration the Platform API will compose. Before designing our own app file, the owner may want a Proposal issue to evaluate Score as that input.

Nothing is adopted without the owner (#332, credit what we use). If the owner chooses to build on or adopt a tool, that decision becomes an ADR; otherwise this page is the record.

docs.text:

  • Kratix: documentation, Promises, Destinations, repository.
  • KusionStack: documentation, Projects, repository, CNCF project page.

  • KubeVela: documentation, core concepts, repository, CNCF project page.
  • kro: overview, repository.

docs.title: Production-grade checklist
docs.text:
Recommendations, not a gate

This page is a reference for opportunities Nereus may take up, one day or never. It is not a list of requirements: no slice, Nereid, reef or PR has to tick these items, and no check enforces them. When one of them becomes work, it starts as an issue and, if it is a new capability, as an API group (API groups).

The list follows the production-grade infrastructure checklist in Yevgeniy Brikman's book Terraform: Up & Running: Writing Infrastructure as Code, Second Edition. The descriptions below are our own words; the tools are examples, not choices. Where a task fits the model, a short note says how it could map to a reef or a Nereid (The CLI design, ADR 0002 (the conceptual model: reefs, Nereids, Mandates)); those notes are ideas, not decisions.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Get the software and everything it depends on onto the machine or into the image, in a way that can be repeated.

  • Example tools: Bash, Ansible, Chef, Puppet, container images built by Docker or Buildpacks.
  • In Nereus: a Nereid ships as a container image, so installing it is pulling that image; the release reef (with the flux Nereid) already installs Helm charts.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
Set how the software behaves when it runs: ports, certificates, how services find each other, which node leads, how data is replicated.

  • Example tools: Ansible, Chef, Puppet, Helm values, Kustomize, ConfigMaps.
  • In Nereus: the spec of a reef's object carries the configuration the API writes, and the Nereid turns it into the tool's own settings (ADR 0005 (one writer per field: the API writes spec, the Nereid writes status)).

docs.title: Provision
docs.text:
Create the infrastructure itself: servers, networks, load balancers, firewall rules, identities and their permissions.

  • Example tools: Terraform, OpenTofu, CloudFormation, Crossplane, Pulumi.
  • In Nereus: the cloud reef (spec 0005) and the environment reef are where provisioning lands; a Terraform or Crossplane Nereid could serve them behind a Mandate, so the tool can be swapped.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Put the service on top of the infrastructure and roll out new versions without taking it down, gradually or side by side.

  • Example tools: Kubernetes, Helm, Flux, Argo CD, Argo Rollouts, Flagger, ECS.
  • In Nereus: the release reef; blue-green, rolling and canary strategies could become fields of a release, served by a Nereid that wraps Flagger or Argo Rollouts.

docs.title: High availability
docs.text:
Keep working when a process, a server, a service, a data centre or a whole region fails.

  • Example tools: replicas across zones, multi-region replication, load balancers, auto scaling, PodDisruptionBudgets.
  • In Nereus: an availability level could be a field of an environment or a release, which the Nereid translates into replicas, zones and disruption budgets; the chaos step of the walkthrough (When the Nereid stops) is the first taste of it.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
Grow and shrink with the load, by adding more copies (out) or bigger machines (up).

  • Example tools: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, KEDA, Karpenter, Cluster Autoscaler, sharding, caches.
  • In Nereus: scaling rules could sit beside availability in the same objects; KEDA fits well where an event bus (the messaging reef) drives the load.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Use CPU, memory, disk, network and GPU well, and know it from measurement: profiling, benchmarks, load tests, query tuning.

  • Example tools: k6, JMeter, Locust, pprof, py-spy, Pyroscope, Dynatrace.
  • In Nereus: the init time SLO (spec 0004) is already one measured target; a load test could become a command of a reef, run against an Instance before a release is promoted.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Addresses, ports, DNS, how services discover each other, firewalls, and how people reach machines (SSH, VPN).

  • Example tools: VPCs, security groups, CoreDNS, ExternalDNS, Cilium, Tailscale, WireGuard, Cloudflare Tunnel.
  • In Nereus: the planned edge reef with a cloudflare Nereid publishes a hostname as a Route (Publish at a hostname); DNS and private access could follow as reefs of their own.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Encrypt data on the wire and at rest, know who is calling and what they may do, keep secrets out of code, harden what runs.

  • Example tools: cert-manager, Let's Encrypt, OpenBao, Vault, KMS, Keycloak, Kyverno, Trivy, CIS benchmarks.
  • In Nereus: the secrets reef (the openbao Nereid, with client-side encryption by the CLI) and the authentication reef (the keycloak Nereid) cover part of it already; certificates and policy could be reefs too. "Security from the first slice" is already a pillar (Rules).

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Measure whether the system is up and doing its job, from the business down to the server, trace requests, and alert a person when it matters.

  • Example tools: Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Alertmanager, Datadog, Honeycomb.
  • In Nereus: an observability reef could let a Nereid publish its metrics and traces the same way whatever the backend; the notifications reef idea (#278 (spoken summaries as notifications)) could carry the alerts.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Keep logs from filling the disk, and gather them in one place where they can be searched.

  • Example tools: Fluent Bit, Vector, Loki, OpenSearch, the ELK stack, CloudWatch Logs.
  • In Nereus: the same observability reef could take logs, with a Loki or OpenSearch Nereid behind a Mandate.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text:
Copy databases, caches and other data on a schedule, keep a copy in another region or account, and prove that it restores.

  • Example tools: Velero, CloudNativePG backups, restic, snapshots of managed databases, cross-region replication.
  • In Nereus: a backup reef could ask for a schedule and a retention on an Instance, served by a Velero Nereid; a restore test could be one of its commands.

docs.title: Cost optimization
docs.text:
Pick the right machine sizes, use spot and reserved capacity, scale down when idle, and remove what nobody uses.

  • Example tools: OpenCost, Kubecost, Karpenter, spot and reserved instances, auto scaling, cloud-nuke.
  • In Nereus: costs are a lever among the pillars (Vision); the cost reef idea (#277 (the AI-usage Nereid of the cost reef)) could grow to infrastructure costs with an OpenCost Nereid.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Write down the code, the architecture and the practices, and keep runbooks for the incidents that will happen.

  • Example tools: MkDocs, Backstage TechDocs, ADRs, runbooks, READMEs.
  • In Nereus: this site, the ADRs and the walkthrough already do much of it; a reef or Nereid could publish its own runbook next to its commands.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Test the infrastructure code automatically, on every change and on a schedule.

  • Example tools: Terratest, Chainsaw, kuttl, InSpec, conftest, pytest.
  • In Nereus: the scene (make scene) and Nereid conformance (spec 0003) are the start; conformance tests could become what every Nereid passes before a Mandate may point at it.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text: • Yevgeniy Brikman, Terraform: Up & Running: Writing Infrastructure as Code, Second Edition: the production-grade infrastructure checklist this page follows, read from a one-page copy of the checklist on 2026-10-29.

docs.title: 0001. First slice: init, Nereid list, and a fake Nereid that publishes commands
docs.text:
Status: Done (2026-10-17)

Its commands and kind follow ADR 0011 since #98: the controller commands live under system, and the Controller kind is named Nereid (Implementation in the current code, to be renamed).

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: Prove the two ideas the project rests on, end to end, with the least code: init only prepares a cluster (ADR 0003), and an installed Nereid adds its own commands to the CLI (ADR 0004). Nothing real is installed: the first Nereid is a fake whose commands only simulate their output.

docs.title: The scene that ends the slice
docs.text:
nereus init --target k3d --create-cluster --name platform-local   # creates the k3d cluster, sets the kube context
nereus nereid list                                 # empty
nereus nereid apply fake \
  --reef release \
  --image <registry>/fake-controller:0.1.0
nereus nereid list
# NAME  STATUS
# fake  Ready
nereus fake --help                                                # shows the commands the fake Nereid published
nereus fake repo add example https://charts.example.com
nereus fake repo list
# NAME     URL
# example  https://charts.example.com
nereus nereid delete fake
nereus fake --help                                                # gone

The project is platform-api (github.com/getnereus/nereus) and the CLI binary is nereus. Keep the binary name in one place, so a later rename is a one-line change.

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
1. init
  2. --target k3d --create-cluster --name <name>: creates a k3d cluster (fails with a clear message when k3d or docker is missing), points the kube context at it, applies the project's CRDs (the Nereid kind), and records the cluster and context in the CLI config.
  3. Running it again reuses the existing cluster.
  4. Without --create-cluster, it uses the cluster of the current kube context.
  5. The Nereid CRD
  6. spec: image, written by the CLI.
  7. status: conditions (Ready) and commands, the command description of ADR 0004, written by the Nereid (ADR 0005).
  8. nereid list | apply | delete
  9. Until the Platform API exists, the CLI talks to the cluster with the kubeconfig.
  10. apply creates the Nereid object and a Deployment plus Service running the image.
  11. delete deletes all three.
  12. Dynamic commands
  13. The CLI caches each Nereid's status.commands (refreshed by nereid list and nereid apply), builds a command group named after the Nereid, and sends each run to its Nereid through the Kubernetes API Service proxy. It prints what comes back.
  14. The fake Nereid image
  15. Follows the runner pattern: an entrypoint that sets umask 0002 and runs the requested command, with a work directory on a volume (an emptyDir is enough for this slice).
  16. It serves a tiny HTTP endpoint that runs its scripts.
  17. On start, it writes its status.commands and Ready.
  18. repo add appends to a file in the work directory, and repo list reads it.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Every rule in CLAUDE.md and docs/adr/ applies, especially "public by design" (ADR 0007) and "one writer per field" (ADR 0005).
  • Walking skeleton first: the scene above working once beats any part done well on its own.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. The CLI's language: Python with uv and typer (ADR 0008).
  2. The API group of the CRDs: platform.wasp.silvios.me (current code, to be renamed core.getnereus.dev), for the proof of concept (ADR 0009).

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text: • Walking skeleton (Alistair Cockburn; WalkingSkeleton on the C2 wiki): "a tiny implementation of the system that performs a small end-to-end function"; the scene of this slice is one.

docs.title: 0002. Reef at runtime: a reef added from the CLI, and the reference Nereid installed into it from its image label
docs.text: Status: Done (2026-10-17)

docs.title: Intent
docs.text: Prove ADR 0010 end to end from the CLI with the least new code, the way the first slice proved ADRs 0003 and 0004: a reef is an object added at runtime, a Nereid is installed into the reef its image declares, and the command group is named after the reef, not the Nereid (ADR 0011). It is the second cut of #45 (#99), after the system group of #98, and the first part of layer 1 of spec 0003: the reef label, read from the registry.

docs.title: The scene that ends the slice
docs.text:
nereus init --yes                                   # also creates the local registry localhost:5111
make reference                                             # builds the reference image with its label, pushes it there
nereus reef apply release --from-file ./reefs/release/
nereus reef list
# NAME     NEREID
# release  -
nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --reef release \
  --image localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0
nereus release --help                               # the group is named after the reef
nereus release repo add example https://charts.example.com
nereus release repo list
nereus nereid list
# NEREID             REEFS    IMAGE                                              STATUS  AGE
# reference-release  release  localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0  Ready   5s
nereus nereid delete reference-release
nereus release --help                               # the reef stays: no Nereid installed
nereus reef delete release

test/scene runs it on a throwaway k3d cluster, and also checks the two refusals: installing before the reef was added, and an image with no reef label.

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
1. The Reef kind (CRD, cluster-scoped): only a name for now. spec.active comes with #72; the contract of a reef with #18. Written by the CLI (ADR 0005).
  2. The reefs on the Nereid kind, spec.reefs, required, written by the CLI.
  3. nereus reef apply | list | delete.
  4. apply refuses a name that is not a command name or that a command of the CLI already uses (init, system), and is idempotent.
  5. list shows each reef with the Nereid installed into it.
  6. delete is refused while a Nereid of the reef is installed, naming the nereus nereid delete to run.
  7. nereus nereid apply <name> --image <ref> [--reef <reef>] follows steps 1, 3 and 4 of spec 0003's layer 1, with its messages:
  8. It reads the label <API_GROUP>/reef (cli/src/nereus/names.py) from the registry. Its value is a comma-separated list.
  9. With --reef, it uses that reef, which must be one the label lists when there is a label.
  10. With no --reef, it uses the one name the label lists; it refuses several names or none.
  11. It refuses a reef that was not added (nereus reef apply <name> --from-file ./reefs/<name>/).
  12. The registry client (cli/src/nereus/registry.py), standard library only, behind one function, labels(image, platform):
  13. References are read as Docker reads them (reference-release-controller is docker.io/library/reference-release-controller).
  14. GET /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>; for an index, the manifest of the platform of the cluster's first node (attestation entries have none and are skipped); then GET /v2/<name>/blobs/<config digest> and its .config.Labels.
  15. A 401 with a Bearer challenge gets an anonymous token from its realm, scoped to repository:<name>:pull.
  16. HTTPS, except for localhost, *.localhost and loopback addresses, as Docker does.
  17. Command groups named after the reef (ADR 0004, ADR 0010). The cache holds one entry per reef with its Nereid and the commands it published. A group with no Nereid says so, with the install hint. The first slice's group named after the Nereid is gone.
  18. The local registry. nereus init --create-cluster on k3d creates the registry k3d-nereus-registry.localhost on port 5111 of the loopback (names.REGISTRY, names.REGISTRY_BIND, names.REGISTRY_PORT; #654: it has no authentication, so nothing on the local network reaches it), or reuses it. It creates the cluster with --registry-use, and with a mirror of localhost:5111 to that registry, so one reference serves docker push on the machine, the CLI's read and the cluster's pull. One registry serves every cluster init creates. Docker pushes over plain HTTP to localhost:<port>, but not to k3d-*.localhost:<port>, so the mirror is needed.
  19. The reference image gets LABEL ${API_GROUP}/reef=${REEF}. API_GROUP is a build argument with no default, passed from names.py by make reference and test/scene, so a rename stays a one-line change. REEF defaults to release; empty, it builds an image that declares no reef, for the scene's refusal.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. One Nereid per reef until #72. Installing a second one into a reef was refused, naming the one to uninstall: before spec.active existed, nothing said which one the group's commands would go to. Superseded (owner, 2026-11-19, #1894): a reef takes several Nereids, one the default and the others reached through a Mandate (ADR 0011).
  2. nereus init creates and owns the local registry, shared by every cluster it creates, on a fixed port so the reference reads the same in the docs and on every machine. A cluster reused by init keeps the registries it was created with.
  3. The platform of an index is the first node's. Mixed-architecture clusters wait for a need.
