  4. The labels the image declares beyond reef (requires, nereid, the version) are spec 0003's, not this slice's.

docs.title: Security and quality attributes
docs.text:
Under the lens of #28, this slice is alpha: a proof that works end to end on a throwaway cluster, never production.

  • Read before run. The reef is read from the registry before anything is pulled or run, two or three small requests and no layer, so a wrong image is refused before it reaches the cluster.
  • What the CLI trusts from a registry.
  • References are validated before they become a URL.
  • A manifest fetched by digest, and the config blob, are checked against their digest.
  • Responses are capped at 4 MiB.
  • Redirects are followed by hand: the token is dropped when the host changes, and HTTPS never falls back to HTTP.
  • Label values are checked as command names before they name a group.
  • The digest gap, closed by #126. The labels were read from a tag, and the cluster pulled the same tag: a tag pushed again between the read and the pull ran an image whose labels were never read. The install now resolves the tag to the digest of the manifest it read and records spec.image as <repository>@sha256:... (spec 0003, Good Citizen rule 3), so the cluster pulls what was read. Signature verification comes later (#126).
  • Anonymous only. A registry that asks for credentials is refused with a message that points to #87. Private registries and their credentials are #87.
  • Plain HTTP only for this machine's registry, the local one init creates.
  • What beta would need:
  • two Nereids of one reef, with one active (#72), instead of refusing the second;
  • private registries (#87);
  • the rest of spec 0003's layer 1: requires checked, the Nereid's name and version from its labels.
  • Fitness functions:
  • unit tests of the registry client against a local HTTP registry: a plain manifest, an index, a missing label, the bearer challenge, a refused 401, a config that does not match its digest;
  • unit tests of every refusal;
  • test/scene end to end.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Every rule in CLAUDE.md and docs/adr/ applies, especially "one writer per field" (ADR 0005) and "the API never names a Nereid": the CLI reads the reef from the image, never from a list of known Nereids.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Fitness functions come from Building Evolutionary Architectures (Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, O'Reilly, 2017; evolutionaryarchitecture.com): an automated check that a quality of the architecture holds, run on every change. This spec lists its own under "Security and quality attributes".
  • OCI image annotations (opencontainers/image-spec): the standard keys an image's labels use (spec 0003).

docs.title: 0003. Nereid conformance
docs.text: Status: Proposed (2026-10-17)

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
A Nereid is an image, and the image carries its own contract: the reef it implements, the reefs it requires (#84), its version and the commands it publishes (ADR 0004). nereus nereid apply keycloak then needs only a name (ADR 0011). This spec decides what the image declares, how the platform reads it, and how it checks that a Nereid honours what it declares, in three layers: at install (layer 1, the MVP), at start (layer 2) and before the Nereid registry lists it (layer 3, #22).

The platform checks rather than trusts: images outside the Nereid registry may run, but only conformant ones become Ready and get their commands routed.

docs.title: Precedents
docs.text:
• Crossplane packages. A crossplane.yaml inside the package image declares metadata and dependsOn (other packages, with version constraints), and the package manager resolves them. Taken: the image is the unit of distribution and carries its own metadata. Not taken: the file sits in a layer, so it must be pulled to be read, and dependsOn names packages, not APIs.
  • OLM ClusterServiceVersion. An operator declares the CRDs it owns and the ones it requires; OLM installs it only when every required API is provided, whoever provides it. Taken: dependencies name the API (the reef), never the operator (the Nereid), as #84 asks and ADR 0002 requires.
  • OCI image labels and annotations. The image spec predefines org.opencontainers.image.* keys (version, source, title, licenses, ...) and lets anyone add namespaced keys. Labels written by a Dockerfile LABEL live in the image config blob, a small JSON document readable from a registry without pulling any layer. Taken: the standard keys where one exists, and the platform's own keys only for what the standard lacks.
  • Kubernetes and Gateway API conformance. Sonobuoy runs the Kubernetes conformance suite against a cluster; Gateway API ships a suite per feature profile, and each implementation publishes a versioned ConformanceReport. Taken for layer 3: a suite per reef, a report per image, the Nereid registry listing only images with a passing report.
  • terraform-packager. A Stack image answers info through its entrypoint. Taken for layer 2: the running image answers a cheap call describing itself. The reference Nereid already answers GET / with its name and commands.

docs.title: The image's metadata
docs.text:
Labels in the image config (LABEL in the Dockerfile). The platform's keys use <API_GROUP>/ as prefix (core.getnereus.dev, the core reef's group, ADR 0009; cli/src/nereus/names.py), the same key as the Kubernetes labels of the Mandate (ADR 0011), as #99 fixed. OCI recommends reverse-domain keys; the Kubernetes form is kept on purpose, so one key reads the same on the image, the Mandate, the Deployment and the pods.

Key Required Value Example <API_GROUP>/reef yes the reefs it implements, comma-separated release, or sast,dependency-scan <API_GROUP>/requires no the reefs it requires, comma-separated; absent means none auth,secrets <API_GROUP>/nereid yes the Nereid's name, the default for nereid apply's name keycloak <API_GROUP>/reference no true for a reference Nereid, a test stand-in never next to another kind of Nereid in its reef (#552, #1423) true org.opencontainers.image.version yes the Nereid's version, shown in nereus status 0.1.0 org.opencontainers.image.title no the repository's name auth-keycloak-controller org.opencontainers.image.source no where its code lives https://github.com/example/auth-keycloak-controller 
LABEL core.getnereus.dev/reef=release \
      core.getnereus.dev/nereid=reference-release \
      core.getnereus.dev/reference=true \
      org.opencontainers.image.version=0.1.0 \
      org.opencontainers.image.title=reference-release-controller
  • Several reefs (#72) share one key, comma-separated (decided by the owner, rather than one key per reef: a Kubernetes label on a Mandate carries one value anyway, and the CLI splits it once). --reef <reef> picks one; it must be one of the listed names. An image installed twice, once per reef, is two Nereids (two Mandates, ADR 0011).
  • Required reefs name reefs, never Nereids (#84, ADR 0002). Contract versions (auth@v1alpha1) wait for #18 to version contracts.
  • The commands description stays out of the labels. It can be long, it changes with the code, and labels would duplicate it. It stays a file in the image (commands.yaml today), published by the running Nereid in its status (ADR 0004) and returned by the contract call of layer 2.
  • Labels are identical across the platforms of a multi-arch image, a Good Citizen rule: the platform reads one of them.

docs.title: Layer 1: at install, from the labels (MVP)
docs.text:
nereus nereid apply [<name>] --image <ref> [--reef <reef>] reads the labels before anything runs in the cluster; the name defaults to the nereid label, an explicit one wins, and neither is refused:

  1. From the registry, before any pull or run (decided by the owner on #85 and #45; #99 implements it). Through the OCI Distribution API: GET /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>; when it returns an index, the manifest of the cluster nodes' platform (linux/amd64 or linux/arm64); then GET /v2/<name>/blobs/<config digest>, whose .config.Labels holds the labels. Two or three small requests, no layer downloaded, and never docker image inspect: the same code serves the CLI, the Platform API and a future operator, none of which can assume a local Docker daemon. The client is a small one of our own, behind one function (decided by the owner): standard library only (token dance, manifest, config blob), no oras-py, crane or skopeo, so the CLI gains no binary dependency and the Platform API can reuse it. Anonymous bearer tokens cover public registries (the Nereid registry is public); private registries and credentials are #87.
  2. Local runs use a registry too. On k3d the image is pushed to a k3d local registry (k3d registry create) instead of k3d image import, so a local run reads its labels the same way.
  3. Resolve the reef. From --reef when given, else from the label. Refuse when the label lists several and no --reef is given, when --reef names one the label does not list, or when there is neither (decided by the owner on #45: no command group named after the Nereid any more).
  4. Check the reef exists (nereus reef apply, #99).
  5. Check every required reef has an installed Nereid (an active one once #72 brings spec.active). Refuse naming each missing one and the command that fixes it. When the required reef has Nereids but none is Ready (its Nereid is not healthy), go ahead and warn that the required reef has a problem (decided by the owner on #85).
  6. Record spec.image by digest (ADR 0003): <repository>@sha256:..., the digest of the manifest (or index) the labels were read from, so a tag pushed again later never changes what runs (#126); a reference given by digest is kept as is and checked, spec.reefs, spec.requires, spec.version and spec.controller (from org.opencontainers.image.title), written by the CLI (ADR 0005). spec.requires keeps in the cluster, not in local files, what answers "who requires this reef". A Nereid of the local Nereids applied by its name alone records the CLI's version as spec.version, as thetis does, not its image's label: make release reuses an image whose inputs did not change (#1574), and its label keeps the version it was built at (#2000).
  7. At nereid delete, refuse the last Nereid of a reef that installed Nereids require (read from their spec.requires), naming them; --force goes ahead (decided by the owner on #85).

The messages:

$ nereus nereid apply my-tool \
  --image example/my-tool:0.1.0
error: example/my-tool:0.1.0 declares no reef (label core.getnereus.dev/reef).
       Add the label to the image, or pass --reef <reef>.

$ nereus nereid apply snyk \
  --image example/snyk-controller:0.1.0
error: example/snyk-controller:0.1.0 implements several reefs: sast, dependency-scan.
       Choose one with --reef sast or --reef dependency-scan.

$ nereus nereid apply snyk \
  --reef iac-scan \
  --image example/snyk-controller:0.1.0
error: example/snyk-controller:0.1.0 does not implement iac-scan; it implements sast, dependency-scan.

$ nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --reef release \
  --image example/reference-release-controller:0.1.0
error: reference-release implements release, and reef release does not exist.
       Add it first: nereus reef apply release --from-file ./reefs/release/

$ nereus nereid apply inception \
  --image example/inception-controller:0.1.0
error: inception requires reefs with no Nereid installed: auth, exposure.
       Install a Nereid of each first: nereus nereid apply <name> --reef <reef> --image <image>

$ nereus nereid apply inception \
  --image example/inception-controller:0.1.0
warning: inception requires reef auth, which has a problem: keycloak is CrashLoopBackOff.
         See 'nereus nereid list'.

$ nereus nereid delete keycloak
error: keycloak is the last Nereid of reef auth, which installed Nereids require: inception.
       Uninstall them first, or go ahead with: nereus nereid delete keycloak --force

$ nereus nereid apply \
  --image example/my-tool:0.1.0
error: example/my-tool:0.1.0 declares no Nereid name (label core.getnereus.dev/nereid).
       Add the label to the image, or pass the name: nereus nereid apply <name> --reef <reef> --image example/my-tool:0.1.0

$ nereus nereid apply reference-release \
  --reef release \
  --image registry.example.com/reference-release-controller:0.1.0
error: could not read the labels of registry.example.com/reference-release-controller:0.1.0: 401 Unauthorized.
       Private registries are not supported yet (#87): push the image to a public or local registry.

docs.title: Layer 2: at start, Ready means it honours the contract
docs.text:
A Nereid is Ready when its readiness and liveness probes pass and its contract call succeeds. Until then it never becomes the active Nereid of its reef and the CLI routes none of its commands; it keeps running, so its logs explain why.

The contract call is GET /contract on the Nereid's Service port, reached like every command (the Service proxy today, the Platform API later). It is cheap and side-effect free, so it runs at start and again on every probe period:

{
  "contract": "v1alpha1",
  "implementation": "keycloak",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "implements": ["auth"],
  "requires": ["secrets"],
  "commands": [{"path": ["user", "list"], "help": "List the users."}]
}

The check passes when the answer parses, implements contains spec.reefs, implements, requires, implementation and version match the labels recorded at install, and commands is valid against the command schema of ADR 0004. Each failure is a reason: contract call failed: no 'implements', contract call timed out, requires differs from the image label: secrets.

status, one writer per field (ADR 0005). The Nereid reports; a checker that is not the Nereid judges:

Field Writer Meaning spec.image, spec.reefs, spec.params, spec.requires, spec.version the CLI (the API later) what was asked, and the labels read at install status.commands the Nereid its commands (ADR 0004), as today status.conditions[type=Serving] the Nereid it started and serves its endpoint status.state the checker Pending, Ready or NotConformant status.reason the checker why, when not Ready status.source the checker registry when the digest has a passing report in the Nereid registry (layer 3), else local status.checkedAt, status.digest the checker when it last checked, and the digest it checked

The checker reads the Deployment's availability (the kubelet runs the probes) and makes the contract call. The CLI routes a command only when status.state is Ready.

docs.title: What every Nereid answers
docs.text:
Honouring the contract means more than answering the contract call: a Nereid answers every object of every kind its reef exposes, the same way in every reef (owner, 2026-10-29, #524, #525).

  1. Every verb of every kind. A Nereid serves create, apply, get, list and delete (ADR 0013, the command conventions) of every CRD labelled core.getnereus.dev/reef: <reef>, even when it does nothing with some of them. A reef that exposes no CRD has no Ready Nereid.
  2. The status follows the kind's schema. What a Nereid writes in status follows that kind's CRD: the fields it declares, with the types and values it allows. A Target gets status.ready even when the Nereid creates no namespace. A reason the contract does not declare is not allowed; when "does not apply" is needed, the contract declares it, for every Nereid of the reef.
  3. The common contract. Every kind of every reef shares the fields of cli/src/nereus/interfaces/common.yaml, which the CLI merges into the status of every CRD it applies (a reef's own declarations kept):
  4. The Ready condition in status.conditions (type, status, reason, message, lastTransitionTime), with the common reasons NotApplicable (the Nereid does nothing with this kind) and CleanupFailed (a delete could not remove what was made). A reef declares its own reasons in the annotation core.getnereus.dev/reasons of each CRD, comma-separated; the common ones are implied.
  5. status.observedGeneration: the metadata.generation the status answers.
  6. status.steps, for a kind whose work has several steps: each with a name, a state (Done, InProgress, Pending or Failed), startedAt only once it started, finishedAt only once it ended, and a message. With one step only, or NotApplicable, steps may be empty and the Ready condition is enough.
  7. One Kubernetes Event per change of a step, on the object: its reason is the step's state and its message the step's message. That is the history kubectl describe shows, kept when the Nereid restarts.
  8. The finalizer <reef>.getnereus.dev/cleanup. The Nereid adds it to every object of every kind of its reef it answers, and removes it only once everything it made for the object is gone; with nothing made (NotApplicable), at once. On a failure the object keeps the finalizer, with Ready=False, reason: CleanupFailed and a message naming what is left: a finalizer is never removed while something it guards still exists. Meanwhile the object shows Terminating, kubectl's word for an object with metadata.deletionTimestamp set and finalizers left. The finalizer is the one field outside status a Nereid writes (ADR 0005 keeps spec the CLI's): its Role allows patch on its reef's kinds for it, which RBAC cannot narrow to metadata.finalizers, so the CLI applies with the Nereid's RBAC a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and its binding (controller-<nereid>-finalizer-only), matched on the Nereid's service account and on updates of its reef's kinds (never their status). The policy is an allowlist (#552): every root key but metadata and status, and every metadata key but finalizers and the ones the API server writes (resourceVersion, generation, managedFields), keeps its old value, present or absent, and no finalizer is added or removed but <reef>.getnereus.dev/cleanup. It fails closed: the CLI creates the policy and its binding before the ClusterRole that grants patch, and on a cluster that does not serve admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (Kubernetes older than 1.30) it installs nothing and says which version is needed.
  9. A reference Nereid never shares its reef with another kind of Nereid (#552, per reef since #1423). The reference Nereids (controllers/reference: reference-release for the release reef, reference-secrets for the secrets reef) are test stand-ins: each answers every object of its reef and keeps the reef's one finalizer whatever the Mandate. Their image declares <API_GROUP>/reference=true, which nereid apply records as the same label on the Nereid. Installing a reference Nereid while one of its reefs has a Nereid without the label is refused, and so is installing a Nereid without the label in a reef a reference one serves; Nereids of other reefs, of either kind, run next to each other, as the catalog Nereid next to the reference ones in make scene-core (owner, 2026-11-13); the error names the Nereids in the way and the fix, delete them first. Several reference Nereids run together: the release reef's asks the secrets reef's for its bindings (#533). The other Nereids are multi-Nereid by design: each object goes to the Nereid of its Mandate (spec.mandate, else the reef's default Mandate), so two real Nereids never answer the same object, and the finalizer keeps its one name per reef.
$ nereus nereid apply flux --reef release
✗ nereid flux was not installed: its reef has the reference Nereid reference-release, a test stand-in. A reference Nereid never shares its reef with another kind of Nereid (spec 0003).
  Why: it answers every object of its reef and keeps the reef's one finalizer, such as release.getnereus.dev/cleanup, whatever the Mandate, so another Nereid could lose its cleanup to it.
  Check: nereus nereid list
  Fix: delete them first, then apply flux again:
    nereus nereid delete reference-release
    nereus nereid delete reference-secrets
Nothing was installed.

Messages: clarity over brevity. A message is a full sentence that says what was done, is being done or is left, or why the kind does not apply to this Nereid; never a terse word such as NoOp. It is a guideline, not a length a check enforces.

A kind the Nereid does nothing with:

conditions:
  - type: Ready
    status: "True"
    reason: NotApplicable
    message: "The openbao Nereid keeps no state for a Target: OpenBao has no namespaces, so nothing is created."

A kind whose delete has several steps, half done:

steps:
  - name: node-pool
    state: Done
    startedAt: "2026-10-29T21:02:11Z"
    finishedAt: "2026-10-29T21:04:40Z"
    message: "Deleted the node pool demo-pool (3 nodes)."
  - name: aks-cluster
    state: InProgress
    startedAt: "2026-10-29T21:04:41Z"
    message: "Deleting the AKS cluster demo-aks in eastus; Azure reports Deleting."
  - name: resource-group
    state: Pending
    message: "Delete the resource group rg-demo once the cluster is gone."

Implemented (#525): the common contract. interfaces/common.yaml and its merge in cli/src/nereus/contracts.py; the release reef's four kinds take it and declare their reasons. Its two Nereids, flux and reference, keep the finalizer release.getnereus.dev/cleanup and write observedGeneration: a Release keeps it until its Flux HelmRelease is gone, a Repository until its HelmRepository is gone, a Source and a Target lose it at once. What the CLI shows while an object is Terminating is #526; NotConformant for a Nereid that does not answer its reef's kinds is #527; the check, kind by kind, is #528.

Implemented (#527): NotConformant from the reef's kinds. A Nereid declares the kinds it serves in status.kinds, a list of <plural>.<group> (for example targets.release.getnereus.dev), which it writes (ADR 0005); when the contract call exists, it carries the same list. Until the checker exists, the CLI computes the state, writing no status field (cluster.assess): a Nereid whose Ready condition is True is Unavailable when its Controller has no pod serving (that wins: with no pod, nothing serves), else NotConformant when one of its reefs exposes no kind (no CRD labelled core.getnereus.dev/reef: <reef> in the reef's own group) and has none by design (authentication, portal and metrics, #794), or exposes a kind missing from its status.kinds, else Ready; a Nereid whose condition is not True keeps its own reason. The reef's kinds come from one list of the labelled CRDs per command, never one call per row. The reason is a full sentence naming the reef, the kind and the fix: nereus nereid get prints it on a Reason line, and nereus status --output json|yaml as the reason field of each row (null when there is none). The CLI sends no command to a NotConformant Nereid, naming the reason, as it sends none to an Unavailable one. core is built into the CLI and stays Ready. flux and reference declare the release reef's four kinds; openbao and keycloak declare none, and are NotConformant until their reefs get kinds (#529, #535). nereus init waits on the Nereid's own Ready condition, so it works while openbao is NotConformant.

$ nereus nereid get my-auth
...
Status:       NotConformant
Reason:       The auth reef exposes no kind, so my-auth serves no verb: a reef needs at least one CRD labelled core.getnereus.dev/reef=auth.

docs.title: The conformance check, kind by kind (#528)
docs.text:
The rules above are checked, not trusted: test/conformance <reef> --nereid <nereid> drives nereus and kubectl on a throwaway k3d cluster where the Nereid is installed, Ready and named by the reef's default Mandate, and proves every verb of every kind the reef exposes. The reference Nereid passes first; make scene-release runs it against the reference Nereid (reference-release), then against flux.

A sample per kind, in the contract the CLI pins: cli/src/nereus/interfaces/<reef>/samples/<kind>.yaml, the objects the kind needs first (a Release's Repository, Source and Target), then the kind's object as created, then the same object with a change to its spec, the one apply makes. A kind whose CRD keeps every spec field as created (a rule self == oldSelf of the field's own, or a rule of spec comparing self.<field> with oldSelf.<field>: the edge reef's Route and Zone) has no change to make, so its sample holds the object once and step 4 is skipped, said in a line (#2006); a sample holding it once for a kind whose spec can change is refused. REEF_GROUP stands for the reef's group, as in the CRDs. The release reef's samples name a chart of example.com: the check proves the status a Nereid writes, not that a chart installs, so flux answers them as a repository it could not read and a release that failed or is still trying, with reasons the contract declares, and installs nothing.

For each CRD labelled core.getnereus.dev/reef: <reef> in the reef's own group:

  1. create: nereus <reef> apply --from-file with the sample; --dry-run first changes nothing, then the line names the object by its full path (release/releases/conformance created).
  2. The status answers the object's generation (status.observedGeneration reaches metadata.generation) and follows the CRD read from the cluster, the common fields merged in: every field present is declared, with its type, its enum and its limits; the Ready condition is there, its reason one the contract declares (the common ones or the CRD's core.getnereus.dev/reasons), its message not empty; each step has a message, startedAt only once it started and finishedAt only once it ended. A message's clarity is a guideline, not checked.
  3. The finalizer <reef>.getnereus.dev/cleanup is on the object.
  4. apply of the changed sample says configured, raises metadata.generation, and the status answers the new one, checked as in 2; skipped for a kind whose spec cannot change.
  5. get and list show the object.
  6. delete: --dry-run changes nothing; then, the check holding a finalizer of its own so the state is seen whatever the Nereid's pace, delete --wait=false says Terminating and list shows it; the Nereid removes its finalizer once what it made is gone; the check releases its own and the object is gone. The objects it needed are then deleted, each delete waiting for its Nereid (#526).

The status is checked by python -m nereus.conformance status (cli/src/nereus/conformance.py) with the small subset of OpenAPI v3 the contracts use (type, enum, properties, required, items, maxItems, maxLength, pattern, format: date-time, x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields), not jsonschema: no new dependency, and a contract using another keyword fails the check, naming it, rather than passing unchecked. Each failure names the kind, the object and the field:

FAIL: Target nereus-system/conformance: status.conditions[type=Ready].reason: 'NoOp' is not a reason the contract declares (NotApplicable, CleanupFailed, Reference, InCluster)
FAIL: Target nereus-system/conformance: status.observedGeneration: missing; the Nereid writes the metadata.generation its status answers
FAIL: Target nereus-system/conformance: status.steps[name=quota].finishedAt: set on a Pending step, which has not ended

The check refuses any kube context but a k3d one, and k3d-nereus, the kept cluster (docs/agent/rules.md): it creates and deletes objects. A Nereid that writes no status.steps (flux today, #567) passes; steps are checked only when present.

$ test/conformance release --nereid reference-release
...
== Release (releases.release.getnereus.dev)
✓ Release nereus-system/conformance: status conforms (generation 1, Ready True, Reference)
✓ Release nereus-system/conformance: status conforms (generation 2, Ready True, Reference)
✓ Release: create, apply, get, list and delete, the status as the contract says
...
✓ reference-release serves every verb of every kind of the release reef and honours its contract: Release Repository Source Target

docs.title: Layer 3: a conformance suite per reef, gating the Nereid registry (outline)
docs.text:
Layer 3 grows from the check of layer 2: the same steps, the samples the contract ships, and the same validator, run by the CLI against an image rather than by a script against the Nereid installed. #109 builds it.

  • One suite per reef, versioned with its contract (#18): it installs the image on a throwaway k3d cluster, creates the reef's Instances from the samples of its contract (interfaces/<reef>/samples/), runs the check of layer 2 kind by kind, and adds the commands it must publish and the Good Citizen rules below.
  • A report per image digest, after Gateway API's ConformanceReport: Nereid, version, digest, contract version, suite version, the result of each test. Signed later (Sigstore attestations, #22).
  • The Nereid registry (#22) lists only digests with a passing report, and that is what makes status.source read registry.
  • Anyone can run the suite locally (nereus nereid conformance <reef> --image <ref>, a provisional shape, replacing test/conformance), so the docs and courses (#33) teach building a Nereid that passes before submitting it.

docs.title: Good Citizen rules (candidates)
docs.text:
The rules every Nereid follows to run on the platform, checked by the platform rather than trusted. Layer 1 checks the first three, layer 2 the next four, layer 3 all of them.

  1. Carries the labels above, well-formed, identical across platforms.
  2. Requires reefs, never Nereids.
  3. Is installed by digest.
  4. Serves readiness and liveness probes.
  5. Answers the contract call within two seconds, matching its labels.
  6. Writes only its own status fields, never spec (ADR 0005); checked from the object's managedFields.
  7. Publishes a command description valid against the schema, every command and argument with help and every command with examples that call it (#676, #132); its output is text (ADR 0004).
  8. Runs as non-root, with no privilege escalation (the reference image runs as 65532).
  9. Touches only its own reef's objects; its RBAC is scoped to them.
  10. Declares resource requests and limits.
  11. Shuts down cleanly on SIGTERM.
  12. Later: exposes metrics and writes structured logs to stdout (#68).

docs.title: nereus nereid list
docs.text:
One row per Nereid, with the reason of a NotConformant one.

Illustrative output: the values are examples, replaced by real output when the code prints this table.

$ nereus nereid list
NEREID             REEFS    IMAGE                                              STATUS         AGE
keycloak           auth     example/auth-keycloak-controller:0.1.0             Ready          3d
auth0              auth     example/auth-auth0-controller:0.1.0                Ready          3d
my-auth            auth     example/my-auth-controller:dev                     NotConformant  2h
                   (contract call failed: no 'implements')
reference-release  release  localhost:5111/reference-release-controller:0.1.0  Pending        5s

docs.title: nereus nereid get
docs.text: One Nereid in full: its reefs, image and digest, parameters and status, and the image's OCI labels org.opencontainers.image.title and org.opencontainers.image.description, which nereid list leaves out. The title still matters: it names the controller a person sees.

docs.title: What the MVP implements
docs.text:
• Layer 1, all of it: the labels above on the reference image; reading them from a registry (#99 brings the read of the reef label and the k3d local registry; this spec adds requires, nereid and the version); resolving the reef; refusing a missing reef or a missing required reef, with the messages above.
  • The list's STATUS from what exists: the Nereid's Ready condition as today, computed by the CLI with no new status field.
  • Not in the MVP: the contract call and the checker (layer 2), the suite and the Nereid registry gate (layer 3). The check of a reef's kinds (layer 2, #528) runs from test/conformance, in make scene-release.

Implemented (#99, #85, #107): layer 1, all of it. The name, the reef, requires, the version and the title read from the registry; the name argument optional, defaulting to the nereid label (an explicit name wins; neither is refused); a missing reef or required reef refused, a required reef with no Ready Nereid warned about; spec.requires, spec.version and spec.controller (the title) recorded; the uninstall of the last Nereid of a required reef refused unless --force; nereid list with the columns above.

Hostile labels (#134). Labels are untrusted input: before any is used or shown, nereid apply refuses a label it reads that holds a control character or is longer than 128 characters (a Docker tag's limit), naming the label, and writes nothing to the cluster. The scene checks it with a hostile reference image.

Implemented (#133): the first check of layer 2. The CLI reads the availability of each Nereid's Deployment: a Nereid with no pod serving shows Unavailable in STATUS (computed by the CLI, no status field written), and its commands are refused with a message and a non-zero exit code instead of reaching a proxy with nowhere to go. The scene kills the pod of a Nereid and scales its Deployment to zero, and checks the message, the exit code and that the commands work again once the pod is back.

docs.title: Decisions on the open questions
docs.text:
• What "has a Nereid" means for a required reef before #72 (decided by the owner on #85): one installed. With none, nereid apply is refused; with one that is not Ready, nereid apply goes ahead and warns that the required reef has a problem. With #72, the active one.
  • Uninstalling the last Nereid of a required reef (decided by the owner on #85): refused, naming the installed Nereids that require it; --force goes ahead.
  • Versions in requires (decided by the owner on #85): names only until #18 versions the contracts, then auth@v1alpha1, checked against the contract version the reef serves.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Who runs the checker of layer 2 before the Platform API exists. The CLI at nereid apply and at every nereid list, or a system controller that init would install (against ADR 0003's "init installs nothing"). Recommendation: the CLI until the Platform API exists, then a controller inside the Platform API.
  2. Should the contract call move into the image as a command, like terraform-packager's info, so layer 1 can run it without a cluster? Recommendation: no for now; labels cover install, and the call is cheap once it runs.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text: • The precedents above, each with what is taken from it: Crossplane packages; OLM's ClusterServiceVersion; OCI image annotations; Sonobuoy and Gateway API conformance.

docs.title: 0004. Init time SLO: a fitness function caps how long nereus init takes
docs.text: Status: Proposed (2026-10-18)

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
nereus init brings the platform up, and how long it takes is a quality the project measures and guards (#141): an SLO (service level objective) of 8 minutes on the local k3d undercloud, and 20 minutes on a cloud (Azure first) once the AKS overcloud (#92) and the pivot (#61) exist. A fitness function fails CI when init misses its time objective by more than a tolerance, naming the slowest steps; the progress of #88 colours the clock by the share of the time objective used, so a person sees the drift long before CI fails.

Every value is a setting with a default in code. The values a person changes live in one object of the platform's API group in the nereus namespace, so the pivot (#61) moves them to the overcloud with the rest of the platform's state, as Cluster API's clusterctl move moves objects, and nothing is reconfigured by hand.

Provisional. The word (SLO), the kind (ServiceLevelObjective), the config group and the shape of the object are chosen for the initial configuration and the tests of this slice. They are expected to change with use: when more objectives arrive (per-step objectives, the first login of docs/inception.md, the measurements of #102), a new spec revisits them.

docs.title: The scene that ends the slice
docs.text:
nereus init --yes                                   # the total ends with the SLO: "slo 8m, 3% green"
nereus config slo show
# SETTING    VALUE  SOURCE
# local      8m     default
# ...
nereus config slo set --local 4m --tolerance 5
nereus config slo show                              # local and tolerance now come from the cluster
nereus config slo reset                             # back to the defaults in code
nereus init --yes --check-slo                       # what test/scene and CI run: fails above the SLO + tolerance

docs.title: The object
docs.text:
One ServiceLevelObjective object (short name slo), named default, in the nereus namespace (names.NAMESPACE), of the platform's API group (names.API_GROUP, v1alpha1); its CRD is cli/src/nereus/crds/servicelevelobjective.yaml, applied by init with the other kinds.

Field Type Default (constant in cli/src/nereus/slo.py) Meaning spec.targets.local duration 8m (LOCAL) The time objective of init on the local target (k3d), from the start of its steps to the end of the last one. spec.targets.cloud duration 20m (CLOUD) The time objective on a cloud (Azure first), from init's start until the overcloud is up and has taken over after the pivot. Keyed by the cloud reef, never by a Nereid's name (#313). Recorded, not enforced, until #92 and #61. spec.bands.yellow percent 50 (YELLOW) From this share of the time objective, the clock is yellow. spec.bands.orange percent 75 (ORANGE) From this share, orange, and the slowest step so far is shown. spec.bands.red percent 100 (RED) Above this share, red: the objective is missed, and init still finishes. spec.tolerance percent 20 (TOLERANCE) The fitness function fails above the time objective plus this share of it (120% by default).
  • A duration is minutes and seconds, 5m, 4m30s or 90s (pattern ^([0-9]+m)?([0-9]+s)?$, validated with re.fullmatch by the CLI and by the CRD), never zero.
  • The bands must rise: yellow < orange <= red. The CLI refuses a set that breaks the order.
  • Spec only. The CLI writes spec (ADR 0005); there is no Nereid and no status. init's timings are printed, not stored: a run's history is #102's.
  • Only the fields set are written. A field the object leaves out falls back to its default in code, so a change of a default reaches every cluster that did not choose its own value.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
Each value, on its own: the object's field, else the default in code. nereus config slo show prints each value with its source (cluster or default), as init prints its settings.

The first init. The cluster, and so the object, does not exist when init starts. init starts with the defaults, and reads the object in its kinds and namespace step, once the kinds are applied in the cluster it is preparing; from that step on, the bands and the check use what it read. On a cluster created by that same run, there is no object yet, so the defaults hold for the whole run; on a cluster reused, the object read in the last step decides the total and the check. init never writes the object, and the settings file of init (settings.py) does not carry these values: one place for each value, the cluster, with the defaults in code.

After the pivot (#61). The object moves to the overcloud with the rest of the platform's objects, and the CLI reads it there.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
nereus config is a new group for the platform's own settings kept in the cluster; system stays for reefs and Nereids (ADR 0011). nereus config slo:

  • show: the six values, each with its source.
  • set --local <duration> --cloud <duration> --yellow <percent> --orange <percent> --red <percent> --tolerance <percent>: writes the options given, keeps the fields already set, and prints the values as show does. At least one option.
  • reset: deletes the object; every value falls back to its default.

docs.title: The bands in the progress
docs.text:
The share is the time since init's steps started over the time objective of its target.

Band Share of the time objective On a terminal (the card of #88) Anywhere else (plain lines) green under yellow the clock next to the objective, 18.7s of ~8m expected nothing on the step lines yellow yellow to orange the clock in yellow slo 54% yellow on the line of the step that crossed into it orange orange to red the clock in orange, and the slowest step so far slo 82% orange on the line that crossed red over red the clock in red, and the slowest step so far slo 104% red on the line that crossed

The plain total line ends with the time objective and the band reached: total 18.7s slo 8m, 3% green. The share is rounded down, so 99% is never shown red.

docs.title: The fitness function
docs.text:
nereus init --check-slo runs init as usual, then compares its total with the time objective plus the tolerance. Above it, init fails (exit code 1) after the cluster is ready and the config saved, with the total, the limit and the three slowest steps:

✗ init took 9m41s, over its time objective of 8m plus the 20% tolerance (9m36s); slowest steps: cluster nereus-scn-main-a3f9c2 9m12s, kinds and namespace 21.3s, registry localhost:5111 7.1s; shorten them, or raise the objective: nereus config slo set --local 10m

Between the objective and the limit, it warns and passes, with the same slowest steps and the same suggestion (#857). Without --check-slo, every init on the local target warns past the objective and exits 0, since the cluster is ready by then. The scenes that install the profile pass --check-slo too. test/scene runs init with --check-slo, so the scene job of CI fails when the local objective is missed. The check lives in the CLI, not in the script: the scene does not parse durations, and the output a person reads in the walkthrough stays the same. A CI runner is slower than a laptop: if the first runs show a steady gap, it is recorded on #141 rather than loosening the objective silently.

The cloud target is recorded (the default CLOUD and the field spec.targets.cloud), not enforced: init has no target on a cloud yet. When #92 and #61 add it, init maps that target to cloud as it maps k3d to local, and the same check applies.

The former key (#313). Before #313 the cloud target was keyed spec.targets.azure, the name of a Nereid, which the CLI never names (ADR 0002, ADR 0011). For one release the CRD keeps that field, so the API server does not prune it: the CLI reads any key of spec.targets that is no target's own as cloud when cloud is not set, config slo show warns with the command that moves it (nereus config slo set --cloud <duration>), and any config slo set writes it at cloud and drops the former key. The release after removes the field from the CRD.

docs.title: Security and quality attributes
docs.text:
Under the lens of #28, this slice is alpha.

  • Performance, as a fitness function: the time of init is checked on every pull request, against a value in code that a one-line PR changes with its reason.
  • What a person sets is validated before it reaches the cluster (durations with re.fullmatch, percents in range, bands in order), and again by the CRD's schema.
  • Fitness functions of the slice: unit tests of the bands, the plain and live output, the check and the command; the CRD contract tests; test/scene end to end, with --check-slo.
  • What beta would need: per-step objectives from the median of earlier runs (#141), and the history of runs (#102).

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Service level objectives (Chris Jones, John Wilkes and Niall Murphy, with Cody Smith, "Service Level Objectives", in Google's Site Reliability Engineering book; sre.google): a target value for a measured quality; here, the time of init.
  • Fitness functions come from Building Evolutionary Architectures (Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, O'Reilly, 2017; evolutionaryarchitecture.com): an automated check that a quality of the architecture holds, run on every change. init --check-slo is one.
  • Cluster API's clusterctl move (cluster-api.sigs.k8s.io): the pivot of the objects from the undercloud to the overcloud.

docs.title: 0005. Cloud reef: how the platform presents itself to a cloud
docs.text: Status: Accepted (2026-10-19)

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The platform reaches a person's cloud resources (the Key Vault of #81, the Terraform Stacks of #92 and #93) as identities of its own, with no credential kept anywhere: no client secret, no certificate, no copy of the person's login. This spec turns the decisions of #82 and the owner's answers on PR #151 into a design:

  • The connection to a cloud is a reef, cloud (decision 2). Each connection is an Instance, and azure is its first Nereid. Nereids that reach a cloud declare requires: cloud, which layer 1 of spec 0003 already checks when a Nereid is added.
  • The platform proves who it is through workload identity federation, from the k3d undercloud too (decision 1). The cluster's service-account tokens are trusted by the cloud because the cluster's OIDC issuer is public: k3d's is published on public storage, AKS publishes its own.
  • One identity per reef and per installation (answer 2): a user-assigned managed identity named <installation>-<reef>-<role>, such as tailwind-secrets-reader, where tailwind is the installation's name (#154, spec 0006), with no platform prefix (answer 15). The identity is named after the reef, never the Nereid, so swapping the Nereid keeps the identity and its grants. It is the same identity before and after the pivot (#61).
  • One resource group per installation holds everything the installation creates in a subscription (answer 15): <installation>-platform (tailwind-platform), like the address platform.tailwind.com. Nothing is shared between installations in a subscription.
  • The person's own login creates what is needed, through requests the Nereid publishes (answer 1, decision 3): the azure Nereid decides which cloud requests to make; the CLI shows each one and runs it on the person's machine with their short-lived az token, after the person approves it.
  • The undercloud is born with the cloud reef (owner, 2026-10-19): nereus init --target azure creates the k3d cluster with its issuer URL already computed from the installation's id, adds the cloud reef, adds the azure Nereid, and that Nereid plans the bootstrap (the installation's resource group, the issuer storage, the person's grant on it, the issuer documents) that the person approves and the CLI runs with their az login, through the same request protocol. Publishing a cluster's issuer is how the platform presents itself to a cloud, so it belongs to the cloud reef's contract, not to a separate reef, and the CLI holds no Azure call of its own.
  • The first overcloud is AKS (owner's condition on decision 1): the first choice, for the owner's experience with Azure and because AKS provisioned faster than EKS when this spec was written (October 2026); EKS, GKE and other managed Kubernetes follow, each with its cloud Nereid. The k3d federation is the undercloud's stage of the same mechanism, which the overcloud keeps after the pivot.
  • Every cloud resource created as the platform says which installation created it and who asked (the requester-tags requirement on #82, the contract of #155).

Not the authentication of the platform's own users (ADR 0006, authentication is a reef: OIDC inwards, any protocol outwards): this is the platform authenticating outward.

The spike of #82 passed: a pod of a k3d cluster named undercloud, service account nereus-system/keyvault, read a test secret from a test vault through workload identity federation, with nothing stored. Its findings are design inputs below.

docs.title: The scene that ends the slice
docs.text:
A person with an Azure login, on a laptop with Docker and k3d. It needs a cloud, so it runs by hand in the owner's sandbox subscription (test/scene-azure), not in CI (answer 6, see Walkthrough and scene).

# journey step 0: the person's own login
az login

# tailwind-undercloud with its computed issuer; adds the cloud reef, adds the azure Nereid, shows the bootstrap plan
# (tailwind-platform, issuers<id16>, the person's grant, the issuer documents, tailwind-cloud-provisioner)
nereus init \
  --target azure \
  --yes

nereus reef apply secrets --from-file ./reefs/secrets/

# requires cloud: shows the plan for tailwind-secrets-reader and its federated credential
nereus nereid apply keyvault --reef secrets

# every request waiting for approval, in plain words
nereus system access list
# REEF       REQUEST   WHAT                                                              STATE
# secrets    r-01jaqb  grant Key Vault Secrets User on vault-<id16> to tailwind-secrets-reader  Pending

# runs them with the person's az login
nereus system access approve secrets

nereus init with no --target azure creates nereus, and nothing here changes it.

Approving in one step (owner, 2026-10-19). In the MVP the person who installs approves their own requests; handing them to someone else (a plan file, an approver role, a pull request) is #259's.

  • nereus system access approve --all shows one plan with every waiting request, numbered (1/3 secrets, 2/3 terraform, 3/3 cloud), each with its role, scope, identity and description, then asks once. A failed request does not undo the others; running it again applies only what is missing.

  • An access request in a plan (owner, 2026-10-19) is one sentence, then its purpose under a why: label, in the same words as the resource's nereus-purpose:

    access  grant Storage Blob Data Contributor on issuers<id16> to maria@example.com
        why: To publish the issuer documents of the undercloud of installation tailwind.

    With colours on, the verb, the role, the resource and who receives it each have their own colour, and the purpose is grey; with NO_COLOR or outside a terminal, the same text. - --approve-access on nereus init and nereus nereid apply approves, during that run, every access request the run itself makes, after printing them in the plan, without a second question: the demo runs end to end with one command. Without it, an interactive run asks; a run that is not interactive stops before the first grant and prints nereus system access approve --all. - --dry-run (#242) on any of them prints the access requests as part of the plan and runs none.

docs.title: The neutral words, mapped before the contract is fixed
docs.text:
"Subscription" and "tenant" are Azure's words. The contract names only what every cloud has (decision 2), and this table checks the third cloud on paper before the first is built.

Neutral word Azure AWS GCP account: where the platform acts and is billed subscription (00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000) account (123456789012) project (example-project) organization (optional): above the account Entra ID tenant: always present, so the azure Nereid requires it organization (o-a1b2c3d4e5), optional organization (organizations/123456789012), optional identity: who the platform presents itself as, one per reef user-assigned managed identity, by its client id IAM role, by its ARN service account, by its e-mail (tailwind-secrets-reader@example-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com) principal: what roles are granted to the managed identity's principal (object) id the role's ARN the service account trust: what accepts the cluster's tokens a federated identity credential on the managed identity (issuer, subject, audience) an IAM OIDC identity provider, plus the role's trust policy on sub and aud a workload identity pool and its OIDC provider, plus an IAM binding on the subject audience the token carries api://AzureADTokenExchange sts.amazonaws.com the provider's resource name exchange: the token traded for a cloud token Entra ID token endpoint, client assertion STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity STS token exchange, then impersonation of the service account public issuer for a local cluster discovery document and JWKS on public blob storage the same, on public S3 not needed: an OIDC provider accepts an uploaded JWKS grant: a role on a scope role assignment (role definition, ARM resource id) an IAM policy on the role, naming resource ARNs an IAM policy binding on the resource where identities live, outliving any cluster a resource group of the installation the account (IAM is global to it) the project resource attributes (see Requester tags) tags tags labels the person's login the CLI uses az aws gcloud

What the table shows: the subject is the same string everywhere (system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<serviceaccount>), the issuer is the same URL, and every cloud has an identity that roles attach to and that trusts an issuer with no secret. So the contract carries the reef, the issuer and the audience; how identities, trust and grants are written stays in each Nereid.

docs.title: The objects
docs.text:
Where they come from (owner, 2026-10-18; the details are #18's): the reef ships its own CRDs, never its first Nereid. nereus reef apply cloud --from-file ./reefs/cloud/ applies the version this CLI pins, and fails when the reef exists, as kubectl create does, printing the apply commands to run instead (pinned version, --image, --path); nereus reef apply cloud creates or updates, to the pinned version, or from --image <ref> (an OCI package) or --path <file or folder> (local YAML). Every command that changes something has --dry-run (#242): nereid apply azure --dry-run and access approve --dry-run show the plan's requests and run none.

ADR 0011's shape: a Mandate per Nereid, an Instance with generic parameters, and the Reef object naming the reef's default Instance.

apiVersion: core.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Mandate
metadata:
  name: azure
  labels:
    core.getnereus.dev/nereid: azure
    core.getnereus.dev/reef: cloud
spec:
  reef: cloud
  nereid: azure
  default: true
---
kind: Cloud
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  mandate: azure
  account: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  organization: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  issuers:
    - {cluster: undercloud, url: "https://issuers<id16>.blob.core.windows.net/oidc/undercloud/"}
  access:
    - {reef: cloud, request: r-01jaq3}
    - {reef: secrets, request: r-01jaq7}
    - {reef: secrets, role: Key Vault Secrets User, scope: /subscriptions/.../vaults/vault-<id16>, request: r-01jaqb}
  approved: [r-01jaq3, r-01jaq7]
status:
  installation: {id: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000, name: tailwind, cluster: undercloud}
  issuer: https://issuers<id16>.blob.core.windows.net/oidc/undercloud/
  audience: api://AzureADTokenExchange
  issuers:
    - {cluster: undercloud, url: "https://issuers<id16>.blob.core.windows.net/oidc/undercloud/", state: Published, jwks: "sha256:<hex>", publishedAt: "2026-10-19T12:00:00Z"}
  identities:
    - {reef: cloud, name: tailwind-cloud-provisioner, identity: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000, principal: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000, state: Applied}
    - {reef: secrets, name: tailwind-secrets-reader, identity: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000, principal: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000, state: Applied}
  plans:
    - request: r-01jaqb
      reef: secrets
      requests:
        - {method: PUT, url: "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/.../roleAssignments/...?api-version=...", body: {...}}
  conditions:
    - {type: Ready, status: "True", reason: TokenExchanged}
Field Writer (ADR 0005) Meaning spec.mandate the CLI the Mandate, so the Nereid spec.account the CLI the account, in the cloud's own form spec.organization the CLI the organization above it, when the cloud has one; empty otherwise spec.resourceGroup the CLI where the installation's resources live in the account, <installation>-platform: a full name from the naming function, never one the Controller composes (#307) spec.issuers[] the CLI the issuers the installation's clusters need published, each a cluster role (undercloud) and its URL, which init --target azure computes with the naming function before the cluster exists; no entry for a cluster whose cloud publishes its own issuer (AKS) (owner, 2026-10-19) spec.access[] the CLI what a reef needs from the cloud: its identity, and optionally a role on a scope, each with a request id spec.access[].name the CLI the identity's full name, <installation>-<reef>-<role>, from the naming function (#307) spec.access[].identity the CLI an identity an admin created, adopted instead of creating one (--param identity=<id>) spec.approved[] the CLI the request ids whose plan the person approved and the CLI ran status.installation the Controller the installation's id and name (#154, spec 0006) and the cluster's role (undercloud, overcloud), read from the installation's object status.issuer the Controller the issuer the cluster presents, read from the cluster's own /.well-known/openid-configuration status.audience the Controller the audience a projected token must carry for this cloud status.issuers[] the Controller per entry of spec.issuers[]: its state (Pending until its plan runs, Published, Stale when the cluster's JWKS differs from the published one), the digest of the JWKS published and when status.identities[] the Controller per reef: the identity's name, its id, its principal and its state (Applied, Pending while it propagates, Refused with a reason) status.identities[].request, .credential the Controller the request whose answers wrote the identity (or whose entry it refused before any plan), and the federated credential that trusts its reef's Nereid now; Retiring marks an identity a role word replaced, deleted by a plan of its own (#310) status.grants[] the Controller per access entry with a role: its request, role, scope and principal, Applied or Refused with what an administrator has to run, so a run again applies only what is missing (#310) status.plans[] the Controller per request id not yet approved: the cloud requests it needs, exactly as the CLI will run them; an access entry of another reef keeps its plan, unchanged, until its answers come back (#310) status.conditions the Controller Ready when its own token exchange passes; Stalled (True, with a reason, a message (at most 300 characters) and the observedGeneration it was written for, and the refusal's cause (300), check (200) and fix (200) when it knows them, ADR 0012) when it refuses the Instance as it is and plans nothing until its spec changes (#318, #327)
  • Keyed by reef, never by Nereid. No Nereid's name or kind sits in the reef's objects (ADR 0002, ADR 0011). The service account a federated credential trusts is found from the Nereid added for that reef (its Nereid object's reef); a swap changes that, and the Controller plans the new credential.
  • Values in the cloud's own form are opaque to the contract. account, organization, identity, role and scope are strings the reef does not parse; the Nereid validates them. A role name or a resource id is a value of the cloud, not of a Nereid.
  • The subject is never written: it is always system:serviceaccount:nereus-system:<serviceaccount>, and the service account is the one the CLI creates per Nereid (cluster.workload).
  • One Instance, default, per Nereid, as ADR 0011 says. Several accounts at once wait for a need.
  • spec.issuers[] says what to publish, never what the cluster presents: status.issuer is still read from the cluster, and the Controller refuses an entry for its own cluster whose URL differs from it, so the two never disagree.

docs.title: What every cloud Nereid adds and validates itself
docs.text:
Azure (azure) AWS (later) GCP (later) account a GUID 12 digits a project id, ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{4,28}[a-z0-9]$ organization required, a GUID optional, ^o-[a-z0-9]{10,32}$ optional, ^organizations/[0-9]+$ identity (adopted) a managed identity's client id, in account a role ARN in account a service account e-mail in account identity names letters, digits, - and _, 3–128 characters 64 characters 6–30 characters: <installation>-<reef>-<role> may need shortening there scope of a grant an ARM id starting with /subscriptions/<account>/ an ARN in account a resource name in account role of a grant a role definition that exists, never Owner, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator a managed or customer policy, never AdministratorAccess or IAMFullAccess a role, never roles/owner or roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin issuer https, publicly reachable, or not yet published when its own plan publishes it (bootstrap mode) the same the JWKS read from the cluster

The Nereid refuses an issuer that is not public (Kubernetes' default issuer, https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local) with the fix: nereus init --target azure. Bootstrap mode (owner, 2026-10-19): an issuer not yet published is accepted when spec.issuers[] lists it for the Controller's own cluster, under the installation's issuer storage, because the Nereid's own plan publishes it; the Controller is Ready only once it is published and its token exchange passes. Kubernetes' default issuer can never be published, so it is refused in every mode. A refusal is final for the spec it read (#318): the Controller writes no plan, sets Ready to False and Stalled to True, both with the reason and the message, and Stalled names the Instance's metadata.generation in observedGeneration. The refusal's fields (ADR 0012, #327): the message (at most 300 characters) says what happened, naming the cluster by its role and installation (the undercloud of installation tailwind, or the cluster of installation tailwind when the role is unknown), never by its Kubernetes distribution; Stalled adds, when the Controller knows them, cause (the probable cause, at most 300 characters), check (a command that confirms it, 200) and fix (a command ready to copy, 200), which the CRD keeps. For Kubernetes' default issuer the Controller writes: message the undercloud of installation tailwind presents Kubernetes' default issuer https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local, which Azure cannot reach; cause probably created by nereus init without --target azure (k3d is the default): the issuer is set when the cluster is created and never changes after; check kubectl get --raw /.well-known/openid-configuration; fix nereus init --target azure --installation-name <installation>. The CLI stops waiting for the plan as soon as it reads a Stalled for the current generation, and prints the reason, then one line per field (what, cause, check, fix) and Nothing ran in the cloud. (the closing line is the caller's, where it holds: nereid apply's plan step adds it, system access approve does not), each cleaned like any text a Nereid publishes and cut at its limit, never naming the Nereid; a refusal with only a message prints as one line, the reason and the message; a Stalled of an earlier generation says nothing about the spec the CLI just wrote. The name follows the Stalled condition of Kubernetes' kstatus.

docs.title: How the Nereid acts with the person's login: the request protocol
docs.text:
Creating identities and grants needs the person's rights, which only the person's machine holds. Azure code inside the CLI would name a Nereid (ADR 0002), and sending the person's token to a pod would put a broad Entra ID token inside an image that may come from outside the catalog (#85). So the CLI is the hands and the Nereid is the brain (answer 1):

  1. The image declares the login it needs, in the label <API_GROUP>/login, one of the Tools the CLI knows: az, later aws, gcloud. The CLI keeps one fixed entry per Tool: how to get a short-lived token for each of its hosts (for az: az account get-access-token --resource <host>, for management.azure.com, and with --resource https://storage.azure.com/ for the blob host of the issuer storage account named in spec.issuers[], which the bootstrap publishes to; graph.microsoft.com only if an app registration is ever needed, #234) and the current account and organization from the same answer. The label only selects an entry; no command is built from it.
  2. The CLI writes what is asked, an access entry in spec.access with a new request id, and the requester's annotations (Requester tags).
  3. The Controller plans: it writes in status.plans the cloud requests the entry needs, each with its method, https URL and JSON body, its tags already in the body. A request may use a field of an earlier answer of the same plan, written ${<n>.<json path>} (the principal id of an identity created by request 0, for a role assignment), so the whole plan is shown before anything runs.
  4. The person approves, and the CLI runs the plan with the person's token, in order, printing each request; nothing runs without approval (answer 5). The CLI then records the request id in spec.approved and posts the answers to the Controller (POST /cloud/answers), which reads the result into status. A refused request (403) stops the plan; the Controller turns it into what an admin has to run.
  5. What the CLI accepts in a plan: https only; the hosts of the declared Tool only; no header but Content-Type (the CLI adds Authorization, and for a blob host the fixed x-ms-blob-type and x-ms-version of the Tool's entry); bodies up to 64 KiB, answers capped at 1 MiB; at most 50 requests per plan; a substitution only from an earlier answer of the same plan, only into a string, and only when the value is a short string of letters, digits, -, _, . and /; text from the Controller shown as text (ADR 0004's rule).

The token never leaves the person's machine, every change is listed before it runs, and the cloud's code lives in the Nereid's repository (cloud-azure-controller).

docs.title: nereus nereid apply azure
docs.text:
nereus init --target azure runs it for the undercloud (see The k3d undercloud issuer); a person runs it by hand on a cluster that already exists (#77) or to pick another subscription. The image declares reef=cloud, nereid=azure, login=az. After layer 1 of spec 0003:

  1. The login. The CLI reads a token and the current account and organization from az. --param account=<id> picks another subscription of the same login.
  2. The Instance. The CLI writes the Mandate of the cloud reef, the Cloud Instance default (account, organization, and location: --param location=<region>, else the Instance's own, else the person's az default, az config get defaults.location; with none, the CLI stops before writing anything, and the Controller refuses an Instance without one, Stalled, #319) and the access entry of the cloud reef itself. The Controller starts, not Ready yet, and plans:
  3. the installation's resource group <installation>-platform (answer 15), which holds everything the installation creates in the subscription and outlives the undercloud; the plan's PUT is idempotent, so the same plan serves init --target azure and an installation into a cluster that already exists (#77);
  4. the bootstrap, when spec.issuers[] lists an issuer not yet published (bootstrap mode): the issuer storage, the person's grant on it and the issuer documents, before the identity (see The k3d undercloud issuer);
  5. the identity <installation>-cloud-provisioner, with no role: it proves the federation end to end before any other reef needs it, and makes the Controller Ready;
  6. its federated credential <cluster>-azure (tailwind-undercloud-azure), named by the CLI's naming function into spec.access[].credential, the cluster's role from the entry of spec.issuers[] whose URL is the issuer the cluster presents (#319): the issuer from status.issuer (trailing slash kept), the subject system:serviceaccount:nereus-system:azure, the audience api://AzureADTokenExchange.
  7. The approval. The CLI shows the plan and asks; with the person's yes, it runs it.
  8. Ready. The Controller exchanges its own projected token. A new credential takes about a minute to apply (the spike's finding): the first exchanges are refused, so the Controller retries with backoff for up to five minutes, and the CLI waits on Ready, saying why.
$ nereus nereid apply azure --reef cloud
✓ image                    0.4s  cloud-azure-controller:0.1.0 implements cloud, login az
✓ login                    0.9s  az, account 00000000-…, organization from the login
✓ plan                     1.2s  3 requests for cloud (r-01jaq3)
  create  resource group        tailwind-platform
          why: To hold what installation tailwind creates in this subscription.
  create  managed identity      tailwind-cloud-provisioner
          why: To prove the federation of the cloud reef of installation tailwind.
  create  federated credential  tailwind-undercloud-azure  in tailwind-cloud-provisioner
Run these 3 requests with your az login? [y/N] y
✓ requests                 3.4s  3 applied
✓ token exchange          48.2s  accepted after 6 tries (Azure applies a new credential in about a minute)
  total                   54.1s
✓ azure installed into cloud · instance default · identity tailwind-cloud-provisioner

A plan reads in plain words (owner, 2026-10-19): each step is a verb a person knows (create, grant, publish, delete), the kind of resource and its name; the HTTP method and URL a step runs (PUT management.azure.com/...) show only with --show-requests, and the audit log (#256) keeps them always. The request protocol (above) is unchanged: the words are derived from it by the CLI, never sent by the Nereid.

No Entra ID role is needed. Managed identities and their federated credentials are Azure resources: creating them needs Contributor (or Managed Identity Contributor) on the installation's resource group, and creating that group needs Contributor on the subscription. A grant needs a role-assignment right on its scope. When the person lacks a right, the request is refused (403), the CLI stops, lists what ran and what did not, and prints what an admin has to run:

✗ requests  create managed identity tailwind-cloud-provisioner refused: the signed-in account cannot create managed identities in tailwind-platform
An administrator can create the identity, and give you Managed Identity Contributor on it:
  az identity create --resource-group tailwind-platform --name tailwind-cloud-provisioner
  az role assignment create --assignee <your-object-id> --role "Managed Identity Contributor" --scope <identity-id>
Then run:
  nereus nereid apply azure --reef cloud --param identity=<client-id>
  • --param identity=<id> adopts an identity an admin created (answer 5, provisional). For any Nereid that requires cloud, and for azure itself, the CLI takes it for the access entry of that Nereid's reef in the Cloud Instance, not for the Nereid's own Instance. The plan then checks it is in account and adds only the federated credential, which Managed Identity Contributor on the identity allows.
  • Role assignments are created with the principal's id and type ServicePrincipal, so a principal created seconds earlier is accepted before Entra ID replicates it; a PrincipalNotFound is retried.

docs.title: A dependent Nereid: the Key Vault of #81
docs.text:
A Nereid that reaches the cloud declares requires: cloud. It acts as its reef's identity, never with a secret of its own:

  1. When it is added (nereus nereid apply keyvault --reef secrets), the CLI, for any Nereid that requires cloud:
  2. adds a projected serviceAccountToken volume to its Deployment, with the audience the active Cloud Instance publishes in status.audience (validated as a short printable string before it becomes a pod field), one hour long, at /var/run/secrets/<API_GROUP>/cloud/token, and the variable CLOUD_TOKEN_FILE naming it. The spike showed this is enough: the Azure Workload Identity webhook is not needed;
  3. lets its service account get the Cloud Instances, where it reads its reef's entry in status.identities, the organization and the account;
  4. writes the access entry of its reef ({reef: secrets}); the Controller plans the identity <installation>-secrets-reader when it does not exist yet, and the federated credential <cluster>-keyvault; the CLI shows the plan and runs it once approved.
  5. When it needs a role, the Key Vault Nereid says so in its own Instance's status.cloudAccess ({role: Key Vault Secrets User, scope: <vault id>}), once it knows the vault (#81 decides when). It never grants itself anything.
  6. The person approves. nereus system access list shows what Nereids ask in their Instances and every plan waiting, each request exactly as it will run; nereus system access approve secrets copies what the reef's Nereid asked into the Cloud Instance's spec.access, waits for the plan, shows it, and runs it. The azure Nereid validates the role and the scope (the table above) before planning, and retries while the grant applies.

A swap keeps the identity. When another Nereid takes over the secrets reef, adding it plans one request pair: delete the old federated credential, create one for the new Nereid's service account. The identity and its role grants stay, so the new Nereid reads the same vault with no new approval of roles.

A Stack runner reaches Azure the same way (#93): <installation>-terraform-runner, its federated credentials on both clusters, and the projected token passed to azurerm as ARM_USE_OIDC=true, ARM_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE_PATH, ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_TENANT_ID and ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, the state backend (the storage account state<id16>, container terraform) with use_oidc and use_azuread_auth. In terraform-packager this is an additive path, chosen only by an explicit signal: the service-principal path and the Azure CLI fallback (no ARM_* set) behave as today (the owner's decision on #93).

The spike found that Owner of the subscription can neither read nor write secrets in a vault that uses RBAC: writing a secret needs Key Vault Secrets Officer on the vault. Which role the Key Vault asks for, and when, is #81's; this spec gives it the way to ask.

docs.title: Identity, credential and federation
docs.text:
Three Azure words this spec uses together:

  • Managed identity: the identity itself, an Azure resource that roles are granted to.

  • Federated credential: a rule inside the identity: tokens from this issuer, for this subject, with this audience, are accepted as the identity. One per cluster.

  • Workload identity: the exchange itself: a pod trades its service account token at Entra ID for a token of the identity, then calls Azure as that identity.

docs.title: The k3d undercloud issuer
docs.text:
nereus init --target azure makes the k3d cluster an undercloud, and the cluster is born with the cloud reef (owner, 2026-10-19). k3s takes its issuer as an argument, so the issuer's URL is computed before the cluster exists, from the installation's id alone; its documents are published after, by the azure Nereid, through a plan the person approves. The word azure in --target azure is the person's input naming the Nereid init adds, not code of the CLI: the CLI holds no Azure call of its own, so cli/tests/test_boundaries.py needs no exemption.

  1. The installation. init creates the installation's object of #154 (its name, tailwind, and its id, spec 0006) when it does not exist, and records the cluster's role, undercloud.

  2. The cluster <installation>-undercloud, with two k3s arguments and k3s's own signing key. The URL comes from the naming function (issuers<id16>, or the override issuer.storage), with nothing created in Azure yet:

    --k3s-arg "--kube-apiserver-arg=service-account-issuer=https://issuers<id16>.blob.core.windows.net/oidc/undercloud/@server:*"
--k3s-arg "--kube-apiserver-arg=service-account-jwks-uri=https://issuers<id16>.blob.core.windows.net/oidc/undercloud/openid/v1/jwks@server:*"

  3. The cloud reef and the azure Nereid. init runs nereus reef apply cloud --from-file ./reefs/cloud/ and nereus nereid apply azure --reef cloud, and writes the undercloud's entry in the Cloud Instance's spec.issuers[] with the same URL. The Nereid accepts that issuer before it is published, because its own plan publishes it (bootstrap mode).

  4. The names, checked before anything is created. The Nereid's first plan is read-only: Azure's checkNameAvailability for the storage account and a GET of the resource group. A taken name stops init before any create, with the suggestion of Naming conventions. The CLI runs this plan without a question, before it shows the bootstrap plan, only when every request is, whole URL and body, one it composes itself from the person's login and the naming function (the forms fixed in the Tool's entry): the checkNameAvailability POST of the issuer storage's name, the GET of the resource group naming.resource_group names, and the GET of the storage account naming.issuer_storage names in it (#335). Any other request, even a read, would let the Nereid read with the person's login what it was never given, so the plan is shown in plain words and approved by the same path as the bootstrap plan (step 6), never run unasked. A 404 ends it as an answer (#263). The answers posted back to the Controller carry each status and, for the check, nameAvailable and reason only, never a body (#335).
  5. The bootstrap plan. The Nereid plans, in order: the installation's resource group tailwind-platform; its issuer storage account issuers<id16>, which allows anonymous blob access and no shared key; the container oidc, with anonymous read of blobs only (access level blob, so nobody can list it); the grant of Storage Blob Data Contributor on that account to the person; the documents and the manifest under oidc/undercloud/; then the identity tailwind-cloud-provisioner and its federated credential, as nereus nereid apply azure says. The uploads use the person's login, so they wait for that grant, and are retried while it applies: Owner alone does not give data access, as the spike found for Key Vault. The account belongs to the installation alone, so only its administrators hold that right and nobody else can replace its keys. When the person lacks a right, the CLI prints what an admin has to run, as for any plan.
  6. The approval, by the same path as any plan: the CLI shows it in plain words and asks; --approve-access approves it during the run, --dry-run prints it and runs none, --show-requests adds each step's method and URL, and a run that is not interactive stops before the first grant and prints nereus system access approve --all.
  7. The documents. The Controller reads /.well-known/openid-configuration and /openid/v1/jwks from its own cluster's API (its service account is bound to system:service-account-issuer-discovery) and writes them into the plan's bodies, to the same paths under the container, as application/json; the person sees them before approving, and they hold public keys only.
  8. The manifest (owner, 2026-10-18). Next to the documents, manifest.json explains each file in the folder: its path, what it is, which cluster it belongs to, and when it was published. A folder whose cluster publishes its own issuer still holds a manifest, with no documents, saying where that cluster's issuer is and why nothing is published here: a managed overcloud's oidc/overcloud/manifest.json (AKS, EKS, GKE) points to the issuer its cloud publishes. So every installation's issuer reads the same way, whatever its clusters.
  9. Republishing. A recreated cluster has new signing keys. The Controller compares the published JWKS with its cluster's, marks the entry Stale in status.issuers[] when they differ, and plans the upload; every init --target azure approves it. The federated credentials need no change: the issuer URL and the subjects stay the same, so they serve the new cluster as soon as its keys are published.
  10. A taken storage name changes the issuer URL (owner, 2026-10-19).
