The URL holds the storage account's name, so once the person accepts a suggested name (or records one with nereus config installation set --naming-override), init recreates the k3d cluster with the new issuer, which takes seconds, and adds cloud and azure again; the plan then runs. It is rare: 16 hex characters of a random id make a chance collision near impossible.

The trailing slash stays in all three places: the k3s argument, the uploaded issuer, and every federated credential (the spike's finding). k3s writes the document's issuer from its argument, so one constant feeds both.

undercloud only when init targets a cloud. A plain nereus init names its cluster nereus: a cluster that only receives the platform is not an undercloud. It is the same case as a cluster someone created beforehand and installs the platform into, later through the operator and GitOps (#77). A cluster is an undercloud only when it bootstraps a cloud and hands over to the overcloud at the pivot (#61); then it is named <installation>-undercloud (tailwind-undercloud), so two installations on one machine never collide (owner, 2026-10-19).

New steps of init's progress (#88), with the same marks and times: cluster tailwind-undercloud with its issuer, reef cloud, the steps of nereid apply azure (image, login, names, plan, requests), issuer documents published (or unchanged) and token exchange. They count against the Azure SLO of spec 0004 once init has that target.

$ nereus init \
    --target azure \
    --approve-access
✓ installation             0.1s  tailwind
✓ cluster                 18.4s  tailwind-undercloud, issuer https://issuers<id16>.blob.core.windows.net/oidc/undercloud/
✓ reef                     0.6s  cloud 0.1.0
✓ image                    0.4s  cloud-azure-controller:0.1.0 implements cloud, login az
✓ login                    0.9s  az, account 00000000-…, organization from the login
✓ names                    1.1s  tailwind-platform and issuers<id16> are free
✓ plan                     1.3s  9 requests for cloud (r-01jaq3)
  create   resource group        tailwind-platform
           why: To hold what installation tailwind creates in this subscription.
  create   storage account       issuers<id16>
           why: To publish the OIDC issuers of the clusters of installation tailwind.
  create   container             oidc  in issuers<id16>
  access   grant Storage Blob Data Contributor on issuers<id16> to maria@example.com
           why: To publish the issuer documents of the undercloud of installation tailwind.
  publish  issuer documents      oidc/undercloud/  openid-configuration, jwks, manifest
  create   managed identity      tailwind-cloud-provisioner
           why: To prove the federation of the cloud reef of installation tailwind.
  create   federated credential  tailwind-undercloud-azure  in tailwind-cloud-provisioner
✓ requests                12.7s  9 applied
✓ issuer documents         0.2s  published
✓ token exchange          48.2s  accepted after 6 tries (Azure applies a new credential in about a minute)
  total                   84.0s

docs.title: The overcloud and the pivot
docs.text:
The first overcloud is AKS, created with its OIDC issuer and workload identity on; EKS and GKE work the same way, each publishing its own issuer. AKS publishes its own issuer (https://<region>.oic.prod-aks.azure.com/<tenant>/<id>/), so nothing is uploaded there.

The undercloud and the overcloud are one installation (#154), so they share its identities. What the pivot (#61) does:

  • The objects move, as clusterctl move moves them: the cloud reef, its Mandate, the Cloud Instance with its spec.access and spec.approved, the installation's object, and the Nereids.
  • The identities stay, and so do their grants. Each identity gains a federated credential for the AKS issuer, <installation>-overcloud-<serviceaccount> (tailwind-overcloud-keyvault), planned by the Controller and approved by the person running the pivot. Each holds two of its 20 federated credentials only during the pivot.
  • The undercloud's credentials go with the undercloud: when the k3d is deleted, its undercloud-... credentials are removed, and so are the documents in its issuer folder (oidc/undercloud/), whose manifest then says the undercloud is gone. The identities and the issuer's storage account live in the installation's resource group, so deleting the undercloud deletes none of them.
  • status is never moved: the Controller in the overcloud recomputes it (issuer, identities, plans), as every Controller writes only its own status (ADR 0005).
  • The undercloud on demand (destroy or recovery) brings a new k3d, republishes its keys, and gets its undercloud-... credentials back through a plan.
  • No certificate or client secret at any stage: the same mechanism from the first init to the overcloud.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
From decision 4 and answers 2 and 15. <installation> is the installation's name, the metadata.name of its object (spec 0006), which never changes; <id16> is the first 16 hex characters of the installation's id, dashes removed; <reef> is the reef's name; <cluster> is the cluster's role. Subscription and tenant ids never go in this repository, nor in a name.

Resource Pattern Example The installation's resource group: everything the installation creates in a subscription <installation>-platform tailwind-platform Managed identity, one per reef and installation <installation>-<reef>-<role> tailwind-cloud-provisioner, tailwind-secrets-reader, tailwind-terraform-runner Federated credential, one per cluster and Controller, inside its identity <cluster>-<serviceaccount>; the namespace is always nereus-system, so it is left out tailwind-undercloud-keyvault, tailwind-overcloud-keyvault Issuer storage account (3–24 lowercase letters and digits, unique in Azure) issuers<id16>, 23 characters issuers<id16> OIDC issuer of a cluster that publishes none (k3d, a k3s overcloud) the public-read container oidc of the issuer storage account, a folder per cluster role https://issuers<id16>.blob.core.windows.net/oidc/undercloud/ Terraform state storage account (3–24 lowercase letters and digits, unique in Azure, private) state<id16>, 21 characters state<id16> Terraform state container terraform, blob stacks/<stack>/<STACK_INSTANCE_NAME>.state.json, one state per instance of a Stack terraform/stacks/azure-cluster/default.state.json Key Vault (3–24 characters, unique in Azure) vault-<id16>, 22 characters vault-<id16> Clusters, by role <installation>-undercloud (the k3d cluster, when init targets a cloud; nereus otherwise), <installation>-overcloud tailwind-undercloud, tailwind-overcloud
  • Names after the installation, with no prefix (answer 15, 2026-10-18, superseding parts of answers 7, 8, 11, 13 and 14 and of decision 4): the installation's name plays the role a company prefix played in the owner's sandbox, so no generated name carries a platform prefix. The tags keep their fixed platform- keys (#155), which a SIEM filters on.
  • An identity is named for what it does (owner, 2026-10-19): <installation>-<reef>-<role>, where <role> is one word the reef's contract fixes for its identity (cloud: provisioner, secrets: reader, terraform: runner), never chosen by a Nereid. A role that grows later (a reader that also writes) changes the word, and the identity is recreated (next item).
  • A role that changes recreates the identity (owner, 2026-10-19): Azure does not rename a managed identity, so when a reef's role word changes (reader to manager), its Controller plans a swap the person approves, like any plan: create the new identity with its grants and one federated credential per cluster, wait for the grants to apply, point the Controller's service account to it and restart it, then delete the old one. Both exist during the swap, so access never stops, and the name always says what the identity does. The same swap replaces a compromised identity. The cloud's log shows another identity from then on; the platform's audit log (#256) and the installation's tags keep the continuity.
  • <installation>-<what> where the length allows, <id16> where it does not. Storage accounts and Key Vaults are unique across Azure and allow 24 characters, while an installation's name may have 63, so they take a fixed word and <id16> (64 bits of the random id). The subscription id is never part of a name.
  • One resource group per installation, <installation>-platform, like the address platform.tailwind.com: it holds everything the installation creates in a subscription (its identities, its issuer storage account, its state storage account, its vault), outlives the undercloud, and is deleted with the installation. The azure Nereid's plan creates it with an idempotent PUT, during init --target azure or nereid apply azure. Two installations in one subscription share nothing.
  • The issuer belongs to the installation (answers 11 and 13, as changed by answer 15): its storage account issuers<id16> holds the public-read container oidc (anonymous read of blobs, no listing) and, inside it, undercloud/ and overcloud/, each with its manifest.json; overcloud/ holds documents only when the overcloud publishes no issuer of its own (a k3s overcloud, #182), and a managed overcloud's (AKS, EKS, GKE) holds only its manifest. Only the installation's administrators may write to that account, so nobody else can replace its keys and pass as its clusters. The pivot deletes undercloud/'s documents; deleting the installation deletes its resource group, and the account with it. The state's account, state<id16>, is a separate one and stays private.
  • A generated name can be taken. A global name (issuers<id16>, state<id16>, vault-<id16>) may belong to someone else. The error says what to run (ADR 0012), with a name checked free a moment ago (Azure's checkNameAvailability, run as a request of the Nereid's plan), and it is kept in the installation's spec.naming.overrides (issuer.storage, state.storage, secrets.vault), validated against that resource's own rules, and used from then on (owner, 2026-10-18):

- **Every name at once, before anything is created** (owner, 2026-10-18): the plan checks every name it would use before its first request runs: the global ones for availability, the others for an existing resource of the same name in their scope (a resource group the company already has). All collisions are reported together, so a person never fixes one, runs again and meets the next. Running the command again after recording the names resumes where it stopped: what exists is not created again. `--dry-run` (#242) shows the same check.
- **The suggestion keeps the generated name and adds a try number** (owner, 2026-10-19): the kind, the whole installation id, then a number, within the resource's limit: `issuers<id16>2` to `9`, `state<id16>02`, `vault-<id16>-2`. Never a name in another form, never a cut id. With colours on, the CLI prints the kind, the id and the try number each in its own colour, so a person sees which part is the installation's id; with `NO_COLOR` or outside a terminal, the same text without colour:

    ```text
    ✗ storage account issuers0b7e4c1a93d24f6e is taken in Azure
    ? Use issuers0b7e4c1a93d24f6e2 for issuer.storage? (Y/n)
    ```

- **Why a generated name is taken:** 16 hex characters make a chance collision near impossible; the likely causes are a deleted installation's resource with the same id, or a Key Vault Azure keeps for 90 days after deletion (soft delete). When the CLI finds one of these, the message says so and offers to recover or purge it before it offers a new name.
- **Interactive** (a terminal): the CLI asks whether to use the suggested name; with a yes, it records the override and goes on.
- **Not interactive** (`--yes`, CI, a workflow): it fails at once, with a non-zero exit code and the commands in the message; it never picks a name on its own, since a name chosen anew on every run would differ between runs.
- **Where it is kept:** the `Installation` object is the source of truth; when the installation came from a settings file, the command writes the file too, so a later `init` from it keeps the new name. The command says what it changed, one line each (owner, 2026-10-18):

    ```text
    $ nereus config installation set --naming-override issuer.storage=tailwindissuers01
    ✓ installation tailwind  naming.overrides.issuer.storage = tailwindissuers01
    ✓ file ~/.config/nereus/init.yaml  updated
    ```

- **An override names a resource to create, it never renames one** (owner, 2026-10-19): once the resource exists, `set --naming-override` for it fails and says only that the resource exists; nothing is changed:

    ```text
    $ nereus config installation set --naming-override issuer.storage=othername01
    ✗ issuer.storage: storage account tailwindissuers01 already exists
      for installation tailwind. Nothing was changed.
    ```

- The name ties resources to the installation; the id identifies it (answers 8 and 14, as changed by answer 15): the installation's name is its object's metadata.name, which Kubernetes never lets change, so one installation never mixes two names. What listings show is the alias (spec.alias, nereus config installation set --alias), which changes no resource name. A company that wants its resources under another name gets a new installation and migrates to it (#249). The id in #155's tags ties a cloud resource to its installation. - Names are composed in one place, and automation receives full names (owner, 2026-10-18): one naming function turns this table's patterns, the installation's name and id, and its naming overrides into full names. Everything that creates or reads a resource (the azure Nereid's plans, the Terraform Stacks of #93, the scripts and the scene) takes the full name as an input, never composes one itself, so changing a pattern or adopting a customer's own naming convention changes one function, not every automation.

docs.title: Requester tags
docs.text:
In the cloud's activity log, the caller of everything the Controllers do is an identity of the platform, so the installation and the person or agent behind a request are lost unless the platform writes them. Every control-plane resource a Nereid creates through the cloud reef carries these attributes, in its cloud's own form (Azure tags, AWS tags, GCP labels), the contract of #155:

Tag Value Example nereus-installation-id the installation's id, a UUID (#154, spec.id in spec 0006) 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 nereus-installation its name (#154, metadata.name in spec 0006) tailwind nereus-requested-by who asked: cloud-<object id> of the person's cloud login until nereus login (#90; old form; users come through SSO (authentication reef); nereus user commands will be designed when Nereus needs them) exists, then the nereus user's id with its own prefix; an agent's identity (#25, #40) cloud-00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 nereus-request an id that also appears in the platform's own audit log (#256), so the two join r-01jaqb nereus-instance the Instance that asked, <namespace>_<name> nereus-system_default nereus-purpose why the resource exists, one sentence in English, at most 256 characters, one of the sentences the reef's contract fixes (below); in the resource's description instead when it has one (owner, 2026-10-19) To act as the secrets reef of installation tailwind.
  • Names neutral across clouds, values for the strictest one. GCP labels are the strictest: keys and values up to 63 characters, lowercase letters, digits, - and _, keys starting with a letter. Azure tags (names up to 512 characters, values up to 256, no <>%&\?/ in names, 50 per resource) and AWS tags (keys up to 128, values up to 256, aws: reserved, 50 per resource) accept the same strings. So one value reads the same in every cloud: _ separates namespace and name (Kubernetes names never hold it). A value is lowercased; one that still holds another character, or is over 63 characters, has those characters replaced by -, keeps its first 54 and ends with - and 8 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the whole value, so two values rarely read the same (values that differ only in case do, and a short hash is no proof of uniqueness), the full value staying in the audit log under the request id (#155: maria@example.com reads maria-example-com-<8 hex>). The prefix nereus comes from names.py; tags.value in the CLI is the reference, and the azure Nereid's contract test checks its own against it.
  • The purpose is written by the contract, not improvised (owner, 2026-10-19): a person who finds tailwind-secrets-reader in the portal reads why it exists without asking anyone. Each reef's contract fixes one sentence per kind of resource it creates, starting with To, so it reads after the plan's why:; the resource's own description holds it when it has one (Azure role assignments, GCP service accounts and buckets), else the tag nereus-purpose (Azure and AWS tag values allow 256 characters and spaces). GCP labels allow neither, so on GCP a resource with no description gets only the other attributes and the purpose stays in the audit log.

  • Where the sentences live (#155): in the annotations <API_GROUP>/purpose.<kind> of the reef's CRDs, next to the role word of its identity, so a new version of the contract changes them and no Nereid writes its own. Each is filled in by replacement, in one pass, with {installation}, {reef} (the reef of the plan) and {cluster} (a cluster role of spec.issuers[]). The cloud reef fixes five:

    Kind Sentence On resource-group To hold what installation {installation} creates in this subscription. the installation's resource group provisioner To prove the federation of the cloud reef of installation {installation}. the cloud reef's own identity identity To act as the {reef} reef of installation {installation}. another reef's identity, and a grant to it issuer-storage To publish the OIDC issuers of the clusters of installation {installation}. the issuer storage issuer-grant To publish the issuer documents of the {cluster} of installation {installation}. the person's grant on the issuer storage

  • The CLI checks every plan before it shows it (#155), as it checks the request protocol: every resource a plan creates or changes (a PUT or a PATCH on the Tool's own hosts: a PATCH can remove the tags) carries the five ids and a purpose of the contract, the installation's id and name and the Instance equal to this installation's, the request equal to the plan's, who asked equal to the requester the CLI wrote on the Cloud Instance (annotation <API_GROUP>/requested-by, from the person's own token), never whoever approves. An empty installation id or requester stops before the plan is shown; a purpose or a description that is not text is refused like a wrong one. A grant carries <purpose> Request <request id>. in its description instead. The kinds of the Tool with neither tags nor description (untagged, each under its own parent: federated credentials of a managed identity and blob containers of a storage account for az) and the uploads of the issuer documents are left to the audit log; a purpose any request carries anyway (its tag, or a grant's description, whatever the method) is still one of the contract's, since the plan shows it under why:. A plan that breaks it runs nothing and says what to add instead (ADR 0012); a cluster whose cloud reef fixes no purpose says to apply it again. The plan shows each resource's purpose under why:, a grant's without the request id the plan already names, and --show-requests adds the other tags under each request, so the person sees who asked and which request before approving. This is the first check of the cloud reef's conformance suite (spec 0003, layer 3), run on every plan until that suite exists.

  • One attribute each, never a combined value (#155): GCP values forbid @, and separate attributes filter better in a SIEM.
  • Ids always, names behind a policy. The ids are always written; the requester's name, personal data, is written only when the platform's compliance policy allows it (#155), and is off until that policy exists. The prefix of nereus-requested-by says where the id came from (answer 4).
  • The contract carries the requester, so no Nereid invents it. The CLI (the Platform API later) writes two annotations on every object it writes, <API_GROUP>/requested-by and <API_GROUP>/request; the installation comes from the Cloud Instance's status. A cloud Nereid, and every Nereid acting through it, copies them into the tags of each resource it creates; the azure Nereid writes them into the bodies of its plans, where the person sees them before approving. Who asked is the person's own cloud login, the object id in the claims of the token the CLI already reads (no Graph call; owner, 2026-10-19), until nereus login (#90).
  • Where a resource has no tags, the request id goes in its description or is left to the audit log: Azure role assignments carry a description (<purpose> Request <request id>.), federated credentials and blob containers none; GCP IAM bindings and service accounts carry no labels.
  • Control plane only. A data-plane call, such as reading a secret, leaves no resource to tag; it is attributed through the platform's own audit log (#256), joined to the cloud's log by time and identity. Since each reef has its own identity, the cloud's log already says which reef made a call.
  • Never trusted for authorisation. Anyone with write access to a resource can change its tags; they are for attribution and inventory, never for a decision.
  • Resources the platform adopts (an existing vault, #81; an identity an admin created, --param identity=) are left untouched, with the adoption in the audit log (#155): a plan only reads them (GET), and the CLI checks only what a plan creates.

docs.title: The audit trail
docs.text:
Every action a Controller takes in a cloud answers four questions (answer 10): which identity, which Controller, on whose request (a person, or nobody: the Controller acting on its own), and which request. Security comes with the design from the first slice (owner, 2026-10-18), so the trail is part of the cloud reef's contract, not added later.

Part of the trail Where it is written Its limit identity and Controller Entra ID's sign-in log of the managed identity records the federated credential used, and each active Nereid has its own (tailwind-undercloud-keyvault) the cloud never knows the person: a managed identity's token carries no user on whose request, and the request id the platform's audit log (#256), when the request is made the only source of the person, so the audit log is required, never optional the resource created the tags above: the installation, nereus-requested-by, nereus-request control plane only the link between the cloud's log and the audit log the Controller sends the request id on every call to the cloud (ARM's client request id header) whether Azure's activity log keeps it is checked by the slice's spike, before the contract is fixed
  • A person's request: the CLI writes <API_GROUP>/requested-by and <API_GROUP>/request on the object; the Controller acting on it copies both into every call and every resource.
  • An autonomous action (a rotation, a reconciliation nobody asked for): the Controller makes the request id itself and nereus-requested-by names it, controller-<namespace>_<serviceaccount> (controller-nereus-system_keyvault), so "nobody asked" is written, never left blank.
  • Several active Nereids in one reef (#72) share the reef's identity and its grants, since they fulfil the same contract; each gets its own federated credential, well within 20, and that credential is what tells their calls apart in the cloud's log.

docs.title: The journey, the walkthrough and the scene
Journey steps it changes (docs/inception.md)
docs.text:
• Step 0 gains: the az login has Contributor on the subscription (or on the installation's resource group) and a role-assignment right on the vault, or an admin hands over an identity (--param identity=). No Entra ID role is needed.
  • Step 1 becomes nereus init --target azure: the installation gets its identity (#154), the k3d cluster is the undercloud, named tailwind-undercloud, born with the cloud reef and the azure Nereid, and the person approves the bootstrap plan that publishes its issuer and creates <installation>-cloud-provisioner in the installation's resource group; the CLI proves the token exchange.
  • Step 2, nereus reef apply cloud --from-file ./reefs/cloud/ then nereus nereid apply azure --reef cloud, runs inside step 1; a person runs it by hand only on a cluster that already exists (#77).
  • Step 3 gains the plan for <installation>-secrets-reader and its federated credential at nereus nereid apply keyvault --reef secrets, and nereus system access approve secrets for its role on the vault.

The inception page changes with the PR that builds step 1, so it never describes what does not run.

docs.title: Walkthrough and scene
docs.text:
• New walkthrough pages, each with the output it really prints, in the PRs that build them: "Prepare the undercloud" (init --target azure: the cluster with its computed issuer, the cloud reef, the azure Nereid and the bootstrap plan), "Connect to the cloud" (nereid apply azure by hand, --param account=, and the admin path), "When a name is taken" (the three steps of the collision flow: the command stops before creating anything, config installation set --naming-override records the names in the cluster and the file, the run goes on to the end, init recreating the undercloud with its new issuer when the issuer storage's name changed; owner, 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-19), "Grant access" (nereid apply keyvault, access list, access approve).
  • CI runs no scene for this slice (owner, 2026-10-19): the cloud reef will change, so a fake cloud Nereid in test/scene costs more than it proves for the MVP. CI keeps the unit tests of the request protocol's limits against recorded plans (#170's recommendation): they are cheap, and they guard the rule that what a Nereid publishes is untrusted input, validated before the CLI runs it with the person's login.
  • test/scene-azure runs the whole scene by hand in the owner's sandbox subscription, by the owner or an agent with the owner's go-ahead (answer 6), with its own XDG_CONFIG_HOME and the CLI of the checkout, and deletes what it created by deleting the installation's resource group. Whether CI ever runs it, federated from GitHub Actions' own issuer, is #170.

docs.title: Security and quality attributes
docs.text:
Under the lens of #28, this slice is alpha: it runs in a sandbox subscription, never against production.

  • What is published is public keys only, as AKS, EKS and GKE publish for every cluster with workload identity. The secret is k3s's service-account signing key (service.key), which never leaves the cluster.
  • Who can write the issuer container can impersonate the cluster: a JWKS of their own would make their tokens valid. Only the installation's administrators hold Storage Blob Data Contributor on its issuer account, which no other installation shares, shared keys are off, and the state lives in another, private account.
  • Trust is narrow: one issuer per cluster, one subject per reef (its active Nereid's service account), the audience api://AzureADTokenExchange, and roles on single resources. The azure Nereid refuses privileged roles and scopes outside the account.
  • One identity per reef, so a read-only Nereid never holds another reef's write role, and the cloud's log tells the reefs apart. Several Nereids active in one reef (#72) share its identity, each with its own federated credential (see The audit trail).
  • The person's token stays on the person's machine, and nothing runs before the person approves its listed requests. A malicious cloud Nereid could still plan any request the person may make, shown before it runs; trusted catalog images (#22) come before beta.
  • No credential kept, at any stage, and no Entra ID role or consent needed: managed identities are Azure resources, created with rights on a resource group.
  • Federated credentials: Entra ID allows 20 per identity; each identity uses one, two during the pivot.
  • What beta would need: catalog-signed images for cloud Nereids (#22); drift detection of access entries (a grant removed in the cloud shows in status); the platform's audit log (#256); the compliance policy for names (#155); the threat model of #28 and #70.
  • Fitness functions: unit tests of the request protocol's limits (hosts, schemes, headers, sizes, counts, substitutions); of the tag values' encoding against each cloud's rules; of the azure Nereid's validations (bootstrap mode accepted only for its own cluster's entry of spec.issuers[], Kubernetes' default issuer always refused, naming the cluster by its role and installation, with its cause, check and fix) and of its plans against recorded answers, the bootstrap plan included (names, storage, grant, documents, a taken name); cli/tests/test_boundaries.py unchanged, with no exemption: the CLI holds no Azure call; the CRD contract tests of Cloud and CloudClass; test/scene for the generic side; test/scene-azure by hand; a check that every resource a plan creates carries the ids (#155).

docs.title: What is left to other issues
docs.text:
• #81: the secrets reef and the Key Vault Nereid: create or adopt, which role it asks for (Key Vault Secrets User or Officer) and when, its Instance's fields.
  • #61: the pivot's mechanics, the undercloud on demand, and the AKS cluster itself (with #92).
  • A cluster reef (creating AKS, #92, and the pivot, #61), noted only (owner, 2026-10-19): this spec's bootstrap creates no cluster in a cloud.
  • #93: terraform-packager's additive federated path, as decided there.
  • #154, #251: the installation's object, its name, id, alias and naming overrides, and the command that shows them (spec 0006).
  • #155: the identification contract: key names, names behind a compliance policy, adopted resources, and its check.
  • #7: who may run a Nereid's commands, and who may approve an access entry.
  • #256: the platform's audit log, which attributes data-plane calls: what an entry holds, where it is stored (a private, immutable storage first), who writes and reads it.
  • #28, #70: the threat model and the maturity of each part.
  • #77: installing into a cluster that already exists, with the issuer the cluster already publishes.
  • #90: the nereus user's id behind nereus-requested-by.
  • #170: whether CI runs a real Azure test.
  • #260: a cloud-neutral access request. The MVP's requests and plans use Azure's role assignment (grant <role> on <resource> to <principal>), accepted as is (owner, 2026-10-19); what a Nereid asks for on AWS (an IAM policy) or GCP (a binding) is #260's.
  • #234: the platform's own identity towards external systems ("Platform API" as an application, like a GitHub App: Microsoft Graph, GitHub, Slack, the portal acting on the platform's behalf). This spec needs no app registration: the access identities are managed identities (answer 9).

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: None: every question is answered on PR #151.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Every rule in CLAUDE.md and docs/adr/ applies: the API never names a Nereid, so the CLI knows the cloud reef and the Tools, never azure (in --target azure the word is the person's input naming the Nereid to add), and the cloud's identities are named after reefs; one writer per field (ADR 0005); what a Nereid publishes, plans or answers is untrusted input; public by design (ADR 0007), so no subscription, tenant or object id enters the repository, its docs or its tests.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• kstatus (kubernetes-sigs/cli-utils): the Stalled condition, a Controller that cannot progress without help, and the observedGeneration it is written for; with the Kubernetes API conventions on status (a reason for machines and a message for people).
  • Workload identity federation (Microsoft Entra, "Workload identity federation"): a cloud trusts the tokens a cluster signs, so the platform keeps no secret.
  • ULID (ulid/spec): the request id, sortable by time.
  • Cluster API's clusterctl move (cluster-api.sigs.k8s.io): the pivot from the undercloud to the overcloud.
  • Fitness functions come from Building Evolutionary Architectures (Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, O'Reilly, 2017; evolutionaryarchitecture.com): an automated check that a quality of the architecture holds, run on every change. This spec lists its own under "Security and quality attributes".

docs.title: 0006. Installation identity: a name, an id and an alias for each installation
docs.text:
Status: Proposed (2026-10-18)

Changed by answer 15 on PR #151 (spec 0005); built by #251.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
Every installation of the platform has a unique, stable identity (#154), so that whatever it creates outside itself (cloud resources and their tags, spec 0005 and #82; cost data, #64; the stricter tag rules of #155) can be traced back to it without ambiguity, even when several installations share a cloud account.

The identity is three values: a name a person chooses or accepts (tailwind), which never changes and is the installation's part of every name the platform generates outside itself; an id (a random UUID, version 4) that never changes either; and an alias, what listings show, which may change. All live in one object of the platform's API group in the nereus namespace, as the SLO of spec 0004 does, so the pivot (#61) moves it to the overcloud with the rest of the platform's objects: the undercloud and the overcloud are one installation, one identity (owner, #82). The role (undercloud or overcloud) is a separate attribute, not part of the identity.

docs.title: The scene that ends the slice
docs.text:
nereus init --yes                                      # step "installation": created, with its name
nereus config installation show
# NAME            ALIAS           ID
# nereus-local  nereus-local  3f2c0d4e-...
nereus init --yes                                      # step "installation": kept; the name and the id are the same
nereus config installation set --alias acme-prod       # the alias changes, the name and the id do not

docs.title: The object
docs.text:
One Installation object in the nereus namespace (names.NAMESPACE), of the platform's API group (names.API_GROUP, v1alpha1), named after the installation; its CRD is cli/src/nereus/crds/installation.yaml, applied by init with the other kinds.

kind: Installation
metadata:
  name: tailwind
spec:
  id: 0b7e4c1a-…
  alias: Tailwind Prod
  naming:
    overrides:
      issuer:
        storage: tailwindissuers01

The init file holds the object itself (owner, 2026-10-18): nereus init --generate-file writes two documents, how to build the platform from this machine and the installation exactly as it goes to the cluster, and the first init writes the generated id back into it, so recreating the undercloud from the file (#61) keeps the same installation:

# how to build the platform from this machine
apiVersion: platform.example.com/v1alpha1
kind: InitConfig
spec:
  # the target cloud; without it, only the local cluster
  cloud: azure

  # this machine's k3d cluster
  undercloud:
    create: true
    name: tailwind-undercloud

  # the cloud cluster, created at the pivot (#61)
  overcloud:
    create: true
---
# the installation, as it goes to the cluster
apiVersion: platform.example.com/v1alpha1
kind: Installation
metadata:
  name: tailwind
spec:
  # written by the first init
  id: 0b7e4c1a-…
  alias: Tailwind Prod

installationName leaves InitConfig, and createCluster becomes undercloud.create. With its id, the file is the installation's definition: two machines with the same file are the same installation.

Field Type Written by Meaning metadata.name string, the installation's name init, once The installation's name, which Kubernetes never lets change, so it is the installation's part of every generated name: its resource group tailwind-platform, its identities tailwind-<interface> (spec 0005). A company that wants its resources under another name gets a new installation and migrates to it (#249). spec.id string, a UUID init, once The identity. Generated by the CLI with uuid.uuid4() when the object is created; the CRD refuses any change to it (self == oldSelf). Its first 16 hex characters, dashes removed (<id16>), name the cloud resources whose names are global and short (spec 0005). spec.alias string, free text (owner, 2026-10-18), at most 63 characters, no control characters init when it creates the object, equal to the name; nereus config installation set --alias later What listings show. Changing it changes no resource name; the name in #155's tags is the installation's name. spec.naming.overrides map, grouped by what a resource serves, then its kind the person: the answer to the CLI's question, or nereus config installation set --naming-override <path>=<name> The names a person gives when a generated one is taken by someone else (spec 0005): issuer.storage, state.storage, secrets.vault. Each is validated against its resource's own rules, and cannot change once its resource exists.
  • A name is lowercase letters, digits and -, starts with a letter, and has at most 63 characters: [a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,62}, validated with re.fullmatch by the CLI and by the CRD's pattern. A name is a valid Kubernetes object name, a GCP label value and the start of an Azure resource name (#82). Further rules of other clouds are #155's.
  • Spec only. The CLI writes spec (ADR 0005); there is no Nereid and no status.
  • spec.id and spec.alias required. An object without an id is never valid.
  • One object per installation. A namespace holds the platform of one installation, so init and the command read the only Installation there; a second one is an error that names both.

docs.title: Where the name comes from
docs.text: init takes it from a setting, installation_name (flag --installation-name, or the metadata.name of the settings file's Installation), else from the cluster name (the name setting, nereus-local by default), with the source cluster name. A name that breaks the rules stops init before anything changes, naming the setting to fix; a cluster name that is not a valid name (2026-demo, starting with a digit) asks for --installation-name. --generate-file writes the Installation with its name, so the file is the installation's definition (#251).

docs.title: What init does
docs.text:
A new step, installation, after kinds and namespace:

  • No object yet: it generates the id, creates the object with the name and an alias equal to it, and prints created <name>.
  • An object already there: it changes nothing and prints kept <name>. The name and the id never change; the alias is nereus config installation set's. When a name was given (flag or file) and differs from the one in the cluster, the line says so: the name cannot change, so a different name means a new installation.
  • Two init runs at once cannot create two identities: the object is created, never replaced, and the run that loses the race reads the other's.

A recreated cluster (nereus-local deleted and created again) is a new installation, with a new id, unless it is restored from a backup that carries the object.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
The walkthrough shows it: The installation.

nereus config installation, next to nereus config slo (spec 0004):

  • show: one row, NAME, ALIAS and ID. With no object, it fails and asks for nereus init.
  • set --alias <alias> and set --naming-override <path>=<name>: change the alias and the overrides, keep the name and the id, and print one line per change: the object's field and its new value, then the settings file it updated, with its path, when the installation came from one (owner, 2026-10-18). It never creates the object: only init makes an id.

There is no reset and no rename: deleting the identity would make a new installation.

docs.title: Security and quality attributes
docs.text:
Under the lens of #28, this slice is alpha.

  • An id identifies, it does not authenticate. Nothing grants rights because a tag carries it; a collision or a spoofed tag misleads a report, never an access decision.
  • The name and the id cannot drift: Kubernetes never changes an object's name, the CLI never writes the id after creation, and the CRD refuses a change, so a hand edit fails too.
  • What a person types is validated before it reaches the cluster (re.fullmatch), and again by the CRD's schema; each naming override against its resource's own rules.
  • Fitness functions of the slice: unit tests of the name rules, of the overrides' validation, of init's step and of the command; the CRD contract tests; test/scene checks the object exists and its id stays the same across a second init.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• UUID version 4 (RFC 9562): the installation's id, random.
  • Fitness functions come from Building Evolutionary Architectures (Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, O'Reilly, 2017; evolutionaryarchitecture.com): an automated check that a quality of the architecture holds, run on every change. This spec lists its own under "Security and quality attributes".

docs.title: 0007. Invitation: a link and a QR code that let one person in, for a while
docs.text:
Status: Proposed (2026-10-26)

From the owner's voice session of 2026-10-26 (raw data in Drive #pontos/raw/2026-10-25, voice files 113 to 119; order 20261026-0610), and the invitation slides of the first PoC's walkthrough deck (found by order 20261026-0042), ported after a public-by-design pass (ADR 0007).

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The first dive is a recorded conversation between two people on one Nereus. The owner has to let the second person in during the call, with no account set up beforehand: an invitation shown as a QR code on the screen, accepted on the phone through single sign-on (SSO), with access that ends by itself.

The slice is the walking skeleton of people coming into Nereus: one command prints a link and its QR code, accepting it creates the person as a User of core (ADR 0006), and both the invitation and the access it grants expire, each on its own clock. That access ends on its own, in front of everyone, is part of what the slice shows.

Simple on the surface, consistent underneath (the owner's design principle, voice file 113): the root form nereus invitation create is the familiar, welcoming one; underneath, the invitation is a kind of the authentication reef with the same verbs, output and errors as every other noun (ADR 0013).

docs.title: The scene that ends the slice
docs.text:
# On the owner's machine: invite one person; the QR code goes on the screen of the call
nereus authentication invitation create dive-01 \
  --to maria@example.com

# The same command, through the root alias
nereus invitation create dive-01 \
  --to maria@example.com

# Maria scans the QR code, signs in with Google through SSO, and lands in Nereus as a User

# The owner sees who accepted and until when the access lasts
nereus authentication invitation get dive-01

# 24 hours after accepting (2 minutes with --access-expires 2m, in a demo), Maria's next call is refused
nereus status

What create prints:

invitation/dive-01 created
to:       maria@example.com
link:     https://nereus.example.com/invitations/accept#k7Qp3...
expires:  in 5m (06:47) · the link and the invitation
access:   24h after accepting

[the QR code of the link, drawn in the terminal]

Next steps:

  nereus authentication invitation get dive-01

docs.title: The commands
docs.text:
The canonical form lives in the reef (ADR 0013, ADR 0010): nereus authentication invitation <verb> <name>. The root form nereus invitation <verb> is an alias: the CLI runs exactly the same command, the way kubectl aliases do, and never adds behaviour of its own. Docs, --help, --examples and errors always show the canonical form; aliases exist only for the most used actions (voice file 113).

Verb Does create <name> Creates the invitation and prints its link and QR code; fails when it exists, listing apply and delete (ADR 0013). apply <name> Creates it, or, while nobody has accepted it, issues a new link with a new expiration: the old link stops working (invitation/dive-01 configured). Refused once accepted, naming create with another name. get <name> Shows one: to whom, the state (pending, accepted, expired), when it expires, who accepted it and until when their access lasts. Never the link. list One row per invitation: NAME, TO, STATE, EXPIRES, ACCESS, AGE. delete <name> Closes the door: the link stops working at once. It expels nobody: whoever accepted keeps their access until it expires (from the first PoC).

The options of create and apply:

Option Default Meaning --to <email> none The only verified e-mail that may accept it. Without it, any verified e-mail of the authentication Mandate's allowed domains may. --invitation-expires <duration> 5m How long the link stays valid. The link (and its QR code) and the invitation are the same thing: unused in time, create another. --access-expires <duration> 24h How long the access lasts, counted from accepting. --qr-file <path> none Also saves the QR code as a PNG, to show in a call. --dry-run Shows the object that would be created, with link: <generated on create>, and changes nothing. --examples The examples, each with a line saying what it does.

--invitation-expires and --access-expires replace the first PoC's --expires and --access-for: two expirations, each named for what it ends, so nobody has to guess which one a flag sets (voice file 115). "Expires" rather than "expiration", since the value is a duration and reads as "expires in 24h".

Durations follow Go's (time.ParseDuration), with d added: one or more numbers each followed by s, m (minutes), h or d, such as 90s, 30m, 1h30m, 2d. There is no month unit, since m already means minutes: thirty days is 30d. Validated with re.fullmatch(r"(\d+[smhd])+", value), and the total must be greater than zero.

The QR code is drawn with segno, the open source library docs/presentations/render-outline already uses: QRCode.terminal(compact=True) in the terminal, QRCode.save(path) for --qr-file (PNG with no other dependency). With --output json or yaml, the output carries the link and leaves the QR code out.

docs.title: Accepting
docs.text:
1. The link opens a page served by core: https://<the API's public host>/invitations/accept#<token>.
  2. The page sends the person to sign in through the authentication reef's default Mandate (Keycloak brokering Google, ADR 0006), keeping the token in the browser.
  3. Back from the login, the page posts the token. Core checks, in this order: the token's hash matches an invitation; it has not expired; nobody accepted it; with --to, the token's verified e-mail is exactly that address; without --to, the verified e-mail's domain is one the Mandate allows.
  4. Core creates the User (ADR 0006: the platform generates its id, and the identity is the token's issuer and sub) with the access's end, and writes the acceptance in the invitation's status. The page says until when the access lasts.

From then on, any client of the API (the CLI's nereus login, the claude.ai connector of the API's /mcp) works as that User until the access ends. After that, every call is refused with ADR 0012's message.

Accepting creates the person in core, never in Keycloak (voice file 116). Core owns users and their linked identities (issuer and subject); an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0) is a Nereid that only proves "this person is this subject at this provider". Swapping the provider loses no User.

An identity is never linked by e-mail. If the signed-in identity already belongs to a User, accepting is refused ("you already have access here; sign in"). Linking a second identity to a User is out of this slice; when it comes, it happens only while signed in with an identity the User already has, or by an admin (voice file 116).

docs.title: The objects
docs.text:
Invitation, a kind of authentication.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1 (ADR 0009), in the nereus namespace:

apiVersion: authentication.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Invitation
metadata:
  name: dive-01
spec:
  to: maria@example.com
  expiresAt: "2026-10-26T06:47:00-03:00"
  accessExpires: 24h
  tokenHash: sha256:9f2c...
  createdBy: u-7f3k2p
status:
  acceptedAt: "2026-10-26T06:44:12-03:00"
  acceptedBy: u-2m8q4x
  accessExpiresAt: "2026-10-27T06:44:12-03:00"
Field Written by Meaning spec.to the API, from the CLI The only e-mail that may accept; absent for an open invitation. spec.expiresAt the API, from --invitation-expires When the link stops working; apply moves it with a new token. spec.accessExpires the API The access's length, as given. spec.tokenHash the API The SHA-256 of the link's token. The token itself is printed once and stored nowhere. spec.createdBy the API The User who created it. status.acceptedAt, status.acceptedBy, status.accessExpiresAt core The acceptance, written once.

One writer per field (ADR 0005): the API writes spec; core writes status, as the static Nereid it exposes itself as (voice file 117, below). Core writes the acceptance with the object's resourceVersion, so two people racing for one invitation cannot both get in.

User (core, ADR 0006) gets two fields, written by core: spec.invitation (the invitation it came from) and spec.accessExpiresAt. Removing spec.accessExpiresAt makes the access permanent; the command that does it comes with the nereus user commands.

Core exposes itself like a Nereid (voice file 117): listed with the others, with the same contract, but static, neither replaceable nor deletable, the way the kubelet starts static pods and the API server shows them as mirror pods (Kubernetes, static pods). For now it runs inside the API, with no deployment of its own.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every message says what happened and how to fix it (ADR 0012), and shows the canonical form:

$ nereus authentication invitation create dive-01
✗ invitation dive-01 already exists (pending, expires in 3m). Run one of:
  nereus authentication invitation apply dive-01   # a new link; the old one stops working
  nereus authentication invitation delete dive-01  # close it

$ nereus authentication invitation create dive-02 --access-expires 1mo
✗ --access-expires 1mo is not a duration. Use numbers with s, m (minutes), h or d, such as 30m, 2h or 30d; there is no month unit.

$ nereus invitation create dive-03
✗ the authentication reef is not installed. Install it with:
  nereus init --profile internal-developer-platform

$ nereus status
✗ your access to this Nereus ended at 06:44, as set by invitation dive-01. To come back, ask for a new invitation.

On the acceptance page: an expired or deleted invitation says so and asks for a new one; an e-mail that is not the invited one is refused without showing the invited address; a domain outside the allowed ones names neither the domains nor the invitation's address.

docs.title: From the first PoC
docs.text: The first PoC This slice platform authentication invite create nereus authentication invitation create <name>, with the root alias nereus invitation create; the noun invitation was decided on 2026-10-22. --expires (the invite), --access-for (the guest's access) --invitation-expires (default 5m), --access-expires (default 24h). --guest <email>, a nominal invitation, always with a deadline --to <email>. --type qr, the QR code in the terminal for a kickoff Always printed; --qr-file saves it. SSO plus the e-mail verified and in allowedDomains as the real gate Kept: the invitation says where you go; SSO says who you are. invite delete: closes the door, expels nobody Kept. The guest's access ending mid-conversation, with a message that says what happened and what to do Kept, through ADR 0012. --organization, --project Left out: Nereus has neither yet (#21). --max-uses, --type email, a directory target (an OU, a group) Left out of the first slice: one invitation lets one person in. The evaluation licence, its waiting queue and license get Parked as an idea (below).

docs.title: Out of this slice
docs.text:
• Sending the invitation by e-mail. The first dive needs only the QR code and SSO; e-mail delivery comes through a notification reef, and only if it is easy (voice file 118).
  • Evaluation licences with a waiting queue (voice files 118, 119): a demo instance limited to a few users, the next ones waiting on a screen until the representative approves more seats from a push notification, all audited and replayed. Kept as an idea, back when the sales demo is built.
  • --max-uses and invitations for many people at once.
  • Linking a second identity to a User, and making an access permanent from the CLI (nereus user commands).
  • Who may create invitations beyond the installation's admins: comes with authorization.

docs.title: Security and quality attributes
docs.text:
Under the lens of the OWASP Top 10:2025, this slice touches:

  • A01 Broken Access Control. Core checks every condition when accepting, not the page: the token, the expiration, single use (the resourceVersion write), the invited address or the allowed domains. The access ends on the server, at spec.accessExpiresAt, whatever the client holds. Only admins create invitations.
  • A04 Cryptographic Failures. The token has 256 random bits (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)); only its SHA-256 is stored, so reading the object does not reveal a link that works. It travels in the URL's fragment (RFC 3986, section 3.5), which browsers do not send in the request line, so it stays out of access logs and proxies.
  • A06 Insecure Design. A shared QR code alone is weak: a photo can leave the call. SSO is the real gate, the link lasts 5 minutes by default, it lets one person in, and delete closes it at once.
  • A07 Authentication Failures. No identity is linked by e-mail (account takeover); a User comes only from an invitation accepted with a verified e-mail. The accepting identity must not belong to another User.
  • A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures. Core records a Kubernetes Event on the invitation for every create, new link, acceptance, refusal (with its reason, never the token) and delete; the platform's own audit trail and its replay come later.

Fitness functions of the slice: unit tests of the duration rule, of the checks in the acceptance order above, of the single-use race, and of the alias running the canonical command; a test/scene step that creates an invitation, accepts it with a test identity, and sees a call refused once a --access-expires 5s access ends.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• ADR 0006 links a new sub only after an e-mail code; voice file 116 links a new identity only while signed in with an existing one, or by an admin. Which one holds, or both?
  • Should --invitation-expires have a maximum (for example 7d), so a link cannot live for months?
  • Is --qr-file the right name for saving the QR code as an image?

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• The two expirations, the nominal guest invitation and "closes the door, expels nobody" come from the first PoC's walkthrough deck (2026-10-22).
  • Durations: Go's time.ParseDuration, whose units are ns, us, ms, s, m and h; this slice keeps s, m and h and adds d.
  • QR codes: segno, a QR code library in pure Python.
  • Identity brokering: Keycloak, Server Administration Guide, where Keycloak brokers an external identity provider such as Google.
  • Static pods and mirror pods: Kubernetes documentation; the analogy for core was brought by Claude (Anthropic) in voice file 117.
  • Security categories: OWASP Top 10:2025.

docs.title: 0008. Portal: the first slice, a PWA that says who you are
docs.text:
Status: Proposed (2026-10-31)

From the owner's session of 2026-10-31 (refining #46, the web portal, with a clickable prototype on the phone). Raw data in the session's Pontos log.

docs.title: Intent
docs.text:
The walking skeleton of the portal (#46): open https://portal.getnereus.dev on the phone, install it on the home screen, sign in with Google, see who is signed in, sign out, and sign in again. Nothing else. Every later screen (reefs, Nereids, commands as forms, push for #278) grows on top of this slice.

The portal is installed the way every capability is: a reef, portal, and a Nereid that implements it, nereus-portal, applied from the CLI. Without it the platform works from the CLI alone; with it, the platform gains a graphical client (#46, the owner's comment: the portal itself is swappable).

docs.title: The scene that ends the slice
docs.text:
# Apply the portal reef (with no kinds of its own, as authentication)
nereus reef apply portal

# Install its Nereid, published at the portal's public address
nereus nereid apply nereus-portal \
  --reef portal

nereus mandate apply nereus-portal \
  --reef portal \
  --nereid nereus-portal \
  --param publicUrl=https://portal.getnereus.dev

# The portal answers, and so does the API behind it
curl https://portal.getnereus.dev/healthz
curl --include https://portal.getnereus.dev/v1/me

ok
HTTP/2 401

Then, on the phone:

  1. Open https://portal.getnereus.dev: the start screen ("Entre com a sua conta para continuar.", Entrar). The browser offers "Add to Home screen"; the icon is the honeycomb, the name Nereus.
  2. Entrar goes to the realm's login (auth.getnereus.dev, always dark), where Entrar com Google signs in.
  3. Back on the portal: name, e-mail, groups, "entrou com Google · auth.getnereus.dev", and Sair.
  4. Sair ends the session in the portal and in Keycloak, and shows "Você saiu" with Entrar de novo, which shows the login again (not a silent return).

Steps 1 to 4 also work from the installed app, opened from the home screen.

docs.title: The screens
docs.text:
The reference is the canvas of the session (dark and light rows, and a clickable prototype): the start screen, the login, the signed-in screen, the signed-out screen. In words:

  • The mark appears once per screen: the honeycomb with "Nereus" beside it. No title repeats the name (the same change made the login card say only "Entrar", #734, the login page says Nereus twice).
  • Theme follows the device (prefers-color-scheme), with no switch in this slice. Dark: the login theme's palette (#598: page #000, card #0c0c0c, lines #262626, text #f5f5f5, primary button white on black). Light: its mirror (page #fafafa, card #fff, lines #e5e5e5, text #0a0a0a, primary button black on white).
  • The login stays dark in both themes: it is Keycloak's theme (#598), out of this slice.
  • Languages: pt-BR and en, from the browser's language, the login's texts style (no gendered words).
  • Touch targets of at least 44 px; text contrast of at least 4.5:1.

docs.title: The portal reef
docs.text:
portal.getnereus.dev/v1alpha1, the capability of a graphical client of the platform. In this slice it has no kinds of its own: the Mandate's parameters carry what the Nereid needs (publicUrl, and gateway, the <namespace>/<name> of the Gateway its route attaches to, istio-system/ingress by default). nereus reef apply portal takes no flag: a reef the CLI pins no contract for is created with no kinds, as authentication is. A kind comes when the portal has state of its own (a theme, a menu); Open questions.

It requires the authentication reef (its login), and reaches the Nereus API (ADR 0018, the API is the one door) for everything it shows.

docs.title: The nereus-portal Nereid
docs.text:
One image, nereus-portal-controller, under controllers/nereus-portal/, the shape of the other local Nereids (server.py, /contract, a Dockerfile, tests), listed in NEREIDS (Makefile) and TOOLS (cli/src/nereus/local_nereids.py), so make nereids builds it and nereus nereid apply nereus-portal needs no --image.

  • It serves the portal's files: a static single-page app, no build step, no framework: index.html, one script, one stylesheet, the web app manifest, the service worker and the icons. A small app with no build keeps the slice cheap; a framework comes when a screen needs one.
  • It forwards /v1/* to the Nereus API (http://nereus-api.nereus-system.svc:8080), on the same origin, so the browser needs no CORS and the API no public hostname of its own. The forward adds nothing and decides nothing: the API checks the token on every request. It is not a backend of the portal (#46: the portal must not grow one the API later replaces).
  • It serves /config.json, from the Mandates: the issuer (the authentication reef's default Mandate's status.oidc), the client id (nereus-portal, a constant on both sides while the client is a stand-in) and its own Mandate's publicUrl. The page reads it at start, so no address is baked into the files.
  • Its Content Security Policy is built from the same issuer, so connect-src names https://auth.getnereus.dev on the kept cluster and the Environment's own issuer elsewhere.
  • /healthz answers ok.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
• Authorization Code with PKCE (S256), a public client, through oidc-client-ts (Apache-2.0), vendored as one file (open source first).
  • The client nereus-portal in the realm nereus: public, standard flow only, redirect https://portal.getnereus.dev/callback, post-logout redirect https://portal.getnereus.dev/signed-out, web origin https://portal.getnereus.dev, the nereus-api audience and the groups claim (as nereus-cli has them).
  • Who registers it: the keycloak Nereid, beside nereus-cli, claude and triton. It reads the publicUrl of every Mandate of the portal reef (every Nereid may read Mandates) and sets the client's redirects from them, so nobody repeats the portal's address on the keycloak Mandate (mandate apply replaces a Mandate's whole spec, and would drop the Google parameters). With no portal Mandate, the client exists with no redirect. This is a stand-in: a reef asking the authentication reef for a client of its own is the feature that retires it (#535, the authentication reef's Client kind).
  • Tokens live in memory only, never in localStorage. Reopening the app finds no token and goes through the login again by itself, a redirect with prompt=none that shows nothing (#1256): while Keycloak's session lasts it returns at once to the signed-in screen, else Keycloak answers login_required and the start screen shows Entrar, with no error line. One attempt per tab (a sessionStorage flag, cleared by a login that works), never on /signed-out, never offline. A hidden iframe (signinSilent) was turned down: it needs Keycloak's cookie as a third-party cookie, which Safari and Chrome's tracking protection block. While signed in, the access token is renewed with the refresh token (#1758): a minute before it expires, and at once when the API answers 401, then the call is sent again once; one renew at a time, since Keycloak rotates refresh tokens. signinSilent uses the refresh token here, never the iframe.
  • Sign out is the RP-initiated logout of OpenID Connect: the end-session endpoint with id_token_hint and the post-logout redirect, so the next Entrar shows the login for real.

docs.title: What GET /v1/me answers
docs.text:
The signed-in screen shows the name and how the person signed in, so the API grows two fields (owner, 2026-10-31), both read from the token it already checks:

{"sub": "…", "email": "maria@example.com", "name": "Maria Silva", "groups": ["nereus-users"], "identityProvider": "google"}
  • name from the name claim (Keycloak's profile scope).
  • identityProvider from an identity_provider claim, which the keycloak Nereid adds to the clients nereus-portal and nereus-cli with a User Session Note mapper of the session note Keycloak sets on a brokered login (identity_provider). A login with a local user has no such note: the field is absent, and the screen shows only the issuer's host.
  • nereus whoami keeps its output; showing the provider there is a later choice.

docs.title: The PWA
docs.text:
• A web app manifest: name and short name "Nereus", the honeycomb icons (192, 512 and maskable), display: standalone, theme and background colours of the dark palette, start_url: /.
  • A service worker that caches only the app's shell (the static files), never /v1/*, /config.json or the login. It is what the browsers ask for before offering to install; offline use and Web Push are out of this slice (#278).
  • iOS: the apple-touch-icon and apple-mobile-web-app-* tags. The login leaves the app for auth.getnereus.dev and must come back to it: the slice proves this on the owner's iPhone or Android, and if the return opens in the browser instead, that is recorded on the issue before widening.

docs.title: Reaching the internet
docs.text: The Nereid publishes portal.getnereus.dev with a Gateway API HTTPRoute on the entrance's Gateway (#727, #728), to the portal's own port (8081), so its controller endpoints (port 8080, /contract, /metrics) stay inside the cluster. The named Cloudflare tunnel (deploy/edge/cloudflared.yaml) lists each hostname it sends to the gateway, portal.getnereus.dev among them (#732); the owner runs one DNS route once (cloudflared tunnel route dns nereus portal.getnereus.dev). The DNS route by hand is a stand-in for the edge reef (#470), which retires it.

docs.title: Security (OWASP)
docs.text:
• A01 Broken Access Control: the portal shows only what GET /v1/me answers for the token; the forward passes the Authorization header unchanged and nothing else.
  • A02 Cryptographic Failures: HTTPS only (Cloudflare's edge); tokens never stored by the page.
  • A05 Security Misconfiguration: a strict Content Security Policy (default-src 'self', connect-src 'self' https://auth.getnereus.dev, frame-ancestors 'none'), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.
  • A07 Identification and Authentication Failures: PKCE S256, exact redirect URIs, state and nonce checked by the library, the logout ending the Keycloak session.
  • A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures: the vendored library pinned by version and hash, served from the portal itself (no CDN).

docs.title: From zero
docs.text:
The owner's direction (2026-10-31): a fresh Nereus, in a new Environment (today a vcluster inside the k3d cluster, #568), must be able to stand the portal up with Nereus's own commands, from nothing. So:

  • Everything the portal needs is a command of the scene above, run against a cluster with only nereus init and the authentication reef: no file edited by hand, no kubectl apply of the portal's own manifests.
  • What still needs a hand is listed as a stand-in below, with the feature that retires it: today the client in the realm (decided by the keycloak Nereid's code) and the public hostname (the tunnel). An Environment reaches the portal through its own entrance, never a port-forward (owner, 2026-10-31): a port of the k3d load balancer, opened when the cluster is created, to an ingress gateway (Istio's, once an Environment installs the mesh) that routes by hostname to the portal. The portal then publishes its route as a Gateway API HTTPRoute, which Istio and other gateways implement alike, so the portal never names the gateway. The entrance comes first (owner, 2026-10-31): #727 installs Istio's ingress gateway through the release reef behind a k3d port, and #728 sends auth. and triton. through it; the portal then only adds its HTTPRoute.
  • The review of everything else a fresh instance needs is its own issue (#726, Nereus from zero, with #24, #61 and #568).

docs.title: Stand-ins
docs.text:
• The client nereus-portal registered by the keycloak Nereid; retired by a reef asking for its own client (#535).
  • The DNS route by hand; retired by the edge reef (#470).

docs.title: 729 (the slice, part of #46), in three sub-issues: #730 (GET /v1/me answers name and identityProvider), #731 (the keycloak Nereid registers nereus-portal), #732 (the reef and the Nereid). Depends on #727 (the entrance).
Done when
docs.text:
• make lint test deck-test docs-build shellcheck passes, with tests for the Nereid (files served, /config.json from the Mandates, the /v1 forward, the headers) and for the keycloak Nereid's new client.
  • On the kept cluster, the scene above prints what it shows, and on the owner's phone steps 1 to 4 work in the browser and from the installed app, in the dark and the light theme.
  • The portal reef's deck (docs/specs/cli/reefs/portal.yaml) has every command above; README.md has the Nereid's row; docs/features.md lists the two stand-ins.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Kinds of the portal reef: none in this slice; whether a Portal kind (hostname, theme) comes next, or the Mandate keeps carrying it.
  • The Nereid's name: nereus-portal (our own portal), leaving room for a backstage Nereid of the same reef.

docs.title: What is left to other issues
docs.text: Push notifications (#278), the reefs' and Nereids' screens and commands as forms (#46), a light login theme, a theme switch, offline use, a public api.getnereus.dev.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Progressive Web Apps (web.dev): the manifest, the service worker and installability.
  • OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications (IETF draft): Authorization Code with PKCE for a public client, tokens kept out of storage.
  • OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0: the sign-out.
  • oidc-client-ts: the library the page uses.
  • Walking skeleton (Alistair Cockburn, Crystal Clear): the thinnest slice that runs end to end.

docs.title: 0009. The build reef's security design: what a hostile Dockerfile can reach
docs.text:
Status: Accepted (the owner's word, 2026-11-05, #1006), with the decisions below taken by the owner; the code of #848 (the build reef) may start once #847 (the registry reef) is done.

A link is the source of a claim. A sentence marked (judgement) is this design's own reading. Nothing here ran: no cluster was used, and every claim about a running cluster goes to what the scene must prove.

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
• A hostile Dockerfile gets no credential unless it escapes the container. A fetch Job clones the source into a claim of that Build and runs no user code (#1141); then one Job, three containers in order: build runs the Dockerfile on that claim, read-only, and holds nothing secret, token and push hold a push token of ten minutes and run only after build is dead (#1010).
  • It keeps what it needs to build: its own source, DNS, and the package hosts of an egress proxy's list (#1142): a RUN reaches the internet only through Smokescreen, which allows the main package hosts and those the build reef's default Mandate adds, and nothing else. It can send its source to a listed host, as an upload to a package index.
  • NetworkPolicy stops another namespace, Triton's Pods and other nodes, and on k3s the Pod's own node too. Kubernetes allows a CNI to let that traffic through; k3s's policy controller does not, so the builds' egress policies stop the kube-apiserver, the kubelet and every NodePort, Triton's NATS included, at every address of the node (#1009). On a CNI that lets it through, the buildkit Nereid's probe reaches the kubelet and the Nereid runs no build (#1128).
  • The weak point is the kernel. With seccomp off, the whole kernel is exposed to hostile code, and nothing here closes an escape. On k3d the kernel is the machine's: an escape reaches Triton, every Secret on the node and the owner's machine.
  • So: the first slice builds only the scene's own Dockerfiles on a throwaway cluster. That proves the containment; it does not make the kernel safe, since a throwaway k3d cluster shares the same machine. Any other Dockerfile, builds on the kept cluster and #914 (a webhook starts a build) should wait for a kernel of their own, a VM.
  • BuildKit Jobs, not Shipwright, Tekton or Cloud Native Buildpacks: a Job and its init containers already give the lifecycle, and each of the others adds controllers without removing the exception. Shipwright's split between building and pushing is copied.

docs.title: Decided (owner, 2026-11-05)
docs.text:
# Decision Decided Why 1 Where builds run Throwaway clusters and the scene's own Dockerfiles for #848; anything else, the kept cluster and #914 only on a VM with its own small cluster The kernel is the one risk this design cannot contain 2 kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns on the machine Do not change it on the owner's machine; try an AppArmor profile, then a VM BuildKit's fix weakens the whole machine 3 Egress during a build Public internet on 80 and 443 for the first slice; closed behind a mirror later (since #1142, an egress proxy with a host list) Closed breaks every RUN apt-get, and no credential is there to steal 4 The git credential A GitHub App's installation token, per build, for one repository with contents: read, minted by the github Nereid as the authentication reef's Token (ADR 0006, #1274) and asked by the buildkit Nereid, which never holds the App's key (#1070) It expires in an hour and needs no port 22; a deploy key never expires; the App's key stays with the one Nereid that is the platform's identity towards GitHub 5 The push credential in #847 (the registry reef) One per repository, read and create only One shared credential would let any build overwrite any image 6 One Job, or a second Job to publish One Job, as #848 decided A second one closes only a bug in the push tool, and costs a volume between Pods

The two points of #1004's own "To decide" are followed here: the design is the next free spec, and every Dockerfile is hostile, whoever wrote it.

docs.title: What runs
docs.text:
$ nereus build create hello-a1b2c3d \
    --workload hello \
    --commit a1b2c3d
build/builds/hello-a1b2c3d created
Order Container Runs Holds Sees 0 (fetch Job, #1141) fetch git, on the Workload's repository at the commit, in a Pod of its own nothing secret (a public repository) writes the claim source-<build> 1 (init) build BuildKit, and every RUN of the Dockerfile nothing secret the claim source-<build> read-only; writes an OCI layout to image 2 (init) token one printf in busybox, pinned by digest the projected push token writes config.json to an in-memory docker volume 3 push a small push tool with no shell the push token, in config.json image and docker read-only

Each init container must complete before the next starts, and they can hold Secrets other containers cannot. A build's processes die with its container, because containers of a Pod do not share a PID namespace unless asked to (judgement). Shipwright mounts the push Secret only on its image-processing step; Cloud Native Buildpacks keeps its registry phases in separate containers "to avoid exposing sensitive data to buildpacks". This takes the same shape.

docs.title: The credentials
docs.text:
The credential cannot sit beside BuildKit. The Kubernetes example runs --oci-worker-no-process-sandbox, which lets a RUN kill, and depending on seccomp ptrace, any process in the daemon's container. Seccomp is off here, and a RUN as root is the daemon's own UID 1000, so a RUN can read anything the daemon holds (judgement). That rules out BuildKit's own git and push paths, and Shipwright's strategy-managed push.

Git credential Push credential Who holds the long-lived part the github Nereid: the GitHub App's key is a param of its authentication Mandate, a secret of the secrets reef (ADR 0006; ADR 0002: credentials live with the Nereid); the buildkit Nereid holds no key the registry reef's Nereid; the person uses only their own login, as #847 decided What a build receives a token for one repository, contents: read (GitHub: limits on repositories and permissions): the buildkit Nereid asks a Token named after the Build, owned by it, in builds, only when an authentication Mandate's allow covers builds and the Workload's repository; otherwise the fetch is anonymous a token of the Repository's ServiceAccount builds/push-<repository>, for one Registry's audience nereus-registry-<registry>; zot maps it to a user bound to the ServiceAccount's uid, read and create on one repository path (zot: OIDC bearer and per-user policies) Lifetime one hour, minted per build ten minutes, the least kubelet asks for a projected token; kubelet renews it at 80% of that, so a push may start with about two minutes left Where it sits the Secret token-<build> the github Nereid writes in builds, which the buildkit Nereid never reads; mounted read-only only in the fetch Pod (#1141), the admission policy of builds admits no other Secret; git reads the file through a fixed credential helper, only after GitHub answers 401, so the token reaches no argv, environment or .git; the Token is deleted once the fetch ends, and its Secret with it a projected volume mounted only in token, which writes it to memory for push; no Secret holds it If stolen reads the repository the build already has adds new tags to that one repository; cannot move a tag or touch another repository

The registry CA, copied, not a credential (#1064): the Registry answers only over TLS, so push checks its certificate. The buildkit Nereid reads the CA's certificate the Registry publishes in its ConfigMap zot-ca (get on that name only, cluster-wide), copies it to the ConfigMap registry-ca-<registry> in builds, one per Registry (#1152), and mounts it read-only in push alone at /etc/nereus/registry; SSL_CERT_FILE points crane there, which in Go replaces the system roots, so push trusts that CA and nothing else, and never takes --insecure. It holds a certificate, no key: a hostile build that reads it learns nothing secret. The admission policy admits a ConfigMap named registry-ca- and a DNS label as a volume, besides emptyDir and secret. The Nereid's HEAD for the digest trusts the same CA alone.

The repository comes from the Workload and the destination from the registry reef, never from free text on a Build, so a credential goes only where it belongs (judgement, the same rule as ADR 0020's on server-side request forgery). The tag is the Build's name, unique, which is why update is not needed. The Nereid reads the digest from the registry, not from anything the Pod wrote.

What a hostile Dockerfile can read during a build:

Thing Reads it? What stops it Left open The source at that commit Yes Nothing; it needs it It can send it out Git token No Only the fetch Pod, another Pod, holds it; the claim it writes holds no .git A copy in tmpfs on the node until the fetch Pod goes Push credential No Not mounted in build, and push has not started The same copy on the node ServiceAccount token No automountServiceAccountToken: false None Service addresses in the environment No enableServiceLinks: false DNS still answers Other builds No One Pod per build, no shared cache Slower builds BuildKit's process and state Yes Nothing It can alter its own image, which it controls anyway The next container Indirectly image is read-only in push, which refuses anything but regular files and checks digests A bug in the push tool would run with the credential and the internet Build secrets and SSH agent Nothing to read The first slice offers none to RUN --mount None

The tmpfs copy is Kubernetes' behaviour: a Secret reaches a node only if a Pod there needs it, and the kubelet keeps it in tmpfs until the Pod is deleted. Mounting it in one container hides it from the others, not from the node. So an escape reads both credentials of its own build.

The push credential expires (#1010). zot v2.1.23 takes Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens through http.auth.bearer.oidc, from one issuer: the cluster's own.
